<meta>This is the title page of the work. No previous page translation exists.</meta>

# Johann Andreas Eisenmenger’s /
->Professor of Oriental Languages at the<-
->University of Heidelberg<-

# Judaism Unmasked /
->Or<-

## A Thorough and True Account /
->In which manner<-
->The stubborn **Jews** blaspheme and dishonor the Most Holy **Trinity/**<-
->**God the Father, Son,** and **Holy Spirit/** in a terrifying way;<-
->disdain the Holy Mother of Christ; treat the New<-
->Testament, the Evangelists, and Apostles, and the Christian religion<-
->with mockery; and despise and curse all of Christendom to the<-
->utmost degree;<-

->**Wherein also many other** things and great errors of the Jewish<-
->religion and **theology/** previously either not at all or only<-
->partially known among **Christians,** as well as many ridiculous<-
->and entertaining fables and other absurd matters,<-
->are brought to light.<-

->**All of which is powerfully proven** from their own books—of which<-
->very many were read through with great effort and tireless<-
->diligence—including the extraction of the Hebrew words and their<-
->faithful translation into the **German language;**<-
->And<-

## Composed in Two Parts
->Each of which<-

->contains its proper **chapters,** each dealing in detail with a<-
->certain **subject matter.**<-

->Prepared for the sincere information of all Christians, and<-
->provided with complete **indexes.**<-

->**With His Royal Majesty in Prussia’s Most Gracious**<-
->**Special Privilege.** <note>original: "Special-Privilegio"; This refers to a royal license granting the author or publisher exclusive rights to print the work, a precursor to modern copyright.</note><-

---

->Printed at Königsberg in Prussia, in the year after Christ’s birth 1711.<-

<summary>This is the title page of Johann Andreas Eisenmenger's infamous polemical work, "Judaism Unmasked," a foundational text of modern anti-Semitism that claims to expose Jewish blasphemy and "fables." Published posthumously in 1711, it presents itself as a scholarly study of Jewish texts by a Professor of Oriental Languages.</summary>

<keywords>Johann Andreas Eisenmenger, Judaism Unmasked, Entdecktes Judenthum, anti-Semitism, University of Heidelberg, polemic, Jewish-Christian relations, printing privilege, Königsberg, 18th century</keywords>

<meta>This page contains the Royal Privilege (copyright grant) from King Frederick I of Prussia for the publication of Johann Andreas Eisenmenger's work. It follows the title page and establishes the legal protection for the book's distribution within Prussian territories.</meta>

# We, Frederick, by the Grace of God,
## King in Prussia / Margrave of Brandenburg /
## Arch-Chamberlain and Prince-Elector of the Holy Roman Empire / Sove-
reign Prince of Orange / Neufchatel and Valengin, Duke of Magdeburg / Cleves / Jülich / Berg / Stettin / Pomerania / of the Cassubians and Wends / of Mecklenburg / in Silesia / and of Crossen / Burgrave of Nuremberg / Prince of Halberstadt / Minden / Kammin / Wenden / Schwerin / Ratzeburg and Moers / Count of Hohenzollern / Ruppin / the Mark / Ravensberg / Hohenstein / Tecklenburg / Lingen / Schwerin / Buren and Leerdam / Marquis of Veere and Vlissingen / Lord of Ravenstein / of the Lands of Rostock / Stargard / Lauenburg / Bütow / Arlay and Breda etc. Make it known and give it herewith to be known: Whereas We, for moving reasons, have most graciously found it good / to have the book of the former Professor of Oriental Languages at Heidelberg / Johann Andreas Eisenmenger, titled *Judaism Unmasked* / printed at Königsberg / in Our Kingdom of Prussia / and to provide it with a Privilege <note>original: "Privilegio"; a royal license granting exclusive rights to print and sell a work, similar to a modern copyright.</note>; Therefore, We have herewith and by virtue of this decree privileged the same in such a manner / that for a period of twenty years, neither in Our Kingdom of Prussia / nor the Electorate of Brandenburg / nor in Our other provinces and lands / under penalty of the confiscation of the copies and a fine of one hundred ducats / to be paid to Our Treasury <note>original: "Fisco"; the state or royal treasury.</note> / shall it be reprinted by any printer / nor shall / if it has already been printed elsewhere / or should be printed in the future / any copies be imported into Our lands under the aforementioned penalty. In this manner We most graciously command all and each of Our Governors / Governments / High and Chamber Courts / and in general all and each of Our high- and low-ranking officials / but especially the Offices of the Treasury <note>original: "Officiis Fisci"</note> in every place, to obediently observe this / to uphold this Our Privilege with due emphasis / and to proceed against violators with the penalty contained therein. Witnessed under Our own signature and the attached Royal Feudal Seal; Given at Cölln on the Spree <note>Cölln was the sister-city of old Berlin; today it forms the central "Museum Island" and Mitte area.</note> on the sixth of March, after the birth of Christ in the year One Thousand / Seven Hundred / and Eleven.

->Frederick.<-

<image-desc>A decorative circular woodcut border containing the letters "L.S." standing for "In place of the seal" <note>original: "Loco Sigilli"</note>.</image-desc>

->M. L. von Printzen.<- <note>Magnus Friedrich von Printzen (1670–1732) was a high-ranking Prussian diplomat and court official who co-signed royal decrees.</note>

# of the First Part.

Ch. I. Concerning the Jews' improper teaching of **God** the Father, etc. <note>original: "2c."; an abbreviation for "et cetera," commonly used in this period to indicate that the chapter title continues or covers related sub-topics.</note>

# Register of the Hebrew Books /
## which are cited in the first and second part of this work.

->A.<-

**A**barbenel. Look for Isaac Abarbenet.

אבקת רוכל *Afkáth róchel* <note>original: "Afkáth róchel"; likely *Avkat Rochel* (The Merchant’s Powder), a work on eschatology and the afterlife.</note>, was written by Rabbi Makkir and printed in Augsburg in quarto format in the year 300 according to the Jews' small count / that is / in the year of Christ 1540. It deals with the pains to be endured at the time of the Messiah / as well as death / hell / eternal life / and the resurrection. <note>The "small count" refers to the Hebrew calendar year omitting the thousands digit; for example, the year 5300 is written as 300.</note>

*Ahabbáth ólam* <note>The Love of the World</note> look for *Sepher Ahabbáth ólam*.

עקדת יצחק *Akedáth Jizchak* <note>The Binding of Isaac</note>, was written by R. Isaac Arâma and printed in folio in Venice / in the year 307 i.e. 1547. It is a commentary on the 5 Books of Moses.

Old *Nizzáchon*, look for *Sepher Nizzáchon*, etc.

עמודי גולה *Ammúde gólah* <note>Pillars of the Exile</note>, was written by R. Isaac, the son of R. Joseph of Corbeil / and printed in Cremona in quarto in the year 317, which is / 1557. It deals with the 613 commandments of the Jews.

עמודה שבעה *Ammudeha schibba* or *schifa* <note>Its Seven Pillars</note>, was written by R. Bezáleel and printed in Dyhernfurth in quarto in the year 453 i.e. 1693. It is a figurative interpretation of many verses of the Old Testament.

ארבע טורים *Arba turim* <note>The Four Rows</note> was written by R. Jacob bar Asher and printed in Krakow in folio in the year 375 i.e. 1615. It deals with Jewish customs and laws.

ערוך של רבי נתן *Aruch* or Lexicon of R. Nathan / was printed in Venice in folio in the year 295, which is / 1535.

עשרה מאמרות *Afaráh maamaróth* <note>Ten Utterances</note>, was written by R. Asárja Mippâno <note>Azariah da Fano</note> and printed in quarto with the commentary of Joel Moshe in the year 304, which is / 1544. These are Kabbalistic matters.

עבודת הקודש *Avodáth hakkodesch* <note>Service of the Holy</note>, was written by R. Meir ben Gábbai and printed in Krakow in folio in the year 337 i.e. 1577. It deals with the unity of God / and His service / as well as the purpose of man / and his creation / and the secrets of the Law.

->B.<-

**B**ábo Móse <note>likely the *Porta Mosis* (Gate of Moses)</note> was written by R. Moshe bar Majemon <note>Maimonides</note> in Arabic with intermixed Hebrew / and printed in quarto in Oxford with Pococke’s Latin translation.

*Bammidbar rábba*. look for *Rabbóth*.

פרוש ר' בחיי על התורה *Bechai*’s Commentary on the 5 Books of Moses, printed in Venice in folio in the year 306, which is 1546.

בן דעת *Bén dáath* <note>Son of Knowledge</note>, written by R. Achilrad <note>likely Isaac Albelda</note> and printed in quarto in Hanau / in the year 376, which is 1616. It is a commentary on the Psalms.

# Index of the Hebrew Books cited in this Work.

באר הגולה **Beér haggóla** <note>original: "Beér haggóla"; The Well of the Exile</note>, written by Rabbi Judah Loew ben Bezalel <note>A famous scholar from Prague, often associated with the legend of the Golem.</note>, and printed in Prague in folio <note>A large book format made by folding sheets of paper once.</note> in the year 358 <note>The Jewish "small count" year, which corresponds to 1598 AD.</note>. It is an interpretation of those things in the Talmud which appear to be absurd or inconsistent.

**Benschbuch** <note>A Yiddish term for a book containing the Grace After Meals.</note>, look for **Bircháth hammáſon**.

**Bereſchíth rábba**, look for **Rabboth** <note>A collection of ancient rabbinic interpretations of the Book of Genesis.</note>.

ברית מנוחה **Beríth menúcha** <note>original: "Beríth menúcha"; Covenant of Rest</note>, written by Rabbi Abraham Merimon <note>Also known as Abraham ben Isaac of Granada.</note>, and printed in Amsterdam in quarto <note>A medium book format where sheets are folded twice to create four leaves.</note> in the year 408 / that is / 1648. It is a Kabbalistic book <note>A work concerning Jewish mysticism and esoteric traditions.</note>.

**Hebrew Bible** with the Chaldean translation <note>The Targum, or Aramaic translation of the Hebrew Scriptures.</note>, and the interpretations of many Rabbis, printed in large folio in Basel, in the year 378 / that is / 1618.

**Hebrew Bible** also with the Chaldean translation, and the interpretations of many Rabbis, printed in large folio in Venice, in the year 285 / that is / 1525, and in the year 307 / that is / 1547.

ברכת המזון **Bircháth hammáſon** <note>original: "Bircháth hammáſon"; Blessing of the Food</note>, called the *Benschbuch* by the Jews, printed in Frankfurt am Main in quarto in the year 442 / that is / 1682. It consists of prayers.

->C.<-

כד הקמח **Cad hakkémach** <note>original: "Cad hakkémach"; The Flour Jar</note>, written by Rabbi Bechai <note>Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century Spanish scholar.</note>, and printed in Venice in folio, in the year 306 i.e. 1546. It is a spiritual and moral book.

כפתור ופרח **Caphtor uphérach** <note>original: "Caphtor uphérach"; Knop and Flower</note>, written by Rabbi Jacob <note>Likely referring to Estori ha-Parhi, though the text attributes it to "Rabbi Jacob".</note>, and printed in Basel in quarto in the year 341 i.e. 1581. It is an interpretation of Talmudic history, narratives, and metaphorical speeches.

**Chapters of Rabbi Eliezer.** Look for **Pirke Rabbi Eliezer**.

חדושי אגדות **Chiddúſche aggadóth** <note>original: "Chiddúſche aggadóth"; New Interpretations of the Lore</note>, written by Rabbi Samuel Eliezer <note>Samuel Eidels, known as the Maharsha.</note>, and printed in Frankfurt am Main in folio, in the year 442 / that is / 1682. It also concerns the Talmudic fables and narratives.

חזוק אמונה **Chiſſúk emunáh** <note>original: "Chiſſúk emunáh"; Strengthening of the Faith</note>, is a refutation of the Christian faith, written by Rabbi Isaac ben Abraham <note>Isaac of Troki, a Karaite scholar.</note>, and is found in the book of the highly learned Doctor Wagenseil, which is called *Tela ignea Satanæ* <note>Latin: "The Fiery Arrows of Satan", a collection of Jewish anti-Christian polemics published by Johann Christoph Wagenseil.</note>, and was printed in 1681 in Altdorf in quarto.

**Chóſchen hammiſchpat.** Look for **Schýlchan áruch** <note>The "Breastplate of Judgment," one of the four sections of the Shulchan Aruch, dealing with Jewish civil and criminal law.</note>.

חומש עם ג' תרגומים ופרש ר"שי **Chúmaſch** <note>The Pentateuch or five books of Moses.</note> or 5. B. Mos. with the triple Chaldean translation, and the commentary of Rabbi Solomon Jarchi <note>Rashi, the preeminent medieval commentator.</note>. Printed in Amsterdam in quarto in the year 433 / that is / 1673.

כל בו **Col bo** <note>original: "Col bo"; Everything is within it</note>, the author of which is unknown, printed in Venice in the year 307 / that is / 1547. It deals with Jewish statutes and laws.

**Commentary on the Machsor** <note>The Machsor is the prayer book for Jewish festivals.</note>, which has not yet been printed and whose author is unknown; however, a Jew named Rabbi Veis Welhäußer, who lives as a *sekunder* <note>A term likely referring to a secondary resident or a specific professional role in the community.</note> in Wetzlar, lent it to me to read when he still lived in Frankfurt.

כוזרי **Coſri** <note>The Kuzari</note>, written by Rabbi Judah <note>Judah Halevi, a Spanish Jewish physician, poet, and philosopher.</note>, and printed in Basel in 4. with the [commentary] of Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf the Younger, a famous Christian Hebraist.</note>

# Index of the Hebrew Books Cited in This Work.

**Jechiel’s Disputation**, which he held with Brother Nicholas <note>original: "Nicolaus"; This refers to the Disputation of Paris in 1240, where Rabbi Jechiel of Paris defended the Talmud against the apostate Nicholas Donin.</note> / is found in the aforementioned book by Doctor Wagenseil <note>Johann Christoph Wagenseil (1633–1705), a Christian Hebraist.</note> / which is titled **The Fiery Darts of Satan** <note>original: "Tela ignea Satanæ"; a collection of Jewish anti-Christian polemics published with Latin refutations.</note> / and was printed in Altdorf in quarto <note>A book size where each sheet is folded twice to create four leaves.</note> in the year of Christ 1681.

**Foundation of Songs** <note>original: "יסוד שירים Jesód Schirim"</note>, which is also called **Golden Apples** <note>original: "תפוחי זהב Tappúche Sáhaf"</note> / was written by Rabbi Eliezer / and printed in Tübingen in quarto / in the year 320 / that is / 1560. It is an interpretation of the little Book of Ruth.

**Epistle of the Living Beings** <note>original: "אגרת בעלי חיים Iggéreth baalé chajim"</note> / was translated from Arabic into Hebrew by Rabbi Kalonymus / and printed in Mantua in octavo <note>A book size where each sheet is folded three times to create eight leaves.</note> / in the year 317 / that is / 1557. It is a dialogue between humans and the tame and wild animals / as well as the creeping creatures <note>A famous fable known as "The Animals' Lawsuit against Humanity."</note>.

**Epistle to Yemen** <note>original: "אגרת התימן Iggéreth hattéman"</note> / was written by Rabbi Moses bar Maimon <note>Maimonides, the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher.</note> / and printed in Amsterdam in quarto / at the back of his book / which is titled **Book of Commandments** <note>original: "Sepher mizvóth"</note> / in the year 420 / that is / 1660. Therein / the Jews are exhorted to remain steadfast in the faith / and in the enduring of exile <note>original: "exilii"</note> or misery.

**Epistle of the Dispute** <note>original: "אגרת הויכוח Iggéreth havicuach"</note> / written by Rabbi Shem Tov / and printed in Prague in 8vo. in the year 370 / that is / 1610. It is a disputation between philosophy and theology.

**Epistle of the Paths of the World** <note>original: "אגרת ארחות עולם Iggéreth orchóth ólam"</note> is written by Rabbi Abraham Farissol / and printed in Venice in octavo / in the year 347 / that is / 1587. It is a short description of the world <note>One of the first Hebrew works to describe the discovery of the New World (America).</note>.

**Yoreh De'ah** <note>original: "Joréh déa"; one of the four sections of the Jewish legal code.</note>, see **Shulchan Aruch**.

**The commentary of Joseph**, son of David ibn Yahya / on the little books of Ruth / Esther / The Song of Songs / and Ecclesiastes / and the Lamentations of Jeremiah / as well as the Hagiographa <note>The "Kethuvim" or Writings, the third section of the Hebrew Bible.</note> / was printed in Bologna in folio <note>The largest standard book format.</note> in the year 298 / that is / 1538.

**Josippon**, or **Joseph ben Gorion** <note>original: "יוסיפון יוסף בן גוריון Josippon"</note> / which is the Hebrew Josephus / printed in Basel with Sebastian Münster’s Latin translation / in the year 1529 / in octavo.

**City of Heroes** <note>original: "עיר גבורים Ir gibbórim"</note> / was written by Rabbi Ephraim <note>Ephraim Luntschitz (1550–1619), a famous preacher from Prague.</note> / and printed in Basel in folio / in the year 340 / that is / 1580. It contains sermons on the Five Books of Moses.

**Isaac Abarbanel’s** interpretation of the Five Books of Moses / printed in Venice in folio / in the year 344 / that is / 1584.

The same author’s interpretation of the **Former Prophets** <note>The books of Joshua, Judges, Samuel, and Kings.</note> / printed in Leipzig in folio in the year 446 / that is / 1686 / as well as in Hamburg / also in folio / in the year 447 / that is / 1687 / with the commentary of Rabbi Jacob Fidanque upon them.

The same author’s commentary or interpretation of the **Latter Prophets** <note>The books of Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the Twelve Minor Prophets.</note> / was printed in Amsterdam in folio / in the year 401 / that is / 1641.

->K.<-

**The Tradition of the Ravad** <note>original: "קבלת הראב"ד Kabbaláth haraavád"; Abraham ibn Daud's 'Sefer ha-Qabbalah,' a history of Jewish tradition.</note> / was written by Rabbi Abraham ben David / and printed in Basel in octavo in the year 340 / that is / 1580 / after the booklets *Seder Olam Rabbah* and *Sotah*. It is a small book of history.

**Pure Line** <note>original: "קו ונקי Kav venáki"</note> is a commentary on the Psalms / and written by Rabbi Shallum / and printed in Hanau in quarto / in the year 381 / that is / 1621.

# Index of the Hebrew Books Cited in This Work.

**Summary of the Beginning of Wisdom** <note>original: "קיצור ראשית חכמה Kizzur reschíth chóchma"</note>, which is also called the **Book of Golden Apples** <note>original: "ספר תפוחי זהב Sepher tappúche sahaf"</note>, is a brief compendium of the book *The Beginning of Wisdom* in octavo <note>A book size where each sheet is folded three times to create eight leaves</note>. The year when and the place where it was printed are not stated within it.

**Voice of the Weepers** <note>original: "קול בוכים Kol bóchim"</note>, which is also called the **Lamentation of Secrets** <note>original: "קינת סתרים Kináth Setharím"</note>, is a commentary on the Lamentations of Jeremiah written by Rabbi Abraham Galante <note>A 16th-century Kabbalist based in Safed</note>; it was printed in Prague in quarto <note>A book size where each sheet is folded twice to create four leaves</note> in the year 381, that is, 1621.

->L.<-

**The Lion’s Heart** <note>original: "לב אריה Lefarjéh"</note> is a commentary on the Five Books of Moses <note>The Torah</note> written by Rabbi Löb and printed in Wilmersdorf in folio <note>A large book size made of sheets folded only once</note> in the year 434, that is, 1674.

**Levi ben Gerson’s Interpretation of the Five Books of Moses** <note>Levi ben Gerson (1288–1344), also known as Gersonides, was a prominent philosopher and commentator</note> was printed in Venice in folio in the year 307, that is, 1547.

**The Royal Garment** <note>original: "לבוש מלכות Levusch malchúth"</note> was written by Rabbi Mordechai Jaffe <note>A 16th-century scholar famous for his ten-volume work of Jewish law</note> and printed in folio in Lublin in the year 350, that is, 1590. It treats Jewish statutes and laws.

**Lipmann’s Poem** <note>original: "Lipmanns Carmen"</note> or Song, which is called **The Record of the Book of Victory** <note>original: "Sichron Sepher Nizzáchon"</note>, was printed in Altdorf in the year 1681 in quarto and is found in Doctor Wagenseil’s book titled **The Fiery Darts of Satan** <note>original: "Tela ignea Satanæ"; a collection of Jewish polemical texts published with Latin refutations</note>.

**Lipmann’s Book of Victory** <note>original: "Sepher Nizzáchon"</note>, look under *Nizzáchon*.

->M.<-

**Treatise on the Resurrection of the Dead** <note>original: "מאמר תחיית המתים Maamár techiáth hamméthim"</note>, *written by Rabbi Moses bar Maimon <note>Maimonides (1138–1204), the most influential Jewish philosopher of the Middle Ages</note> and printed in Amsterdam in quarto, following his book titled the **Book of Commandments** <note>original: "Sepher mizvóth"</note>, in the year 420, that is, 1660.*

**The Order of Divinity** <note>original: "מערכת האלהות Maaréchet haëlahúth"</note> was written by Rabbi Perez and printed in Ferrara in quarto in the year 451, that is, 1691. It is a Cabbalistic <note>Kabbalistic; referring to Jewish mysticism</note> book.

**The Arranger of the Ranks** <note>original: "מעריך המערכות Maarich hammaarachóth"</note> is a Hebrew Lexicon <note>Dictionary</note> written by a Jew named Michael, who afterwards became a Christian and was called Philippus Aquinas. It was printed in Paris in folio in the year 1629.

**The Work of the Lord** <note>original: "מעשה השם Maaséh haschém"</note> was written by Rabbi Eliezer and printed in Venice in folio in the year 343, that is, 1583. It treats the work of Creation, the deeds of the Patriarchs, what occurred in Egypt, as well as the Law.

**The Jerusalemite Tale** <note>original: "מעשה ירושלמי Maaséh Jeruschálmi"</note> was printed in Venice in octavo in the year 304, that is, 1544, after the little book called **The Book of the Words of the Days of Moses** <note>original: "Sepher divré hajamím schel Mosche"</note>; it reports how a learned Jew married the daughter of the devil Asmodeus <note>original: "Aschmedai"; a prominent king of demons in Jewish folklore</note> and what occurred during it.

**The Work of the Law of Our Holy Rabbi** <note>original: "מעשה תורה רבינו הקדוש Maaséh Thóra Rabbenu hakkádosch"</note> was printed in Amsterdam following the little book of *Ben Sira* in decimo-sexto <note>A small pocket-sized book</note> in the year 457, that is, 1697.

**Cycle** <note>original: "מחזור Machsor"</note> was printed in Prague in the year 373, that is, 1613, with a commentary in folio; it is the Jews' prayer book for their festivals.

### Index of the Hebrew Books Cited in This Work.

**Festival Prayer Book** <note>original: *Machsor*—a collection of prayers for the Jewish festivals</note> [printed] in Venice in folio <note>A large book size made of sheets folded once</note>, also printed with a commentary in the year 314, that is, 1554.

**Shield of Abraham** <note>original: "מגן אברהם Maggen Abraham"</note>, written by Rabbi Abraham Farissol <note>original: "Abraham Perizol," a 15th-16th century scholar and geographer</note>, and never yet printed; however, it was lent to us in Amsterdam for four weeks by a Portuguese Jew named Rabbi Joseph Franco, who was my teacher in the Talmud.

**Fountain of Wisdom** <note>original: "מעין חכמה Maján chóchma"</note>, written by Rabbi Abraham and printed in Amsterdam in quarto in the year 411, that is, 1651. It is a Kabbalistic book <note>Kabbalah refers to the Jewish mystical tradition</note>.

**Fountains of Salvation** <note>original: "מעיני ישועה Majené jeschúah"</note>, written by Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel <note>A prominent 15th-century philosopher and biblical commentator</note>, and printed in Amsterdam in quarto in the year 412, that is, 1652. It is a commentary on the prophet Daniel.

**The Lesser Light** <note>original: "מאור הקטן Máor hakkáton"</note>, written by Rabbi Meir Tranpel and printed in Fürth <note>OCR: "Ferd"</note> in folio in the year 457, that is, 1697. It is a commentary on the Five Books of Moses <note>The Torah</note>.

**The Second Chariot** <note>original: "מרכבת המשנה Markéveth hammischneh"</note>, written by Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel and printed in Sabioneta in folio in the year 311, that is, 1551. It is a commentary on the Fifth Book of Moses <note>Deuteronomy</note>.

**Herald of Salvation** <note>original: "משמיע ישועה Maschmía jeschúah"</note>, written by the aforementioned Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel and printed in Amsterdam in quarto in the year 407, that is, 1647. Within it, the prophecies concerning the future redemption <note>Messianic prophecies</note> are discussed.

**The Travels of Rabbi Benjamin** <note>original: "מסעות ר' בנימין Masseóth Rabbi Binjamin"</note>, printed in Amsterdam behind the small book *The Hope of Israel* <note>original: "Mikvéh Jisraél"</note> in decimo-sexto <note>A small book size where the sheet is folded four times into sixteen leaves</note> in the year 458, that is, 1698; it is a travelogue <note>Benjamin of Tudela's famous 12th-century journey</note>.

**The Tradition of Tradition** <note>original: "מסורת המסורת Massóreth hammassóreth"</note>, written by Rabbi Elijah <note>Elijah Levita, a renowned grammarian</note> and printed in Venice in quarto in the year 306, that is, 1546. It is a key to the Masorah <note>The traditional system of notes on the textual details of the Hebrew Bible</note>.

**The Rod of Aaron** <note>original: "מטה אהרן Mattéh Aharon"</note>, written by Rabbi Aaron; it is a commentary on the Haggadah <note>The text recited during the Passover Seder</note>.

**Mechilta** <note>original: "מכילתא Mechilta"—a collection of early legal interpretations</note>, written by Rabbi Ishmael and printed in Venice in folio in the year 310, that is, 1550. It is an ancient commentary on a portion of the Second Book of Moses <note>Exodus</note>.

**Midrash on Psalms, Proverbs, and Samuel** <note>original: *Médrasch Tillim, Mischle, Schemuel*</note>, was printed in Venice in folio <note>A large book format where sheets are folded once</note> in the year [5]306, that is, 1546. It is an allegorical commentary on the Psalms, the Proverbs of Solomon, and the two books of Samuel.

**The Midrash "And He Saved"** <note>original: *Medrasch Vajóscha*</note>, was printed in Constantinople in quarto in the year [5]284, which is 1524. It deals with the deliverance from Egypt.

**Revealer of Depths** <note>original: *Megalléh amykkóth*</note>, was written by Rabbi Nathan Spira and printed in Fürth <note>original: "Ferd"</note> in the year [5]451, which is 1691, in quarto. It is a multifaceted interpretation of the prayer of Moses found in Deuteronomy 3:24–25.

**Source of Life** <note>original: *Mekór chájim*</note>, written by Rabbi Samuel Zirza, printed in Mantua in folio in the year [5]319, which is 1559. It is a commentary on Abraham ibn Ezra's <note>A celebrated 12th-century Spanish-Jewish scholar</note> interpretation of the Five Books of Moses.

**Menahem of Recanati’s Explanation of the Five Books of Moses** <note>original: *Menáchem von Rekanat Auslegung*</note> was printed in Venice in quarto in the year [5]305, which is 1545.

**Candelabrum of Gold** <note>original: *Menoráth fáhabh*</note>, was written by the aforementioned Rabbi Isaac Aboab and printed in Krakow in quarto without an indicated year.

**Light of the Eyes** <note>original: *Meór enáim*</note>, was written by Rabbi Azariah <note>Azariah dei Rossi, a famous 16th-century Italian-Jewish physician and scholar</note> and printed in Mantua in quarto in the year [5]334, i.e., 1574. It contains various historical and philological matters.

**Perfection of Beauty** <note>original: *Michlál jóphi*</note>, is a commentary on the entire Old Testament written by Rabbi Solomon ben Melech, printed in Amsterdam in folio in the year [5]445, i.e., 1685.

**The Letter of Resurrection** <note>original: *Michtáf hattechiah*</note>, was written by Rabbi Judah Sabdaa and printed in Venice in octavo <note>A smaller book size where sheets are folded three times</note> at the end of Rabbi Moses ben Maimon's <note>Maimonides, the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher</note> booklet, **Treatise on the Resurrection of the Dead** <note>original: *Maamár techiáth hammethím*</note>. It deals with the resurrection of the dead.

**A Golden Poem to David** <note>original: *Michtám le-David*</note>, is a commentary on the 13 Jewish Articles of Faith <note>The fundamental principles of Judaism as codified by Maimonides</note>, written by Rabbi David bar Solomon and printed in Venice in octavo in the year [5]307, which is 1547.

**Holy Convocations** <note>original: *Mikráë Kodesch*</note>, was written by Rabbi Joseph Samiga and printed in Venice in quarto in the year [5]346, i.e., 1586. It deals with the commandments, the fear and love of God, the mysteries of the Law, festivals, and customs.

**The Hope of Israel** <note>original: *Mikvéh Jisraél*</note>, was written by Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel <note>A famous 17th-century Portuguese rabbi and diplomat based in Amsterdam</note> and printed in Amsterdam in decimo-sexto <note>A very small "pocket" format where each sheet is folded into 16 leaves</note> in the year [5]458, which is 1698. In it, the future redemption is discussed.

### Index of the Hebrew Books Cited in This Work.

**New Light** <note>original: *Or chádasch*</note> was written by Rabbi Hayyim, and printed in quarto <note>a book size where the printing sheet is folded twice to create four leaves</note> in Amsterdam in the year [5]431, which is 1671. It deals with various thanksgivings and blessings.

**Way of Life** <note>original: *Orach chájim*</note>, see the *Shulchan Aruch* <note>The "Set Table," the most authoritative legal code of Judaism</note>.

**Paths of Life** <note>original: *Orchóth chájim*</note>, was written by Rabbi Eliezer the Great, and printed in Amsterdam in decimo-sexto <note>a small pocket-sized book</note> behind the small book *Ben Sira* in the year [5]457, which is 1697. It is an instruction that he gave to his son.

**Paths of the Righteous** <note>original: *Orchóth Zaddikim*</note>, the author of which is unknown; it was printed in Frankfurt am Main in folio <note>a large book size</note> in the year [5]447, which is 1687, and deals with various virtues and vices.

**The Letters of Rabbi Akiva** <note>original: *Othióth Rabbi Akkíva*</note>, was written by Rabbi Akiva, and printed in Krakow in quarto in the year [5]344, which is 1584, as well as in Venice in the year [5]306, which is 1546, also in quarto. It is a Cabbalistic book <note>referring to Jewish mysticism</note>.

->P.<-

**The Orchard of Pomegranates** <note>original: *Pardes Rimmónim*</note>, was written by Rabbi Moshe Cordovero <note>a leading figure in the Safed school of Kabbalah</note>, and printed in Krakow in folio in the year [5]392, which is 1632. It is a Cabbalistic book.

**Commentary on the Torah by Rabbi Jacob** <note>original: *Perusch hattóra schel Rabbi Jaacob*</note>, is a very brief interpretation of the Five Books of Moses, written by Rabbi Jacob, and printed in Venice in quarto in the year [5]304, which is the year 1544.

**The Greater Pesikta** <note>original: *Pesíkta rábbetha*</note>, was printed in Prague in quarto, without mention of the year. <note>A collection of homiletic teachings for the festivals</note>.

**The Lesser Pesikta** <note>original: *Pesíkta sotárta*</note>, is a very ancient commentary <note>original: *Commentarius*</note> on the third, fourth, and fifth books of Moses, and was printed in Venice in folio in the year [5]306, which is 1546.

**The Passing of Moses** <note>original: *Patiráth Mosche*</note>, was printed in Venice in octavo in the year [5]304, which is 1544, after the small book *The Book of the Words of the Days of Moses* <note>original: *Sepher divré hajamím schel Mosche*</note>. It deals with the death of Moses.

**The Chapters of Rabbi Eliezer** <note>original: *Pirke Rabbi Elieser*</note>, or the chapters of Rabbi Eliezer, printed in Prague in quarto without mention of the year; it is a history book.

**Polish Prayer Books** <note>original: *Siddurim*</note>, see *Tephilloth* <note>Prayers</note>, etc.

->R.<-

**The Great Midrashim** <note>original: *Rabbóth*</note>, was written by Rabbi bar Nachmani, and printed in Wilmersdorf in folio in the year [5]433, which is 1673, with the commentary **The Gifts of the Priesthood** <note>original: *Mattenóth kehúnna*</note>. It is an allegorical and historical commentary on the five books of Moses and the five **Scrolls** <note>original: *Megillóth*</note>, namely the books of Ruth, Esther, Ecclesiastes <note>original: *den Prediger*</note>, and the Song of Solomon <note>original: *Hohe Lied Salomons*</note>, as well as the Lamentations of Jeremiah. It is named **The Great Genesis** <note>original: *Bereshíth rábba*</note> over the first book of Moses, **The Great Exodus** <note>original: *Schemóth rábba*</note> over the second, **The Great Leviticus** <note>original: *Vajikra rábba*</note> over the third, **The Great Numbers** <note>original: *Bammidbar rábba*</note> over the fourth, and over the fifth it is called **These are the Words** or **The Great Deuteronomy** <note>original: *Elléh haddevarím* or *Devarím rábba*</note>. Over the Lamentations of Jeremiah it is called **The Great Lamentations** <note>original: *Echa rábbathi*</note>, and over the Song of Solomon, **The Great Song of Songs** <note>original: *Schir haschírim rábba*</note>, etc.

**The Book of Raziel** <note>original: *Sepher Rasiel*</note>, is a handwritten and not yet printed book, which the aforementioned Jew living in Wetzlar, Rabbi Veis Gelhäußer, lent to me when he still lived in Frankfurt; attached to it is a treatise called **Special Remedies** <note>original: *Segullóth*</note>

# Register of the Hebrew Books Cited in This Work.

**Signs and Amulets from the Angel Raphael** <note>original: *Ióth ukemeóth mimmálach Rafiel*</note>. This is a Cabbalistic <note>relating to Jewish mystical tradition</note> book which Adam is said to have received from the Angel Raphael.

**The Beginning of Wisdom** <note>original: *Reschíth chochma*</note>. Written by Rabbi Elijah de Vidas, and printed in Prague in quarto <note>a book size where the printing sheet is folded twice to create four leaves</note> in the year [5]354, which is 1694. It contains theological commonplaces <note>general principles or topics for study</note> and other matters.

**The Pinnacle of Faith** <note>original: *Rosch Amanáh*</note>. Written by Rabbi Isaac Abarbenel <note>a prominent 15th-century Jewish statesman and philosopher</note>, and printed in Venice in quarto in the year [5]305, which is 1545. It deals with the fundamental articles of faith.

---

->S.<-

**Gates of Light** <note>original: *Schaaré órah*</note>. Written by Rabbi Joseph ben Gekatília <note>Gikatilla</note>, and printed in Mantua in quarto in the year [5]321, which is 1561, and also printed in Riva di Trento in quarto. It is a Cabbalistic book.

**Gates of Righteousness** <note>original: *Schaaré Zédek*</note>. Written by Rabbi Joseph ben Karnitol, and printed in Riva di Trento in quarto in the year [5]321, which is 1561. It is also a Cabbalistic book.

**The Chain of Tradition** <note>original: *Schalschéleth hakkabbála*</note>. Written by Rabbi Gedaliah <note>ibn Yahya</note>, and printed in Amsterdam in the year [5]457, which is 1697, in octavo <note>a book size where each sheet is folded to create eight leaves</note>. It is a book of chronology and history.

**The Scepter of Judah** <note>original: *Schébhet* or *Schevet Jehuda*</note>. Written by Rabbi Solomon ben Verga, and printed in Amsterdam in octavo in the year [5]415, which is 1655. It deals with the persecutions that the Jews have endured.

**The Forgotten Gleanings** <note>original: *Schechecháth léket*</note>. Written by Rabbi Nathan, and printed in Prague in quarto in the year [5]412, which is 1652. It consists of commonplaces that were collected from many books.

**Questions and Answers of Rabbi Jacob Weil** <note>original: *Scheelóth utheschuvóth*</note>, that is, legal inquiries and responses written by Rabbi Jacob Weil, and printed in Venice in quarto in the year [5]309, which is 1549. They consist of legal matters.

**An Abundance of Dew** <note>original: *Schéfa tal*</note>. Written by Rabbi Sheftel Horwitz, and printed in Hanau in the year [5]372, which is 1612, and is a Cabbalistic book.

**The Great Exodus** <note>original: *Schemóth rabba*</note>, see **The Great Midrashim** <note>original: *Rabbóth*</note>.

**The Two Tablets of the Covenant** <note>original: *Schené luchóth habberíth*</note>. Written by Rabbi Isaiah <note>Horowitz</note>, and printed in Wilmersdorf in folio <note>a large book size where the printing sheet is folded only once</note> in the year [5]446, which is 1686, as well as in Amsterdam in the year [5]413, which is 1653, also in folio. It deals with theological and moral matters.

**The Song of Songs** <note>original: *Schir haschírim*</note>, see **The Great Midrashim** <note>original: *Rabbóth*</note>.

# Register of the Hebrew Books Cited in This Work.

**The Four-Fold Table** <note>original: *Schylchan árba*</note>, written by Rabbi Bahya <note>Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century Spanish scholar</note> and printed in Venice in folio <note>a large book size made by folding a sheet of paper once</note> in the year [5]306, which is 1546. It deals with what a person should observe while eating, and with the great banquet of the future <note>referring to the messianic feast in Jewish tradition</note>.

**The Set Table** <note>original: *Schylchán aruch*</note>, written by Rabbi Joseph Karo <note>the definitive codification of Jewish law</note> and printed in Amsterdam in small octavo <note>a portable book size</note> in the year [5]421, which is 1661. It consists of four parts, which are called **The Way of Life** <note>Orach chájim</note>, **The Breastplate of Judgment** <note>Chóschen hammischpat</note>, **The Teacher of Knowledge** <note>Jore dea</note>, and **The Stone of Help** <note>Even haéser</note>. It deals with Jewish laws and statutes.

**The Passover Sacrifice** <note>original: *Sebhach pésach*</note>, written by the aforementioned Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel and printed in Venice in quarto in the year [5]305, which is 1545. It is a commentary on the Haggadah <note>the text recited at the Passover Seder</note>, or the historical reading of the Passover festival.

**The Order of the Burial Society** <note>original: *Séder chafrútha de kafránim*</note>, printed in Frankfurt am Main in the year [5]457, which is 1697, in octavo. It consists of the prayers of those appointed for the burial of the dead.

**Small Order of the World** <note>original: *Seder olam sóta*</note>, a small chronological book or chronicle, printed in Basel in the year [5]340, which is 1580, following the booklet **Great Order of the World** <note>Séder olam rábba</note>.

**Signs and Amulets from the Angel Raziel** <note>original: *Segullóth ukemeóth mimmalach Rasiel*</note>, see **Raziel**.

**Penitential Prayers** <note>original: *Selichóth*</note>, printed in Prague in folio in the year [5]347, which is 1587. It is one of the prayer books of the Jews arranged for the festival days.

**Penitential Prayers** <note>original: *Selichóth*</note>, printed in Frankfurt am Main in quarto in the year [5]425, which is 1665.

**The Book of Faith** <note>original: *Sepher amanáh*</note>, written by a converted Jew in defense of the Christian religion, and printed in Isny in quarto in the year [5]302, which is 1542.

**The Book of Ben Sira** <note>original: *Sepher ben Sira*</note>, printed in Amsterdam in decimo-sexto <note>a very small, pocket-sized book</note> in the year [5]457, which is 1697. It deals with Ben Sira <note>also known as Sirach</note> and his wisdom.

**The Book of the Pious** <note>original: *Sepher chasidim*</note>, written by Rabbi Judah <note>Judah ben Samuel of Regensburg</note> and printed in Sulzbach in quarto in the year [5]445, which is 1685. It is a theological and ethical book.

**The Book of the Chronicles of Moses our Teacher** <note>original: *Sepher diré hajamím schel Mosche Rabbénu*</note>, printed in Venice in octavo in the year [5]304, which is 1544. It is a description of Moses and the events that occurred during his time.

**The Book of Eldad the Danite** <note>original: *Sepher Eldad hadáni*</note>, also printed in Venice in the year [5]304, which is 1544, following the previously mentioned booklet *The Book of the Chronicles*, etc., in octavo. It deals with the Jews who are said to live beyond the Sambation River <note>a legendary river that stops flowing on the Sabbath</note> and that same region.

# Register of the Hebrew Books Cited in This Work;

**Book of Reincarnations** <note>original: *Sepher gilgulim*</note>, was written by Rabbi Isaac Luria <note>a foundational figure in Jewish mysticism known as the Ari</note>, and printed in Frankfurt am Main in quarto <note>a book size made by folding a sheet of paper twice to form four leaves</note> in the year [5]444, which is 1684. It deals with the journey of souls from one body or place to another.

**Book of the Gathering** <note>original: *Sepher ha-aguddah*</note>, was written by Rabbi Alexander [Susslin of Frankfurt] and printed in Kraków in folio <note>a large book size made by folding a sheet of paper once</note> in the year [5]331, which is 1571. It contains Talmudic statutes.

**Book of the Bright** <note>original: *Sepher ha-bahir*</note>, was written by Rabbi Nehuniah ben ha-Kanah and printed in Amsterdam in quarto in the year [5]411, which is 1651. It is a Kabbalistic book <note>referring to Jewish mystical tradition</note>.

**Book of Intentions** <note>original: *Sepher ha-kavanot*</note>, was composed by Rabbi Isaac Luria and printed in Venice in quarto in the year [5]384, which is 1624; in it, the mysteries of the prayers are explained.

**Book of Life** <note>original: *Sepher ha-chayim*</note>, was written by Rabbi Hayyim ben Bezalel <note>brother of the famous Rabbi Judah Loew of Prague</note> and printed in Prague in quarto without the inclusion of the year. It deals with merits, nourishment and preservation, the good life, forgiveness, and redemption.

**Book of Beliefs** <note>original: *Sepher ha-emunot*</note>, was written by Rabbi Shem Tov [ibn Shem Tov] and printed in Ferrara in quarto in the year [5]216, which is 1556. It deals with faith.

**Book of Beliefs and Opinions** <note>original: *Sepher ha-emunot ve-ha-deot*</note>, was written by Rabbi Saadia [Gaon] and printed in Amsterdam in quarto in the year [5]413, which is 1653. It deals with the one God, human conduct, the soul, the resurrection, etc.

**Book of the Upright** <note>original: *Sepher ha-yashar*</note>, the author of which is unknown, was printed in Prague in quarto in the year [5]428, which is 1668. It deals with history from Adam until after the Exodus from Egypt.

**Book of the Offering** <note>original: *Sepher ha-terumah*</note>, was written by Rabbi Baruch [of Worms] and printed in Venice in quarto in the year [5]283, which is 1523. It deals with the statutes and rights of the Jews.

**The Tishbite** <note>original: *Sepher ha-Tishbi*</note>, was written by Rabbi Elijah [Levita] and printed in Basel in quarto in the year [5]361, which is 1601. It is a dictionary.

**Book of Principles** <note>original: *Sepher Ikarim*</note>, was written by Rabbi Joseph Albo and printed in Venice in quarto in the year [5]304, which is 1544. It deals with the foundations of the Jewish faith.

**Instructor of Sinners** <note>original: *Sepher yoreh chataim*</note>, was printed in Fürth <note>original: *Ferd*</note> in the year [5]451, which is 1691, in duodecimo <note>a small, pocket-sized book</note>; it deals with sins.

**Book of Lineage** <note>original: *Sepher yuchasin*</note>, was written by Rabbi Abraham Zacuto and printed in Kraków in quarto in the year [5]340, which is 1580. It is a book of history.

**Gift of God** <note>original: *Sepher Mattat Yah*</note>, was written by Rabbi Mattathiah Libermann and printed in Frankfurt am Main in folio in the year [5]456, which is 1696. It is an interpretation of the Books of Moses.

**Illumination of Praises** <note>original: *Sepher Meir Tehillot*</note>, is a commentary on the Psalms written by Rabbi Meir Arama and printed in Venice in quarto in the year [5]350, which is 1590.

**Book of Holy Convocations** <note>original: *Sepher mikráë kódesch*</note>, see *Holy Convocations*.

**Book of Customs** <note>original: *Sepher minhagím*</note>, was printed in Amsterdam in small octavo <note>a standard portable book size</note> in the year [5]439, which is 1679. It deals with Jewish customs and traditions.

**Book of Commandments by Rambam** <note>original: *Sepher mizvôth schel Rambam*</note>, was written by Rabbi Moses bar Maimon <note>known as Maimonides</note> and printed in Amsterdam in quarto <note>a medium-sized book format</note> in the year [5]420, which is 1660. In it, the 613 commandments are discussed.

**Great Book of Commandments** <note>original: *Sepher mizvôth gadôl*</note>, was written by Rabbi Moses of Coucy and printed in Venice in folio in the year [5]307, which is 1547. It also discusses the commandments.

**Book of Victory by Rabbi Lipman** <note>original: *Sepher Nizzáchon*</note>, was printed in Nuremberg in quarto in the year 1644 and was written as a refutation of the Christian religion.

**Book of Victory by Rabbi Mattathiah** <note>original: *Sepher Nizzáchon des Rabbi Mattátja*</note>, which is called the *Old Nizzáchon* in this work, was printed in Altdorf in quarto in the year 1681 and is contained in Mr. Wagenseil's aforementioned book, which is titled *The Fiery Darts of Satan* <note>original Latin: *Tela ignea Satanæ*</note>.

**Book of Roots** <note>original: *Sepher Saharaschím*</note>, was written by Rabbi David Kimchi and printed in Venice in folio in the year [5]294, which is 1534. It is a lexicon <note>a dictionary focusing on the root forms of Hebrew words</note>.

**Book of Zerubbabel** <note>original: *Sepher Serubábel*</note>, was printed in Constantinople in quarto in the year [5]284, which is 1524, and contains a dialogue between Zerubbabel and the Archangel Michael.

**Book of the Generations of Adam and Eve** <note>original: *Sepher toledóth Adam ve Chávva*</note>, was written by Rabbi Jerucham and printed in Venice in folio in the year [5]313, which is 1553. It deals with Jewish laws and customs.

**Book of the Hooks of the Pillars** <note>original: *Sepher Váve ammudím*</note>, see *Hooks of the Pillars*.

**Seed of Abraham** <note>original: *Séra Abraham*</note>, was written by Rabbi Abraham and printed in Sulzbach in quarto in the year [5]445, which is 1685. It contains sermons on the Five Books of Moses.

**Memorial of the Book of Victory** <note>original: *Sichron Sepher Nizzáchon*</note>, see *Lipman’s Song* <note>original Latin/German: *Lipmanns Carmen*</note>.

**Lips of the Sleepers** <note>original: *Siphté jeschením*</note>, was written by Rabbi Shabbethai [Bass] and printed in Amsterdam in quarto in the year [5]440, which is 1680. It is a catalogue of Hebrew books.

**The Splendor** <note>original: *Sohar*</note>, was written by Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and printed in Sulzbach in folio in the year [5]444, which is 1684; it is a Kabbalistic <note>mystical</note> interpretation of the Books of Moses.

**New Splendor** <note>original: *Sohar chádasch*</note>, was printed in Kraków in quarto in the year [5]363, which is 1603, along with the *Hidden Midrash* <note>original: *Médrasch néelem*</note>, the *Rectifications* <note>original: *Tikkúnim*</note>, as well as the *Midrash on the Song of Songs and Lamentations* <note>original: *Medrasch Schir haschírim veécha*</note>.

**Hope of Israel** <note>Hebrew: *Mikvéh Jisraél*</note> was written by Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel in Portuguese, translated into German by another, and printed in Amsterdam in octavo in the year [5]451, which is 1691. It deals with the future redemption.

**Penitential Prayers** <note>Hebrew: *Selichóth*</note>, printed in Amsterdam in quarto <note>a medium-sized book format</note> in the year [5]435, which is 1675. It is a prayer book.

**Book of the Regions of the Land of Israel** <note>Hebrew: *Sepher gelilóth érez Jisraél*</note> was written by Rabbi Joseph and printed in Fürth <note>original: "Ferd"</note> in the year [5]451, which is 1691. It is a description of the Land of Israel and other places, as well as the land beyond the River Sambation.

**Book of Customs** <note>Hebrew: *Sepher minhagim*</note> was printed in Dyhernfurth in quarto in the year [5]452, which is 1692. It deals with Jewish customs and rituals.

**Go Forth and Behold** <note>Hebrew: *Zeénah ureénah* (Tseno Ureno)</note> was written by Rabbi Jacob and printed in Frankfurt am Main in folio <note>a large book size</note> in the year [5]453, which is 1693. It is a commentary on the Five Books of Moses <note>The Torah</note>.

### In which is shown what improper and, in part, very blasphemous things the hardened Jews teach and write concerning God the Father.

<margin>The Jews are a blind and hardened <note>The term "hardened" (German: *verstockt*) refers to the theological concept of "obduracy," where a person's heart is closed to spiritual truth.</note> people.</margin>
One reads in the fifth book of Moses <note>The Book of Deuteronomy</note>, in the 28th chapter, that when Moses, the pious and faithful servant of God, zealously and earnestly commanded the children of Israel to keep and observe the commandments of God, he gave them to understand that if they diligently took heed of them and properly obeyed the holiest will of the Most High, they should be blessed in all places and in all things: On the other hand, however, if they did not live according to the voice of the Almighty and did not submit to His laws, they should be cursed in every way and struck with madness, blindness, and hardening of the heart.

But the malicious Jews did not heed such sharp threats at all, but stubbornly despised God's word; therefore it has also come to pass that they have been visited with all kinds of well-deserved punishments, among which blindness and the hardening of their hearts is the greatest. Of this hardening and spiritual blindness of theirs, God speaks in Isaiah <note>original: "Esaiæ"</note> 6:9–10 to the prophet

They teach that there are academies in heaven in which the Law is studied and disputed.</margin> Thirdly, they teach that in the firmament of heaven there are academies <term>Hohe Schulen: Literally "high schools," referring to academies or universities of religious study, known in Hebrew as Yeshivot</term> in which the deceased Rabbis and others—yes, even the devils themselves—diligently study; and that in these same academies, a sharp dispute was once conducted against God, and He was overcome by the disputation. Concerning these celestial academies, it is written in the book *Yalkut Reuveni the Great*, folio 159, column 3, and furthermore from the book *Peliah* as follows: <note>original Hebrew: "דע לך שאין ישיבה שלמטה שאין נגדה למעלה וכל אחד מבני הישיבה יש לו למעלה כח וצל כנגדו. ואם אלף ישיבות למטה כנגדן אלף למעלה"</note> that is, **"Know that there is no academy here below (on the earth) that does not have one above (in heaven) corresponding to it. In the *Genesis Rabbah* <note>original: *Beréshis rábba*; a collection of ancient rabbinic interpretations of the Book of Genesis</note>, folio 44, column 3, in the 49th section, and folio 57, column 4, in the 64th section, it is written: <note>original Hebrew: "Every day the Holy One, blessed be He, innovates a law in the Heavenly Court; what is the reason? In the *Sépher Chasîdim* <note>original: *Sefer Hasidim*, "The Book of the Pious"</note>, number 455, it is read: <note>original Hebrew: "נשמות יש להם ספרים ערוכים על השולחן כמו שרגילים בחייהם ללמוד כן במותם לומדים"</note> **"The souls have their books ready upon the table; just as they were accustomed to learning in their lives, so they learn in their death."** And immediately following in number 456: <note>original Hebrew: "מעשה שעברו נכרים דרך בית הקברות בליל שבת וראו יהודי אחד יושב וספרו על שלחנו וקרא בו"</note> **"A story occurred where foreigners passed by a burial place on the Sabbath eve and saw a Jew who had his book upon the table and was reading from it."**

<margin>The devils also study in the heavenly Academy.</margin>
That even devils <note>demons or spirits</note> come into the upper Academy <term>Academy: the Hebrew *Metivta*, a celestial school for the study of the Law</term> and are said to study there can be proven from the Talmudic tractate *Gittin*. There, on folio 68, column 1, it is reported that when a question was once asked regarding a certain worm called *Schámir* <note>the Shamir, a legendary creature/substance capable of cutting stone, used to build Solomon's Temple</note>—where it had gone—the answer was given that Ashmedai <note>Asmodeus</note>, the King of the Devils, would undoubtedly know. When asked where he might be encountered and found, the answer was: <note>original Aramaic: "בטורא פלן כריא ליה כירא ומליא ליה מיא ומכסיא בטינרא וחתמיא בגושפנקיה וכל יומא סליק לרקיעא וגמר מתיבתא דרקיעא ונחית לארעא וגמר מתיבתא דארעא וגו' "</note> **"On such-and-such a mountain, he has dug a pit for himself and filled it with water and covered it with a stone, and also sealed it with his signet ring. Every day he ascends into the firmament and learns in the Academy there; thereafter, he comes back down to the earth and studies in the Academies of the earth, etc."**

# Of the Jews’ Unbridled Doctrine of God the Father. #
B 3
<meta>catchword: the</meta>

<margin>A sharp dispute is said to have once been held against God.</margin> In what manner a sharp dispute was once held against God in the Academy of the Firmament, and how He was contradicted by all the heavenly academies, is taught to us by Rabbi Bechai in his book *Cad hakkémach* <note>original: *Kad HaKemach*, "Jar of Flour," a work on ethics by the 13th-century scholar Bahya ben Asher</note>, folio 78, column 1, from the Talmudic tractate *Báva mézia* <note>original: *Bava Metzia*, "The Middle Gate," a tractate primarily concerning civil law and property</note>, folio 86, column 1, at the bottom:

> Rabba bar Nachmani was studying and heard them disputing 
> in the Academy of the Firmament: if a bright spot <note>original Hebrew: *baheret*, a specific type of skin lesion</note> precedes white hair, it is unclean; if white hair precedes the bright spot, it is clean. The Holy One, blessed be He, 
> says "clean," and the entire Academy of the Firmament says "unclean." They said: "Who shall decide?" Rabba bar Nachmani, for Rabba bar 
> Nachmani said: "I am unique in the knowledge of skin diseases <note>original: *nega'im*</note> and I am unique in the knowledge of purity in tents <note>original: *ohelot*</note>." They sent a messenger after him, but the Angel of Death 
> was not able to approach him, because his mouth did not cease from study. Meanwhile, a wind blew and made a rustling among the reeds; he thought it 
> was a troop of horsemen. He said: "Let that man's soul rest <note>a self-referential way of saying 'I would rather die'</note> and not be handed over to the government." As his soul was departing, he said: "Clean! 
> Clean!" A Heavenly Voice <note>original: *Bat Kol*</note> went out and said: "Blessed are you, bar Nachmani, for your body is clean and your soul has departed in purity."

That is: Rabba bar Nachmani read and heard that those in the Academy of the Firmament were quarreling with one another whether it is unclean when a pustule <term>Blatter: a skin lesion or pustule, often associated with the biblical skin disease *tzara'at*, traditionally translated as leprosy</term> comes before the white hair; or whether it is clean when the hair comes before the pustule. This was in doubt. GOD said it was clean, but all the high schools of the Firmament said it was unclean. Thereupon it was asked who should prove this and settle the dispute; and Rabba bar Nachmani was proposed. For Rabba bar Nachmani said: "I alone am the one who understands the strokes (of the leprosy of men); I alone know the leprosy of the tents." <note>This refers to the intricate Jewish laws regarding ritual purity and skin diseases found in the books of Leviticus and the Mishnaic orders of *Nega'im* and *Ohelot*.</note> Thereupon a messenger was sent for him; but the Angel of Death could not come near him because his mouth did not cease from reading <note>In Jewish folklore, a scholar cannot be taken by death as long as he is actively speaking words of Torah</note>. Meanwhile, a wind began to blow and made a noise among the reeds (wherein he was stuck in the marsh), so that he thought it was a troop of horsemen (who wanted to take him prisoner). Then bar Nachmani said: "I must die, and I shall not be surrendered into the hands of the King (who pursues me)." When he now died, he said: "It is clean" (thus he held with God and was of the same opinion, against all the high schools of the Firmament). Then a voice came from heaven and spoke: "You, bar Nachmani, are blessed, for your body is clean, and your soul has departed in purity." From this absurd and godless fable of the Talmud, it is to be seen that God, according to the opinion of all the Heavenly High Schools, erred and judged wrongly, and that He is not to be believed in all matters. And this agrees with what is written in the book *Zéda ledérech* <note>original: *Tzedah LaDerekh*, "Provision for the Journey," a 14th-century work by Menachem ibn Zarach</note>, in the *Parascha Ki tiffa* <note>original: *Parashat Ki Tissa*, the Torah portion in Exodus 30:11–34:35</note>, folio 83, column 2, concerning Moses: that he also did not believe God, where the words read thus:

<margin>Moses is said not to have believed God.</margin>
> At the hour when the Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: "Go, descend, for your people have corrupted themselves," he was holding the Tablets and did not believe that Israel had sinned. He said: 
> "If I do not see, I do not believe," as it is said: "And it came to pass, as soon as he came nigh unto the camp..." <note>Exodus 32:19</note> for he did not repent <note>of his disbelief</note> until he saw it with his own eyes.

<margin>Firstly, because of the destruction of the Temple.</margin>
Regarding the first cause of God’s weeping, namely the destruction of the Temple, it is written in the Talmudic tractate *Chagiga* <note>Tractate Hagigah, which deals with temple service and pilgrimage</note> folio 5, column 2, concerning the words of Jeremiah 13, verse 17: *Veim lo tischmauha bemistarim tifkéh nafschí mippené géva* <note>original Hebrew: ואם לא תשמעוה במסתרים תבכה נפשי מפני גוה</note>, that is, **"But if you will not hear it, my soul shall weep in secret because of such pride,"** it is written as follows: **"The Holy and Blessed God has a place where He weeps (as is added in the book *Nezach Iisraél* <note>The "Eternity of Israel," written by the Maharal of Prague in the 16th century</note> folio 16, column 4, in the 9th Chapter, and in the book *En Iisraél* <note>The *Ein Yaakov*, a famous collection of the non-legal (aggadic) portions of the Talmud</note> folio 154, column 1), which is called *Mistarim* (or *Mistorim*), that is, a hidden place. What, then, is the meaning of the words *mippené géva* <note>original: "because of the pride/loftiness"</note>, that is, because of the splendor (or the glory)? Rabbi Samuel, the son of Isaac, says: because of the glory of Israel, which was taken from them and given to the nations of the world (God weeps). Rabbi Samuel, the son of Nachman, says: because of the glory of God (which is despised because of the Jews' captivity and misery). What! Does the Holy and Blessed God weep then? Indeed, Rav Papa says: there is no sadness before God, as it is said (1 Chronicles 16:27): 'Splendor and majesty are before Him; strength and joy are in His place.' (To this it is answered:) This objection is not significant, for this (namely, that God weeps) is to be understood as occurring in the inner chambers; whereas that (that He does not weep) refers to the outer dwellings (of heaven). What! Does God not also weep in the outer dwellings? Indeed, it is written (Isaiah 22:12): 'On that day the Lord, the Lord of Hosts, called for weeping and mourning, for baldness and wearing sackcloth.' (To this the answer is given:) The destruction of the Temple is a different matter, for even the angels of peace wept over it, as it is written (Isaiah 33:7): 'Behold, their messengers (or mighty ones) cry without; the angels of peace weep bitterly.'"**

In the book *Rabboth* (or *Rabbos*) in *Petichach echa rabbathi* (or *Petichas echa rabbasi*) <note>This refers to the *Petichta* or "proem" (introductory section) of *Lamentations Rabbah*, a collection of ancient homilies and stories related to the Book of Lamentations</note> on folio 289, column 4, the following is also read: <margin>How God is said to have behaved before and after the destruction of the Temple.</margin> At the hour when the Holy One, Blessed be He, sought to destroy the Holy Temple, He said: "As long as I am within it, the nations of the world will not touch it. Rather, I will hide my eyes from it and swear that I will not attend to it until the time of the end; then the enemies shall come and destroy it." Immediately, the Holy One, Blessed be He, swore by His right hand and turned it behind Him, as it is written: "He has drawn back His right hand from before the enemy" <note>Lamentations 2:3</note>. At that time, the enemies entered the sanctuary and burned it. When it was burned, the Holy One, Blessed be He, said: "I no longer have a dwelling place on earth; I will remove my Presence <note>The *Shekhinah*, or the divine indwelling</note> from it and ascend to my former habitation," as it is written: "I will go and return to my place, until they acknowledge their offense and seek my face" <note>Hosea 5:15</note>. 

At that hour, the Holy One, Blessed be He, was weeping and saying: "Woe is me! What have I done? I caused my Presence to dwell below for the sake of Israel, and now that they have sinned, I have returned to my former place. Heaven forbid that I should be a laughingstock to the nations and a mockery to the creatures!" At that hour, Metatron <note>In Jewish mystical tradition, the highest of the angels who serves as a celestial scribe</note> came and fell on his face and said before Him: "Lord of the Universe, let me weep, but You do not weep." He replied to him: "If you do not let me weep now, I will enter a place where you have no permission to enter, and I will weep there," as it is written: "But if you will not hear it, my soul shall weep in secret places because of pride" <note>Jeremiah 13:17</note>. 

The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to the ministering angels: "Come, let us go, I and you, and see my house, what the enemies have done to it." Immediately, the Holy One, Blessed be He, went, and the ministering angels and Jeremiah were before Him. When the Holy One, Blessed be He, saw the Temple, He said: "Surely this is my house and this is my resting place, where enemies have come and done as they pleased!" At that hour, the Holy One, Blessed be He, was weeping and saying: "Woe is me for my house! My children, where are you? My priests, where are you? My beloved ones, where are you? What shall I do for you? I warned you, but you did not repent." 

The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Jeremiah: "Today I am like a man who had an only son and made a wedding canopy for him, and he died within his canopy. And you feel no pain for me or my son? Go and call Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Moses from their graves, for they know how to weep." Jeremiah said before Him: "Lord of the Universe, I do not know where Moses is buried." The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to him: "Stand on the bank of the Jordan and raise your voice and call: Son of Amram, son of Amram, stand and see your flock, which the enemies have swallowed up!" 

Immediately, Jeremiah went to the Cave of Machpelah <note>The burial place of the Patriarchs in Hebron</note> and said to the fathers of the world: "Arise, for the time has come when you are required before the Holy One, Blessed be He." They said to him: "Why?" He said to them: "I do not know," because he was afraid they might say: "In your days this happened to our children!" Jeremiah left them and stood on the bank of the Jordan and called: "Son of Amram, son of Amram, arise, the time has come when you are sought before the Holy One, Blessed be He." Moses said to him: "What makes this day different from other days, that I am sought before the Holy One, Blessed be He?" 

Moses left him and went to the ministering angels, whom he had known from the time the Torah was given. He said to them: "Ministers of the Heights, do you know why I am sought before the Holy One, Blessed be He?" They said to him: "Son of Amram, do you not know that the Temple is destroyed and Israel is exiled?" And he cried out and wept until he reached the fathers of the world. Immediately, they too tore their garments and placed their hands upon their heads, and were crying and weeping until they reached the gates of the Temple. When the Holy One, Blessed be He, saw them, immediately: "The Lord GOD of hosts called in that day to weeping, and to mourning, and to baldness, and to girding with sackcloth" <note>Isaiah 22:12</note>. And were it not for the scripture being written, it would be impossible to say such a thing <note>This is a common Rabbinic phrase (*kavyachol*) used when attributing human emotions or actions to God that might otherwise seem disrespectful</note>. And they were weeping and walking from this gate to that gate like a man whose dead lies before him, and the Holy One, Blessed be He, was lamenting and saying: "Woe to the King who in His youth succeeded, but in His old age did not succeed!"

That is: **At the time when God wanted to have the Temple destroyed, He said: As long as I am within it, the nations of the world will not touch it; but I will hide my eyes from it and swear that I will not concern myself with it until the time of the end, and the enemies shall come and devastate it.** Thereupon God immediately swore by His right hand and turned it behind Him: This is what (in the Lamentations of Jeremiah, chapter 2, verse 3) stands written: **He has drawn back his right hand when the enemy came.** In that same time, the enemies entered the Temple and burned it. **First Part.**

### On the Jews’ Unbecoming Doctrine of God the Father ###

Erster Theil. C <meta>Part One, Sig. C. Catchword: Then</meta>

In the book *Rabboth* (or *Rabbos*) <note>original: *Midrash Rabbah*, a classic collection of ancient Jewish homiletic interpretations of the Bible</note> in *Petichach Echa Rabbathi* (or *Pesichas Echa Rabbathi*) <note>original: the "proems" or introductory section to the Midrash on Lamentations</note>, on folio 289, column 4, the following is also read: <margin>How God is said to have behaved before and after the destruction of the Temple.</margin> 

<note>The following is a translation of the Hebrew passage from the Midrash:</note> At the hour when the Holy One, blessed be He, sought to destroy the Temple, He said: "As long as I am within it, the nations of the world will not touch it. Rather, I will hide My eyes from it and swear that I will not attend to it until the time of the end; then the enemies shall come and destroy it." Immediately, the Holy One, blessed be He, swore by His right hand and pulled it back behind Him; this is what is written (in Lamentations 2:3): **"He has drawn back His right hand from before the enemy."** 

At that hour, the enemies entered the Sanctuary and burned it. Once it was burned, the Holy One, blessed be He, said: "I no longer have a dwelling place on earth; I will remove My *Shekhinah* <term>Shekhinah: the dwelling presence of God on earth</term> from it and ascend to My first dwelling place." This is what is written (in Hosea 5:15): **"I will go and return to My place, until they acknowledge their offense and seek My face."** At that hour, the Holy One, blessed be He, was weeping and saying: "Woe is me! What have I done? I caused My *Shekhinah* to dwell below for the sake of Israel, and now that they have sinned, I have returned to My first place. Heaven forbid <note>original: *chas ve-shalom*</note> that I should become a laughingstock to the nations and a mockery to the creatures." 

At that hour, Metatron <note>one of the highest archangels in Jewish mystical tradition, often described as the celestial scribe</note> came and fell upon his face, saying before Him: "Lord of the Universe, let me weep, but You must not weep." God replied: "If you do not let me weep now, I will enter a place where you have no permission to enter, and I will weep there," as it is said (Jeremiah 13:17): **"My soul shall weep in secret places for your pride."** The Holy One, blessed be He, said to the ministering angels: "Come, let us go, I and you, and see what the enemies have done in My house." Immediately, the Holy One, blessed be He, went with the ministering angels, and Jeremiah <note>the prophet associated with the destruction of Jerusalem</note> before Him. When the Holy One, blessed be He, saw the Temple, He said: "Surely this is My house and this is My resting place, where enemies have come and done as they pleased." 

At that hour, the Holy One, blessed be He, was weeping and saying: "Woe is me for My house! My children, where are you? My priests, where are you? My beloved ones, where are you? What shall I do for you? I warned you, but you did not return in repentance." The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Jeremiah: "I am like a man today who had an only son; he prepared a wedding canopy for him, and the son died within his canopy. And you feel no pain for Me or My son? Go and call Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Moses from their graves, for they know how to weep." Jeremiah said before Him: "Lord of the Universe, I do not know where Moses is buried." The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: "Stand on the bank of the Jordan and raise your voice, calling: Son of Amram, son of Amram, arise and see your flock, which the enemies have swallowed up!" 

Immediately, Jeremiah went to the Cave of Machpelah <note>the traditional burial site of the Jewish patriarchs and matriarchs in Hebron</note> and said to the Patriarchs of the world: "Arise, for the time has come when you are summoned before the Holy One, blessed be He." They said to him: "Why?" He said to them: "I do not know," for he was afraid they would say: "This happened to our children in your days!" Jeremiah left them and stood on the bank of the Jordan and called: "Son of Amram, son of Amram, arise! The time has come when you are summoned before the Holy One, blessed be He." Moses said to him: "What makes this day different from other days, that I am summoned before the Holy One, blessed be He?" 

Jeremiah left him, and Moses went to the ministering angels, whom he had known since the time the Law was given. He said to them: "O celestial ministers, do you know why I am summoned before the Holy One, blessed be He?" They said to him: "Son of Amram, do you not know that the Temple is destroyed and Israel is gone into exile?" Then he cried out and wept until he reached the Patriarchs of the world. Immediately, they too tore their garments and placed their hands upon their heads, crying and weeping until they reached the gates of the Temple. When the Holy One, blessed be He, saw them, it was as written (Isaiah 22:12): **"And in that day did the Lord God of hosts call to weeping, and to mourning, and to baldness, and to girding with sackcloth."** Were it not for the scripture which says this, it would be impossible to say it <note>a Rabbinic expression used when describing God in very human or daring terms</note>. And they went weeping from one gate to another, like a person whose dead relative lies before him. And the Holy One, blessed be He, lamented, saying: "Woe to the King who succeeded in his youth but did not succeed in his old age!"

*This is:* At the time when God wanted to have the Temple destroyed, He said: "As long as I am within it, the nations of the world will not touch it; but I will hide my eyes from it and swear that I will not take care of it until the time of the end, and the enemies shall come and lay it waste." Thereupon, God immediately swore by His right hand and turned it behind Him: This is what is written (in the Lamentations of Jeremiah, chapter 2, verse 3): **"He has drawn back His right hand when the enemy came."** At that same time, the enemies entered the Temple and burned it:

<margin>How God is said to have conducted Himself before and after the destruction of the Temple.</margin>

"At the hour when the Holy One, blessed be He, sought to destroy the Holy Temple, He said: 'As long as I am within it, the nations of the world will not touch it. In that hour, Metatron <note>Metatron: a high-ranking angel in Jewish mystical tradition, often described as a celestial scribe or the "Prince of the Countenance"</note> came and fell upon his face and said before Him: 'Lord of the Universe, let me weep, but You must not weep.' They said to him: 'Why?' He said to them: 'I do not know,' because he was afraid they might say: 'In your days, this has happened to our children!' Jeremiah left them and stood on the bank of the Jordan and called: 'Son of Amram! Son of Amram! Arise, the time has come that you are requested before the Holy One, blessed be He.' Moses said to him: 'What is different about this day from other days, that I am requested before the Holy One, blessed be He?' Moses left him and went to the ministering angels, whom he had known since the time the Law was given. He said to them: 'You heavenly ministers, do you know why I am requested before the Holy One, blessed be He?' They said to him: 'Son of Amram, do you not know that the Temple is destroyed and Israel is gone into exile?'

Then he cried out and wept until he reached the Fathers of the world. Immediately, they too rent their garments and placed their hands upon their heads, and they were crying out and weeping until they reached the gates of the Temple. When the Holy One, blessed be He, saw them, immediately: 'The Lord God of Hosts called in that day to weeping, and to mourning, and to baldness, and to girding with sackcloth' <note>Isaiah 22:12</note>. And were it not for the scripture that is written, it would be impossible to say such a thing. And they went weeping from one gate to another like a man whose dead lies before him. And the Holy One, blessed be He, lamented, saying: 'Woe to the King who succeeded in his youth, but in his old age did not succeed!'"

*This is:* **At the time when God intended to have the Temple destroyed, He said: As long as I am within it, the nations of the world will not touch it; but I will hide My eyes from it and swear that I will not concern Myself with it until the time of the end, and the enemies shall come and devastate it. Thereupon God immediately swore by His right hand and turned it behind Him. This is what is written (in the Lamentations of Jeremiah, chapter 2, verse 3): He has drawn back His right hand when the enemy came. At that same time, the enemies entered the Temple and burned it.**

# Of the First Part of *Judaism Unmasked*, Chapter I.

...[that] the holy and blessed God might now deal with me as He did in previous months, during the time of the parting of the Red Sea; for at that time He allowed Himself to be released from His oath: Oh, that He would also now allow Himself to be released from His oath! For this reason He said (from Job 29:2): *Mi jittenéni* <note>original: "מי יתנני"</note>, that is, "Who will give to me?" (meaning, "Who will grant that I were as in months past?"). For the one who wrote the book *Megalléh amukkóth* <note term="Megalleh Amukot">"Revealer of Depths," a 17th-century Kabbalistic work by Nathan Nata Spira known for its complex numerical and mystical interpretations.</note> reports in the third *Ofan* <note term="Ofan">Literally "wheel"; here it refers to a section or chapter of the mystical text.</note> that the angel who releases the holy and blessed God from His oath is named *Mi* <note>In Hebrew, "Mi" (מי) is simply the word for "who," used in questions. Here, the author critiques a mystical interpretation that transforms this pronoun into the proper name of an angel.</note>. And this is what is written in Job 29:2: *Mi jittenéni kejárche kédem* <note>original: "מי יתנני כירחי קדם"</note>, that is, "Who will give to me, that I were as in months past?" Consider the word *Mi*, which signifies the angel called *Mi*: may that same one do for me now what he did in the former months, when he released the holy and blessed God from His oath.

May he also now release the holy and blessed God from His oath, who has sworn that I shall not enter the Land of Israel. One must also say that this (which stands in the cited passage of Job) also has a meaning referring to those aforementioned words spoken by a heavenly voice <note term="Bath Kol">Literally "daughter of a voice"; a divine echo or heavenly proclamation.</note> which said: "Woe is me, that I have sworn! But now that I have sworn, *Mi méfer li*" <note>original: "מי מפר לי"</note>, that is, "Who will release me from my oath?" Consider the word *Mi*: and it means as much as: "The angel who is named *Mi* shall bring my oath to nothing." These are the words of the book *Ammudéha Schifa* <note term="Ammudeha Shiva">"The Seven Pillars," a work of homilies and explanations.</note>. Since the angel *Mi* is appointed for the purpose of releasing God from His oath and vow, those who scolded the Rabba <note>Referring to Rabba bar bar Hana, mentioned on the previous page.</note> as a donkey and a fool for not freeing God from His oath and releasing Him from it had no reason to do so. However, all of this is a Jewish madness; and the fools want to make an angel out of the word *Mi*, which is a *pronomen interrogativum personæ* <note>Latin: "interrogative pronoun of a person."</note> and means "who."

To return, however, to the words "Woe is me" which God is said to have spoken, it is written thus in the Talmudic tractate *Berachóth* <note term="Berachot">The first tractate of the Talmud, dealing with prayers and blessings.</note> (or *Beróchos*), folio 3, column 1:
