<margin>How it is foolishly proven from Isaiah that there are six orders in the Talmud.</margin>
That there are six *Sedarim* <term>Sedarim</term><note>The primary "Orders" or divisions of the Mishnah and Talmud.</note> or orders in the Talmud is proven in the Talmudic tractate *Shabbath* (or *Shabbas*), folio 31, column 1, in a very subtle <note>The author uses "subtle" sarcastically here to mock Rabbinic logic.</note> manner from the words of Isaiah 33:6: **And there shall be *emunath* (the faith) *ittecha* (of your times), *chosen* (the strength), *yeshuoth* (of the salvations), *chochmath* (the wisdom), and *daath* (the knowledge)** etc., in the following way: <note>original Hebrew: אמונת סדר זרעים עתך זה סדר מועד חוסן זה סדר נשים ישועות זה סדר נזיקין חכמת זה סדר קדשים ודעת זה סדר טהרות ואפילו הכי יראת יי' היא אוצרו</note> that is: (The word) *emunath*, (that is) the **faith**, signifies the order of *Zeraim* <term>Zeraim</term><note>Seeds; the order dealing with agricultural laws.</note>, or of the **seeds**. (The word) *Ittecha*, that is **of your times**, (signifies) the order of *Moed* <term>Moed</term><note>Appointed Times; the order dealing with the Sabbath and festivals.</note> or the **festivals**. (The word) *chosen*, that is the **strength**, (signifies) the order of *Nashim* <term>Nashim</term><note>Women; the order dealing with marriage and family law.</note> or the **women**. (The word) *Yeshuoth*, that is of the **salvations**, (signifies) the order of *Nezikin* <term>Nezikin</term><note>Damages; the order dealing with civil and criminal law.</note> or the **damages**. (The word) *Chochmath*, that is the **wisdom**, (signifies) the order of *Kodashim* <term>Kodashim</term><note>Holy Things; the order dealing with sacrifices and the Temple.</note> or the **holy things**. And (the word) *Daath*, that is the **knowledge**, (signifies) the order of *Tohoroth* <term>Tohoroth</term><note>Purities; the order dealing with ritual purity and uncleanness.</note> or the **purities**. Is this not a magnificent proof? The most understanding and subtle Christian would not have been so clever as to bring such a secret meaning to light from the words of Isaiah. Similarly, in the *Yalkut Chadash* <note>The "New Collection," a 17th-century compilation of Midrashic and Kabbalistic teachings.</note>, folio 173, column 1, number 117, under the title *Torah*, it is proven from Psalm 19:8, 9, 10 in just such a tasteless way that there are said six orders.

In exactly such an absurd manner, the highly enlightened Rabbis also prove from the Holy Scriptures of the Old Testament that there is not only a written law, but also an oral law. ### Chapter VIII of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked.

<meta>catchword: It</meta>

word / for according to these words I have made a covenant with you and with Israel, it is written: <note>original Hebrew: בשעה שנגלה הק"ה בסיני ליתן תורה לישראל... "At the hour when the Holy One, Blessed be He, revealed Himself at Sinai to give the Torah to Israel..."</note> At the hour when the Holy One, Blessed be He <note>A standard Jewish honorific for God</note>, revealed Himself at Sinai to give the Torah to Israel, He spoke to Moses according to the order: the Bible, the Mishnah, the Talmud, and the Aggadah. As it is said: "And God spoke all these words." Even that which a student asks his teacher, the Holy One, Blessed be He, told to Moses at that time. After he had learned it from the mouth of the Holy One, Blessed be He, He said to him: "Teach it to Israel." Moses spoke before Him: "Lord of the world, I will write it down for them." God, however, said to him: "I do not wish to give it to them in writing, because it is revealed before Me that the Idolaters <term>Abgöttische</term><note>Eisenmenger uses the German "Abgöttische" to translate terms referring to non-Jews or Gentiles in the Hebrew text, reflecting his polemical tone.</note> will one day rule over them and take it from them, and they will be held in contempt among the Idolaters. Rather, the Bible I give to them in writing; but the Mishnah, the Talmud, and the Aggadah I give to them by word of mouth, so that when the nations of the world come and make them subjects, they may be distinguished from them." He said to the prophet: "If I were to write for him the multitude of my Law, they would be accounted as a stranger." <note>A reference to Hosea 8:12.</note> What then shall I do for them? I will give them the Bible in writing, but the Mishnah, the Talmud, and the Aggadah by word of mouth. The words "Write these words" refer to the Bible; and the words "For according to the tenor of these words" refer to the Mishnah and the Talmud, which create a distinction between Israel and the Idolaters. 

That is: In that time when the holy, blessed God had revealed Himself on Mount Sinai to give the Law to the Israelites, He spoke the same to Moses according to the order of the Bible, the Mishnah, the Talmud (that is, the Gemara, which, as already mentioned, is sometimes called the Talmud on its own), and the Aggadah (that is, the amusing stories and little tales) <note>Eisenmenger often dismissively refers to Aggadah—the non-legal, narrative portion of the Talmud—as "tales."</note>, just as it is written in Exodus 20, verse 1: **"And God spoke all these words."** Even everything that a disciple might ask his master, God told to Moses at that same time. Now, after he had learned it from the mouth of God, and He had commanded him to teach the same to the Israelites, Moses said to Him: "You Lord of the world, I will write it down for them." But God gave him as an answer: "I do not desire to give it to them in writing, because I well know that the Idolaters shall rule over them and take it away from them, and they shall also be despised among the Idolaters. The Bible I will give to them in writing, but the Mishnah, the Talmud, and the Aggadah they shall receive from Me orally, so that when the nations of the world come and make them subjects, they may be distinguished from them." He said to the prophet: "If I compose the greatest part of my Law in writing for him (namely, the people of Israel), they will be regarded as a stranger." What shall I then do with them? I will give them the Bible in writing, but the Mishnah, the Talmud, and the Aggadah orally. The words **"Write these words"** signify the Bible; and the words **"For after these words"** signify the Mishnah and the Talmud, which make a distinction between Israel and the Idolaters. 

The very same thing is also to be found in the *Yalkut Shimoni* regarding the five books of Moses, number 405, though with fewer words; and more can be found on this in the book called *Sefer Maor HaKaton*, folio 48, column 3 and 4, in the *Parashah Vayakhel*. <note>Eisenmenger provides citations to standard Jewish anthologies and commentaries to support his claims about Jewish beliefs regarding the Oral Law's superiority.</note>

# Of the Talmud.
<center>Pp 3</center>

<margin>Refutation of the proof used by the Jews that "Al pi" signifies an oral law.</margin>It is, however, a completely tasteless matter that the Jews wish to prove that there is an oral law based on what is written in Exodus 34, verse 27: **Write these words; for al pi had-devarim ha-ele karatti ittecha berit** (or *beris*), **that is—as the Jews interpret it—According to the mouth of these words I have made a covenant with you.** <note>original Hebrew: עַל־פִּי הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה כָּרַתִּי אִתְּךָ בְּרִית; Eisenmenger is arguing against the literal translation of "mouth" (*pi*) here.</note> From this they wish to force the conclusion that an oral law must be understood here, because *al pi* means **according to the mouth** or **through the mouth.** I answer them, however, that while *al pi* does indeed mean **according to the mouth** or **through the mouth** when mention is made of a thing that literally or figuratively has a mouth: thus it stands in Genesis 45, verse 21, *Al pi Pharoh*, **that is, according to the mouth (meaning the command) of Pharaoh;** and Numbers 4, verse 27, *Al pi Aharon*, **that is, according to the mouth of Aaron;** and Deuteronomy 17, verse 6, *Al pi shenayim edim*, **that is, according to the mouth of two witnesses** <note>Eisenmenger writes "two tongues" in the German text, likely a slip of the pen or a reference to the "mouths" of the witnesses.</note>; there are many such places in the Scriptures. But where a matter is dealt with that has no mouth, then *al pi* signifies as much as **According to** or **In proportion to,** as it is used in Leviticus 27, verse 18, where one reads *Al pi ha-shanim han-notarot*, which means **According to the remaining years,** and not **According to the mouth of the remaining years,** for years have no mouth. In this same sense, *al pi* is also used in Leviticus 27, verse 8; Numbers 26, verse 56; Deuteronomy 17, verse 10; Proverbs 22, verse 6; as well as Amos 6, verse 5. Since words have no mouth, the interpretation of the Jews is not only false but also completely foolish.

But to return to the reason why the Talmud was not also given in writing: in the *Sefer Yuchasin* <note>The "Book of Genealogies," a 16th-century work of Jewish history by Abraham Zacuto.</note>, folio 160, column 1, the following is read: <note>original Hebrew: לא נכתבה התורה שבעל פה להיות כי ארוכה מארץ מדה לכן כתב הקב"ה זכרון המצוות בקיצור בתורה שבכתב ופירושיהן בעל פה. ועוד טעם אחר אמרו בפרקי רבי אליעזר מפני שראה הקב"ה שעתידין האומות להעתיק התורה שבכתב לכן מסר למשה סימנים בעל פה:</note> <margin>Another reason why the Talmud was not given in writing.</margin>**that is: The Oral Law was not written down because its measure is longer than the earth; therefore, the Holy One, Blessed be He, wrote the remembrance of the commandments briefly (and with few words) in the Written Law, but gave the interpretations of them orally.** Another reason is also mentioned in the *Chapters of Rabbi Eliezer* <note>A famous midrashic work (Pirkei De-Rabbi Eliezer) traditionally attributed to the 1st-century sage Eliezer ben Hyrcanus.</note>, namely, because God saw that the nations of the world would translate the written law (into their languages); therefore, He delivered oral signs to Moses. So also writes Rabbi Isaac in his book *Ammude ha-Golah* <note>The "Pillars of the Exile," also known as the Sefer Mitzvot Katan or SeMaK, written by Isaac ben Joseph of Corbeil.</note>, folio 39, concerning this: <note>original Hebrew: אל תחשוב כי עיקר התורה בכתב כי אדרבה עיקרה אותה שבעל פה ועל תורה שבעל פה נכרת ברית דכתיב כי על פי הדברים האלה כרתי אתך ברית וזן אוצרו של הקב"ה כי היה גלוי לפניו שהיו ישראל עתידין להיות גולין בין האומות ויעתיקו הגוים ספריהם</note> **that is: Do not think that the essence of the Law is in the writing; for on the contrary, its essence is that which is oral, and the covenant was made concerning the Oral Law, as it is written: "For according to the mouth [Al pi] of these words I have made a covenant with you." And it is the treasure of the Holy One, Blessed be He; for it was revealed before Him that Israel was destined to be in exile among the nations, and the Gentiles would copy their books—**

[can any] Jew [say] to whom such a revelation occurred? If it was not revealed to anyone else at that time, one would certainly like to know where they obtained it from.

From this, one can reasonably conclude that there was no Oral Law at that time, since it is reported here that Joshua had all the words of the Law proclaimed as they were described in the <term>Book of the Law<gloss>The Torah or Pentateuch</gloss></term>. It follows that there was no word commanded by Moses that was not announced; by which it is understood that the written Law was entirely perfect, because everything that was announced was contained within it. Why then would an oral one have been necessary?

Furthermore, in Deuteronomy 31, verses 9, 10, 11, and 12, we read that after Moses had written the Law, he gave it to the priests and commanded that every seven years, at the <term>Feast of Tabernacles<gloss>Sukkot; a harvest festival commemorating the wandering in the desert</gloss></term>, it should be proclaimed before all Israel, so that they might learn it, keep it, fear their God, and do all the words of this Law. From this it follows that they were to be instructed solely from such a written Law, and that it was perfect enough to teach them the true fear of God; and no mention of an oral law is made therein. Moreover, in Deuteronomy chapter 30, verse 10, it is read: **For the Lord will turn, that he may rejoice over you for good, as he rejoiced over your fathers: because you obey the voice of your God, to keep his commandments and statutes which are written in the book of this law.** And in 2 Kings 17, verses 36 and 37, it is written that it was said to the children of Israel: **The Lord, who brought you out of the land of Egypt with great power and an outstretched arm, Him shall you fear, Him shall you worship, and to Him shall you sacrifice. And the customs, statutes, laws, and commandments which He wrote for you, these you shall observe.** Now, if God rejoiced over those who kept His commandments and statutes which are written in the Law of Moses, and commanded that only the written commandments should be observed, then surely no Oral Law can have been given by Him. For if He had given one—and indeed one which, according to the teachings of the Jews, was to be held in higher regard than the written Law—He would certainly have commanded that it be kept as well. In addition, it should be well noted that the written Law of Moses was perfect and clear enough for the Israelite people, to which nothing was to be added, as can be seen in Deuteronomy 4, verses 1, 2, 8, and chapter 12, verse 32; therefore it is said in Psalm 19, verse 8—

[...that God] covered Israel and said to them: if you accept the Law, it is well; but if not, there shall be your grave beneath it. This is also read in the <term>Talmud<gloss>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism</gloss></term>, in the Tractate *Shabbath*, folio 88, column 1; and in the <term>Yalkut Shimoni<gloss>A popular medieval midrashic anthology</gloss></term> on the five books of Moses, number 283, folio 80, column 1; as well as on Isaiah, number 116, folio 50, column 4. And in <term>Jonathan’s Chaldean Translation<gloss>The Targum Jonathan, an Aramaic translation and interpretation of the Hebrew Bible</gloss></term>, the aforementioned seventeenth verse of Exodus 19 is given thus: <note>original Aramaic: "ואנפק משה ית עמא לקדמות שכינתא דיי' מן משריתא ומן יד חלש מארי עלמא ית טורא וזקפה באוירא וזהר זיג הי כאספקלריא ואתעתדו תחותי טורא"</note> which is to say: **And Moses led the people out of the camp to meet the Majesty of the Lord; and immediately the Lord of the world uprooted the mountain and lifted it up into the air, and it (the mountain) shone like a mirror; and they stood under the mountain.**

<margin>Such compulsion is only to be understood as applying to the Oral Law, for they are said to have accepted the written one willingly.</margin>
However, <term>Rabbi Bechai<gloss>Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century Spanish rabbi and commentator</gloss></term> writes in his commentary on the 5 Books of Moses, in the section *Vayishlaḥ Yitro*, folio 87, columns 1 and 2, regarding the words of Exodus 19, verse 8, **"All that the Lord has spoken, we will do,"** that God had to force the Israelites in the aforementioned manner only to accept the <term>Oral Law<gloss>The traditions and legal interpretations believed by Rabbis to have been given to Moses alongside the written Torah</gloss></term>, but not the <term>Written Law<gloss>The Five Books of Moses</gloss></term>; where those same words read as follows: <note>original Hebrew: "הודו וקבלו עליהם עול התורה והמצוות ועשו כן ברצונם, ומה שדרשו רבותינו ז"ל: כפה עליהם הר כגיגית ואמר להם אם אתם מקבלים את התורה מוטב ואם לאו שם תהא קבורתכם על התורה שבעל פה היה שיש בה אזהרות ועונשים וכמה סייגים וגדרים אבל התורה שבכתב הכל הודו מרעתם בחפץ גדול בשמחה ובטוב לבב ולא הוצרכו כפיה אלא בתורה שבעל פה"</note> that is: **They made their confession and took upon themselves the yoke of the Law and the commandments, and did so willingly. But as for what our Rabbis—of blessed memory—report, that He (namely God) covered the mountain over them like a tub and said to them: "If you accept the Law, it is well; but if not, there shall be your grave beneath it," this occurred because of the Oral Law, which contains warnings and punishments within it, and has many hedges and fences around it** (that is, many difficult commandments which surround the commandments found in the written Law like fences, so that one does not transgress them). **But as for the written Law, all acknowledged it knowingly with great desire, with joy, and with a good heart, and had no need for covering** (or for compulsion, for <note>original Hebrew: כפה</note> *Capha* also means to compel).

<margin>Moses is said to have received the Law in Heaven.</margin>
Concerning the place where Moses is said to have received the Law, the "highly rational" Rabbis teach that this occurred in Heaven, though Moses faced many obstacles until he arrived there, as mentioned in the great <term>Yalkut Reuveni<gloss>A 17th-century collection of Kabbalistic midrashim by Reuben Hoeshke</gloss></term>, in the section *Mishpatim*,

In the hour when Moses ascended on high, a cloud came and crouched before him, and he did not know whether to ride upon it or to take hold of it. Immediately, the cloud opened its mouth and Moses entered inside it; he walked through the firmament like a man walking upon the earth, as it is written in the <term>Torah<gloss>The first five books of the Hebrew Bible</gloss></term>: **"And Moses went into the midst of the cloud."** 

There met him **Kemuel**, the officer appointed over twelve thousand angels of destruction who stand at the gates of the firmament. He rebuked Moses with anger and said to him: "What is it to you, son of Amram, to come to the place of the angels of fire?" Moses said to him: "I have not come of my own accord, but by the permission of the Holy One, Blessed be He, to receive the Torah and bring it down to Israel." Since the angel would not allow him to pass, Moses struck him and dealt him a wound to destroy him from the world. 

Moses continued walking in the firmament until the angel **Hadarniel** met him. It is said of the angel Hadarniel that he is higher than his fellows by sixty myriads of <term>parasangs<gloss>An ancient unit of distance, roughly 3.5 to 4 miles</gloss></term>, and with every single word that comes out of his mouth, twelve thousand lightning bolts of fire issue forth. When he saw Moses, he rebuked him and said: "What is it to you, son of Amram, in the place of the supreme holy ones?" 

When Moses heard the sound, he was terrified by him, his eyes shed tears, and he sought to fall from the cloud. Immediately, the mercies of the Holy One, Blessed be He, were stirred, and He said to Hadarniel: "From the day I created you, you have been masters of strife. In the beginning, when I sought to create Man, you brought an accusation before Me and said, 'What is man that You are mindful of him?' <note>Psalm 8:4</note> I even burned and beat you down into small groups with my little finger. And now you strive with the **faithful one of My house** <note>original Hebrew: "ne’eman beyti"</note>, whom I have brought up here to receive the Torah and bring it down to My chosen children? For if it were not for the Torah that Israel receives, you would have no dwelling in the firmament." 

When Hadarniel heard this, he immediately trembled before the Holy One, Blessed be He, and said: "Lord of the Universe, it is revealed and known before You that I did not know he came here with Your permission. Now I shall be his messenger and walk before him like a student before his master." Immediately Hadarniel ran and bowed himself and walked before Moses like a student before his master until they reached the fire of **Sandalphon**. Hadarniel said to Moses: "Go back, for I cannot restrain myself before the fire of Sandalphon, lest he burn me." 

When Moses saw Sandalphon, he was immediately terrified and hurried to fall from the cloud; his eyes shed tears and he sought mercy before the Holy One, Blessed be He. Because of the goodness and grace of Israel, the Holy One, Blessed be He, Himself descended from the **Throne of Glory** and stood before Moses until he had passed before the fire of Sandalphon; and of that hour it is written: **"And the Lord passed before him and proclaimed."** <note>Exodus 34:6</note> 

When Moses had passed Sandalphon, he encountered **Rigyon**, the river of fire, whose streams burn the ministering angels, and in which they all immerse themselves; it issues from beneath the Throne of Glory from the sweat of the **Living Creatures** <note>The "Chayot," high-ranking angels described in Ezekiel's vision</note>. Immediately the Holy One, Blessed be He, helped him across. Then he met **Galizur**, who is also called **Raziel** <note>Often identified in mysticism as the angel who reveals divine secrets</note>. When Moses saw him, he trembled. Immediately the Holy One, Blessed be He, took him and helped him pass. 

Then he met a great troop of angels of terror who surround the Throne of Glory; they are mightier and more powerful than all the other angels. They sought to burn him with the breath of their mouths. Immediately, the Holy One, Blessed be He, spread the radiance of His glory over him and said to Moses: "Give them an answer." 

Moses said to them: "What is written in the Torah? **'I am the Lord your God who brought you out of the land of Egypt.'** Were you enslaved to Egypt and then set free, that you should need the Torah? It is written: **'You shall have no other gods.'** Is there idolatry among you, that you should need the Torah? It is written: **'You shall not take the name of the Lord in vain.'** Is there business among you that you should need to take an oath? It is written: **'Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy.'** Is there labor among you that you should need to rest on the Sabbath? It is written: **'Honor your father and your mother.'** Do you have fathers and mothers that you should need to honor them? It is written: **'You shall not murder.'** Is there any shedding of blood among you? It is written: **'You shall not commit adultery.'** Are there women among you? It is written: **'You shall not steal.'** Is there money in the firmament? It is written: **'You shall not bear false witness.'** Is there false testimony among you? It is written: **'You shall not covet.'** Are there houses, fields, and vineyards among you that you should need the Torah?" 

Immediately, all the ministering angels turned back and conceded to the words of the Holy One, Blessed be He, and said: **"O Lord, our Lord, how majestic is Your name in all the earth, who has set Your glory above the heavens."** <note>Psalm 8:1</note> And the Holy One, Blessed be He, taught him the entire Torah in forty days. 

But when he was about to descend and saw the dread of the angels—the troops of angels of terror, angels of sweat, angels of quaking, and angels of trembling—he was immediately seized by trembling and forgot everything in one hour. Immediately, the Holy One, Blessed be He, called to **Yefefiyah**, the Prince of the Torah, and delivered the Torah to him.

# Of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked, Chapter VIII. #

> The Law <note>original: התורה (HaTorah)</note> is set in order and preserved in all things; all the ministering angels became his friends, and each one handed over to him a remedy and the secret of names which proceed from every single section, along with all their uses. Thus it is written: **"Thou hast ascended on high, thou hast led captivity captive, thou hast received gifts."** <note>Psalm 68:18</note> Even the Angel of Death handed over something to him, for so it is written: **"And he put on the incense and made atonement for the people."** <note>Numbers 16:47; the midrashic idea is that the Angel of Death taught Moses that incense stops plagues.</note> This is the glorious service which the angels delivered to him through **Yefifiah** <gloss>The Prince of the Torah, a high-ranking angel in mystical lore</gloss>, the Prince of the Law, and through **Metatron** <gloss>The "Prince of the Face" or "Prince of the Presence," often considered the highest of angels in the Kabbalah</gloss>, the Prince of the Presence; and Moses delivered it to **Eleazar**, and Eleazar to **Phinehas** his son, who is in great and precious joy.

<margin>How this came to pass, and what he encountered there.</margin>
That is: At the time in which Moses was to travel on high (that is, into heaven), a cloud came and crouched before him; but Moses our teacher—upon whom be peace—did not know whether he should ride upon it or hold onto it. Immediately the cloud opened up, and Moses stepped inside and walked through the firmament <gloss>The expanse of the heavens</gloss> just as a man walks upon the earth; for thus it is written in the Law (**Exodus 24:18**): **And Moses went into the midst of the cloud.**

<margin>How the angel Kemuel addressed him.</margin>
But when the gatekeeper **Kemuel**, the angel who is set over twelve thousand angels of destruction <note>original: מלאכי חבלה (Malakhei Khabalah)</note> who stand at the gates of the firmament, met him, he addressed him with harsh words and said to him: "What have you, son of **Amram** <note>Moses's father</note>, to do in the place of the angels of fire?"

<margin>What Moses answered him, and how he struck him until he was wounded.</margin>
Upon this Moses answered him: "I have not come of my own accord, but with the permission of the Holy and Blessed God, to receive the Law and to bring it down to the Israelites." But since the angel would not let him pass, Moses struck him so that he received a wound, thereby intending to blot him out from the world; and he went into the firmament until the angel **Hadarniel** met him.

<margin>How the angel Hadarniel addressed him harshly.</margin>
It is said of this angel **Hadarniel** that he is sixty times ten thousand (or six hundred thousand) miles higher than his companions, and that with every single word that comes out of his mouth, twelve thousand fiery lightning bolts flash forth. After he saw Moses, he addressed him with rough words and said to him: "What have you, son of Amram, to do in the place of the upper holy ones?" When Moses heard the voice, he was terrified of him, and tears flowed from his eyes, and he was about to fall from the cloud.

<margin>Whereupon God gave him a rebuke.</margin>
The Holy and Blessed God, however, had mercy on him and said to **Hadarniel**: "From the day that I created you, you have been quarrelsome. When I intended to create man in the beginning, you complained against me and said to me: **'What is man, that thou art mindful of him?'** <note>Psalm 8:4</note> Therefore I grew angry with you and burned you in heaps with my smallest finger; and now you quarrel with the one who is faithful in my house, whom I have allowed to come here."

<note>original Hebrew: מנין היה משה יודע ארבעים יום וארבעים לילה שם עם יי' אימתי יום ואימתי לילה כשהיה הק"בה מלמדו תורה שבכתב היה יודע שהוא יום וכשלמדו תורה שבעל פה היה יודע שהוא לילה שהיום והלילה שוין לפני הק"בה שנאמר ונהורא עמיה שרי וכתיב גם חשך לא יחשיך וגו' ועוד דרשו כשהיה רואה הכוכבים והמזלות כורעים ומשתחוים לפני הק"בה היה יודע שהוא יום וכשהיה רואה גלגל חמה כורע ומשתחוה לפני הק"בה היה יודע שהוא לילה שנ' וצבא השמים לך משתחוים</note>

That is, in the **Midrash** <note>A term for ancient Jewish commentaries and interpretations of the Bible.</note> (it is written concerning the words of **Exodus 34, verse 28**): **And he was there with the Lord forty days and forty nights.** From where did Moses know when it was day and when it was night? When the Holy One, blessed be He, taught him the **Written Law** <note>The Torah as written in the Five Books of Moses.</note>, he knew that it was day; but when He instructed him in the **Oral Law** <note>The traditional interpretations and laws passed down verbally, later recorded in the Talmud.</note>, he knew that it was night. For day and night are the same before God, as is said in **Daniel 2, verse 22**: **And the light remains with Him.** So it is also written in **Psalm 139, verse 12**: **The darkness also does not darken before You.** Furthermore, it is interpreted in the Midrash: when he saw the stars and the constellations bowing and prostrating themselves before God, he knew that it was day; but when he saw the sphere of the sun bowing and prostrating itself before God, he knew that it was night, as is said in **Nehemiah 9, verse 6**: **And the heavenly host worships You.**

This is also read in the *Yalkut Shimoni* <note>A significant medieval compilation of Midrashic material.</note> regarding the Psalms, number 672, folio 96, column 2, and regarding the five books of Moses, number 406, folio 111, column 1; in which latter place, however, this is also added:

<note>original Hebrew: כשהיה רואה למלאכים מקלסין אותו בקדוש היה יודע שהוא יום וכשעה שהיה רואה אותן מקלסין בברוך היה יודע שהוא לילה. דבר אחר כשהיה רואה אותן ששוחקין מן להוריד לישראל היה יודע שהוא יום וכשהיה יורד להם היה יודע שהוא לילה</note>

That is: When he saw that the angels praised God with the word **Holy** <note>The "Kadosh" prayer.</note>, he knew that it was day; but when he saw them praising Him with the word **Blessed** <note>The "Barukh" prayer.</note>, he knew that it was night. In another way (this also happened): When he saw that they (namely the angels) were grinding the **Manna** <note>The miraculous "bread from heaven" that fed the Israelites in the desert.</note> to send it down to the Israelites, he knew it was day; but when the Manna descended to them, he knew it was night. All this can also be found in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>The Midrash on the Book of Psalms.</note> folio 18, column 3, concerning the 19th Psalm.

<margin>Although the Talmudic disputes run directly contrary to one another, they are nevertheless all said to be God's Word.</margin> However, despite the fact that such disputes run directly contrary to one another—and thus one side must necessarily be wrong—the Rabbis nevertheless teach that they are all God's Word, as can be seen in the Talmudic tractate *Eruvin*, folio 13, column 2, where it is written: <note>original Hebrew: אמר רבי אבא אמר שמואל שלש שנים נחלקו בית שמאי ובית הלל הללו אומרים הלכה כמותינו והללו אומרים הלכה כמותינו יצתה בת קול ואמרה אלו ואלו דברי אלהים חיים הן והלכה כבית הלל:</note> that is, **Rabbi Abba says that Samuel said: for three years those from the House of Shammai and those from the House of Hillel were in dispute with one another. The text intends to say: these teachings are given by one Shepherd; one God has given them; one Sustainer or Ruler has spoken them. They come from the mouth of the Lord of all works, the blessed God, as is said (Exodus 20, verse 1): "And God spoke all these words." Therefore, let your ears be just like a funnel, and provide yourself with a heart that may hear the words of those who hold a thing to be unclean, and of those who recognize it as clean; the words of those who forbid, and the words of those who permit; the words of those who speak of something as wrong, and the words of those who hold it to be right.** So it is also written in the book *Ammude ha-Shivah* <note>The Pillars of the Seven</note>, folio 42, column 1, under the title *Ammud ha-Revii* <note>The Fourth Pillar</note>, thus

# The Seventh Chapter of the First Part of *Judaism Unmasked* #

<meta>catchword: and</meta>

written: <note>original Hebrew: אף על פי שזה אוסר וזה מתיר אלו ואלו דברי אלהים חיים ויכולים שניהם להתקיים לעתיד:</note> **"Even though one forbids and the other permits, both are the words of the living God, and both can be upheld in the future."** That is: although one person forbids something and another allows the very same thing, both are nonetheless God’s Word and both can be confirmed in due time.

<margin>Moses is said to have learned all Talmudic disputes on Mount Sinai.</margin>
Indeed, they even claim that Moses received all the disputes found in the <term>Talmud</term><note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishnah (laws) and the Gemara (commentary).</note> from God on Mount Sinai, as reported in the *Jalkut Chadash* <note>A 17th-century collection of midrashic and kabbalistic teachings.</note> under the title *Luchoth* (or *Luchos*), number 74, folio 114, column 1, from the book *Megalleh Amukkoth* (or *Amykkos*), folio 20, column 1, in the seventy-fourth <term>Ofan</term><note>Literally "wheel" or "way," referring to a section or method of mystical interpretation.</note>, where the words are as follows: <note>original Hebrew: משה קבל תורה מסיני: אפילו מחלוקת שמאי והילל נרמז במלת מ"שה נוטריקון מחלוקת שמאי והלל הכל שמעו מסיני:</note> that is, **Moses received the Law from (Mount) Sinai; even the dispute between Shammai and Hillel is hinted at in the word "Moshe"** <note>The Hebrew name for Moses, spelled M-Sh-H (משה).</note> (meaning Moses, namely by the letters M, Sh, and H). For through <term>Notarikon</term><note>A method of shorthand or acrostic interpretation where the letters of a word represent the first letters of other words.</note> (read both backwards and forwards) it forms: **"The Dispute of Shammai and Hillel, all was heard from Sinai."** This means that the famous disagreement between Shammai and Hillel <note>Two influential 1st-century BCE scholars whose schools often disagreed on legal points.</note> was already known and heard on Mount Sinai.

<margin>The Law is said to have existed before the creation of the world, and Adam along with some of his descendants were said to have known it.</margin>
Furthermore, they teach that the Law existed before the Creation, and that Adam and some of his descendants knew it before it was given on Mount Sinai. That it existed before the creation of the world is taught by Rabbi Eliezer in his chapters, in the 3rd chapter, with these words: <note>original Hebrew: שבעה דברים נבראו עד שלא נברא העולם ואלו הן תורה: וגיהנם וגן עדן וכסא הכבוד ובית המקדש ותשובה ושמו של משיח תורה מנין שנאמר יי' קנני ראשית דרכו קדם מפעליו מאז קדם ד"ל קודם שלא נברא העולם. גיהנם מנין שנ' כי ערוך מאתמול תפתה מאתמול עד שלא נברא העולם. גן עדן מנין שנ' ויטע יי' אלהים גן בעדן מקדם עד שלא נברא העולם. כסא הכבוד מנין שנ' נכון כסאך מאז מאז עד שלא נברא העולם. בית המקדש מנין שנ' כסא כבוד מרום מראשון מראשון עד שלא נברא העולם. תשובה מנין שנ' בטרם הרים ילדו תשב אנוש טרם עד שלא נברא העולם. שמו של משיח מנין שנ' לפני שמש ינון שמו וכתוב אחד אומר ואתה בית לחם אפרתה צעיר להיות באלפי יהודה ומוצאותיו מקדם מימי עולם:</note> that is: **Seven things were created before the world was created; and these are: the Law (Torah), Hell (Gehenna), Paradise (the Garden of Eden), the Throne of Glory, the Temple, Repentance, and the name of the Messiah.** How is the Law proven? Because it is said (Proverbs 8:22): "The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his way, before his works of old"—where the word "before" refers to the time before the world was created. How is Hell proven? Because it is said (Isaiah 30:33): "For <term>Tophet</term><note>A site in Jerusalem associated with child sacrifice, used here as a synonym for the fires of Hell.</note> is ordained of old"—and "of old" means before the world was created. How is Paradise proven? Because it is said: "And the Lord God planted a garden in Eden from the beginning"—meaning before the world was created. How is the Throne of Glory proven? Because it is said: "Thy throne is established from of old"—meaning before the world was created. How is the Temple proven? Because it is said: "A glorious high throne from the beginning"—meaning before the world was created. How is Repentance proven? Because it is said: "Before the mountains were brought forth... thou turnest man to destruction"—meaning before the world was created. How is the name of the Messiah proven? Because it is said: "His name shall endure as long as the sun"—and another scripture says: "But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah... whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting."

Because it is said (Gen. 2:8): "And the Lord God planted a garden in Eden, *mikkédem*," that is, from eternity <note>original Hebrew: *mi-qedem*, which can mean "from the east" or "from of old." Here the author notes the Rabbinic interpretation of "from before the beginning of time"</note> (as Rabbi Eliezer wishes it to be understood here; and the word *mikkédem* is also used in Hab. 1:12, though here it is usually translated as: "toward the morning" <note>the east</note>; but the word signifies) *mikkédem*, before the world was created. How is the **Throne of Glory** proven? Because it is said (Ps. 93:2): "From of old Your throne is established"; and this "from of old" signifies: before the world was created. How is the **Temple** proven? Because it is said (Jer. 17:12): "A glorious throne, exalted from the beginning"; and the words "from the beginning" signify as much as: before the world was created. How is **Repentance** proven? Because it is said (Ps. 90:2, 3): "Before the mountains were brought forth (that is, created)" etc. *taschéf enosch* <note>original Hebrew: *tashev enosh*, "You turn man back [to dust/contrition]"</note>, that is (as it is incorrectly understood here), You make it so that man should do penance; and the word "Before" signifies: before the world was created. How is the **Name of the Messiah** proven? Because it is said (Ps. 72:17): "His name shall endure before the sun." And another passage (Mic. 5:2) reports: "And you, Bethlehem Ephrata, are you too little to be among the thousands of Judah? yet out of you shall come forth... whose goings forth have been from the beginning, from eternity," before the world was created. This same matter is also read in the <term>Talmudic</term><note>The Talmud is the central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishnah and the Gemara.</note> tractate *Pesachim* folio 54, column 1, and in the tractate *Nedarim* folio 39, column 2, though with some variation.

<margin>How long the Law existed before the world.</margin>
But how long it existed before the creation of the world is taught by the **Talmud** in the tractate *Shabbath* (or *Shabbas*), folio 88, column 2, where it is reported that the angels addressed the Lord God when He wished to give the Law to Moses in heaven: <note>original Hebrew: מה לילוד אשה בינינו אמר להן לקבל תורה בא. אמרו לפניו חמודה גנוזה שגנוזה לך מששת ימי בראשית תשע מאות ושבעים וארבעה דורות קודם שנברא העולם אתה מבקש ליתנה לבשר ודם מה אנוש כי תזכרנו</note> That is: **"What has one born of a woman to do among us?"** When God had answered them, "He has come to receive the Law," they said to Him: **"Will You give that pleasant and hidden [Law], which was kept hidden with You for nine hundred and seventy-four generations before the six days of Creation, before the world was created, to flesh and blood? What is man, that You are mindful of him?"**

It also cites the Talmudic tradition that the Torah existed for 974 generations before the universe was made.</summary>

### Chapter VIII of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked ###

<margin>Whether Adam knew the entire Law.</margin>
That Adam knew the entire Law is written in the book *Lech Aryeh* <note>original: "Les ärje"; likely *Lech Aryeh* or "Heart of the Lion," a rabbinic commentary</note> on folio 96, column 4, as follows: <note>original Hebrew: מחמת האור הגדול שנברא עם אדם הראשון יש לו שכל בהיר והיה מבין כל התורה כולה ולא היה צריך לתורה שבעל פה</note> **That is: Because of the great light which was created with the first man, he possessed a clear understanding and understood the entire Law, and had no need for the Oral Law.** And in the book *Mikra'e Kodesh* <note>Sacred Readings</note>, it is taught by Rabbi Samiga <note>likely Joseph ibn Samiga, a 16th-century Ottoman rabbi</note> in the fourteenth chapter of the first part, folio 42, column 1: <note>original Hebrew: והסתכל היטב וראה שמכל המאמרים שהזכרתי יש לך ראיה גמורה שאדם הראשון קודם חטאו היה מקיים כל התורה כולה ואין צריך להאריך בביאורם . ואין ספק שהמצוה שנצטווה בה אדם הראשון שבה היו נכללים כל המצוות ודאי שהיא אנכי ולא יהיה לך</note> **That is: Consider well, and see that from all the discourses I have mentioned, you have a perfect proof that the first man, before his committed sin, observed and kept the entire Law; and it is not necessary to linger long in explaining them. Likewise, there is no doubt that in that which was commanded to the first man—which is: "I am the Lord your God, etc. You shall have no other gods before me"—all the commandments were certainly included.**

The first man, Adam, knew the Law and left it to his son Seth through a tradition <note>original: *Tradirion*, likely a typo for *Tradition*</note> or oral teaching; thereafter it came to Enoch, until Shem received it and studied therein. 

Rabbi Jose said to him: "If the Law was in Shem's school, why did God find it necessary to command those seven commandments which were given to the children of Noah <note>term: Noahide Laws (Sheva Mitzvot Bnei Noach), seven moral imperatives believed by Jews to be binding on all humanity</note>, since the Law was already written before then?" ...[Jacob] was well-versed in the Bible and the *Mishnah* (that is, in the Talmud), in the *Halakhah* <term>Halakhah: the collective body of Jewish religious laws</term> (or *Halóchos*), that is, legal decisions, as well as the *Aggadah* <term>Aggadah: non-legalistic exegetical texts, often involving stories and folklore</term> (or *Aggódos*), that is, entertaining narratives. Thus it is also written in the *Yalkut Chadash* <note>original: "New Collection," a 17th-century anthology of Midrashic and Kabbalistic teachings</note>, folio 90, column 3, number 140, under the title *Yitzchak* [Isaac], regarding Jacob: <note>original Hebrew: רבי שמואל בר נחמן אמר כל ספר תהילים היה אומר שנ' ואתה קדוש יושב תהילות ישראל</note> that is, **Rabbi Samuel bar Nachman said he recited the entire Book of Psalms, as reported in (Psalm 22, verse 4): "But thou art holy, O thou that dwellest in the praises of Israel."**

<margin>
Refutation of such Jewish folly from their own sources.
</margin>
But how does all this agree with what the aforementioned Rabbi Bechai <note>Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century Spanish commentator</note> teaches in his cited commentary on the *Parashah Vayishmash Yitro* <note>the weekly Torah portion "Jethro," which contains the Ten Commandments</note>, folio 92, column 1? There, he was of a completely different opinion when he said: <note>original Hebrew: כשנברא אדם הראשון נצטווה על ו' מצוות כדי שיתקיים העולם בשש קצוות. בא נח ונצטווה על השביעית זו אבר מן החי אברהם על השמינית זו המילה יעקב על התשיעית זוהי גיד הנשה כשבאו ישראל נתן להם י' הדברות שהן כוללות תרי"ג מצוות ועל זה אמר הכתוב בקרבנו מלאה קט"רת מלאה קט"רת מלאה תרי"ג כי הקו"ף מתחלפת בדל"ת י"ב נשיאים כף אחת עשרה זהב</note> that is, **After the first man [Adam] was created, six commandments were commanded to him, so that the world might exist in its six directions. When Noah came, the seventh commandment was commanded to him—namely, that he should not eat a limb from a living animal. Abraham received the eighth, namely circumcision; but Jacob received the ninth, namely the displaced sinew (Genesis 32, verse 32, that it should not be eaten). But after the Israelites came, the Ten Commandments were given to them, which encompass the six hundred and thirteen commandments.** For this reason, the Scripture says (Numbers, chapter 7) regarding the offerings of the twelve princes: **"A bowl of ten shekels' weight of gold, full of קטרת Ketóreth"** (that is, incense), where the word *Ketóreth* through *Gematria* <term>Gematria: a system of assigning numerical values to Hebrew letters</term> makes six hundred and thirteen; for the letter *Koph* is exchanged for *Daleth* through the *Atbash* alphabet <term>Atbash: a substitution cipher where the first letter of the alphabet is replaced by the last, the second by the second-to-last, etc.</term>. The same is also found in the book *Kad ha-Kemach* <note>original: "The Jar of Flour," a work on ethics by Bahya ben Asher</note>, folio 21, column 3. If, therefore, Jacob only had nine commandments, how could he have kept the six hundred and thirteen, which were supposedly only given on Mount Sinai? Furthermore, it is written in the Talmudic tractate *Avodah Zarah* <note>concerning "Foreign Worship" or idolatry</note>, folio 9, column 1: <note>original Hebrew: תנא דבי אליהו ששת אלפים שנה הוי העולם שני אלפים תוהו שני אלפים תורה שני אלפים ימות המשיח</note> that is, **Those of the House of Elijah teach: The world will stand for six thousand years; two thousand will be the days of desolation; two thousand the days of the Law; and two thousand the days of the Messiah.** And Rabbi Solomon Jarchi <note>known as Rashi, the preeminent medieval commentator</note> writes in his commentary on this: **"Six thousand years are decreed for the world to exist, corresponding to the number of the days of the week."**

Because he was in the Academy from his youth until his old age, expert in the Scripture, in the Mishnah, in legal decisions, and in narratives, as it is said: "And Jacob was an upright man, dwelling in tents."**

### Chapter VIII of Part I of *Judaism Unmasked* ###

<note>original Hebrew: שביעי שבתו ובשבעה אלפים נוח לעולם שני אלפים תוהו אלו שני אלפים תוהו בלא תורה : ושני אלפים תורה בלא ימות המשיח : ושני אלפים ימות המשיח :</note> **That is: Six thousand years are determined for the world, that it shall stand according to the number of the days of the week; but in the seventh day is the Sabbath, and the world shall rest in the seven-thousandth year. Over the first two thousand years, it is determined that they should be empty or desolate, and without the Law; and two thousand should be the time of the Law, without the days of the Messiah; but the last two thousand years should be the days of the Messiah.** Such is also read in the Talmudic <term>Tractate: a specific volume or treatise within the Talmud</term> **Sanhedrin**, folio 97, column 1. If, then, the first two thousand years of the world were supposed to be without the Law, how could it have been known and observed by Adam and others?

<margin>Children also learn the Law in their mother’s womb, but forget it again when they are born.</margin>
Since the Law is being discussed here, I must also point out how the irrational Rabbis claim that children also learn the same in their mother's womb, but as soon as they are born, they are said to forget it again. Regarding this, it is written in the **Yalkut Shimoni** <note>original: "Jalkut Schimóni," a medieval collection of midrash (scriptural commentary) on the Hebrew Bible</note> concerning the first book of Moses <note>the Book of Genesis</note>, folio 10, column 4, number 38: <note>original Hebrew: עד שהולד במעי אמו מלמדין אותו כל התורה כולה : שנאמר ויורני ויאמר לי יתמוך דברי לבך וגו' וכיון שיצא לאויר העולם בא מלאך וסטרו על פיו ומשכח כל התורה שנאמר לפתח חטאת רובץ :</note> **That is: As long as the child is in its mother’s womb, one teaches it the entire Law, as it is said (Proverbs 4:4): "And he taught me, and said to me; let your heart receive my words." But when it comes out into the air of the world, an angel comes and strikes it upon its mouth, and causes it to forget the entire Law again, as it is said (Genesis 4:7): "Sin lies at the door."** This fable is taken from that great book of lies, the <term>Talmud: the central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishnah and the Gemara</term>, in which it is reported in the Tractate **Nidda**, folio 30, column 2, in what manner the child lies in the mother’s womb, and follows with: <note>original Hebrew: ונר דלוק לו על ראשו וצופה ומביט מסוף העולם ועד סופו שנ' בהלו נרו עלי ראשי לאורו אלך חושך ואל תתמה שהרי אדם ישן כאן ורואה חלום באספמיא ואין לך ימים שאדם שרוי בטובה יותר מאותן הימים שנ' מי יתנני כירחי קדם כימי אלוה ישמרנו ואיזה ימים שיש בהם ירחים ואין בהם שנים הוי אומר אלו ירחי לידה ומלמדין אותו כל התורה שנ' ויורני ויאמר לי יתמוך דברי לבך שמור מצותי וחיה ואומר בסוד אלוה עלי אהלי ואומר וכי תימא נביא הוא דקאמר תא שמע בסוד אלוה עלי אהלי וכיון שבא לאויר העולם בא מלאך וסטרו על פיו ומשכחו כל התורה כולה שנ' לפתח חטאת רובץ ואינו יוצא משם עד שמשביעין אותו שנ' כי לך תכרע כל ברך תשבע כל לשון כי לך תכרע כל ברך זה יום המיתה שנ' לפניו יכרעו כל יורדי עפר תשבע כל לשון זה יום הלידה שנ' נקי כפים ובר לבב אשר לא נשא לשוא נפשו ולא נשבע למרמה. ומה היא השבועה שמשביעין אותו הוי צדיק ואל תהי רשע ואפילו כל העולם כולו אומרים לך צדיק אתה היה בעיניך כרשע והוי יודע שהקב"ה טהור ומשרתיו טהורים ונשמה שנתן בך טהורה היא אם אתה משמרה בטהרה מוטב ואם לאו הריני</note> **And a lamp is lit for it over its head, and it gazes and looks from one end of the world to the other, as it is said (Job 29:3): "When his candle shined upon my head, and by his light I walked through darkness." And do not be surprised at this, for a person may sleep here and see a dream in Spain. And there are no days in which a person dwells in greater goodness than those days [in the womb], as it is said (Job 29:2): "Oh that I were as in months past, as in the days when God preserved me." And which are the days that have months but do not have years? One must say these are the months of birth. And they teach it the entire Law, as it is said (Proverbs 4:4): "And he taught me, and said to me: Let your heart receive my words; keep my commandments and live." And it says (Job 29:4): "When the secret of God was upon my tabernacle." And if you should say it was a prophet who said this, come and hear: "When the secret of God was upon my tabernacle." And once it comes into the air of the world, an angel comes and strikes it upon its mouth, and causes it to forget the entire Law, as it is said (Genesis 4:7): "Sin lies at the door." And it does not leave from there until it is made to swear an oath, as it is said (Isaiah 45:23): "Unto me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear." "Every knee shall bow"—this refers to the day of death, as it is said (Psalm 22:29): "All they that go down to the dust shall bow before him." "Every tongue shall swear"—this refers to the day of birth, as it is said (Psalm 24:4): "He that has clean hands and a pure heart, who has not lifted up his soul unto vanity, nor sworn deceitfully." And what is the oath that they make it swear? "Be righteous and be not wicked; and even if the whole world tells you that you are righteous, be in your own eyes as if you were wicked. And know that the Holy One, blessed be He, is pure, and His ministers are pure, and the soul He has placed within you is pure. If you keep it in purity, it is well; but if not, I am..."**

### About the Talmud. ###

<margin><note>original Hebrew: הריני נטלה ממך</note> "Behold, I am taking it from you."</margin> That is: "And upon his head a light burns for him," <margin>They have a light burning over their head.</margin> and he looks and sees from one end of the world to the other, as it is said in Job 29:3: **"When his lamp shone over my head, and I walked through darkness by his light."** You must not wonder at this, for a person here might be sleeping and yet see a dream as far away as Spain <note>This analogy explains how a soul in the small space of the womb can "see" the whole world.</note>. There are also no days in which a person fares better than in those very days (when he is in his mother’s womb), as it is said in Job 29:2: **"O that I were as in months past! in the days when God watched over me."** What kind of days are these that consist of months but not years? Say: these are the months of gestation <note>The text refers to the "months of birth," meaning the time spent in the womb before delivery.</note>.

The child is also taught the entire Law <term>Torah: the body of divine instruction and Law given to Israel</term>, as it is said in Proverbs 4:4: **"And he taught me, and said to me, let your heart receive my words, keep my commandments, and live."** And he (Job) says in his 29th chapter, verse 4: **"When God’s secret was over my tent."** What is this that Job says? Would you then say that he was a prophet, because he said such things? Come here and hear (I answer this by noting it is indeed written that he said): **"When God’s secret was over my tent."** 

However, after the child comes into the air of the world (and is born), an angel comes and strikes it upon its mouth, and causes it to forget the entire Law, as it is said in Genesis 4:7: **"Sin rests at the door."** But the child does not come out until it is put under oath, as it is said in Isaiah 45:23 <note>The original text mistakenly cites verse 32</note>: **"For unto you** (though it should say "unto me") **every knee shall bow, and every tongue shall swear."** <margin>Children do not want to leave their mother's womb until they are put under oath.</margin> The words **"For unto you every knee shall bow"** signify the day of death, as it is said in Psalm 22:30: **"Before me** (it should say "before him") **all who lie in the dust shall bow their knees."** And the words **"And every tongue shall swear"** signify the day of birth, as it is said in Psalm 24:4: **"He who has innocent hands and is of a pure heart; who does not give his heart to vanity, and does not swear with deceit."** 

What kind of oath is it, then, with which the child is bound? One says to it: "Be righteous (or pious) and not godless; and even if the whole world says to you, 'you are righteous,' consider yourself as if you were godless. And know that the Holy and Blessed God is pure, and His servants are pure, and the soul that He has placed in you is pure. If you keep it in purity, it is well; but if not, behold, I will take it away from you."

### Chapter VIII of the First Part of *Judaism Uncovered*. ###

<margin>Further proof that children learn the Law in their mother's womb but forget it again.</margin> In Rabbi Aaron Samuel's book, *The Soul of Man* <note>original Hebrew: *Nishmath Adam*; Aaron Samuel Kaidanover was a 17th-century Talmudist</note>, the following is also read in the 6th chapter of the first column on page 26: 

<note>The following is a translation of the Hebrew passage provided in the text</note> "We can further say, according to the path of our Rabbis of blessed memory, that in his mother’s womb a man learns the entire Torah. But when he emerges into the atmosphere of the world, an angel comes and strikes him upon his mouth, causing him to forget the entire Torah. Afterward, when he grows up, he is like someone who has lost an object and goes about seeking his lost item. If he exerts himself to search for the loss by the light of the intellectual lamp, he then finds the wisdom and knowledge that he had lost. Therefore, Scripture says (Proverbs 3:13), 'Happy is the man who finds wisdom,' using the language of 'finding.' This is similar to what is written (Proverbs 2:4-5): 'If you seek her as silver, and search for her as for hidden treasures; then you shall understand the fear of the Lord, and find the knowledge of God.' It is well known that the contemplation of the Torah is the 'knowledge of God.' And this is what we say regarding the verse (Proverbs 4:22), 'For they are life to those who find them, and health to all their flesh.' The meaning is that the finding of the Torah—which was lost to him when he emerged into the atmosphere of the world—is life in the World to Come, even eternal life. It is also 'health to all his flesh' because he is healed from the blow with which the angel struck him on his mouth, causing him to forget the Torah. Through this [study], he is healed from his wound, for he returns to the state he was in before."

That is: We can also speak further, according to that which our Rabbis, of blessed memory, have said: that a man in his mother’s womb learns the entire Law <term>Torah: the divine instruction and Law</term>; but when he comes out into the air of the world, an angel comes and strikes him on his mouth, and causes him to forget the entire Law. But thereafter, when he grows up and goes about like one who has lost something, seeking that which he has lost, and exerts himself to look for the lost item by the light of the lantern of the intellect, he then finds the wisdom and knowledge which he had lost. For this reason, the Scripture says (Proverbs 3:13): **"Happy is the man who finds wisdom,"** etc., and it uses the word *find*, just as it is written (Proverbs 2:4–5): **"If you seek her (namely, wisdom) as silver, and search for her as for treasures, then you will understand the fear of the Lord, and find the knowledge of God."** Now, it is known that the contemplation of the Law is the knowledge of God; and this is what we say regarding the words (Proverbs 4:22): **"For they (namely, the words of God) are life to him who finds them, and a medicine to all his flesh."** The purpose (and understanding) of this is that the finding of the Law—which he lost when he came into the air of the world—is life, and in the future world eternal life; it is also a medicine to all his flesh, in that he is healed from his blow (with which the angel struck him on his mouth, whereby he forgot the Law) and becomes again as he once was. Regarding this, one may also consult the book *The Service of Holiness* <note>original: *Avodath HaKodesh*</note>, page 42, column 1, in the 23rd chapter under the title *The Part of Service* <note>original: *Chelek HaAvoda*</note>, as well as the book *The Son of Knowledge* <note>original: *Ben Daath*</note>, page 10, column 1, regarding the eighth Psalm.

# Concerning the Talmud. #

...what their Rabbis have taught, and still teach, is necessary to believe and to follow. That the written Law cannot be understood without the oral Law is written in the book *The Flour Jar* <note>original: *Cad hakkémach*; a 14th-century work by Bahya ben Asher</note> on folio 77, column 3, as follows: <margin>The written Law shall not be capable of being understood without the oral Law.</margin> <note>original Hebrew: "ששה סדרים אלו הם תורה שבעל פה..."</note> "These six Orders <term>Sedarim; the six major divisions of the Talmud</term> are the Oral Law, for the foundation or main work of the Law is the Oral Law, because the written Law cannot be explained except through the Oral Law." And in the book *The Golden Altar* <note>original: *Misbéach hassahaf*; by Rabbi Solomon ben Mordecai</note>, the following is read in the fifth chapter: <note>original Hebrew: "אי אפשר לעמוד על עיקר תורתנו הקדושה..."</note> "It is impossible for us to stand upon the foundation of our holy Law, which is the written Law, in any way other than through the Oral Law, which is its interpretation." However, I shall prove that the Talmud is held in higher regard by the Jews than the Bible, because in the Talmudic tractate *The Middle Gate* <note>original: *Báva mezía*</note>, folio 33, column 1, it is written: <note>original Hebrew: "תנו רבנן העוסקין במקרא מדה ואינה מדה..."</note> "Our Rabbis teach: those who study the Bible perform a deed that is a virtue, and yet not a virtue; those who study the *Mishnah* <term>the first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions</term> perform a deed that is a virtue, and receive a reward for it; but those who study the *Gemara* <term>the section of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis and commentary on the Mishnah</term> perform a deed that is the greatest virtue of all." This is also found in the fifteenth chapter of the *Tractate of Scribes* <note>original: *Mafsécheth Sópherim*</note>, folio 13, column 2, and in the *Tractate on the Lesser Way of the World* <note>original: *Mafsécheth dérech érez súta*</note> folio 20, column 4, as well as in the aforementioned book *The Flour Jar*, folio 77, column 3. And in the said *Tractate of Scribes*, in the mentioned fifteenth chapter on folio 13, column 2, it is further read: <note>original Hebrew: "נמשל המקרא למים והמשנה כיין והששה סדרים כקונדיטון..."</note> "The Bible is like water, the Mishnah is like wine, and the six Orders (that is, the Gemara) are like spiced wine <note>original Latin/Greek term: *conditum*; a wine mixed with honey and spices</note>. The world cannot exist without water, and the world cannot exist without wine, and the world cannot exist without spiced wine; and a wealthy man is sustained by all three. Thus, the world cannot exist without the Bible, without the Mishnah, and without the six Orders."

### The Eighth Chapter of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked. ###

...has said: whoever murmurs against his Rabbi does as much as if he murmured against God; as it is said in Exodus 16:8: **Your murmuring is not against us, but against the LORD.** This is also found in the *Yalkut Shimoni* <note>A popular medieval midrashic miscellany or anthology on the Hebrew Bible.</note> on the five books of Moses, number 258, folio 74, column 2, and in the book *Menorat HaMaor* <term>Menorat HaMaor: "The Candlestick of Light," a popular 14th-century ethical work by Isaac Aboab.</term>, folio 20, column 1, under the title *Ner Sheni, Perek Sheni, Kelal Shevii, Chelek Sheni*. In this latter book, the *Menorat HaMaor*, these words precede the quote: <note>original Hebrew: "אף על פי שהחולק עם כל אדם גורם כל הרעות שבעולם החולק עם רבו הוא עון פלילי וחרבן עולם ונחשב לו כאלו חולק עם השכינה"</note> **that is: Although he who quarrels with any man causes all the evil in the world, yet he who quarrels with his Rabbi commits a crime to be brought before the judges, and destroys the world, and it is reckoned to him as if he quarreled with God.**

<margin>Punishment of those who transgress the words of their Rabbis.</margin>

What punishment those deserve who transgress the sayings of the Rabbis, the Talmud teaches in the tractate *Eruvin*, folio 21, column 2, with these words: <note>original Hebrew: "העובר על דברי סופרים חייב מיתה"</note> **that is: He who transgresses the words of the scribes is worthy of death.** By these "words of the scribes," Rabbi Solomon Jarchi <note>Known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent commentator on the Bible and Talmud.</note> understands in his commentary everything that the Rabbis newly introduce and command, and he calls them there: <note>original Hebrew: "דברי סופרים החדשים שנתחדשו בכל דור ודור לגדור גדר וסייג"</note> **that is: The new words of the scribes, which have been newly introduced in every generation to make a hedge and a fence around the Law.** <note>This refers to the concept of 'Seyag la-Torah,' making a fence around the Torah to prevent accidental violations.</note> So it is also read in Rabbi Bechai’s <note>Bahya ben Asher (c. 1255–1340), a Spanish rabbi and kabbalist.</note> commentary on the five books of Moses, in the section *Tazria*, folio 105, column 2: <note>original Hebrew: "עובר על דברי חכמים חייב מיתה שנאמר כה אמר יי' אלהי ישראל ארור האיש אשר לא ישמע את דברי הברית הזאת"</note> **that is: Whoever transgresses the words of the wise is worthy of death, as (Jeremiah 11:3) it is said: Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Cursed be the man who does not obey the words of this covenant.** This is also to be found in the tractate *Avoda Zara*, folio 27, column 2, in the *Tosafot* <note>Medieval supplements or glosses on the Talmud.</note>. And in the book *Shulchan Aruch* <term>Shulchan Aruch: The "Set Table," the most authoritative code of Jewish Law, authored by Joseph Karo in the 16th century.</term>, it is taught in the section *Yoreh De'ah*, number 334, § 43, folio 306, column 1: <note>original Hebrew: "על כ"ד דברים מנדין את האדם ואלו הם א' המבזה את החכם אפילו לאחר מותו. ב' המבזה שליח בית דין. ג' הקורא לחבירו עבד. ד' המזלזל בדבר אחד מדברי סופרים ואין צריך לומר מדברי תורה וגו'"</note> **that is: For twenty-four things (or causes) a man is placed under the ban <note>The 'Herem' or 'Niddui,' forms of ecclesiastical excommunication or social shunning.</note>, and these are the following. First, he who despises a wise man, even if it happens after his death. Second, he who despises a messenger of the court. Third, he who calls his fellow a slave. Fourth, he who treats with contempt any one word of the words of the scribes...**

### Concerning the Talmud. ###
Tt 3

...the scribes have said (and it is not necessary to mention the words of the Law) despiseth, etc. From this, it is to be seen how highly the teachings and statements of the Rabbis are to be esteemed, and how carefully they are to be observed.

<margin>The Rabbis are greatly honored and feared by the Jews.</margin> Since the teaching of the Rabbis is held in such high regard, it is easy to understand that they must also be greatly honored and feared. In the book *Menorat HaMaor* <term>Menorat HaMaor: "The Candlestick of Light," a famous 14th-century work of Jewish ethics and law by Isaac Aboab.</term>, folio 68, column 1, in the first chapter under the title *Ner revii, kelál revii, chelek schéni*, it is taught: <note>original Hebrew: "אף על פי שחייב אדם לכבד לתלמידי חכמים ולירא מהם גדול הוא חייבו בשיכבד את רבותיו ויירא מהם והשוו רבותינו מורא רבו של אדם כמורא שמים כמו ששנינו בפרק שני מאבות ר' אליעזר אומר יהי כבוד תלמידך חביב עליך כשלך וכבוד חברך כמורא רבך ומורא רבך כמורא שמים :"</note> **That is: Although** <margin>Such is commanded to be done.</margin> a man is bound to honor the disciples of the wise (that is, the wise and the learned; in ancient times, not only those who were students of the wise were called "disciples of the wise," but even those who had attained the title of "the Wise" and were the most learned were called "disciples of the wise" out of humility) <note>The term "Talmid Chakham" (disciple of a wise man) remains the standard Jewish term for a Torah scholar, suggesting that no matter how much one knows, one remains a student of the Infinite.</note> and to fear them, he is yet especially bound to honor his own Rabbis or teachers, and to stand in fear of them. Indeed, our Rabbis have equated the fear of a man's Rabbi with the fear of God: as we learn in the second chapter of the tractate *Avot* <note>Also known as "Ethics of the Fathers," a compilation of ethical teachings from the Mishnaic period.</note> that Rabbi Eliezer said: "Let the honor of your student be as dear to you as your own honor, and the honor of your companion like the fear of your Rabbi, and the fear of your Rabbi like the fear of God."

And in the book *Neveh Shalom* <term>Neveh Shalom: "Abode of Peace," a philosophical and homiletic work by Abraham Shalom, printed in 1538.</term>, in the second chapter of the fifth *Maamar* <note>A "Maamar" is a formal discourse or treatise within a larger work.</note>, folio 63, column 1, we read: <note>original Hebrew: "ידוע שהאב הוא המוליד והמצייר החלק הנכבד והמשובח שבאדם הוא ראוי ליקרא אב אמיתי מאותו שלא יוליד רק החלק החסר ולכן ראו שיכובדו החכמים המולידים אמתת העצמות שהוא הצורה השכלית כי הם האבות באמת כמו שאמרו רבותינו ז"ל מורא רבו כמורא שמים ואמרו על רבי מאיר שהיה דורש כל אתין שבתורה וכשהגיע לפסוק את יי' אלהיך תירא נרתע לאחוריו עד שדרש ואמר את יי' תירא לרבות תלמידי חכמים :"</note> **that is: It is well known that the father who begets and forms the most excellent and praiseworthy part of a man [the soul and intellect] is more worthy of being called a "true father" than the one who only begets the deficient part [the physical body]. Therefore, it is right that the wise should be honored, for they beget the true essence, namely the intellectual form or shape; for they are the fathers in truth, just as our Rabbis of blessed memory say: "The fear of your teacher is equal to the fear of God." It is also said of Rabbi Meir that he interpreted every *et* (את)** <note>original: "את". In Hebrew grammar, *et* is a particle that indicates the definite direct object. It has no direct translation but Rabbinic tradition often uses its appearance to suggest an "inclusion" of something additional to the text.</note> **which appears in the Law, and when he came to the verse: "You shall fear the LORD (*et*) your God," he drew back in hesitation until he interpreted it and said: "The word *et* before the name of the LORD is there to include the disciples of the wise."**

...and when he came to the verse (Deuteronomy 6:13 *Eth Jehova Elohécha tira* <note>original: "את יהוה אלהיך תירא"</note>, that is, **You shall fear the Lord your God**), he drew back until he had provided the interpretation for it and said: "You shall fear the Lord—and the disciples of the wise <note>The term *Talmidei Chakhamim* (disciples of the wise) refers to Torah scholars. Rabbinic tradition often interprets the Hebrew word "Et" as an inclusion, suggesting that the fear of God includes the fear of those who teach His Law.</note> are also included (in this commandment)."

Concerning this, Rabbi Moshe bar Maimon <note>Commonly known as Maimonides (1138–1204), one of the most influential Torah scholars and philosophers of the Middle Ages.</note> also writes in his book *Yad Chazakah* <term>Yad Chazakah: "The Mighty Hand," a major code of Jewish law also known as the Mishneh Torah.</term>, in the first part, in the treatise *Talmud Torah* (that is, *On the Study of the Law*), in the fifth chapter, number 1, as follows:

Just as a man is commanded to honor and fear his father, so he is bound to honor and fear his teacher even more than his father; for his father brought him into the life of this world, while his teacher, who taught him wisdom, brings him into the life of the world to come. If he sees a lost object belonging to his father and a lost object belonging to his teacher, the teacher's object takes precedence over the father's. If his father and his teacher are both carrying a burden, he first assists his teacher and then his father. If his father and his teacher are held in captivity, he ransoms his teacher first and then his father. But if his father was a disciple of a wise man, he ransoms his father first. Likewise, if his father was a disciple of a wise man, even if he is not equal to his teacher, he returns his father's lost object first and then his teacher's. There is no greater honor than the honor due to a teacher, and no greater fear than the fear due to a teacher. The Sages have said: "The fear of your teacher should be like the fear of Heaven."

<margin>How greatly they are to be honored.</margin>
That is: Just as a person is commanded to honor and fear his father, so he is also obligated to honor and fear his teacher more than his father; for his father has brought him into the life of this world, but his teacher, who has taught him wisdom, brings him to the future (that is, the eternal) life. When someone has seen something that his father has lost, as well as something his teacher has lost, then that which his teacher has lost takes precedence over that which his father has lost (so that he may return it to him). When his father and his teacher are loaded with a burden, he first helps his teacher and afterward his father. When his father and his teacher sit in captivity, he first sets his teacher free and afterward he also ransoms his father. However, if his father is a disciple of a wise man (that is, a sage or a scholar), then he ransoms his father first. Likewise, if his father is a disciple of a wise man (that is, a scholar), even if he is not equal to his teacher, he nevertheless gives him back his lost property first and afterward returns to his teacher what he had lost. There is no greater honor than that which is due to the teacher, nor any greater fear than that with which the teacher is to be feared. The Sages say: "The fear of your teacher shall be equal to the fear of God." The like is also seen in the book *Shulchan Aruch* <term>Shulchan Aruch: "The Set Table," the most widely consulted code of Jewish law, authored by Joseph Karo in the 16th century.</term>, in the part *Yoreh De'ah*, folio 214, column 1, number 242; and in the previously mentioned place in the first chapter of the book *Menorat HaMaor*, folio 68, column 1. # Chapter VIII of the First Part of Judaism Discovered. #
<meta>The catchword 'lung' from the previous page completes the word 'Versammlung' (assembly) or similar context regarding the honor due to scholars.</meta>

<note>original: "ולומד מחבירו פרק אחד או הלכה אחת או פסוק אחד או אפילו אות אחת צריך לנהוג בו כבוד שכן מצינו בדוד מלך ישראל שלא למד מאחיתופל אלא שני דברים בלבד עשאו רבו אלופו ומיודעו שנאמר ואתה אנוש כערכי אלופי ומיודעי. והלא דברים קל וחומר ומה דוד מלך ישראל שלא למד מאחיתופל אלא שני דברים בלבד עשאו רבו אלופו ומיודעו. הלומד מחבירו פרק אחד או הלכה אחת או פסוק אחד או אפילו אות אחת על אחת כמה וכמה שצריך לנהוג בו כבוד :"</note>

That is: **Whoever learns from his companion one chapter, or one Halakha (or legal ruling), or one verse, or even just a single letter, must honor him. For thus we find regarding David, the King of Israel, who learned only two things from Ahithophel, and yet recognized him as his master, his leader, and his acquaintance, as it is said** (*Psalm 55:14*): **But you are a man of my own rank** (that is, my equal, whom I esteem as myself), **my leader and my acquaintance. Can one not then make an argument here from the lesser to the greater: If David, the King of Israel, who learned only two things from Ahithophel, recognized him as his master, leader, and acquaintance, should not he who learns from his companion a chapter, or a Halakha or ruling, or a verse, or even a single letter, be much more bound to show him honor?**

<margin>One is duty-bound to honor the person from whom one learns anything.</margin>
<margin>King David learned only two things from Ahithophel, and honored him for that reason.</margin>

As for which two things those were, which King David is said to have learned from Ahithophel <note>Ahithophel was King David's counselor who later joined Absalom's rebellion. The Talmudic tradition here focuses on his role as a teacher of Torah before his betrayal.</note>, such is indicated in the commentary upon it with these words:

<note>original: "לפי שמצאו אחיתופל לדוד שהיה יושב ועוסק יחידי בתורה אמר לו למה אתה עוסק בתורה יחידי והלא כבר נאמר חרב על הבדים ונואלו. שוב פעם אחרת מצאו שהיה נכנס לבית מדרשו בקומה זקופה אמר לו והלא כבר נאמר שצריך לו לאדם ליכנס שם במורא כדי שתהי' אימת שמים עליו. ויש אומרים שהיה נכנס לבית המדרש יחידי ואמר לו בית אלהים נהלך ברגש כתיב שחייב אדם ליכנס שם בקיבוץ עם לפי שנ' ברוב עם הדרת מלך :"</note>

<margin>What those two things were.</margin>

That is: **Because Ahithophel found David sitting and studying the Law alone, he said to him: why do you study the Law alone? Has it not already been said** (*Jeremiah 50:36*): **"A sword shall come upon the liars (or diviners) that they may become fools"? On another occasion, he found him again, that he was entering his school** <term>Schule: Here referring to the Bet Midrash, the Jewish house of study and prayer.</term> **with an upright or straight posture, and said to him: Is it not already said that a man must enter there with fear, so that the fear of God may be upon him? But others report that he went into the school alone, and the former said to him: it is written** (*Psalm 55:15*): **"We walked into the house of God in a throng"; for a man is duty-bound to enter there with a congregation**

...to enter into the assembly of the people, as it is said in Proverbs 14:28: *In the multitude of people is the king's glory.*

<margin>No one may teach anything in the presence of his master.</margin>The Talmud also forbids anyone from teaching in the presence of his master, as is indicated in the Tractate Erúvin <note>A volume of the Talmud dealing with the laws of the Sabbath "boundaries" or travel limits.</note> folio 63, column 1, with these words: <note>original: "כל המורה הלכה בפני רבו חייב מיתה"</note> that is, *Whoever teaches a Talmudic ruling in his master's presence is deserving of death.* And soon after it follows: <note>original: "כל המורה הלכה בפני רבו ראוי להכישו נחש"</note> that is, *Whoever teaches a Talmudic ruling before his master is worthy of being bitten by a snake.* Furthermore, in the Tractate Sanhédrin <note>The Talmudic volume concerning the high court and criminal law.</note> folio 131, column 4, it forbids calling a teacher by his name, where one reads: <note>original: "כי שקורא לרבו בשמו הוי אפיקורוס ואין לו חלק לעולם הבא"</note> that is, *Whoever calls his master by his name is an Epicurean,* <note>The term "Epicurer" or "Epicurean" is used in Jewish texts to refer to a heretic or someone who shows contempt for the Law and the Sages.</note> *and has no portion in the eternal life.*

<margin>It is also forbidden to call him by his name.</margin>The Rabbis are even considered to be kings, regarding which the following is written in the Tractate Gittin <note>The volume of the Talmud concerning divorce and legal documents.</note> folio 62, column 1: <note>original: "רב הונא ורב חסדא הוו יתבי חליף ואזיל גניבא אמר ליה חד לחבריה ניקום מקמיה דבר אוריין הוא אמר לו ומקמי פלגאה ניקום אדהכי אתא איהו לגבייהו אמר להו שלמא עלייכו מלכי שלמא עלייכו מלכי אמרו ליה מנא לך דוננן איקרו מלכים אמר להו דכתיב בי מלכים ימלוכו"</note> that is, *Rav Hôna and Rav Chásda were once sitting together when Geniva came by and wished to pass. One said to the other: "Let us stand up for him, for he has studied the Law well." But the other said to him: "Should we stand up for a brawler?"* <note>The term "פלגאה" (palga'ah) refers to a contentious person or someone who causes division.</note> *Meanwhile, Geniva came to them and said: "Peace be unto you, my kings; peace be unto you, my kings." After they asked him, "From where do you prove that the Rabbis are called kings?" he gave them the answer: "Because it is written in Proverbs 8:15: 'By me kings reign.'" Oh, what a glorious proof that these vile Rabbis are kings!* <note>The author adds a sarcastic jab here, typical of 17th and 18th-century polemical writings against the Talmud.</note>

<margin>The Rabbis are considered to be kings.</margin>One is also said to receive a special benefit when sharing a meal with a Rabbi, as the Tractate Berachóth <note>The volume concerning blessings and prayers.</note> (or Beróchos) folio 64, column 1, indicates with these words: <note>original: "אמר רבי אבין הלוי כל הנהנה מסעודה שתלמיד חכם שרוי בתוכה כאילו נהנה מזיו השכינה שנאמר ויבא אהרן וכל זקני ישראל לאכול לחם עם חותן משה לפני האלהים וכי לפני אלהים אכלו והלא לפני משה אכלו אלא לומר לך כל הנהנה מסעודה שתלמיד חכם שרוי בתוכה כאילו נהנה מזיו שכינה"</note> that is, *Rabbi Abbin the Levite said: "Whoever enjoys a meal at which a wise man is present, it is as if he enjoyed the splendor of the Divine Majesty," as it is said in Exodus 18:12: "Then Aaron and all the elders of Israel came to eat bread with Moses' father-in-law before God." What! Did they eat before God?*
