# Chapter VIII of the First Part of *Judaism Unmasked*.

...did they then eat before God? Did they not eat before Moses? But you must say: anyone who enjoys a meal at which a Wise Man <note>A "Wise Man" or *Chakham* refers to a Torah scholar or Rabbi.</note> is present, does as much as if he enjoyed the radiance of the Divine Majesty. Thus it is also read in the book *Nevéh Shalóm* <note>original: "Abode of Peace," a work by Abraham ben Isaac Shalom.</note> folio 156, column 1, at the beginning of the third chapter of the ninth *Maamar*: <note>original: "כל המכניס תלמיד חכם בתוך ביתו ומאכילו ומשקהו ומהנהו מנכסיו מעלה עליו הכתוב כאלו מקריב תמידין בכל יום דכתיב הוא עובר עלינו תמיד"</note> That is: <margin>How highly it is regarded when someone gives a Rabbi and Wise Man food and drink, etc.</margin> Regarding anyone who allows a disciple of a Wise Man (that is, a Rabbi) to enter his house, and gives him food and drink, and allows him to enjoy some of his goods, the Scripture regards it as much as if he offered the daily sacrifice every day, as it is written (2 Kings 4:9, regarding Elisha): **He passes by us continually.** And in the Talmudic Tractate *Kethuvóth* <note>The volume of the Talmud dealing with marriage contracts.</note> it stands written on folio 111, column 2: <note>original: "במשיא בתו לתלמיד חכם והעושה פרקמטיא לתלמידי חכמים ומהנה תלמידי חכמים מנכסיו מעלה עליו הכתוב כאלו מדבק בשכינה"</note> That is: *Whoever gives his daughter to a disciple of a Wise Man (that is, a Rabbi) as a wife, and conducts business <term>Pragmatia<gloss>mercantile trade or business dealings</gloss></term> for the disciples of the Wise, and lets them enjoy his goods, is regarded by Scripture as if he cleaved to the Divine Majesty.* However, without a doubt, the parasitic Rabbis brought this teaching into play for the purpose of ensuring that people would diligently invite them as guests and fill their bellies well, as well as so that they might obtain rich wives and gifts.

<margin>Just as a scholar is highly praised among the Jews, so an unlearned man is greatly despised.</margin> But just as a scholar is held very high and honored among the Jews, so on the contrary, one who has learned nothing at all, and is called an <term>Am haárez<gloss>literally "people of the land," referring to the unlearned or those ignorant of religious law</gloss></term>, is despised by them to the utmost, as is evident from the Talmudic Tractate *Pesachím* <note>The volume concerning the laws of Passover.</note> folio 49, column 2, where it is written: <note>original: "תנו רבנן לעולם ימכור אדם כל מה שיש לו וישא בת תלמיד חכם..."</note> *Our Rabbis taught: A man should always sell everything he has to marry the daughter of a scholar. If he cannot find the daughter of a scholar, he should marry the daughter of the great men of the generation. If he cannot find the daughter of the great men of the generation, he should marry the daughter of the heads of the synagogues. If he cannot find the daughter of the heads of the synagogues, he should marry the daughter of the charity collectors. If he cannot find the daughter of the charity collectors, he should marry the daughter of the teachers of children. But he should not marry the daughter of the unlearned (*Am haárez*), because they are an abomination and their wives are vermin, and regarding their daughters it says: Cursed be he who lies with any beast.* It was taught: Rabbi says: It is forbidden for an unlearned man to eat meat, as it is said: *This is the law of the beast and the fowl.* <note>Leviticus 11:46. The Rabbi's interpretation is that only those who study the "Law" (*Torah*) have the right to eat the animals mentioned in it.</note> Whoever occupies himself with the Torah is permitted to eat the meat of beasts and fowl, but whoever does not occupy himself with the Torah is forbidden to eat the meat of beasts and fowl. Rabbi Eleazar said: It is permitted to stab an unlearned man <note>original: "לנחרו" - specifically to kill by piercing the neck, as opposed to ritual slaughter.</note> on the Day of Atonement that falls on a Sabbath. His disciples said to him: Rabbi, say "to slaughter him" <note>Which would imply a more refined or ritualized death.</note>. He said to them: This [slaughter] requires a blessing, but that [stabbing] requires no blessing. Rabbi Eleazar said: It is forbidden to accompany an unlearned man on a journey, as it is said: *For it is your life and the length of your days.* Since he has no regard for his own life <note>by not studying the Torah</note>, how much less will he care for the life of his companion? Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Yohanan: It is permitted to tear an unlearned man open like a fish. Rabbi Shmuel added: And that from his back. It was taught: Rabbi Akiva <note>One of the most famous Rabbis, who was famously illiterate until the age of 40.</note> said: When I was an unlearned man, I said: Who will give me a scholar so that I may bite him like a donkey? His disciples said to him: Rabbi, say "like a dog"? He said to them: This [a donkey] bites and breaks the bone, while that [a dog] bites but does not break the bone. It was taught: Rabbi Meir used to say: Whoever marries his daughter to an unlearned man is as if he bound her and placed her before a lion. Just as a lion tramples and eats and has no shame, so too...

### Chapter VIII of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked

...to split them.) <note>This continues a sentence from the previous page, likely referring to a physical or metaphorical divide.</note> It is taught that Rabbi Akiva said: "When I was an *am ha’aretz* <term>am ha’aretz: Literally 'people of the land,' referring to Jews who were uneducated in religious Law.</term> or an unlearned man <term>Idiot: In the 18th century, this term referred to a commoner or a layman lacking specialized education, rather than its modern pejorative sense.</term>, I said: 'Would to God I had a wise man, so that I might bite him like a donkey.'" But when his disciples said to him, "Rabbi, say 'like a dog,'" he answered them: "This one (namely the dog) bites and breaks the bone, but that one (namely the donkey) bites and does not break the bone." <note>Akiva implies the donkey's bite is more painful or stubborn, reflecting the deep-seated resentment he once felt toward the scholarly class.</note>

<margin>One should not give his daughter to an unlearned man.</margin>
It is taught that Rabbi Meir said: "Whoever marries his daughter to an unlearned man or a commoner does as much as if he bound her and threw her before a lion: just as a lion tramples (or tears) with its feet and eats and is not ashamed, so also an unlearned man strikes and sleeps with his wife and is not ashamed."

<margin>One should also not study the Law in their presence.</margin>
It is taught that Rabbi Eliezer said: "If we did not need them (the unlearned) for business or trades (that is, for our food and help, as Rabbi Solomon Yarchi <note>original: Rabbi Salomon Jarchi. Better known as Rashi, the preeminent medieval commentator on the Torah and Talmud.</note> explains it), they would kill us." Rabbi Hiyya teaches: "Whoever studies the Law <note>Torah</note> in the presence of an unlearned man does as much as if he slept with his betrothed (bride) before his face, as it is said (Deuteronomy 33:4): 'Moses commanded us the Law as an inheritance' <note>original Hebrew: מורשה moráscha</note>. Do not read it as *morashah* (inheritance), but rather as *me’orasah* <note>original Hebrew: מאורסה meorása</note>, which means 'betrothed.'" <note>This is a wordplay common in Rabbinic literature; it suggests the Torah is the "bride" of the Jewish people, and exposing it to the "unworthy" is like a violation of that marriage.</note> The hatred of the unlearned for the wise is greater than the hatred of the idolaters for Israel, and their wives hate the scholars even more than the men do.

<margin>They are unfit for six things.</margin>
It further follows there: "Our Rabbis teach <note>original Hebrew: Tnu Rabbanan</note> that six things are said of the *amme haárez*, that is, the unlearned. One does not give testimony to them, and one does not accept testimony from any of them. One does not reveal a secret to them. One does not appoint them as guardians over orphans. One does not appoint them over the alms box <note>the community charity fund</note>. One does not join them on a journey. There are also some who say that one should not have their lost property announced, so that they do not recover it in that way." <note>Usually, lost items were announced in the community so owners could claim them; this passage suggests excluding the unlearned from this social courtesy.</note>

<margin>Whatever the Rabbis do, the Jews regard as a keeping of the Law; they learn it and imitate them like apes.</margin>
Because the Jews are so foolish that they believe everything their Rabbis do is done very well and according to the Law, and for that reason they pay close attention to their works so that they may follow them like apes, I must also bring forward something from the Talmud here, where in the tractate Berakhot <note>original: Berachóth or Beróchos; the section of the Talmud dealing with prayers and blessings.</note>, folio 62, column 1, it is written thus:

<margin>The Talmud is not God's Word.</margin>
To return, however, to the Talmud or the oral Law of the Jews: it is known from the preceding that they firmly believe that everything contained therein is God’s Word, which Moses learned on Mount Sinai, or even in Heaven, and brought down. But these hardened people <note>The author uses "verstockte Menschen" (hardened/stubborn people), a common 17th-century polemical term for those who refuse to convert to Christianity.</note> are very much mistaken in their imagination, which I shall prove to them with the following important grounds and significant reasons.

<margin>The first reason is because many things are in it that are contrary to the Majesty of God.</margin>
The first reason is this: because many things stand therein which are belittling, mocking, and contemptuous to the Divine Majesty—indeed, even blasphemous against the same, as was demonstrated at length above in the first chapter. How then can such a book come from God? Would God then have taught Moses such unbecoming things, which run directly contrary to His divine essence? Certainly, no one can say this except one who is deprived of all sound reason and does not know what God is, or in what His attributes consist.

<margin>The second reason is because many things are in it which conflict with the Old Testament.</margin>
The second reason why the Talmud is not God’s Word is this: because many things are taught therein which do not agree at all with that which stands in the Holy Scripture of the Old Testament, but rather seek to maintain the exact opposite. For in the same it is taught that there were men who kept the entire Law, of which it is written in the tractate *Schabbath* (or *Shabbas*) <note>Shabbat: The Talmudic tractate regarding the Sabbath.</note> folio 55, column 1, concerning the words of Ezekiel 9:6, *Umimmikdashí tachéllu*, that is, **"But begin at my Sanctuary"**; it is written thus: <note>original Hebrew: "אל תקרא מקדשי אלא מקודשי אלו בני אדם שקיימו את התורה כולה מאלף ועד תיו"</note> that is, **"Read not *mikdashí*, that is, 'my Sanctuary' or 'Temple,' but *mekuddashai*, that is, 'my Sanctified ones'; and these are those who have kept the entire Law from Aleph to Tau, (that is, from the first letter to the last)."** <note>Aleph to Tau: The first and last letters of the Hebrew alphabet, similar to the Greek "Alpha and Omega."</note> And in the second column of the same it is read: <note>original Hebrew: "הלא משה ואהרן מתו שלא קיימו כל התורה כולה"</note> that is, **"Did not Moses and Aaron die, who yet fulfilled the entire Law?"** With this also agrees Rabbi Bechai <note>Rabbi Bahya ben Asher (c. 1255–1340), a famous Spanish commentator.</note> in the book *Cad hakkemach* <note>Kad Ha-Kemach: "The Jar of Flour," a work on Jewish ethics and philosophy.</note>, folio 5, column 4, and speaks: <note>original Hebrew: "אף הצדיקים הגמורים שלא חטאו מעולם הם בכלל עונש המיתה"</note> that is, **"Even the perfectly righteous who never sinned are included in the punishment of death."**

It is clearly written: **The imagination, that is, the nature or the thought of the human heart, is evil from its youth.** <note>Genesis 8:21</note> This is also confessed by Rabbi David Kimchi <note>A significant medieval Jewish commentator and grammarian, also known by the acronym Radak (c. 1160–1235).</note> in his interpretation of Isaiah 43:27 with these words: <note>original: "האדם מוטבע בחטא כי יצר לב האדם רע מנעוריו"</note> **that is, man is naturally steeped in sin, for the imagination of the human heart is evil from youth.**

<margin>The claim that Hophni and Phinehas did not sin.</margin>
Regarding Eli’s sons, Hophni and Phinehas, it is written in 1 Samuel 2:22 that they sinned against God by lying with the women who served at the entrance of the Tabernacle. In the Talmudic tractate *Shabbath* <note>The tractate of the Talmud primarily concerned with the laws of the Sabbath.</note> however, on folio 55, column 2, it is read: <note>original: "אמר רבי שמואל בר נחמני אמר רבי יונתן כל האומר בני עלי חטאו אינו אלא טועה"</note> **that is, Rabbi Samuel the son of Nachmani said that Rabbi Jonathan said: whoever says that the sons of Eli sinned is merely mistaken.** And this is proven there in a foolish manner, stating: <note>original: "מתוך ששהו את קיניהן שלא הלכו אצל בעליהן מעלה עליהן הכתוב כאילו שכבום"</note> **that is, because they [the priests] delayed the women’s bird offerings so that they could not go to their husbands, the Scripture accounts it to them [Eli’s sons] as if they had actually slept with them.** <note>The Talmudic argument here is that the "sin" was administrative neglect—delaying the sacrifices required for ritual purity after childbirth—which prevented the women from returning home to their husbands, rather than actual adultery.</note>

<margin>The claim that Reuben did not sin with Bilhah.</margin>
Furthermore, in Genesis 35:22, it is read that Reuben slept with his father’s concubine, Bilhah, and thus committed incest, which was a great sin. In the aforementioned Talmudic passage, however, it is taught: <note>original: "אמר רבי שמואל בר נחמני אמר רבי יונתן כל האומר ראובן חטא אינו אלא טועה"</note> **that is, Rabbi Samuel, the son of Nachmani, reports that Rabbi Jonathan said: whoever says that Reuben sinned is merely mistaken.** And it is then stated regarding this: <note>original: "וישכב את בלהה פילגש אביו ומעלה עליו הכתוב כאילו שכב עמה"</note> **that is, the words "And he lay with Bilhah, his father’s concubine" teach that he merely disturbed his father's bed [by rearranging it], which the Scripture regards as seriously as if he had actually slept with her.** <note>The Rabbinic tradition claims Reuben merely moved Jacob’s bed from Bilhah’s tent to his mother Leah’s tent to protest his father's perceived neglect of Leah.</note> How, however, does this foolish interpretation agree with what is written in Genesis 49:4 and 1 Chronicles 5:1, where it is said that he defiled his father’s bed?

<margin>The claim that the sons of Samuel did not sin.</margin>
Furthermore, it is written in 1 Samuel 8:3 that Samuel’s sons turned aside after gain, took bribes, and perverted justice, which was a sin against the Law of Moses in Exodus 18:21 and Deuteronomy 16:19. In the previously mentioned tractate on folio 56, column 1, however, it is taught: <note>original: "א"ר שמואל בר נחמני אמר ר' יונתן כל האומר בני שמואל חטאו אינו אלא טועה"</note> **that is, Rabbi Samuel the son of Nachmani reports that Rabbi Jonathan said: whoever says that Samuel’s sons sinned is merely mistaken.**

Eisenmenger uses this to argue that the Rabbis are making excuses for David's conduct with Bathsheba.</note>

We also read in 1 Kings 11:4–7 that King Solomon, when he grew old, was led astray into heathen idolatry through the incitement of his foreign wives, by which sin God was provoked to anger against him, as is indicated in the following ninth verse. In the <margin>It is claimed that Solomon committed no idolatry.</margin> oft-mentioned Talmudic tractate *Shabbath*, however, on folio 56, column 2, it is denied that he sinned, where the words read as follows: <note>original: "אמר רבי שמואל בר נחמני אמר רבי יונתן כל האומר שלמה חטא אינו אלא טועה"</note> that is, **Rabbi Samuel, the son of Nachmani, says that Rabbi Jonathan said: Whoever says that Solomon sinned is merely mistaken.** And soon after it follows: <note>original: "נשיו הטו את לבבו ללכת אחרי אלהים אחרים ולא הלך והכתיב אז יבנה שלמה במה לכמוש שקוץ מואב שביקש לבנות ולא בנה"</note> that is, **His wives certainly wanted to incline his heart to follow after other gods, but he did not follow them. How so? It is indeed written (verse 7): "Then Solomon built a high place for Chemosh, the abomination of Moab!" (This is to be understood thus:) He wanted to build it, but he did not build it.** Likewise, in the book *Siphre Jeshénim* <note>term: *Sifrei Yeshenim* (Old Books); likely a reference to a bibliographic work or a specific collection of older Rabbinic writings.</note> on folio 32, column 4, <margin>Adam is defended, claiming he did not sin.</margin> number 27, a written book is mentioned which is called *Sachúth Adam*, that is, *The Innocence of Adam*, wherein it is claimed that Adam did not sin when he ate of the forbidden fruit.

Furthermore, it is stated in the Talmudic tractate *Bava Batra* on folio 15, column 2, thus: <note>original: "אמר ר' שמואל בר נחמני אמר ר' יונתן כל האומר מלכת שבא אשה היתה אינו אלא טועה מאי מלכת שבא מלכותא דשבא"</note> that is, **Rabbi Samuel, the son of Nachmani, says that Rabbi Jonathan said: whoever <margin>It is claimed that the Queen of Sheba did not come to Solomon.</margin> says that *Malcath Shebha* (which we Christians correctly interpret as the Queen of Sheba) was a woman, is merely mistaken.** What then does *Malcath Shebha* mean? (It means) the kingdom (that is, the King) of Sheba. On the contrary, 1 Kings 10:1, etc., expressly reports that it was a queen, and consequently a woman; and it is not found in all of Holy Scripture—indeed, nowhere else in any Rabbinic book—that the word *Malca* <note>term: *Malka* (Hebrew: מַלְכָּה). In standard Hebrew, this word exclusively means "queen," while "kingdom" is *malkut*.</note> signifies a kingdom, but rather it always means a queen. But we see from this how the Devil, through the Rabbis in the Talmud, perverts the Scripture and endeavors to twist into a false meaning that which is quite clear and distinct in God's word.

Holy Scripture teaches that God asks no one for advice, for in Isaiah 40:13–14 it is said: **Who has instructed the Spirit of the Lord?**

-># Of the Talmud.<-

X x 2

...and who has instructed Him as a counselor? With whom has He held counsel? In the Talmud, however, in the Tractate *Sanhedrin*, folio 38, column 2, it is written: <margin>The Talmud teaches that God takes counsel with the angels, and does nothing without them.</margin> <note>original Hebrew: אמר ר' יוחנן אין הק"בה עושה דבר אלא אם כן נמלך בפמליא של מעלה שנ' : במירת עירין פתגמא ובמאמר קדישין שאלתא</note> that is, **Rabbi Jochanan said: The Holy One, blessed be He, does nothing unless He first consults with the heavenly household (that is, with the angels), as it is said (Daniel 4:17): "This matter is by the decree of the watchers, and the demand by the word of the holy ones."** Concerning this, Rabbi Bechai <note>Rabbi Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century Spanish scholar and kabbalist.</note> writes in his commentary on the Five Books of Moses, in the section *Bereshith* <note>The portion of Genesis.</note>, folio 8, column 2, as follows: <note>original Hebrew: אין הק"בה עושה דבר עד שמסתכל בפמליא של מעלה : וביאור הענין שהבורא ית' פועל כל פעולותיו על ידי אמצעיים. ומצינו גם כן בפשטי התורה מסייעין אל זה הענין ועל זה אמר בכאן נעשה אדם בלשון רבים להורות על אמצעיים</note> that is, **The Holy One, blessed be He, does nothing unless He first looks upon the heavenly household (namely the angels). This is to be interpreted to mean that the blessed Creator performs all His works through intermediaries. We also find proofs in the literal (or simple) interpretations of the Law which confirm this; therefore, God speaks here in the *plurali numero*, or in the plural: "Let us make man," in order to indicate the intermediaries (that is, the angels, through whose mediation He does something).**

That wisdom comes from God and is given by Him to man, we read in Psalm 51:6 and 94:10, Job 32:8 and 38:36, Daniel 1:17, and Ecclesiastes 2:26. For this reason, Solomon also desired and received wisdom from Him, as seen in 1 Kings 3:9, 11, 12. It is also written in 1 Samuel 2:7 that the Lord God makes poor and makes rich. In the Talmudic Tractate *Shabbath*, however, on folio 156, column 1, it is read: <margin>In the same it is also taught that wisdom and wealth come from the stars.</margin> <note>original Hebrew: רבי חנינא אומר מזל מחכים מזל מעשיר</note> that is, **Rabbi Chanina says that the stars <term>mazal: literally "constellation" or "destiny" associated with astrology</term> make one wise and wealthy.** Yet the Talmud itself, in Tractate *Kiddushin*, folio 82, column 2, teaches the opposite and contradicts itself, where it is written: <note>original Hebrew: רבי מאיר אומר לעולם ילמד אדם לבנו אומנות נקייה וקלה ויבקש רחמים למי שהעושר והנכסים שלו שאין עניות מן האומנות ואין עשירות מן האומנות אלא למי שהעושר שלו שנ' לי הכסף ולי הזהב אמר יי' צבאות</note> that is, **Rabbi Meir says: A man should always let his son learn a clean and easy trade, and pray for mercy to Him to whom wealth and possessions belong. For poverty does not come from the trade, nor does wealth, but rather from Him to whom wealth belongs, as it is said (Haggai 2:8): "The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, says the Lord of Hosts."** Thus it is...

### Chapter 8 of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked.
<page-num>348</page-num>

<margin>Thus, the gift of children, life, and nourishment is also said to originate from the stars.</margin> It is also read in Psalm 127, verse 4, that children are an inheritance or gift from God; however, in the Talmudic tractate *Moed Katon* <note>A tractate concerning laws of the intermediate days of festivals.</note>, folio 28, column 1, and in the aforementioned tractate *Shabbat*, folio 156, column 1, in the *Tosafot* <note>Medieval commentaries on the Talmud.</note>, it is recorded: <note>original Hebrew: אמר רבא בני חיי ומזוני לאו בזכותא תליא מילתא אלא במזלא תליא מילתא</note> That is, **Rabba says: Children, life, and nourishment do not depend on righteousness, but rather depend on the constellation.** <note>The term "Mazzal" refers to the zodiac or planetary influence, indicating a belief in astrological fate.</note>

<margin>The Talmud permits usury.</margin> Usury <note>The charging of interest on loans.</note> is also forbidden in Exodus 22, verse 25, and Leviticus 25, verses 35, 36, and 37. In the Talmud, however, it is permitted in the tractate *Bava Metzia*, folio 75, column 1, where it is taught thus: <note>original Hebrew: אמר רב יהודה אמר שמואל תלמידי חכמים מותרים ללוות אמר רב זה מזה ברבית מאי טעמא מידע ידיעי דרבית אסורה ומתנה הוא דיהבי אהדדי</note> That is, **Rav Yehuda said that Samuel said: It is permitted for scholars to borrow from one another with interest. What is the reason? They know very well that interest is forbidden, and so it is merely a gift that they give to one another.** Rav Yehuda also said that Rav said: It is permitted for a man to lend to his children and his household members with interest, so that they may be made to taste the flavor of usury.

<margin>Drunkenness is commanded.</margin> Drunkenness is forbidden in Isaiah 5, verse 20 <note>The author likely means Isaiah 5:22: "Woe to those who are heroes at drinking wine."</note>, where it is said: "Woe to those who are heroes at drinking wine." In the Talmudic tractate *Megilla*, on the contrary, it is read in folio 7, column 2: <note>original Hebrew: אמר רבא מיחייב איניש לבסומי בפוריא עד דלא ידע בין ארור המן לברוך מרדכי</note> That is, **Rabba said: A man is obligated to drink so much on the feast of Purim until he no longer knows the difference between the words "Cursed be Haman" and "Blessed be Mordechai."** <note>Purim is a Jewish holiday commemorating the saving of the Jewish people from Haman, as recounted in the Book of Esther.</note>

<margin>According to the Talmud, it was permitted for one to let all his children pass through the fire for Molech.</margin> God forbade in Leviticus 18, verse 21, and chapter 20, verses 2 and 3, to give of one’s seed—that is, one’s children—to the idol Molech <note>A Canaanite deity associated with child sacrifice.</note>, that they should be burned or passed through two fires. In the Talmud, however, it is written in the tractate *Sanhedrin*, folio 67, column 2: <note>original Hebrew: אמר רב אחא בריה דרבא העביר כל זרעו פטור שנ' ומזרעך ולא כל זרעך</note> That is, **Rav Acha, the son of Rabba, said: If one causes all his seed (or all his children) to pass through, he is free (namely, from punishment), because it is said (in the mentioned place, Leviticus 18:21): "And of your seed," but not "all your seed."** Is this not once again a perverse interpretation of the Word of God? The foolish Rav Acha should rather have concluded that because it is forbidden to let some of one's seed pass through the fire in honor of Molech, it is even less permissible to lead all of one's children through it.

<margin>He who praises God too much shall be—</margin> That one cannot praise God enough, and that He should be constantly lauded and glorified, is taught by Holy Scripture; for this reason, Da— <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence, likely referring to King David.</note>

# Chapter VIII of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked.

According to this, it is therefore permitted to consult the **demons** <note>original: "Teuffel"; Eisenmenger uses this term for the Hebrew "shedim," often translated as spirits or demons.</note> on weekdays, although Rabbi Jose did not want to allow it because of the danger, but not because it was supposedly forbidden by the Law. Following this, it further says in the same place: <note>original Aramaic: תנו רבנן: שרי שמן ושרי ביצים מותרים</note> **that is, Our Rabbis teach that the Princes of Oil and the Princes of Eggs are permitted.** What these words mean, however, is explained by **Rabbi Salomon Jarchi** <note>Also known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator on the Torah and Talmud.</note> in his commentary on it, with these words: <note>original Hebrew: יש מעשה שדים ששואלין על ידי שמן וקרי להו שרי שמן ויש ששואלין בשפופרת של ביצה וקרי להו שרי ביצים</note> **that is, It is a work of the demons whereby one consults them through oil, and they (the demons) are called "Princes of Oil": some, however, consult them through an eggshell, and those (demons who are thus consulted) are called "Princes of Eggs."** According to this teaching, it is therefore free for the Jews to consult the demons through oil or eggshells. Concerning this, it is also written in the book *Lef tof* <note>Referring to "Lev Tov" (A Good Heart), a popular 16th-century Yiddish book of ethical and practical instruction by Isaac ben Eliakum.</note>, in the third chapter, folio 39, column 1 of the Wilmersdorf edition: <note>original Western Yiddish/Judeo-German: וואו אנבּילאגן מיט שרי זכוכית ושר ידי דאס איז וואס מיר ווען מיין גניבה ווער געטהן דא קענן אזולכי מאכן דען גנב ברענגן אין איין גלאז אדר אין דער הנט פאר אן וואוז אן אפילו אם שבת דען וואו זאכע זונן אין דער וואוכן דאס מיין זא סבת אוך מותר</note> **that is, Regarding the Princes of the Glass (in which there is oil) or the Princes of the Hand: some, when a theft has occurred, can bring the thief into a glass or into the hand; and one may certainly do such a thing even on the Sabbath, for those things which are permitted during the week are also permitted on the Sabbath.**

<margin>
Solomon is said to have asked certain demons where the Shamir worm was.
</margin>

The words of the Talmud, however, read as follows:

**King Solomon said to the Rabbis: "How shall I do this?" They said to him: "There is the Shamir, which Moses brought for the stones of the Ephod." He said to them: "Where is it found?" But when he became thirsty, he could not resist and drank...**

[Benaiah] went down, reached [Asmodeus], and threw the chain upon him, then sealed it. When [Asmodeus] woke up, he struggled to get free. Benaiah said to him: "The Name of your Master is upon you! The Name of your Master is upon you!" As he was leading him away, they reached a tree; [Asmodeus] brushed against it and knocked it down. They reached a house and knocked it down. They came to the hut of a certain widow. She came out and begged him [to spare her home]; he bent his body away from it, but in doing so, a bone within him broke. He said: "This is as it is written: *And a soft tongue breaks the bone* <note>Proverbs 25:15</note>." When he arrived [at the palace], he was not brought before Solomon for three days. On the first day, he asked them: "Why does the King not require me to come before him?" They said to him: "He has been overcome by drink." [Asmodeus] took a brick and placed it on top of another. They went and told Solomon. He said to them: "This is what he meant to tell you: Go and give him [more] to drink." The next day, he asked them: "And why does the King not require me to come before him?" They said to him: "He has been overcome by food." [Asmodeus] took the top brick and placed it on the ground. They went and told Solomon. He said to them: "This is what he meant: Withhold his food from him." At the end of three days, he entered before Solomon. He took a reed, measured four cubits, and threw it before him. He said: "Consider: when that man [you] dies, he possesses nothing in this world but four cubits [the space of a grave]. Now you have conquered the whole world, and yet you were not satisfied until you conquered me as well?" Solomon said to him: "I want nothing from you. I wish to build the Holy Temple, and I require the Shamir <note>A legendary worm or substance capable of cutting through the hardest stone.</note>." Asmodeus said: "It was not handed over to me, but to the Prince of the Sea; and he does not entrust it to anyone except the wild rooster <note>original: תרנגולא ברא (Tarnegola Bara), often identified as the hoopoe or woodcock</note>, who is faithful to his oath. And what does the bird do with it? He carries it to mountains where there is no habitation, and places it upon the peak of a cliff, and the mountain splits. Then he brings seeds from trees and throws them there, and it becomes a place of habitation. And this is why the Targum <note>Aramaic translation of the Bible</note> calls him the 'Mountain-Cutter' [Naggar Tura]." They searched for the nest of a wild rooster that had chicks, and they covered the nest with clear glass. When the bird came, he wanted to enter but could not. He went and brought the Shamir and placed it upon the glass. [Solomon's men] let out a shout; the bird dropped it, and they took it. # Chapter VIII of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked.

...make heavy, rocky mountains fruitful and sow them? Indeed, how can such crude lies be the Word of God?

<margin>When the little worm Shamir was created, how large it was, and how it was preserved.</margin>
Since the little worm Shamir is mentioned here, we shall also investigate when it was created, how large it was, and how it was preserved. Regarding this, the Talmud teaches in the Tractate *Sotah*, folio 48, column 2, the following: <note>original: "תנו רבנן שמיר זה ברייתו כשעורה ומששת ימי בראשית נברא ואין כל דבר קשה יכול לעמוד בפניו. במה משמרין אותו כורכין אותו בספוגין של צמר ומניחין אותו באוטני של אבר מלאה סובי שעורים"</note> that is, "Our Rabbis teach: this Shamir is a creature the size of a grain of barley, and it was created during the six days of Creation, and no hard thing can withstand it. How is it kept? It is wrapped in sponges of wool and placed in a leaden box filled with barley-husks." Regarding the time of its creation, the following is written in the *Pirkei Avot* (or *Ethics of the Fathers*) in the fifth chapter, folio 30, column 1, in the Talmud printed in Amsterdam: <note>original: "עשרת דברים נבראו בערב שבת בין השמשות ואלו הן פי הארץ ופי הבאר ופי האתון והקשת והמן והמטה והשמיר וגו'"</note> that is, "Ten things were created on the (first) Sabbath Eve in the twilight, and they are the following: The mouth of the earth (which swallowed Korah and his company, of which one may read in Numbers 16:30–32), the mouth or opening of the well (mentioned in Genesis 29:2), the mouth of the donkey (belonging to Balaam), the rainbow, the manna, the staff (of Aaron, mentioned in Exodus 7:12), and the Shamir, etc."

<margin>It is said, however, that it has no longer existed since the time the second Temple was destroyed.</margin>
It is said, however, that it has no longer existed since the time of the destruction of the second Temple; therefore, in the aforementioned Tractate *Sotah*, folio 48, column 2, it is written: <note>original: "משחרב בית המקדש בטל השמיר וכו' ת"ר שמיר שבו בנה שלמה את המקדש"</note> that is, "From the time in which the Temple was laid waste, the Shamir has no longer existed, etc. Our Rabbis teach that Solomon built the Temple by means of this Shamir."

Now, since according to the contents of the Talmud, the King of the <term>Devils (demons)</term> had to assist in the building of the Temple and reveal where the Shamir was to be obtained, we shall see further what foolish dreams the nonsensical Rabbis have regarding the help of the devils, which they claim was utilized for this purpose. In the book *Emek HaMelech*, folio 147, column 1, the following is to be read: <note>original: "דרשו רז"ל על פסוק וישב שלמה על כסא יי' למלך מה הקב"ה מושל על העליונים ועל התחתונים אף שלמה המלך ע"ה מלך על העליונים ועל התחתונים ואפלו שדים ורוחין ולילין היו משועבדים לו כי בזמנו היתה הסיהרא קיימא באשלמותא והטוב גבר על הרע ונמתקו ואפילו הגבורות הגדולות הביאו דורונות לבנין בית המקדש וגם הם היו מסייעים"</note> "Our Rabbis of blessed memory interpreted the verse: *And Solomon sat on the throne of the Lord as king*; just as the Holy One, blessed be He, rules over the celestial and the earthly beings, so too King Solomon—peace be upon him—ruled over the celestial and the earthly beings. Even the demons, spirits, and <term>night-monsters (Liliths)</term> were subjected to him; for in his time the moon was at its full perfection, and good prevailed over evil, and [the judgments] were sweetened; and even the great [spiritual] powers brought gifts for the construction of the Holy Temple, and they also assisted."

-># Of the Talmud.<-

<note>original: "מקיים בבניינו כאשר הוא במדרש שיר השירים רבה אבל אחר חטאו שריא סיהרא לאתפגמא שנ' ויעש שלמה הרע בעיני יי' ונמלטו מתחת ידו ולא עבדוהו כנראה ממשלת דאשמדאי מלכא דשידי ואדרבא הוא היה מתיירא מהם מאוד שנ' הנה מטתו של שלמה ששים גבורים סביב לה מגבורי ישראל מחד מפחד בלילות:"</note>
<note>This Hebrew passage from the Midrash explains that Solomon sustained the moon in its fullness through his righteousness; however, after he sinned, the moon began to wane. This is a metaphor for his power: while he was upright, even the demons served him, but after his fall, they escaped his control and he became terrified of them, requiring a guard of sixty heroes.</note>

This is how our Rabbis, of blessed memory, have interpreted the verse in 1 Chronicles 29:23: **"Then Solomon sat on the throne of the LORD as king."** Just as the holy and blessed God rules over the upper and lower worlds, so too did King Solomon (upon whom be peace) rule over the upper and lower worlds. Indeed, even the devils, spirits, and night-demons were subject to him. For in his time, the moon stood in its full perfection, and good held the upper hand over evil. <margin>The devils were subject to King Solomon.</margin> At that time, the devils were even pleasant in their conduct. Thus, the spirits brought the great stones for the building of the Temple and provided assistance in its construction, as can be seen in the *Midrash Shir HaShirim Rabbah* <note>The "Great Midrash on the Song of Songs," a collection of ancient rabbinic homilies and stories.</note>. <margin>They also helped build the Temple.</margin> However, after he had sinned, the moon began to be "cut" (that is, to wane), as it is said in 1 Kings 11:6: **"And Solomon did what was evil in the sight of the LORD."** Consequently, those same spirits and devils withdrew themselves from his authority and served him no longer, <margin>But after Solomon sinned, they no longer served him.</margin> as is seen in the story of Asmodeus <note>original: "Aschmedái"</note>, the King of the Devils. On the contrary, Solomon became very much afraid of them, as is said in the Song of Solomon 3:7: **"Behold his bed, which is Solomon's; threescore valiant men are about it, of the valiant of Israel."** Regarding his power over the devils, more can be found in *Bammidbar Rabbah* <note>The Great Midrash on the book of Numbers.</note>, in the eleventh portion, folio 199, column 3. It is also taught in *Shemot Rabbah* <note>The Great Midrash on the book of Exodus.</note>, in the fifteenth portion, folio 108, column 2, that Solomon ruled over the entire world, from one end to the other. <margin>Solomon is said to have ruled over the whole world.</margin>

They fulfilled all his desires, as it is said (1 Chronicles 29:23): "And Solomon sat on the throne of the Lord as king." He ruled over the upper and lower beings, and they were forced to bring him stones and building materials for the Holy Temple. And when he sought the Shamir <note>A legendary worm or substance capable of cutting through the hardest stone without metal tools.</note>, Ashmedai, the king of the demons, brought it in iron chains and a ring engraved with the Explicit Name. Solomon released him and, at his request, gave him his ring, upon which was engraved the Explicit Name. Solomon trusted him because it was a cause brought about by the Lord to repay him for his deeds—for he had violated three prohibitions <note>Biblical laws in Deuteronomy 17:16-17 forbidding a king from having too many horses, wives, or gold.</note>—that he should go for three years into exile. When the demon took the ring, he threw it into the sea, and a fish swallowed it. Then the demon cast Solomon four hundred leagues away into the land of the heathens and drove him from his kingdom. Solomon lost all his glory, for he was cast far away and begged at doorways. He remained in this suffering for three years because he had transgressed the three commandments of the Torah: that he shall not multiply wives, nor multiply horses, nor greatly multiply silver and gold for himself. He stumbled in all of them. At the end of this time, at the end of the three years, the Holy One, blessed be He, wished to have mercy on him for the sake of David His servant, and for the sake of the righteous Naamah, daughter of the King of Ammon, from whom the Messiah, the son of David, was to descend. So that he might be joined to her and bring her with him to the land of Israel, the Holy One, blessed be He, brought him to the land of Ammon. He came to the royal city, the place of their dwelling, and stood in the street of the city. The King's butler—the chief cook who prepares and cooks the King's food—came to take what was needed for his work and found Solomon standing there. He took him as a hired laborer to carry what he had purchased and led him to the kitchen. He saw what Solomon did, and Solomon said he would stay with him and serve him, wanting nothing but food alone. The butler was pleased and Solomon stayed with him, serving and helping him. After some days, Solomon told him that he would cook dishes for the King in his own fashion, as he was a great master in these foods. The butler agreed, and Solomon prepared and cooked the King's delicacies. When the King ate those treats which the butler brought, and tasted those dishes, the King asked the butler: "Who cooked these foods? For until now you never brought me the likes of them." He told him the whole story of that man, and the King commanded his servants to call him. He came before the King, and the King said to him: "Do you wish to be my butler?" and he said, "Yes." The King sent the former butler away and put Solomon in his place to cook all his food. And it came to pass after these things...

# About the Talmud

[Genesis] **Rabba** <note>original: "Beréschis rábba"; this is the Midrash Rabbah on the book of Genesis.</note> in the 98th **Parashah** <note>A weekly portion or section of the Torah/Midrash.</note>, folio 90, column 4, states that God addressed Joseph thus: <note>original Hebrew: אמר לו הק"בה אתה לא תלית את עיניך והבטת בהן חייך שאתה נותן לבנותי צעירה בתורה מהו צעירה פרשה</note> that is: **The Holy Blessed God said to him: You did not lift up your eyes and look at them (namely the royal daughters who are mentioned there); I swear by your life that you shall give to my daughters a *Zeida* in the Law. What is a *Zeida*? A Parashah or a section of the Law.** <note>The author is citing a midrashic interpretation where Joseph's modesty is rewarded by having a specific section of the Torah (likely the laws of inheritance for the daughters of Zelophehad) associated with his descendants.</note> Conversely, in the Holy Scripture, God swears either by Himself—as can be seen in Genesis 22:16, Isaiah 45:22 and 62:8, Ezekiel 33:27 and 34:8—or by His right hand (Isaiah 62:8), or by His soul (which is also the same as by Himself, Jeremiah 51:14, Amos 6:8), or by His holiness (Amos 4:2 and Psalm 89:35), or else by His great name (Jeremiah 44:26). It is nowhere to be found therein that He ever swore by the life of a human being.

Furthermore, it is taught in the Talmud in the tractate **Berakhot** <note>original: "Berachóth"; the first tractate of the Talmud, dealing with prayers and blessings.</note> folio 33, column 2, as well as in Rabbi **Bahya’s** <note>original: "Bechai"; referring to Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century Spanish rabbi and scholar.</note> commentary on the Five Books of Moses, folio 194, column 4, and folio 195, column 1, in the section **Va'etchanan**: <note>original Hebrew: הכל בידי שמים חוץ מיראת שמים</note> that is: **Everything is in the hand or power of God, except for the fear of God.** <margin>The Talmud teaches that the fear of God does not come from God.</margin> In the Holy Scripture, however, we learn that the fear of God is a gift from God; therefore, God speaks in Jeremiah 32:39: **"I will give them one heart and one way, that they may fear me forever."** And in the following 40th verse, He says further: **"And I will put my fear in their hearts, that they shall not depart from me."** Because of this, King David also prays to God the Lord in Psalm 86:11: **"Unite my heart to the fear of your name,"** or **"to fear your name."**

This is that which is written (in Isaiah 2:22): "Cease ye from man, whose breath is in his nostrils: for wherein is he to be accounted of?"* Shortly thereafter, the same source follows with: <note>original Hebrew: ודאי האדם בכללו הוא רוחני כי תפוח עקבו של אדם הראשון היה מכהה גלגל חמה קלסהר פניו לא כל שכן והוו הענין שטעו בו מלאכי השרת על כן הפיל הק"בה עליו תרדמה שהוא ענין גשמי להורות שהוא גשמי</note> *that is: Certainly, Adam was entirely spiritual, for the ball of the first man’s heel darkened the orb of the sun (which is also stated in the Sepher Gilgulim <note>The "Book of Reincarnations."</note> at the end of the sixteenth chapter, folio 14, column 3), how much more so then the radiance of his countenance! And this was the reason that the ministering angels were mistaken in him. Therefore, God caused a deep sleep to fall upon him, which is a physical matter, to demonstrate that he was physical.*

In the book, however, which is called *Sepher Chasidim* <note>The "Book of the Pious," a central text of the German-Jewish pietists of the 12th/13th centuries.</note>, the following is read in number 500: <note>original Hebrew: אדם הראשון היה מסוף העולם ועד סופו ובקשו מלאכי השרת לומר לפניו קדוש קדוש כי היה מלא כל הארץ בא הק"בה ומעטו ונטל מאבריו קצת והיו מונחים חתיכות בשר סביבותיו אמר אדם להק"בה רבש"ע למה אתה גוזלו לך כי תמאס יגיע כפיך וכתיב ותשת עלי כפך, אמר אני אחזיר לך פרו ורבו ומלאו את הארץ כבראשונה והיינו דאמרינן אין בן דוד בא עד שיכלו כל הנשמות שבגוף. א"ל הק"בה טול אלו חתיכות ותפזרם בכל הארץ ובכל מקום שתוליך ותשליך אותם שם ישובו לעפר כשיהיה מתישב המקום מיועד ובמקום שתגזור ליורך לישראל שם יהיו ולגוים שם יהיו והיינו שנאמר ארץ לא עבר בה איש ולא ישב אדם שם שלא ידע שם מבשרו</note> <margin>How God took large pieces of flesh from Adam and made him smaller.</margin> *that is: The first man reached from one end of the world to the other, and the ministering angels wanted to say before him (the words of Isaiah 6:3) "Holy, holy," because he filled the entire world. But God came and made him smaller, and took some parts from his limbs, and pieces of flesh lay all around*

...placed the flesh (from the flesh that had been removed from him). Then Adam said to God, "O Lord of the world! Why do you rob me? Is it right that you should despise the work of your own hand?" He gave it to Moses for three months, but when he went before Pharaoh, God took it from him until he stood upon Mount Sinai; then He returned that light to him, and he used it every day, so that the children of Israel could not come near him until he put a veil over his face.

<margin>How long Adam is said to have remained in Paradise, and what occurred on the first day of his creation.</margin>
We must now also see how long Adam is said to have remained in Paradise until he was cast out from it; and the <term>Talmudic</term> <note>The Talmud is the central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of legal and legendary discussions.</note> tractate <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>The tractate dealing with the high court and judicial procedures.</note>, folio 38, column 2, teaches us this with these words: <note>original Hebrew: "אמר רבי אחא בר חנינא שתים עשרה שעות הוי היום שעה ראשונה הוצבר עפרו שניה נעשה גולם שלישית נמתחו אבריו רביעית נזרקה בו נשמה חמישית עמד על רגליו שישית קרא שמות שביעית נזדווגה לו חוה שמינית עלו למיטה שנים וירדו ארבעה תשיעית נצטווה שלא לאכול מן האילן עשירית סרח אחת עשרה נידון שתים עשרה נטרד והלך לו שנא' אדם ביקר בל ילין"</note> that is: Rabbi Acha, the son of Channina, has said: The day has twelve hours. In the first hour, the dust (from which God created him) was gathered together; in the second, he was made into a <term>golem</term> <note>A Hebrew term meaning an unformed or shapeless mass.</note>; in the third, his limbs were stretched out; in the fourth, the soul was cast into him; in the fifth, he stood upon his feet; in the sixth, he called out the names (in that he gave a name to every thing); in the seventh, Eve was joined to him; in the eighth, two climbed into the bed and four came down (in that two children, namely Cain and his sister, were conceived and born in that time); in the ninth, he was commanded that he should not eat from the tree (of the forbidden fruit); in the tenth, he sinned; in the eleventh, judgment was held over him; and in the twelfth, he was cast out (from Paradise) and went away, as it is said (Psalm 49:13): **Man does not abide overnight in his dignity.** This fable is also found in Rabbi Bechai’s <note>Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century Spanish rabbi and commentator.</note> commentary on the Five Books of Moses, in the <term>Parashah Bereshith</term> <note>The first weekly Torah portion, covering the beginning of Genesis.</note>, folio 10, column 4, and folio 11, column 1; and in the Great *Yalkut Reuveni*, folio 21, column 3, in the aforementioned *Parashah Bereshith*; as well as in the *Avot* (or *Ovos*) of Rabbi Nathan (or Noton), folio 1, column 3, in the Talmud printed at Amsterdam, and in the 11th chapter of the *Chapters of Rabbi Eliezer*. But regarding the children who were initially conceived, one reads thus in <term>Bereshith Rabbah</term> <note>An ancient midrashic (interpretive) text on the book of Genesis.</note> in the twenty-second *Parashah*, folio 21, column 2: <note>original Hebrew: "א"ר אלעזר בן עזריה ג' פלאים נעשו באותו היום . בו ביום נבראו . בו ביום שמשו . בו ביום הוציאו תולדות"</note> "Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah said: Three wonders were performed on that day: On that same day they were created; on that same day they coupled; and on that same day they brought forth offspring."

<margin>How the serpent seduced Eve.</margin>
As to how it happened regarding the eating of the forbidden fruit, and how Satan seduced Eve to it, this is indicated in the book *Emek Hammelech* <note>The "Valley of the King," a 17th-century Kabbalistic work by Naphtali Herz ben Jacob Elhanan.</note> folio 23, column 3, in the 43rd chapter, under the title *Sha’ar Olam ha-Tohu* <note>The Gate of the World of Chaos.</note> with the following words: <note>original Hebrew: נתקנא הנחש באדם בסיבת חוה והטיל בה זוהמת הנדה ואחר כך השיאה לאכול הפרי וכשראתה שהיא נפלה ברשת יצר הרע בקשה להפיל גם לאדם ונתנה לו ואכל דכתיב ותתן גם לאישה עמה ויאכל ואחר שאכלם בלתי ידיעתו חזר ואכל עם ידיעתו מפני כי תכף שלט בו יצה"ר ואחר שאכל אותן ה' גבורות שהיו ממותקים בח' חסדים חזרו לתקפם וכשנכנס הפרי בבטנו מיד נתהווה בו יצה"ר והיא האכילה ג"כ לכל בעלי חי ונפלו כולם ברשתה חוץ מעוף אחד ששמו חול דכתיב וכחול ארבה ימים</note> that is: The serpent was jealous of Adam because of Eve, and cast into her the impurity of menstruation; thereafter he seduced her to eat of the (forbidden) fruit. After she had seen that she had fallen into the net of the <term>Yetzer hara</term> <note>The "evil inclination" or the innate human drive toward selfishness and sin.</note>, which is the evil and corrupt nature, she sought to make Adam fall as well, and gave some to him, and he ate, as it is written (Genesis 3:6): "And she gave also unto her husband with her; and he did eat." Now when he had eaten of it without his knowledge, he went back and ate of it knowingly, because immediately the *Yetzer hara*, or the evil nature, ruled in him. And once he had eaten them, the five <term>Gevurot</term> <note>Literally "powers" or "severities"; Kabbalistic attributes of judgment.</note>, which had been sweetened by the eight <term>Chasadim</term> <note>Attributes of "kindness" or "mercy."</note>, returned to their original strength. And after the fruit (which he had eaten) had entered his belly, the *Yetzer hara* arose within him. She (Eve) also gave all the animals to eat of it, and they all fell into her net, except for one bird named <term>Chol</term> <note>A mythical bird in Jewish tradition often identified with the Phoenix.</note>, as it is written (Job 29:18): "And I shall multiply my days as the *Chol*," that is, as the <term>Phoenix</term> bird, as it is understood here. These are the words of the book *Emek Hammelech*. However, the word *Chol* in this passage from Job signifies sand, and Job intended to say that he thought he would make his days many, like the sand of the sea—that is, that he would live a long time.

# Chapter VIII of the First Part of Judaism Discovered. #

<margin>Which one is the Phoenix.</margin>
Among the scriptural interpreters of the Jews, however, it must signify a bird that is said to be the Phoenix. This fable of such a bird also appears in Bechai’s <note>Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century Spanish rabbi and scholar.</note> commentary on the five books of Moses, in the portion *Bereshith* <note>The beginning of Genesis.</note> folio 13, column 2; and in the small *Yalkut Reuveni*, under the title *Chajoth* <note>Living Creatures.</note>, numbers 2 and 3; as well as in the book *Zeëna ureëna* <note>Tseno Ureno, a popular Yiddish prose work for women, often summarizing the Torah and legends.</note> folio 4, column 2. In this last book, one reads as follows: <note>original Yiddish: חוא זיא האט אן זידען חיות און עופות און בהמות און חיות פֿון דעם עץ הדעת צו עסן. און זיא האט רבֿי יודן פֿון וועגן רבֿי שמעון דער פֿוגל חול לעבט טויזנט יאר. און נאך טויזנט יאר דא ווערט זיין גוף פֿארדארבן און פֿעדערן פֿאלן אים ארויס און ער בלייבט אן אים אזוי גרויס וויא איין איי. דאס איז ער ווידר יונג.</note> That is: "And she (Eve) gave all the wild and tame animals, and the birds as well, to eat from the apple. Rabbi Joden says, on behalf of Rabbi Simeon: the bird Chol lives for a thousand years; and after a thousand years, its body is decayed and its feathers fall out, and it remains only as large as an egg; then it grows again and becomes young."

Regarding the mentioned monthly impurity of Eve, it is written in the aforementioned book *Emek Hammelech* <note>The Valley of the King, a Kabbalistic text.</note> folio 23, column 3, that this is the impure seed of the serpent—that is, the high devil Sammael—who had intercourse with Eve before Adam did; and the words read thus: <note>original Hebrew: נידה היא הזוהמא וזוהי הטמא של הנחש שבא על חוה קודם שבא עליה אדם</note> <margin>Eve’s monthly impurity is said to have come from the devil Sammael, who lay with her.</margin> That is: "Her (Eve’s) monthly impurity is the uncleanness and the impure seed of the serpent, which lay with Eve before Adam had lain with her." If this were the case, then Eve would have already sinned before she had eaten of the forbidden fruit. For if the serpent lay with her before Adam, then this must have happened—according to what was indicated above from the tractate *Sanhedrin* folio 38, column 2—in the seventh hour, because it was only in the tenth hour that the forbidden fruit was eaten. It is also read in the last-cited place that Eve was afflicted with her impurity when Adam lay with her, for it is written there: <note>original Hebrew: אדם הראשון שכב עם אשתו נידה</note> That is: "The first man lay with his wife while she was afflicted with her impurity."

<margin>Adam is said to have mingled with all the animals.</margin>
Furthermore, in the Talmudic tractate *Jevamot* (or *Yevamos*) folio 63, column 1, it is written of Adam that he lay with all the animals and mingled with them in a shameful manner before Eve was joined to him; there the words read as follows: <note>original Hebrew: אמר רבי אלעזר מאי דכתיב זאת הפעם עצם מעצמי ובשר מבשרי מלמד שבא אדם על כל בהמה וחיה ולא נתקררה דעתו עד שבא על חוה</note> That is: "Rabbi Eliezer said: what is it that is written (Genesis 2:23): 'This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh'? This teaches us that he lay with all cattle and wild beasts, but his mind was not satisfied until he lay with Eve."

# Of the Talmud. #

...until he lay with Eve. Although these words are interpreted quite differently not only by <margin>This has indeed been interpreted differently by some, but they have erred.</margin> some Christians (among whom is also the learned Buxtorf, as can be seen in his *Chaldaic-Talmudic-Rabbinic Lexicon* under the root-word <term>קרא</term> *Karár* <note>Johannes Buxtorf was a famous 17th-century Christian Hebraist; "Karar" or "Kara" is the Hebrew root for "to call" or "to encounter."</note>) but also by Jews—as can be read in Rabbi Lipmann's *Sépher Nizzáchon* <note>The *Sefer Nizzachon* or "Book of Victory" is a famous medieval Jewish apologetic work written to defend Judaism against Christian attacks.</note> number 9—and they wish to have it understood only that Adam went to all the animals and sought a wife but found none, and therefore his spirit was not satisfied, but not that he had carnally mixed with them: yet I am of a completely different opinion than others in this matter. I hold that the actual meaning of the Hebrew words is as I have translated them, just as the convert Hieronymus de sancta fide <note>A 15th-century Spanish physician and convert from Judaism who wrote against the Talmud.</note> understood them in his second book, chapter 1, page 134, as well as the convert Victor von Carben in his *Book of the Jews*, in the seventh chapter. I prove this for the following reasons. Firstly, <margin>First proof.</margin> because Rabbi Salomon Jarchi <note>Commonly known as Rashi, the most influential medieval Jewish commentator on the Bible and Talmud.</note> himself interpreted it so in his commentary on it, where he reports: <term>זאת הפעם מכלל דפעמים אחרים שמש ולא נתקררה דעתו</term> <note>original Hebrew: "This time [implies] from the rule that at other times he had intercourse, but his mind was not cooled [satisfied]."</note> that is, "The words *this is now* were said after he had slept with others (previously), but those (acts of intercourse) were not according to his mind (and did not satisfy him)." And he explains the word <term>בא</term> <note>meaning "came" or "entered," often used euphemistically.</note> which stands in the mentioned Talmudic passage, through the word <term>שמש</term> *shimmesh*, which among the Rabbis means to sleep with [someone]. So it also stands in the book *Zeéna ureéna*, folio 3, column 4: <term>עטליכ' חכמים זאגן אדם הראשון זיין בייא אלן באשעפניש זיין געלעגן אונ' קיינר האט אים ניט געפאלן צו נעמן צו איין ווייב</term> <note>original Yiddish: "Some wise men say the first man lay with all creatures and none pleased him to take as a wife."</note>: Some wise men say the first man lay with all creatures, and none pleased him enough to take as a wife.

"And when I grew up, I went out to see the oppression of my brothers, and I saw an Egyptian man striking a Hebrew man from among my brothers; and I killed him and hid him in the sand. He struck me ten times, but the Holy One, blessed be He, performed a miracle for me, and my neck became like a pillar of marble, and the sword had no power over me. That is: "After I had become grown, I went out to see the oppression of my brothers, and saw an *Egyptian* man who struck a Hebrew man from among my brothers, and I struck him dead and hid him in the sand."

But after he repented, another staff from the Tree of Life was given to him.** <margin>Regarding what kind of tree the staff of Moses was from.</margin> <note>In Jewish mysticism, Matatron is often the supreme archangel, while Sammael is an angelic figure representing severity or the "accuser." The striking of the rock refers to the event in Numbers 20, where Moses was punished for not following God's exact command.</note> The same is also to be found in the aforementioned *New Collection* <note>original: "Jalkut chádasch"</note> folio 130, column 1, under the title "Moses," number 73.

This same angel also lay with the wife of Ham, the son of Noah, at the very time they were to enter the Ark; and she became pregnant and gave birth to Sihon (who became the King of the Amorites, as read in Numbers 21:21) within the Ark; he was Og's brother.**

<margin>Where the giants come from.</margin> It is also claimed that all giants trace their origin to those angels cast out from heaven, concerning which it is written in the *Chapters of Rabbi Eliezer* <note>original: "Rabbi Eliesers Capiteln", also known as Pirkei De-Rabbi Eliezer</note>, in the 22nd chapter, as follows: **That is: The Rabbi says, the angels who had fallen from heaven, the place of their holiness, saw the daughters of Cain walking about with their nakedness exposed, their eyes painted like harlots; and they went astray after them and took wives from among them, as it is said: "And the sons of God saw the daughters of men," etc. Rabbi Zadok says: From them were born the giants who walk with a towering stature.**

# Of the Talmud.

...the radiance of his countenance was like his. But in the following, on folio 83, column 1, number 50, it is reported: <note>original: "בקש להרוג את אליעזר וראה שהיה נוטל ב' גמלים בב' ידיו ומעבירן את הנחל כיון שראו כך אמרו אין אנו יכולין להרגו והניחו לפניו קערה וסם המות בתוכה וזכות אברהם ברתהלפה הקערה ואכל בתואל ממנה ומת שנאמר ויושם לפניו לאין מיושם אלא לשון סם: ומפני מה מת בתואל שהיה דרכו לבעול כל בתולה שנכנסה לחופה וכשבינס את רבקה נתכנסו כל השרים ואמרו נראה אם יעשה כן לבתו ואם לאו נהרוגו לכך מת שניצל אליעזר ורבקה:"</note> **He (Laban) sought to kill Eliezer and saw that he was taking two camels in his two hands and carrying them across the river. When they saw this, they said: "We cannot kill him." And they placed a bowl before him with poison in it. But the merit of Abraham caused the bowl to be switched, and Bethuel ate from it and died, as it is said: "And it was set before him" [Genesis 24:33]. "Vajusam" [it was set] means nothing other than "Sam" [poison]. And why did Bethuel die? Because it was his custom to sleep with every virgin who entered the bridal canopy. And when he brought Rebecca [his daughter] in, all the princes gathered and said: "Let us see if he will do this to his own daughter; if not, we will kill him." Therefore, he died so that Eliezer and Rebecca would be saved.** 

This is to say: He (Laban) sought to kill *Eliezer* <note>Abraham’s servant, sent to find a wife for Isaac</note>; however, he saw that he took two camels in his hands and carried them across the river. When they (Laban and those with him) saw this, they said: "We cannot kill him," and they placed a bowl before him containing poison. But because of the merit of Abraham, the bowls were switched, and Bethuel <note>Rebecca’s father</note> ate from it and died. As it is said in Genesis 24, verse 33: *Vajusam lefanáv leechól*, that is: "And there was set before him to eat." The word *Musam* (which means "set before") is said to mean nothing other than *Sam*, which is poison. Why did Bethuel die, however? Because it was his custom to sleep with every young woman who held a wedding. Now, when he held his own daughter's wedding, all the princes gathered and said: "We shall see if he will deal with his daughter in this manner; if he does not, we will kill him." Therefore, he died so that Eliezer and Rebecca would be rescued. Is this not a frivolous distortion of the Scripture, that from the word *vajusam*, which means "and it was set before," one wants to force the meaning that they intended to present Eliezer with poison, simply because the word ends in *Sam*, which means poison?

<margin>
Laban intended to kill Eliezer with poison, but Bethuel ate it and died.
</margin>

<margin>
Why he died.
</margin>

We read in Genesis 7, verses 19, 20, 21, and 22, that through the waters of the <term>Deluge|The Great Flood of Noah</term> all high mountains under the entire heaven were covered, and that it rose fifteen cubits above them; also that everything that had the breath of life on dry land and was not in the Ark—both humans and other creatures—died. The <term>Talmud|The central body of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</term>, however, teaches in the tractate *Niddah*, folio 61, column 1, that Og also remained alive at that time; where, concerning the words of Genesis 14, verse 13, **"Then one who had escaped came and told it to Abraham the Hebrew,"** it is written thus: <note>original: "אמר רבי יוחנן זה עוג שפלט מדור המבול"</note> That is: Rabbi Jochanan has said, this is Og, who escaped from the generation of the Flood (and was kept alive by the water). Rabbi Salomon Jarchi <note>Also known as Rashi (1040–1105), the most famous medieval commentator on the Torah</note> also includes this in his interpretation of the First Book of Moses regarding the said verse, but adds this as well: <note>original: "לפי פשוטו זה עוג שפלט מן המלחמה"</note> [According to its plain meaning, this is Og who escaped from the war.]

**They said: If the waters of the flood come upon us, we are of great height, and the water will not reach our necks. He made the water of the abyss boiling hot, so that it scalded their flesh and peeled the skin off them, as is said in **Job 6, verse 17**: *At the time when they burn from the heat, they are destroyed; and when it becomes hot, they vanish from their place.* Read not *bechymmó*, that is, "when it becomes hot," but *bechammemó*, that is, "when He makes it hot." <note>This is a classic Rabbinic interpretation technique called "Al Tikrei" (do not read), where a word's vowels are changed to reveal a deeper or alternate meaning in the biblical text.</note>

### Chapter VIII of the First Part of *Judaism Uncovered*. ###

<margin>How long the grave of Shem was.</margin> ...it is said that he traveled through the land of King Og and saw a grave there which was eighty cubits <note>An "Ell" or cubit is an ancient unit of length, roughly 18–22 inches.</note> long; he was told it was the grave of Shem, the son of Noah. Furthermore, he reports in the aforementioned booklet that a human backbone hangs at the castle in Jerusalem which is four fathoms <note>A "Klaffter" or fathom is about 6 feet.</note> long. In the <term>Jalkut Schimóni<gloss>A medieval midrashic anthology on the Hebrew Bible</gloss></term> concerning the Lamentations of Jeremiah, on page 166, column 3, number 1001, it is also read that when the Chaldeans <note>The Babylonians who besieged Jerusalem.</note> besieged Jerusalem, there was a brave hero in Jerusalem at that time, of whom the following is boasted: <margin>What kind of human backbone hung in Jerusalem.</margin> <note>original Hebrew: היו גבורים בירושלים עד אין חקר והיו נלחמים עם הכשדים ומפילים מהם חללים הרבה והיה שם גבור אחד ושמו אביקא בן גבתרי כשהיו אנשי החיל מקלעים באבנים גדולות להפיל החומה היה מקבלם בידו ומשליכן על בני החיל והורג מהם הרבה עד שהתחיל לקבל האבנים ברגלו והיה מחזירן לחיל וגרם העון ובאה הרוח והפילתו מן החומה ונבקע ומת באותה שעה נבקעה ירושלים ונכנסו הכשדים : .b. i.</note>

<margin>What mighty heroes were in Jerusalem.</margin> In Jerusalem there were heroes beyond counting, and they fought against the Chaldeans and slew many of them whom they had wounded. There was a hero there named Afika, the son of Gasteri; and when the (Chaldean) soldiers slung great stones to knock down the city wall, he caught them with one hand and threw them (back) at the soldiers, killing many of them: until he began to catch the stones with his foot and throw them back into the army. But sin caused a wind to come and cast him down from the wall, so that he burst asunder and died. In that same hour, Jerusalem was breached and the Chaldeans entered. It is also written in the book <term>Zeéna ureéna<gloss>Tze'enah uRe'enah, a popular Yiddish-language commentary on the Torah used primarily by women</gloss></term>, page 108, column 1, under the title *Chórban* <note>The Destruction of the Temple.</note>, that when a Roman Emperor besieged the city of Turmålka <note>A legendary Jewish city, often identified as the "King's Mountain" or Har HaMelekh.</note>, there was a great hero named Bar Deróma among the Jews, who could leap an entire mile in a single bound and slew all the Roman people within a mile's distance: along with many other crude and nonsensical fictions to be found there. And in the <term>Máase-Buch<gloss>The Mayse Bukh, a collection of Jewish folktales and legends</gloss></term>, in the 145th chapter, it is reported of Joab that he took the Ammonite city of Rabboth alone and slew many therein, alongside which are found unheard-of lies.

<margin>What great birds, fish, and four-footed animals are described in the Talmud.</margin> Having seen thus far what palpable lies are found in the Talmud and some other Rabbinic books concerning giants and heroes, we will now also consider what foolish fables they shamelessly present regarding great birds, fish, and four-footed beasts. Concerning the birds, it is written in the Talmudic tractate <term>Bechorôth<gloss>A tractate of the Talmud dealing with the firstborn of humans and animals</gloss></term>, page 57, column 2, of a bird called *Bar júchne*: <note>original Hebrew: פעם אחת נפלה ביצת בר יוכני וטבעה ששים כרכים ושברה שלש מאות ארזים ומי שדיא ליה</note> Once the egg of the *Bar júchne* fell and drowned sixty cities and broke three hundred cedars.

### Concerning the Talmud. ###

<margin>Of a great egg of the bird Bar Juchne.</margin>
<note>original Hebrew: אמר רבי אשי ההיא מוזרתא הוא : ליה וזא כתיב כנף רננים נעלסה</note> that is: **Once, the egg of the Bar Juchne fell (out of the nest) and flooded sixty villages, and broke three hundred cedar trees. How so? Did he throw it away? For it is written (Job 39:13, or according to others verse 16): "The wing of the (bird) Renanim flaps joyfully"** (and here, according to the interpretation of <term>Rabbi Solomon<gloss>Refers to Rashi, the famous 11th-century commentator</gloss></term>, the word *Renanim* signifies the bird Bar Juchne; which, however, is a great error, for it refers to peacocks, which are so named for their cry, since *Ranán* means to cry out.) **Rabbi Ashi has said that the same (egg) was worthless and rotten.** It must therefore have been a terrifyingly large bird to have laid such a large egg.

<margin>Of the great bird, which is called Sis.</margin>
Furthermore, concerning a great bird called Sis, it is written in the tractate <term>Bava Batra<gloss>A section of the Talmud dealing with civil law, which often includes legendary stories (Aggadah)</gloss></term> (or Bovo bafro) folio 73, column 2, as follows: <note>original Aramaic: אמר רבה בר בר חנה זימנא חדא הוה אזלינן בספינתא וחזינן ההוא ציפרא דקאים עד קרצוליה במיא ורישיה ברקיע ואמרינן ליכא מיא ובעינן ליהותי לאקורי נפשין ונפק בת קלא ואמר לן לא תיחתו הכא דנפלא ליה חציצא לבר נגרא הא שב שני ולא קא מטיא ארעא לאו משום דנפישי מיא אלא משום דردפי מיא אמר רב אשי ההוא זיז שדי הוא דכתיב וזיז שדי עמדי :</note> that is: **Rabba, the grandson of Channa, said: We were once traveling in a ship and saw a bird that stood in the water up to its shins, and its head reached the firmament of heaven. Then we said: "There is no (deep) water there; let us climb in and cool ourselves." But a voice came from heaven (which, as already mentioned above, is called <term>Bath kol<gloss>Literally "Daughter of a Voice," a divine echo or revelation</gloss></term>) and said to us: "Do not climb in there, for seven years ago a carpenter's axe fell in there, and it has not yet reached the ground (or the bottom); not because there is so much water there (and it is so very deep), but because the current is so strong (that it cannot sink straight down)." Rabbi Ashi said: "That same bird is the Sis of the field, of which it is written (Psalm 50:11): 'The Sis of the field is with me'"** (that is, as Rabbi Solomon mentions in his interpretation of it in the Talmud, it is close to me because its head reaches the firmament and thus is said to be near God. In the Chaldean <note>Refers here to the Aramaic Targum (translation) of the Bible.</note> translation of these words, this bird is called *Tárnegol bára*, that is, **the wild cock**, and it reads as follows: <note>original Aramaic: תרנגול ברא דקרצוליה שריין בארעא ורישיה מטי בשמיא מרנן קדמו :</note> that is: **The wild cock, whose shins are upon the earth, but its head reaches to heaven, sings before me.** <margin>The same is also called a wild cock.</margin> However, the word Sis is understood in the Talmud in a foolish manner as such a large bird, when it usually signifies all animals that move in the field, as it [derives] from the root...

# The Eighth Chapter of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked. #

The root word <term>Ziz<gloss>A giant, mythical bird from Jewish tradition, said to be large enough to block out the sun</gloss></term> originates from a word meaning "to move," as <term>Rabbi Solomon<gloss>Known as Rashi (1040–1105), a premier medieval commentator on the Bible and Talmud</gloss></term> explains in his commentary on the Psalms regarding the cited passage, Psalm 50:11, where he writes: <note>original Hebrew: וזיו השדה זו על שם שהם זיזים ממקום למקום</note> that is: **The creatures of the field are called Ziz because they move from one place to another.** Regarding this bird, the following is also written in <term>Leviticus Rabbah<gloss>An ancient collection of homilies and folklore related to the Book of Leviticus</gloss></term>, in the twenty-second section, folio 155, column 4, as well as in Rabbi David Kimchi's *Book of Roots*, under the word *Ziz*: <note>original Hebrew: אמר רבי יהודה בר סימון בשעה שהוא פורש את כנפיו מכסה גלגל חמה... ולמה נקרא שמו זיז שיש בו כמה מיני טעם מזה ומזה :</note> <margin>He is said to darken the sun with his wings.</margin> that is: **Rabbi Judah, the son of Simon, said that when this bird spreads its wings, it darkens the orb of the sun; and this is what is written in Job 39:26 (or according to others verse 29): "Does the hawk fly by your wisdom, and spread its wings toward the south?" But why is it called Ziz? Because it has many kinds of flavors, from this and that.** <note>The name Ziz (זיז) is here explained as a pun on the Hebrew word "Zeh," meaning "this," implying the bird's meat contains every possible flavor.</note> This Ziz is said to be the aforementioned bird <term>Juchne<gloss>Also known as Bar Juchne, another legendary bird of immense proportions</gloss></term>, as will be shown below in the 15th chapter of the second part, from the commentary of Abraham ibn Ezra on Daniel 12:3.

In the mentioned section of the tractate <term>Bava Batra<gloss>A section of the Talmud dealing with property law, which also contains many "tall tales" or allegories known as Aggadah</gloss></term>, on folio 73, column 2, immediately following what was previously cited, there are also tall tales told regarding large fat geese, where the following is written: <note>original Aramaic: אמר רבה בר בר חנה זימנא חדא הוה קא אזלינן במדברא... עתידין ישראל ליתן עליהן את הדין :</note> <margin>Concerning large fat geese.</margin> that is: **Rabba, the grandson of Channa, said: Once we were walking in a desert and saw geese whose feathers were falling out because of their fatness, and streams of oil flowed from beneath them. I said to them: "Do we have a portion of you in the World to Come?" (that is, when the Messiah arrives). Then one lifted its wing, and another lifted its leg (to indicate: "this is your portion in the future world," as Rabbi Solomon explains). When I came before Rabbi Eleazar, he said to me: "The Israelites must one day give an account because of these geese" (since, through their sins, they cause the Messiah to delay his coming for so long, and these geese must suffer the pain of their excessive fat for that much longer, as the mentioned Rabbi Solomon Jarchi interprets it).**

<margin>Concerning a giant raven, frog, and a snake.</margin> Furthermore, in the same part of the Talmud, a large raven, a frog, and a snake are mentioned, of which the words go as follows: <note>original Aramaic: אמר רבה בר בר חנה לדידי חזיא ההיא אקרוקתא דהויא כי אקרא דהגרוניא... וסליק יתיב באילנא חזי כמה נפיש חיליה דאילנא</note> **Rabba bar bar Channa said: I myself saw a frog that was as large as the fortress of Hagronia <note>A town in Babylonia near Nehardea</note>; and how large was the fortress of Hagronia? It contained sixty houses. Then a snake came and swallowed the frog. Then a giant raven came and swallowed the snake, and went and sat in a tree. See how great the strength of that tree must have been!**

<margin>...as well as a tree.</margin>
<note>original Hebrew: דאילנא אמר רב פפא בר שמואל אי לא דהואי התם לא הימיני</note> that is: **Rabba, the grandson of Channa, said: I myself saw a frog which was as large as the village of Akra in Hagronia.** <note>Hagronia was a district in Babylonia near Nehardea.</note> How large then was the village of Akra in Hagronia? **Sixty houses.** There came a snake and swallowed the frog; after that came a raven and swallowed the snake, and flew onto a tree and perched upon it. See how great the strength of this tree must have been! **Rav Papa, the son of Samuel, said: If I had not been there myself, I would not have believed it.** This tree, however, must surely have been one <margin>Concerning another large tree.</margin> of those cedar trees of which it is written in the <term>Talmudic Tractate Bechorot<gloss>A section of the Talmud dealing primarily with the laws of firstborn animals and humans</gloss></term> (or Bechoros), folio 57, column 2: <note>original Hebrew: פעם אחת נפל ארז אחד שבמקומנו ועברו שש עשרה קרונות על חודו</note> that is: **Once a cedar tree fell which was in our place, and sixteen wagons passed over its sharp edge** (that is, as <term>Rabbi Solomon<gloss>Rashi, the famous 11th-century commentator</gloss></term> explains it: it was so wide that sixteen wagons could drive upon it side by side). Yet such a tree would still likely have been too small and too weak to hold such a massive raven.

<margin>Concerning large fish.</margin>
As far as large fish are concerned, it is written of one such creature in the previously mentioned place in the <term>Tractate Bava Batra<gloss>The "Last Gate," a section of the Talmud dealing with civil law, which also contains many legendary tales known as Aggadah</gloss></term>, folio 73, column 2: <note>original Hebrew: אמר רבה בר בר חנה זימנא חדא הוה קא אזלינן בספינתא וחזינן ההוא כוורא דיתבא ליה אכלתא טינא באוסייה וארדפוהי מיא ושדייה לגודא וחרוב מיניה שיתין מחוזי ואכול מיניה שיתין מחוזי ומלחו מיניה שיתין מחוזי ומלאו מחד גילגלא דעיניה תלת מאה גרבי משחא וכי הדרן לבתר תריסר ירחי שתא חזינן דהוה קא מנסרי מגרמיה מטללתא ויתבי למבנינהו הנך מחוזי</note> that is: **Rabba, the grandson of Channa, said: We were once traveling on a ship, and we saw a fish in whose nostril was a certain worm** (which is otherwise called <term>kilbith<gloss>A small fish or parasite mentioned in the Talmud that was believed to enter the ears or noses of giant sea creatures, causing their death</gloss></term>, and it attaches itself to the ears or noses of large fish, from which they die); **and the water drove it** (because it was dead) **and cast it upon the shore, and thereby sixty cities were devastated** (because the water threw it against the land with such great force that the cities lying on the shore were smashed); **and sixty cities ate from it, and sixty cities salted meat from it, and they filled three hundred barrels of fat from one of its eyeballs.
