What Rabbi Bechai writes of the aforementioned large fish.
</margin>
Indeed, the Jews / when one confronts them with these little fables of the fish / might venture to say / that they are not to be understood according to the letter; however, one can meet them with this / and give as an answer / that indeed the very famous scholar among them, <term>Rabbi Bechai<gloss>Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century Spanish rabbi and kabbalist known for his commentary on the Torah</gloss></term>, in his commentary on the five books of Moses / folio 7 column 2 / on the words Genesis 1:21 "And <term>Elohim<gloss>A Hebrew name for God</gloss></term>, that is / God created great <term>tanninim<gloss>Often translated as sea monsters, dragons, or whales</gloss></term>, that is / whales / takes all of this literally / and according to the literal meaning / where he writes thus:

<note>original Hebrew: על דרך הפשט דגים הם ולהפלגת גודל גופם יחס הבריאה לאלהים כשם שתמצא באדם שיחס הכתוב בריאתו לאלהים הוא שכתוב ויברא אלהים את האדם בצלמו. והכוונה כי הבורא ית' המציא הגופים הגדולים ההם יש מאין. וחכמי הפלוסופים כתבו בספריהם שידעו מהם ארוכים חמש מאות פרסה. גם רבותינו חכמי התלמוד ספרו לנו הפלגות במסכת בבא בתרא והוא שהעיד רבה בר בר חנה וגו' : ופסוק מלא הוא יורדי הים באניות עושי מלאכה במים רבים המה ראו מעשה ה' וגו' :</note>

That is / According to the literal understanding, the word *tanninim* signifies fish / but because of their excessive size, their creation is attributed to *Elohim*, that is / God (which word sometimes signifies a greatness) / just as you find with man / that the Scripture assigns his creation to *Elohim* / as (Genesis 1:27) is written: And *Elohim*, that is / God created man in His image: The purpose is / that the blessed Creator created those same large bodies (of the fish) out of nothing.

They grow for it food for the meal of the righteous, and it eats. What is the reason? And Sharon shall be for a fold of flocks. And the Rabbis say: It is one beast and it crouches upon a thousand mountains, and those thousand mountains grow for it various kinds of animals, and it eats them. What is the reason? As it is said: "And all the beasts of the field play there." And is it possible for one beast to eat another? <note>This refers to the giant ox Behemoth eating other animals, which seems contradictory for a bovine creature.</note> Rabbi Tanchuma said: Great are the works of God, how wondrous are the works of the Holy One, blessed be He! <margin>Where such an ox finds its food.</margin>
Resh Lakisch has said: it is an animal that lies on a thousand mountains, and the thousand mountains bring forth food for it, from the food intended for the righteous, and it eats the same. From where is this proven? (Because in Isaiah 65:10 it stands written:) **And Sharon shall be a dwelling for the flock.** Our Rabbis, however, say: it is an animal that lies on a thousand mountains, and those same thousand mountains raise for it various species of animals, and it eats them. From where is this proven? Because (in Job 40:20) it is said: **And all the wild animals play there.** This is also possible, for there are animals that eat others. Rabbi Tanchuma has said: the works of God are great; how diverse are the works of the holy and blessed **GOD**!

<margin>From where it receives its drink, and how much it takes in one gulp.</margin>

From where is this proven? (Since in Job 40:23 it is said:) **He trusts that he can drink the Jordan into his mouth, etc.** Rabbi Simeon, the son of Jochai, teaches that a river goes out from Paradise which is called *Yuval*, and that he drinks from the same. From where is this proven? Since (in Jeremiah 17:8) it is said: **And is rooted by the Yuval (that is, the stream).** In the commentary of Rabbi Menachem of Recanati <note>Menahem Recanati, an early 14th-century Italian rabbi and kabbalist</note> on the Five Books of Moses, in the section *Bereshith* <note>The first portion of Genesis</note>, folio 10, column 3, the following is also mentioned—

Then he called upon God for mercy, and He returned him to his place. This must indeed have been a terrifyingly great lion to have been able to roar in such a cruel fashion.

<margin>Judah is said to have roared just as terrifyingly, whereupon the same thing occurred.</margin>
However, it was not only this lion who could roar so dreadfully; for in the *Sepher hajaschar* <note>The "Book of Jasher," a medieval collection of Jewish legends and biblical expansions</note>, in the section *Vajiggash* <note>Hebrew for "And he drew near," referring to the weekly Torah portion covering the confrontation between Judah and Joseph in Genesis 44</note>, it is read concerning Judah that when Joseph, being in Egypt, did not wish to let his brother Benjamin go, Judah, along with his other brothers, began to fight with the Egyptians and roared in such a way, of which the words there read as follows:

<note>original Hebrew: וירא יהודה את כל אנשי מצרים סובבים אותם במצות יוסף להפחידם... (The text describes Judah's supernatural roar during his confrontation with Joseph in Egypt.)</note>
And Judah saw all the Egyptian men who had surrounded them at Joseph’s command to strike fear into them. Joseph, however, had commanded them, saying: "Do not touch any of them." Then Judah hurried and drew his sword and cried out with a very great and bitter cry, and he struck with his sword and stomped upon the earth, and Joseph cried out again against all the men. When he did this thing, the Lord caused the fear of Judah and his brothers to fall upon all the warriors and all the men who were around them; and they all fled because of the sound of the cry and the terror; and they fell one over the other, so that many of them died as they fell, and they all fled from Judah and his brothers and from Joseph. While they were fleeing, Judah and his brothers pursued them even to Pharaoh’s house, but they all escaped. Then Judah sat before Joseph and roared at him like a lion, and cried out against him with a very great and bitter cry, so that the same cry was heard from a great distance, and all who dwelt in Sukkot <note>A biblical region in Egypt</note> heard it. Also, the entire land of Egypt shook and trembled at the sound of the cry, and all the walls in Egypt and in the land of Goshen fell down from the quaking of the earth. King Pharaoh also fell from his throne onto his face to the ground; and furthermore...

That is: And Judah saw all the Egyptian men who had surrounded them at Joseph's command to strike fear into them. Joseph, however, had commanded them that they should not touch any of them. Then Judah hurried and drew his sword and cried out very loudly and bitterly, and he struck with his sword, and also leaped upon the earth, and cried out once more against those same men. Now, when he did this, God let the fear of Judah and his brothers fall upon all the heroes and all the men who had surrounded them, and they all took to flight because of the sound of the cry and the fear; and one fell over the other, so that many of them died when they fell, and all fled before Judah and his brothers and before Joseph. <margin>
Concerning a great turnip, as well as a mustard and cabbage stalk.
</margin>
Since the preceding sections have dealt with giant humans, birds, fish, and four-footed animals, I must also mention here something regarding great plants of the earth, which are extravagantly claimed in the Talmud. In the tractate *Ketubot* (or *Kesuvos*) <note>The volume of the Talmud dealing with marriage contracts</note>, *folio 111, column 2*, it is written as follows concerning a great turnip, a branch of a mustard stalk, and a cabbage stalk:

> <note>original Hebrew: אמרו עתידה חטה שתהא כשתי כליות של שור הגדול ואל תתמה שהרי שועל קנן בלפת ושקלוהו ומצאו בו ששים ליטרא של ציפורי תניא אמר רב יוסף מעשה בשיחין באחד שהניח לו אביו שלשה בדי חרדל ונפשח בו אחת מהן וצרו ממנה תשעה קבין של חרדל ועציו סיככו בו סוכת יוצרין אמר רבי שמעון בן חלפתא קלח של כרוב הניח לנו אבא והיינו עולים ויורדים בו בסולם :</note>
> <note>Translation of the Hebrew: They said: In the future, a grain of wheat will be as large as the two kidneys of a great ox; and do not wonder at this, for behold, a fox once made its nest in a turnip, and they weighed it and found it to be sixty pounds of the Sepphoris weight. It was taught that Rav Joseph said: It happened in Shikhin that a certain man's father left him three branches of mustard, and one of them was split and they gathered from it nine kabs of mustard; and its wood was used to roof a potter’s hut. Rabbi Simeon ben Halafta said: Our father left us a cabbage stalk, and we would go up and down it by a ladder.</note>

That is: It is said that in the future (in the time of the *Messiah*) a grain of wheat will be as large as the two kidneys of a great ox. Do not wonder at this, however, for see, a fox once made its lair in a turnip (which he had hollowed out and kept his young within), and they weighed it and found (although it was hollow) that it weighed sixty pounds according to the Cyprian weight <note>The Hebrew text specifies the weight used in the city of Sepphoris (Tzippori), though the German translator refers to it as "Cyprian."</note>. We learn that *Rav Joseph* said it occurred among the bushes that his father left him three branches of a mustard plant, one of which was split (and threshed), and they found nine *kab* <note>An ancient Hebrew measure of volume; the author notes it holds as much as twenty-four chicken eggshells</note> of mustard seeds; from the wood of the same, they covered a potter's hut. Rabbi *Simeon*, the son of *Halafta* <note>Written here as "Tachalifa"</note>, said: "Our father left us a cabbage stalk, and we climbed up and down it (to break off the leaves) with a ladder."

Furthermore, there are many more shameless lies in the *Talmud*, some of which I will show here. # On the Talmud

<note>original Hebrew: שדורא לספינתא הוה הנחו ציפרי מלוחי בהדן אותבינהו עלייהו שקלוה ופרחו להו כהדיה : (Translation: [The stone] was the ballast of the ship; we placed salted birds upon them [the stones], and they took them and flew away with them.)</note>
That is: Rabbi Judah the Hindu related: We were once traveling in a ship and saw a gemstone which a snake had encircled (or surrounded). When a man who was a skilled rower went down (into the water) to retrieve it, the snake came and intended to swallow the ship. Then (the master of the rowers) took the same gemstone and threw it into the ship. We had salted birds with us, and when the gemstone was placed upon them (to test whether they would also return to life), they took the stone and flew away with it.

<note>original Hebrew: רב יהודה הינדוא משתעי... (Translation: Rav Judah the Hindu related: Once we were traveling in a ship and we saw a gemstone which a serpent had surrounded...)</note>

<note>original Hebrew: שחזה לספינתא הוה הנחו ציפרי מלווי בהון אותיבהו עלוהי שקלוה ופרחו להו כחדוה (Translation: When he saw the ship, there were birds accompanying them; they placed [the stone] upon them, they took it and flew away as one.)</note>

That is, Rabbi Yehuda the Hindu related: We were once traveling in a ship and saw a gemstone which a snake had encircled. ### Chapter 8 of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked.

<note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: ותיב לסיפי' דכולהו... ויאמר יי' זעקת סדום ועמורה כי רבה</note>
And he <note>Eliezer, Abraham's servant</note> sat at the very end of them all. Someone said to him, "Who invited you here?" He replied, "You invited me." He then took the cloak of the one sitting next to him and ran outside, and he did the same to all of them until they all went out, and he alone ate the banquet. He saw a certain woman of the house who was bringing out bread in a jar; the matter was revealed, for they had smeared it with honey and placed it upon the top of the wall, and the hornets came and ate it. That is: There were four judges in <term>Sodoma</term> <note>Sodom</note>, who were liars, inciters of lies, falsifiers, and perverters of justice. If someone struck his companion's wife so that she suffered a miscarriage, they would say to him (namely, to the woman's husband): Give her to him (the attacker) so that he may make her pregnant again. If someone had cut off the ear of his companion's donkey, they would say to him (namely, to the owner of the donkey): Give it to him until the ear grows back again. If someone wounded his companion, they would say to him (the wounded person): Give him his wage, because he has let your blood <note>Bloodletting was a common medical practice; the perverse logic here is that the attacker performed a "service."</note>. 

Whoever crossed over the bridge gave four guilders, but whoever went through the water gave eight guilders. Once, a <term>fuller</term> <note>A cloth-worker who cleans and thickens fabric</note> came there, and they said to him, "Give four guilders." When he said to them, "I went through the water," they said to him, "If that is so, then give eight guilders, because you went through the water." 

<term>Eliezer</term>, the servant of <term>Abraham</term>, once came there, and they wounded him. When he came before the judge, the judge said to him, "Give him (the one who wounded you with blows) his wage, for he has let your blood." Then he (Eliezer) took a stone and wounded the judge with it. At this, the judge said to him, "What does this mean?" He replied to him, "Give to this person (the one who wounded me) the wage that is due to me from you (because I have struck you and made you bleed); thus I shall keep my guilders (which I otherwise should have paid)." 

They also had a <term>bedstead</term> in which they laid travelers; if someone was too long for it, they cut off his feet (so that he would fit into it); but if he was too short, they stretched him out <note>This is a Jewish parallel to the Greek myth of Procrustes and his bed.</note>. When Eliezer, Abraham’s servant, arrived there, they said to him, "Go and lie down in the bed." But he said to them, "From the time my mother died, I have made a vow that I will lie in no bed." 

When a poor man came there, everyone gave him a penny upon which his name was written, but they allowed no bread to reach him. When that same man died (of hunger), everyone came and took back his own (namely, his penny). They also had a custom among them that anyone who invited a person to a wedding would have his mantle or coat stripped off (and thus be robbed). ### Chapter 8 of the First Part of Judaism Unveiled.

<note>original: "מַחַשׁ חֵילֵיהּ... וְלֹא תְכַבֶּה אֶת נֵר יִשְׂרָאֵל"</note>
[The Hebrew text translates as:] "His strength weakened, and he killed him. This is what is written: *Then the men of David swore unto him, saying, Thou shalt go no more out with us to battle, that thou quench not the light of Israel.*" [2 Samuel 21:17]. This means: The holy, blessed God said to David: "How long will the sin be hidden in your hand? Because of you, the inhabitants of Nob, the city of the priests (as can be read in 1 Samuel 22:19), were killed. Because of you, Doeg the Edomite <note>A servant of King Saul who informed on David</note> was driven away. Because of you, Saul and his three sons were slain. Do you now wish for your lineage to come to an end, or that you be delivered into the hand of the enemy?" Then David spoke to Him: "Lord of the world, it is better that I be delivered into the hand of the enemy, and that my lineage does not cease."

One day David went hunting, and Satan came and appeared before him in the form of a deer. David shot an arrow at it, but he did not hit it (namely, the supposed deer). However, Satan caused David to follow him until he had brought him into the land of the Philistines.

<margin>How Ishbi sought to kill King David, and how it proceeded further.</margin>

When Ishbi of Nob <note>A giant and brother of Goliath, according to the Talmudic reading of 2 Samuel 21</note> saw him, he said: "This is the one who killed my brother, Goliath." He then bound him, set him down bent over, and threw him under a winepress (in order to crush him to death). But a miracle occurred for him, so that the earth beneath him became soft (and Ishbi could do him no harm). This is what is written (Psalm 18:37): *You have made my steps wide under me, so that my ankles do not waver.*

<margin>The Talmud also teaches that irrational animals, as well as mountains, hills, valleys, trees etc. can speak.</margin>
The Talmud further teaches in a foolish manner that not only irrational animals, but also mountains, hills, valleys, trees, and herbs are said to have particular languages which some individuals have understood. Regarding this, the following is written in the tractate *Sopherim*, folio 13, column 3, in the 16th chapter: <note>original: "אמרו עליו על הילל שלא עזב דברי חכמים שלא למדם אפילו כל הלשונות אפילו שיחת הרים וגבעות ובקעות שיחת עצים ועשבים שיחת חיות ובהמות שיחת שדים ומשלות הכל למד:" — "They said of Hillel that he did not neglect any words of the Sages without learning them: even all the languages, even the speech of mountains, hills, and valleys; the speech of trees and herbs; the speech of wild and domestic animals; the speech of demons and parables; he learned them all."</note> that is: It is said of *Hillel* <note>Hillel the Elder was one of the most important Jewish sages in history, active in the 1st century BCE.</note> that he left no words of the Sages unstudied, but learned them all: Indeed, even the conversation of the mountains and the hills, as well as the valleys; the conversation of trees and herbs; the conversation of cattle and wild animals; the conversation of devils <note>The Hebrew term *shedim* refers to spirits or demons; here it suggests a supernatural knowledge of all realms.</note>; and the parables—he learned all of them together.

And in the Talmudic tractate *Succah*, folio 28, column 1, it is said of *Rabbi Jochanan*, the son of *Saccai* <note>Better known as Johanan ben Zakkai, a primary contributor to the core of the Mishnah.</note>, that he understood the conversation of the ministering angels, as well as that of the devils and the date-palm trees. In the *Maase-Buch* <note>The *Maase-Buch* (Book of Stories) was a famous collection of Jewish folktales and ethical legends, mostly written in Yiddish for a general audience.</note> it likewise states in the 143rd chapter concerning *Rabbi Channina* that he knew the seventy languages of men, as well as the languages of animals and birds. When he had preached to his disciples about the birds, a raven arrived and prayed to God to protect *Rabbi Channina* in the great wealth he would possess, at which the Rabbi was amazed; and many such foolish antics are to be found in the same chapter. Furthermore, in the aforementioned *Maase-Buch*, in the 114th chapter, citing the Talmudic tractate *Gittin*, it is reported of someone that he was knowledgeable in the seventy languages as well as the language of birds. In the same *Maase-Buch*, in chapter 156, one may also read about a conversation that the chickens and geese once held with one another. And in chapter 115 there, it is found how *Rabbi Meir* heard two snakes talking to each other, whom he understood. In the Talmudic tractate *Eruvin*, folio 18, column 2, it is written regarding the dove that Noah released, concerning the words of *Genesis 8, verse 11*: **"And behold, she had plucked off an olive leaf,"** as follows: <note>original: "אמרה יונה לפני הק"בה רבונו של עולם יהיו מזונותי מרורין כזית ומסורין בידך ואל יהיו מתוקין כדבש ותלויין ביד בשר ודם:" — "The dove said before the Holy One, Blessed be He: Master of the Universe, let my food be as bitter as an olive but given by Your hand, and let it not be as sweet as honey but dependent on the hand of flesh and blood."</note>

...when they have studied the Bible, they should deal with the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa <note>The third and final section of the Hebrew Bible (Tanakh), which includes books like Psalms and Proverbs.</note>; but when they have learned the *Mishna* <note>The first major written collection of the Jewish oral traditions, known as the "Oral Torah."</note>, they should deal with the *Mishna*, etc. And in the book *Menorat HaMaor* <note>original: "Menoráth hammaór"; a popular 14th-century work of religious ethics by Isaac Aboab.</note> it stands in folio 54, columns 2 and 3, in the 5th chapter, under the title *The Third Lamp, the Eighth Rule, the Third Part*, written from the book *Midrash Tanchuma*, that the Law <note>The Torah</note> weeps over those who teach and learn when they die: and that once the Talmudic tractate *Hagigah* <note>A tractate concerning festival offerings, here personified as a celestial being.</note> wept greatly over a deceased pious man in the form of a woman, and spoke with the people. But are these not mad Jewish dreams?

<margin>How one may attain the ability to understand the languages of all creatures.</margin>
How one might attain the ability to understand the languages of all creatures is shown in the little book *The Fountain of Wisdom* <note>original: "Maján hachóchma"; a short Kabbalistic text.</note>, which is said to have been given by the Angel Michael to Pali, and from Pali to Moses, in folio 2, column 2, where it is indicated that such can happen if one correctly understands the *Shem HaMephorash* <note>The "Explicit Name" of God, often associated with the 72-fold name in Jewish mysticism.</note>; and it is written there: <note>original Hebrew: "או הבין : מילת אדם ודיבור בהמה וצפצוף עופות ומילת חיות וצעקת כלבים וגו'. שיהיו שדים ושיחות מלאכי ה' המשרתים ושיחת דקלים ותנועות ימים וצירוף לבבות וחזון לשונות וחשבון כליות"</note> That is: Then you will understand the words of men, the speech of cattle, the chirping of birds, the words of wild beasts, and the howling of dogs, etc., the conversation of devils, and the conversation of the ministering angels of the Lord, the speech of palm trees, the movements of the seas, the composition of hearts, the murmuring of tongues, as well as the thoughts of the kidneys <note>In ancient thought, the kidneys were often viewed as the source of counsel or the seat of the conscience.</note>.

### Chapter VIII of the First Part of *Judaism Unmasked*.

<margin>What one should do when one wishes to drink water on Wednesday or Sabbath nights.</margin>
A person should not drink water on the nights of the fourth days (of the week, i.e., on Wednesday nights), nor on the nights of the Sabbaths; and if he drinks, his blood is upon his head (that is, he himself is to blame if a misfortune befalls him) because of the danger. What kind of danger is it? The evil spirit. But if he is thirsty, what remedy should he use (so that he may drink)? He should speak the seven "voices" over the water which David spoke, and thereafter drink, as is said (in Psalm 29, verses 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9): "The voice of the LORD is upon the waters: the God of glory thundereth, the LORD is upon many waters. The voice of the LORD is powerful; the voice of the LORD is full of majesty. The voice of the LORD breaketh the cedars; the LORD breaketh the cedars of Lebanon. The voice of the LORD divideth the flames of fire. The voice of the LORD shaketh the wilderness; the LORD shaketh the wilderness of Kadesh. The voice of the LORD maketh the hinds to calve, and discovereth the forests: and in his temple doth every one speak of his glory." If this is not possible (that is, if he does not wish to do this), he should speak thus: *Lul shafan anigron agärdefon* <note>original: "Lul schafan anigron agärdefon"; these are magical or "sorcerous" nonsense words used as a charm.</note> (which, as Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi (1040–1105), the famous medieval commentator.</note> writes concerning this, are sorcerous words). "I sit between the stars; I walk between lean and fat (people)." If this is not possible, and if a person is with him, he should turn to them and say: "You, N. N. <note>A placeholder for "Name," similar to "John Doe."</note> son of N. N., I am thirsty for water," and thereafter he may drink. If this is not possible, he should knock with a lid against a vessel and drink thereafter. If this is not possible, he should throw something into it and drink thereafter. Upon this further follows:

<note>original: ת"ר לא ישתה אדם מים לא מן הנהרות ולא מן האגמים בלילה ואם שתה דמו בראשו מפני הסכנה מאי סכנה סכנת שברירי ואי צחי מאי תקנתיה אי איכא איניש בהדיא לימא ליה פלניא בר פלניתא צחינא מיא ואי לא נימא איהו לנפשיה פלניא אמרה לי אימי איזהר משברירי ברירי רירי רירי רי צחינא מיא בכסי חיורי</note> Our Rabbis teach: A person should not drink water at night, neither from the rivers nor from the lakes (or ponds). But if he has drunk, his blood is upon his head, because of the danger. What kind of danger is it? The danger regarding blindness (or because of *Shabriri*, the angel of blindness). But if thirst is present, what remedy is there against it? If someone has another person with him, he should say to him: "You, N. N., son of N. N., I am thirsty for water." If, however, no one is with him, he should say to himself: "You, N. N., my mother said to me: beware of the *Shabriri, shabriri, riri, ri* <note>This is a "diminishing" incantation where the demon's name is shortened syllable by syllable to reduce its power.</note>; I am thirsty for water in white cups."

# Concerning the Talmud.

<margin>How Rabbi Akiva climbed a tree because of an imagined woman.</margin>
...laughed at those who had committed a transgression. But it happened one day that the Devil appeared to him in the form of a woman at the top of a palm tree. He grasped the tree and climbed up (to reach the supposed woman). When he was halfway up the palm tree, the Devil let him go <note>The sense here is that the Devil ceased the illusion or stopped tempting him further once he had proved his vulnerability.</note> and spoke (to him): "If it were not proclaimed in the firmament (that is, in heaven), 'Take care with Rabbi Akiva and his Law,' I would not value your life at even two pennies <note>original German: "zween Pfenning"</note>."

<margin>How Rabbi Meir was also tempted by an imagined woman.</margin>
The following is also found there concerning Rabbi Meir: <note>original Hebrew: "Rabbi Meir used to mock transgressors. One day Satan appeared to him in the guise of a woman on the other side of the river. As there was no ferry, he took hold of a rope and crossed. When he reached the middle of the rope, Satan let him go and said: 'If they were not proclaiming in heaven, "Be careful with Rabbi Meir and his Torah," I would have made your blood worth two ma'ah [small coins].'"</note> That is: Rabbi Meir laughed at those who had committed a transgression. It so happened that Satan appeared to him in the form of a woman on the other side of a river; and because there was no bridge (or ferry), he grabbed the rope (which was stretched across the river to pull the ferry back and forth) and crossed by it. When he reached the middle of the rope, (Satan) let him go and said: "If they were not calling out in heaven concerning you, 'Pay attention to Rabbi Meir and his Law,' I would not give two pennies for your life."

<margin>Further report of Rabbi Meir, in which Rabbi Tarpon is mentioned.</margin>
In the aforementioned place, in the second column, it is also read of the said Rabbi Meir that he did not trust himself to be alone with his daughter; likewise of Rabbi Tarpon, that he reminded his household they should not leave him alone with his <term>daughter-in-law|The original German uses the archaic term "Schnur" for a daughter-in-law</term>, and the words are as follows: <note>original Hebrew: "It is taught: Rabbi Meir said, 'Be careful of me because of my daughter.' And Rabbi Tarpon said, 'Be careful of me because of my daughter-in-law.' A certain student laughed at him. Rabbi Abhu said in the name of Rabbi Hanina ben Gamaliel: Not many days passed before that student stumbled with his mother-in-law, or even with an animal."</note> That is: We learn that Rabbi Meir said, "Pay attention to me because of my daughter" (lest I commit unchastity with her). And that Rabbi Tarpon said, "Pay attention to me because of my daughter-in-law." At this, a student laughed, and Rabbi Abhu said in the name of Rabbi Hanina, the son of Gamaliel, that a few days later that same student sinned with his mother-in-law, and even with a beast. These two Rabbis, Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Tarpon, must therefore have been very lustful men, since the former did not trust himself to be alone with his daughter, and the latter with his daughter-in-law.

# The First Part of Judaism Unmasked: Chapter 8.

...were men who had wives, yet when traveling to other places for business and staying for a short time, would each take another wife for that brief duration, whom they would then let go when they returned home. Concerning this, it is written in the Talmudic tractate *Joma* <note>Tractate Yoma 18b; this tractate primarily deals with the Day of Atonement, but includes various legal and biographical anecdotes.</note>, folio 18, column 2, as follows: <note>original Hebrew: "Rav ki mikla le-Darshish makhriz: man havei l'yoma? Rav Nachman ki mikla le-Shachneziv makhriz: man havei l'yoma?"</note> That is: When the *Raf* <note>term: Raf (Rav); a title for a prominent Babylonian teacher, specifically Abba Arika.</note> came to *Tharsiskam*, he had it proclaimed: "Who will be (my wife) for a few days?" When *Raf Nachman* came to *Schachnezibh*, he had it proclaimed: "Who will be (my wife) for a few days?" This is exactly how *Rabbi Salomon Jarchi* <note>term: Rabbi Salomon Jarchi; better known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French commentator on the Torah and Talmud.</note> himself explains it.

<margin>The marriage of Christians and other peoples is said to be no marriage at all.</margin>
By way of this subject, I must also point out here that the Rabbis consider the marriages of Christians, and all other peoples living outside of Judaism, to be no marriage at all. They hold the erroneous opinion that if a Jew lies with the wife of a Christian, he does not commit adultery. For *Rabbi Salomon Jarchi* writes in his commentary on the Five Books of *Moses*, regarding the words of *Leviticus 20:10*, "The man that committeth adultery with another man's wife, the adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be put to death," because he has committed adultery with his neighbor's wife, in this manner: <note>original Hebrew: "asher yinaf et eshet re'ehu—perat le-eshet nochri; lamednu she-ein kiddushin le-nochri."</note> That is: By the words "because he has committed adultery with **his neighbor's** wife," the wife of a stranger <note>original German: "Frembdlings"; here referring to a non-Jew.</note> (who is not the Jew's neighbor) is excluded; and this teaches us that the stranger has no valid betrothal. *Rabbi Bechai* <note>term: Rabbi Bechai; Bahya ben Asher (13th century), a Spanish rabbi and scholar known for his kabbalistic commentary on the Torah.</note> also teaches this in his commentary on the aforementioned words, folio 144, column 3, in the *Parashat Kedoshim* <note>term: Parashat Kedoshim; the weekly Torah portion spanning Leviticus 19:1–20:27.</note>. *Rabbi Levi ben Gerson* <note>term: Rabbi Levi ben Gerson; also known as Gersonides or Ralbag (1288–1344), a philosopher and commentator.</note> likewise writes concerning these words in his commentary, folio 164, column 1, in the last-mentioned *Parasha*, as follows: <note>original Hebrew: "magid she-lo yitchayev mitah ki im al eshet ben brit, ki lo yishlemu tana'ei ha-ishut be-zulat bnei brit."</note> That is: This indicates that one is not guilty of death except because of the wife of a "son of the covenant" (that is, an Israelite); for the conditions of marriage are not fulfilled among others who are not sons of the covenant. This is also confirmed in *Rabbi Moshe bar Maimon's* <note>term: Rabbi Moshe bar Maimon; Maimonides or Rambam (1138–1204).</note> book, which is called *Jad Chasaka* <note>term: Jad Chasaka; literally "The Strong Hand," another name for Maimonides' Mishneh Torah, his comprehensive code of Jewish law.</note>, in the second part, in the second chapter of the tractate concerning Kings and their Wars, numbers 2 and 3, where he teaches thus: <note>original Hebrew: "ben bo'el ishah be-kutiyutah im tekefo yitzro... ein eshet yifat toar muteret ela be-sha'at ha-shivyah... she-ein ishut le-kutim."</note> That is: Thus one may lie with a woman in her state of unbelief (that is, when she is not a Jewess), if his lust overcomes him. However, he should not lie with her and then leave, but rather bring her into his house. For it says: "And you see among the captives a beautiful woman..." <note>A reference to Deuteronomy 21:10–14 regarding a woman captured in war.</note> and it is forbidden to lie with her a second time until he has married her. A "beautiful woman" of this kind is only permitted at the time of captivity, whether she be a virgin, or previously married, or the wife of a man; for there is no [valid] marriage among the heathens <note>original German: "Kuthen" or "Kutiam"; Eisenmenger uses this term, which originally referred to Samaritans, as a general derogatory term for non-Jews.</note>.

### Of the Talmud.

...take her into his house, as it is said in (Deuteronomy 21:11): **And you see among the captives a beautiful woman.** It is forbidden to sleep with her a second time until he has married her. A "beautiful woman" is not permitted except at the time of captivity; she may be a virgin, or one who is no longer a virgin, or even another man’s wife. For the Cuthites <note>term: Cuthites; originally referring to the Samaritans, but used here by the author to imply Christians or other non-Jewish peoples.</note> (that is, the Christians and other peoples, as this word is taken here to mean *Gojim* <note>term: Gojim; Hebrew for "nations," often used to refer to non-Jews.</note>, as frequently happens among the Jews) have no [valid] marriage.

However, this worthless teaching—that Christians and other peoples have no marriage—is taken from the Talmudic tractate *Sanhedrin*, folio 52, column 2. There, regarding the words of Leviticus 20:10, **The man that committeth adultery with another man’s wife, even he that committeth adultery with his neighbor’s wife, the adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be put to death,** it is taught: <note>original Hebrew: "Perat le-eshet acherim"</note> that is, the wives of "others" (that is, of the *Gojim* or Christians, as *Rabbi Salomon* <note>term: Rabbi Salomon; refers to Rashi (1040–1105), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator.</note> explains it) are excepted or excluded. And the aforementioned *Rabbi Salomon* further writes regarding this: <note>original Hebrew: "Ashmeinan she-ein kiddushin le-goi"</note> that is, "We learn from this that a *Goi* (or Christian) has no [valid] marriage." This is also to be found in the *Tosephtot* <note>term: Tosephtot; the "Additions" or "Supplements," referring here to the Tosafot, medieval commentaries on the Talmud.</note> in the same place. We see from this that Friedrich Samuel Brentz, in his *Jewish Snake-Skin* <note>term: Jüdischer Schlangenbalg; a polemical work written in 1610 by Brentz, a Jewish convert to Christianity, attacking his former faith.</note>, in the fourth chapter, writes the truth when he reports that the Jews teach that Christians have no binding marriage, and that a Jew who lies with a Christian’s wife does not commit adultery. On the other hand, *Rabbi Salman Zevi*, according to his custom, maliciously denies this in the fourth chapter of his *Jewish Theriac* <note>term: Jüdischer Theriack; a 1615 defense of Judaism written by Zalman Zevi of Aufhausen in response to Brentz's attacks.</note>, number 14.

<margin>How unchaste Elijah is said to have been.</margin>
I must also report here what is written in the tractate *Joma*, folio 19, column 2, concerning the unchastity of *Elijah* <note>Elijah is a major prophet in the Hebrew Bible, often depicted in the Talmud as a regular visitor to the earthly world who converses with Rabbis.</note>, where the words read as follows:

> <note>original Hebrew: "Amar lo Eliyahu le-Rav Yehuda achvei de-Rav Salla Chasida amritu amai lo ati Meshicha ve-ha idna yoma de-kippuri hu ve-ibbi'ul kamma betulita be-Neharde'a amar leh ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu mai amar amar leh lapetach chatat rovetz"</note>

That is: *Elijah* said to *Rav Judah*, the brother of the pious *Rav Salla*: "You ask why the Messiah does not come? Behold, today is the Day of Atonement (on which one should especially guard oneself against sin), and yet many virgins in Nehardea <note>term: Nehardea; a major center of Babylonian Jewry and home to a famous Talmudic academy.</note> have been slept with." Then he (*Rav Judah*) asked him (*Elijah*): "What does the Holy and Blessed God say to that (when you do such a thing)?" Whereupon he answered him, He says (from Genesis 4:7): **Sin crouches at the door.** That is, as *Rabbi Salomon* explains it in his commentary on the passage: "Evil desire makes him sin against his will." From which it is to be concluded that according to the Talmud’s teaching, God does not particularly regard fornication, even though He has strictly forbidden it.

### Of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked, Chapter VIII.

<margin>Some Talmudic teachers were murderers: for</margin>
<margin>Rabba cut the throat of Rabbi Sira.</margin>
Regarding murder and manslaughter, there were some among the Talmudic teachers who are accused of such heavy sin. In the tractate *Megilla* <note>term: Megilla; the Talmudic tractate primarily concerning the scroll of Esther and the holiday of Purim.</note>, folio 7, column 2, it is read of Rabba that he killed Rabbi Sira in a state of drunkenness. The words there read as follows:

<note>original: "Rabba ve-Rabbi Zira avdu se'udat Purim bahadi hadadei, ibsum, kam Rabba shachatei le-Rabbi Zira. Le-machar be'a rachamei ve-achayei. Le-shana amar lei: neiti mar ve-na'avid se'udat Purim bahadi hadadei. Amar lei: lo be-chol sha'ata ve-sha'ata mitrachish nissa."</note>

*That is: Rabba and Rabbi Sira prepared a meal together on the festival of Purim (which is the Jews' Shrove Tuesday <note>The author compares the Jewish holiday of Purim to the Christian Carnival or Shrove Tuesday because both involve feasting and drinking.</note>). And when they were drunk, Rabba stood up and cut Rabbi Sira's throat. The next day, he called upon God for mercy because of it, and caused him to become alive again. In the following year thereafter, he (Rabba) said to him (Rabbi Sira): "May the master come, that we may hold the meal of Purim together." But he gave him the answer: "A miracle is not performed at every hour," as I was made alive again by a miracle in the past year; and thus he trusted him no more, for fear that he might cut his throat once again.*

<margin>So also the Rabbi, as well as Rabbi Chija, killed someone.</margin>
In the tractate *Shabbat* <note>term: Shabbat; the tractate concerning the laws of the Sabbath.</note>, folio 30, column 2, it is likewise read of the Rabbi <note>term: the Rabbi; usually refers to Judah ha-Nasi, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah.</note> and Rabbi Chija that they committed a murder, of which it is thus written:

<note>original: "Hahu de-ata le-kamei de-Rabbi, amar lei: ishtach ishti u-vanecha banai. Amar lei: retsonecha she-tishte kos shel yayin? Shata u-faka. Hahu de-ata le-kamei de-Rabbi Chiyya, amar lei: imech ishti ve-ata beni. Amar lei: retsonecha she-tishte kos shel yayin? Shata u-faka."</note>

*That is: A man came before the Rabbi and said to him: "Your wife is my wife, and your children are my children." Then he (the Rabbi) said to him: "Do you wish to drink a cup of wine?" When he had drunk, he burst asunder. Another man came before Rabbi Chija and said to him: "Your mother is my wife, and you are my son." Then he said to him: "Do you wish to drink a cup of wine?" When he had drunk, he burst asunder. These two must have given their invited guests poison to drink, because their bodies burst apart.*

# Of the Talmud.

<margin>Rav Hanina and Oshaya created a calf and ate it.</margin>
<margin>The Jews claim / it happens through the *Book of Yetzirah*.</margin>
<note>original Hebrew: "Hanina ve-Rav Oshaya havu yatvei kol ma'alei Shabbata ve-aske'i be-Sefer Yetzirah u-mivru lehu igla tilta ve-achlei lei."</note>
That is: **Rav Hanina and Rav Oshaya sat every Sabbath evening / and studied in the *Book of Yetzirah* <note>term: Book of Yetzirah; also known as *Sefer Yetzirah*, an early Jewish mystical text that describes the creation of the world through the Hebrew alphabet and numbers.</note>, and created for themselves a calf / which was as large as if it were three years old / and ate the same.** This is said to have occurred / according to the testimony of the Jews / through the aforementioned *Book of Yetzirah* (which / as is claimed in the fourth part of the *Book of Kuzari* <note>term: Kuzari; a famous work by Judah Halevi defending Judaism, written in the 12th century.</note>, number 25 / is said to have originated from the *Patriarch Abraham* / though others conversely maintain that *Rabbi Akiva* authored it /). They hold that through this same *Book*, powerful things can be accomplished / which is why it is called *Sepher Jezira*, that is, the *Book of Creation*. And Rabbi Naphtali, in his book *Emeck hammélech* <note>term: Emeq ha-Melekh; "The King’s Valley," a 17th-century Kabbalistic work by Naphtali Herz ben Jacob Elhanan.</note>, folio 10, column 3, in the 55th chapter / under the title *Scháär schaaschüë hammélech* <note>original: "Sha'ar Sha'ashue ha-Melekh," meaning "The Gate of the King's Delights."</note>, gives some small instruction / as to how one should conduct oneself in the use of this book / and how the letters of the alphabet / through which everything is accomplished / are to be arranged / and also how one should bring about a *golem* <note>term: Golem; in Jewish folklore, an animated being created from inanimate matter (usually clay) through mystical means.</note>, that is, such a mute person / like the one *Rabba* made / or else a calf / as *Rabbi Hanina* and *Rabbi Oshaya* have done. So also it is read in the book *Nischmáth chájim* <note>term: Nishmat Chayim; "The Breath of Life," a work on the soul and reincarnation by Menasseh ben Israel.</note>, in the 24th chapter of the third part / folio 136, column 2:

<margin>Rabbi Joshua was able to make *stags* and *roes* from gourds and melons / according to his claim / through the *Book of Yetzirah*.</margin>
<note>original Hebrew: "Bi-Yerushalmi perek Arba Mitot amar Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hanania yakhol ani (al yedei Sefer Yetzirah) likach delu'in ve-avatihim ve-asotan ilim u-tzeva'im mamash."</note>

<margin>But all of this was pure sorcery and delusion.</margin>
However, all of this is certainly nothing other / than a godless sorcery / and therewith a delusion of the Devil / for the creation of any creature / belongs to God alone. One reads in the description of Doctor *Faustus* <note>A legendary German scholar and sorcerer who was said to have made a pact with the devil; here the author uses him as a parallel for "Jewish magic."</note> / that he was able to present all sorts of things before one's eyes / and made five fat pigs / as well as a horse / which was nevertheless nothing other / than a delusion. Many such things are read of sorcerers / in their descriptions.

Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel also writes of this in his aforementioned book *Nischmáth chájim*, folio 136, column 2, in the 24th chapter of the third *Ma'amar* <note>term: Ma'amar; a discourse or treatise.</note> as follows:
<note>original Hebrew: "Amar Rabbi Yannai mahalech hayiti be-shuk zeh shel Tzippori..."</note>
That is / **Rabbi Jannai said: I was walking in the market of Sepphoris and I saw a sorcerer take a pebble and throw it upward, and it came down and became a calf. And when they questioned him based on what Rabbi Eleazar said in the name of Rabbi Yose ben Zimra—that if all the inhabitants of the world gathered together, they could not create a single gnat and breathe a soul into it—he replied to him that the possibility of the thing was because the sorcerer called to his demon who is in charge of sorceries, and this [demon] steals a calf from the cattle and brings it to him. And Rabbi Hinana ben Rabbi Hinanya said: I was walking at the place of the gate-hinges of Sepphoris and saw a sorcerer take a stone and throw it, and it became a calf. I came and told my father; he said: if you ate from it, believe the deed; but if you did not eat from it, then believe it was vanity and an optical illusion from the power of demons.**

That is / **Rabbi Jannai**

### Chapter VIII of the First Part of *Judaism Unmasked*.

Jannai <note>likely referring to Rabbi Yannai, a prominent teacher in the Land of Israel in the 3rd century</note> said, "I was walking in the market in the city of Zippore <note>term: Zippore; the ancient city of Sepphoris in Galilee, once a center of Jewish learning</note>, and I saw a sorcerer who took a stone and threw it up into the air; but when it came back down, it had become a calf." When it was pointed out to him (Rabbi Jannai) that Rabbi Eliezer had said, in the name of Rabbi Jose, the son of Simra, that even if all the people in the whole world were to come together, they could not create a single gnat and put a soul into it: he gave the answer that the thing had been possible because the sorcerer had called upon his devil, who is placed over sorcery, and the devil had stolen a calf from a cow and brought it to him. Also, Rabbi Chinnana, the son of Rabbi Chanánja, said, "I was walking in Zippore, at the place where the gates close, and I saw a sorcerer who took a stone and threw it, and a calf came from it. I went and told it to my father, but he said to me, 'If you had eaten of it, you could believe in the work; but since you certainly did not eat of it, believe that it was nothing but a delusion through the power of the devil.'" Just as the devil, in Rabbi Jannai’s opinion, could have brought a calf to the sorcerer in the city of Zippore, or as it was a delusion according to Rabbi Chanánja’s statement; so one can also say that the devil brought a calf to Rabbi Channina and Rabbi Oschája every Sabbath evening. I would rather hold, however, that he, as a deceptive spirit, brought them a dead beast and carrion, or perhaps a pig, and so blinded their eyes that they looked upon it as a living calf and ate of it.

<margin>Rabbi Jannai transformed a woman into a donkey through sorcery.</margin>
Of this Jannai, it is read in the Tractate Sanhédrin <note>one of the books of the Talmud dealing with law and criminal procedures</note>, folio 67, column 2, that he transformed a woman into a donkey through sorcery and rode upon that same donkey to the market; regarding which it is written there as follows:

> <note>original Aramaic: יאנאי אקלע לההוא אושפיזא אמר להו אשקין מיא קריבו שתיתא חזא דקא מרחשן שפוותה שדא פורתא מינה הוו עקרבי אמר להו אנא שתיתי אתון נמי שתו מדידי אשקייה הואי חמרא רכבה סליק לשוקא אתא חברתה פשרה לה הוייה דרכיב וקאים איתתא בשוקא</note>

That is: Jannai came to an inn and said to them (namely, the innkeeper's people), "Give me water to drink." But they brought him a drink in which flour was stirred into water, which is called <term>Schethita</term>. And he saw that the lips of the woman who brought it were moving (and he realized thereby that she was a sorceress); then he poured a little of it out, and scorpions came from it. Thereupon he said to them, "I have drunk of yours, so now you drink of mine." After he had given her to drink, she turned into [a donkey]—

In the 173rd chapter <note>Eisenmenger is citing the *Maase-Buch*, a popular 16th-century collection of Jewish folk tales and legends</note>, it is also read of Rabbi Elieser that he traveled from Regensburg to Mainz in only a few hours. Likewise, in the 174th chapter, a strange story is found which is said to have occurred between a Bishop of Salzburg and Rabbi Judah of Regensburg; and if the matter is true, this same Rabbi Judah must have been a genuine sorcerer. <margin>
Abraham is said to have taught magic to the children he fathered with his concubines.
</margin>

However, it is no wonder that the Jews learn sorcery and make use of such diabolical arts, since the Rabbis teach that the pious Patriarch Abraham gave the art of sorcery as a gift to the children of his concubines. Regarding this, it is written in the Talmudic tractate *Sanhedrin* <note>The section of the Talmud dealing with legal and court procedures</note>, folio 91, column 1, concerning the words of Genesis 25:6 ("But to the sons of his concubines, Abraham gave gifts"): <note>original Hebrew: מאי מתנות אמר רבי ירמיה בר אבא מלמד שמסר להם שם טומאה</note> that is: **What does the word "gifts" signify? Rabbi Jeremiah, the son of Abba, said: This teaches us that he gave them the Name of Impurity.** But as for what is to be understood by such a "Name of Impurity," Rabbi Solomon Jarchi <note>term: Jarchi; an older name for Rashi (1040–1105), the most famous medieval commentator on the Bible and Talmud</note> teaches in his commentary on the passage with these words: <note>original Hebrew: שם טומאה כשוף ומעשה שדים</note> that is: **The Name of Impurity signifies sorcery and the work of devils.** This is also found in the *Sepher ha-Emunoth* <note>The Book of Beliefs</note> by Rabbi Shem Tov, folio 54, column 1, in the fourth chapter of the fifth part; and in the book *Sha'are Tzedek* <note>Gates of Justice</note> folio 17, column 1; as well as in the book *Mekor Chayim* <note>Source of Life</note> folio 17, column 3. And in the book *Zioni* <note>a mystical commentary by Menahem Zioni</note>, it is written on folio 20, column 2, concerning the aforementioned words of Genesis 25:6: <note>original Hebrew: אמרו חכמינו ז"ל : שם בטומאה מסר להם שהיו משתמשים בהם בטומאת הגוף וזאת היתה חכמת בני קדם שהיו בני הפלגשים שנ' וישלחם אברהם מעל יצחק בנו בעודנו חי קדמה אל ארץ קדם הרומז לכח בני קדם שנ' מן ארם ינחני בלק מהררי קדם וכחות הטומאה החיצונות מסר להם והם מעשה שדים וכשפים</note> that is: **Our Sages, of blessed memory, say that he gave them impure names, which they used in the impurity of the body; and this was the wisdom of those who lived toward the East, who were the children of the concubines, as it is said (Gen. 25:6): "And Abraham sent them away from his son Isaac, while he yet lived, eastward unto the east country." This indicates the power of those who dwell in the East, as it is said (Numbers 23:7): "Balak hath brought me from Aram, out of the mountains of the East." And he delivered to them the external powers of impurity, which are the works of devils and sorceries.**

# About the Talmud.

Balak, the King of Moab, had me fetched from Syria, from the mountains toward the East. <note>Eisenmenger is referencing the biblical story of Balaam (Numbers 23:7), whom Balak summoned to curse the Israelites. He interprets this "East" as the place where magical knowledge was sent.</note> And he is said to have given them the external powers of impurity, which consist of the work of the Devil and of sorceries. Thus it is also written in the book *Nischmath Chájim* <note>original: "Nischmath chájim," a work on the soul by Menasseh ben Israel (1604–1657)</note>, folio 145, column 2, at the beginning of the 29th chapter, under the title *Maamar Schelischi* <note>meaning "Third Discourse"</note>, as follows: <note>original Hebrew: חז"ל על פסוק ולבני הפלגשים נתן להם מתנות אמרו שם טומאה מסר להם. ושאברהם אבינו עשה מסכתא שהיו סדורים בה כל סדרי הכשוף ופעולותיו מכחות הטומאה כמו שחבר ספר יצירה משמות הקדושים</note> that is: "Our Sages, of blessed memory, say regarding the verse: 'But to the children of the concubines he had, he gave gifts' <note>Genesis 25:6</note>, that he gave them names of impurity: and that our father Abraham composed a tractate in which all the orders of sorcery and its operations from the powers of impurity (that is, the impure spirits) were arranged one after another, just as he prepared the book *Jezira* <note>The *Sefer Yetzirah* or "Book of Creation," an early work of Jewish mysticism</note> from the holy names." <margin>The same is also said to have written a book about sorcery.</margin> According to all of this, the pious Patriarch Abraham is accused by his degenerate, insane descendants of having been a sorcerer and of having taught his children born of concubines such a godless practice, with which the Devil is served, whereby the art of sorcery was spread throughout the entire land toward the East.

Furthermore, they also teach that all who sat in the *Synedrio* <term>Sanhedrin: the supreme council and tribunal of the Jews</term> or High Council were required to understand sorcery, as is indicated in the book *Emeck hammelech* <note>The "Valley of the King," a Kabbalistic work by Naftali Herz Bacharach</note> folio 108, column 2, in the 111th chapter, under the title *Scháar Kirjáth árba* <note>The Gate of the City of Four</note>, with these words: <note>original Hebrew: הסנהדרין היו מחוייבים לידע כישוף כדי שיהיו יודעים איזהו מעשה ואיזהו אחיזת עינים</note> <margin>All who were in the Great Council at Jerusalem were also expected to have understood sorcery.</margin> that is: "Those in the *Synedrio* had to know sorcery so that they could know which was a (true) deed and which was a delusion of the eyes." And in the book *Juchasin* <note>A genealogical and historical work by Abraham Zacuto</note> it is written on folio 17, column 1: <note>original Hebrew: הסנהדרין צריך שידעו כשוף בעבור שידעו הדין על איזה כשוף יהרגו המכשף. אבל פירש רש"י בפרק האומר שאם יהא הנידון מכשף ויעשה האור שלא ישלוט בו יעשו הם מכשפות וימיתוהו</note> that is: "The *Synedrium* needed to understand sorcery so that they could rightly know for which sorcery the sorcerer should be put to death. *Rabbi Salomon Jarchi* <note>Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French commentator on the Torah and Talmud</note> however, explains it in the chapter which begins *Haómer* <note>a section of the Talmudic tractate *Kiddushin*</note> as follows: If the one upon whom judgment was passed was a sorcerer and had acted such that the light <note>perhaps referring to the "light" of justice or a specific magical protection</note> did not prevail over him, they would then use sorcery themselves and kill him with it:"

that is, **Rabba, the grandson of Channa, said: "When we followed Rabbi Jochanan <note>Rabbi Yochanan bar Nafcha, a leading 3rd-century scholar in the Land of Israel</note> to eat the fruits of Ginnosar <note>Ginnosar or Gennesaret, a fertile plain on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee</note> (which is the region in Galilee lying by the Lake of Gennesareth, which bore the best fruits), and if there were a hundred of us, each of us would take ten for Rabbi Jochanan. But if there were ten of us, each of us would take a hundred for him; and a hundred of these fruits would fit into a basket that held three seahs <note>A "seah" is an ancient Hebrew dry measure, roughly equivalent to 7 or 8 liters</note>; and he ate them all, and yet he swore that he had tasted no food." What do you think? (That he had sworn he had eaten no food?) I would rather say, he swore that he had received no nourishment from it (since it was as if he had eaten nothing at all). Rav Abhu ate until a fly slipped off his forehead (that is, until his face was so fat and greasy from eating and drinking that no fly could keep its footing because of the slipperiness). Rav Ammi and Rav Assi ate until their hair fell out. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish ate until he became confused in his head.** Regarding Jochanan, the son of Narbai, the following is read in the Tractate *Pesachim*, folio 57, column 1:

> <note>original Hebrew: אמרו עליו על יוחנן בן נרבאי שהיה אוכל שלש מאות עגלים ושותה שלש מאות גרבי יין ואוכל ארבעים סאה גוזלות בקינוח סעודה :</note>

that is, **It is said of Jochanan, the son of Narbai, that he ate three hundred calves, and drank three hundred bottles of wine, and ate forty seahs <note>About 300 liters</note> of young pigeons as a dessert or confection.** It is true that Rabbi Solomon Jarchi <note>A common name for Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator</note> writes in his interpretation that this man fed many priests at his table, and that is why so much was consumed; however that may be, a great gluttony must have taken place. > <note>original Hebrew: מארת ה' בבית רשע זה פקח בן רמליהו היה אוכל ארבעים סאה גוזלות בקנוח סעודה. ונוה צדיקים יברך זה חזקיה מלך יהודה שהיה אוכל ליטרא ירק בסעודה :</note>

that is, (referencing the words of Proverbs 3:33): **"The curse of the Lord is on the house of the wicked" refers to Pekah, the son of Remaliah <note>A King of Israel mentioned in 2 Kings 15</note>, who ate forty seahs of young pigeons as a dessert. "But He blesses the home of the just" refers to Hezekiah, King of Judah, who ate only a pound of vegetables at a meal.**

<margin>The Jews spend their holidays very much with eating and drinking.</margin>
The Jews also hold that they must spend their holidays only with gluttony and drinking, because in the Talmudic Tractate *Pesachim, folio 68, column 2*, it is read as follows: <note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: שמחת יום טוב נמי מצוה היא דתניא רבי אלעזר אומר אין לו לאדם ביום טוב אלא או אוכל ושותה או יושב ושונה רבי יהושע אמר חלקהו חציו לאכילה ושתיה וחציו לבית המדרש:</note> that is, the joy of a festival is also commanded, for we learn that *Rabbi Eliezer* says: A **man** has nothing to do on a holiday except that he eat and drink, or sit and learn. But *Rabbi Joshua* has said: divide the day, and use one half of it for eating and drinking, and the other half for the school <note>The "Schul" or "Beth Midrash," the house of study</note>. ...not have been of much use. Who then would want to consider their traditions as God's Word?

<margin>Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Jose tore the book of the Law.</margin>
Regarding Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Jose, it is also read in the Talmudic tractate *Yevamot* <note>Tractate Yevamot deals primarily with levirate marriage, but like much of the Talmud, contains various historical and biographical anecdotes.</note> (or *Yevomos*) folio 96, column 2, that they became contentious with one another during a disputation and, in their anger, tore the book of the Law <note>The Torah scroll.</note> into pieces. From this, one may judge that they were worthless fellows, since they treated the Word of God so mockingly.

<margin>Some Talmudic teachers doubted their own salvation.</margin>
As for those who doubted their own salvation, the following is written in the Talmudic tractate *Berakhot* <note>Tractate Berakhot deals with prayers and blessings.</note> (or *Berokhos*) folio 28, column 2, concerning Rabban Yohanan, the son of Zakkai:

When Rabban Yohanan, the son of Zakkai, became ill, his disciples entered to visit him. When he saw them, he began to weep. His disciples said to him: "Light of Israel, right pillar, mighty hammer <note>These are traditional honorifics for a great scholar; the "mighty hammer" refers to his ability to shatter difficult legal problems.</note>, why do you weep?" He answered them: "If I were being led before a king of flesh and blood, who is here today and in the grave tomorrow, and if he were angry with me, his anger would not be an eternal anger; and if he bound me, his binding would not endure forever; and if he put me to death, the death he inflicted on me would not last into eternity; and I could appease such a king with words and bribe him with money—even so, I would weep. But now that I am to be brought before the King of all kings, the Holy and Blessed God, who lives and exists forever and for all eternity—if He is angry with me, His anger is eternal; if He binds me, His binding is eternal; and if He kills me, I must be dead eternally; and I can neither appease Him with words nor bribe Him with money. Furthermore, there are two paths before me: one to Paradise and the other to Hell <note>The original uses *Gehenna*.</note>, and I do not know upon which one I shall be led—should I then not weep?" 
<note>original Hebrew: כשחלה רבן יוחנן בן זכאי נכנסו תלמידיו לבקרו כיון שראה אותם התחיל לבכות אמרו לו תלמידיו נר ישראל עמוד הימיני פטיש החזק מפני מה אתה בוכה א"ל אילו לפני מלך בשר ודם היו מוליכין אותי שהיום כאן ומחר בקבר שאם כועס עלי אין כעסו כעס עולם ואם אוסרני אין איסורו איסור עולם ואם ממיתני אין מיתתו מיתת עולם ואני יכול לפייסו בדברים ולשחדו בממון אע"פ כן הייתי בוכה ועכשיו שמוליכין אותי לפני מלך מלכי המלכים הקב"ה שהוא חי וקיים לעולם ולעולמי עולמים שאם כועס עלי כעסו כעס עולם ואם אוסרני איסורו איסור עולם ואם ממיתני מיתתו מיתת עולם ואיני יכול לפייסו בדברים ולא לשחדו בממון ולא עוד אלא שיש לפני שני דרכים אחת של ג"ע ואחת של גיהנם ואיני יודע באיזו מוליכין אותי ולא אבכה:</note>

That is: When Rabban Yohanan, the son of Zakkai, was ill, his disciples went in to visit him; but after he saw them, he began to weep. Then his disciples spoke to him: "You light of Israel, you right pillar, you strong hammer, why do you weep?" Even if it were only this, I would weep. <margin>The sixth reason why the Talmud is not God's Word.</margin>
<margin>Indecent and coarse ribaldry is found in the Talmud.</margin>
The sixth reason why the Talmud is not God's Word is because there are indecent things in it, mixed with shameless, gross lies and scandalous ribaldry. I was indeed in doubt whether I should include such unseemly things here and make mention of them; but because one can see all the more from them what a worthless book it is, I have decided to mention them here. In the tractate *Sanhedrin*, folio 22, column 1, the words of 1 Kings 1:1–3 are cited, in which it is reported that for King David, who was old and could not get warm, they sought a young maiden who should sleep in his arms and warm him; and that Abishag of Shunem was chosen for this purpose. Following this, it further describes what occurred when she lay with King David, and the words run thus: <note>original: "אמרה נינסבן אמר לה אסורת : לי אמרה ליה חסריה לגנבא נפשיה לשלמא נקיט אמר להו קראו לי לבת שבע וכתיב ותבא בת שבע אל המלך החדרה. אמר רב באותה שעה קינחה בת שבע בשלש עשרה מפות :"</note> that is,

<margin>Concerning King David and Abishag of Shunem.</margin>
**Then she (namely, Abishag) said to King David: "Marry me." And he answered her, "You are forbidden to me" (because I already have eighteen wives <note>According to Talmudic interpretation of Deuteronomy 17:17, a king was permitted no more than eighteen wives.</note>). She then replied: "When a thief lacks a place (where he can steal anything), he keeps himself peaceful and quiet." <note>This is a proverb implying that David was only claiming she was "forbidden" because he was now impotent due to old age.</note> Then the King said to them (namely, to his servants): "Call Bathsheba to me"; for (in the 15th verse of the cited place, 1 Kings 1) it is written: *And Bathsheba went in to the king into the chamber.* The Rav <note>A title often referring to the 3rd-century scholar Abba Arika, founder of the academy at Sura.</note> has said that Bathsheba wiped herself in that same hour with thirteen napkins.** These are the words of the Talmud. But as for what the words of Abishag mean when she said, "When a thief lacks a place, he keeps himself peaceful," Rabbi Salomon Jarchi <note>Known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French commentator on the Torah and Talmud.</note> teaches in his commentary on this that she meant the following: <note>original: "מפני שזקנת ותשש כחך אתה אומר שאיני אסורה לך"</note> that is, **"Because you are old and your strength has failed, you say that I am forbidden to you."**

But how it is to be understood that the Rav <note>original: "Raf"; a title for the 3rd-century Babylonian scholar Abba Arika</note> said Bathsheba wiped herself with thirteen napkins, the aforementioned Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator on the Torah and Talmud.</note> explains it thus: <note>original: "קינחה בת שבע שבא עליה י"ג ביאות ומקנחה בין תשמיש לתשמיש ובמקרא : הוה כתובין י"ג תיבות ותבא אל המלך החדרה והמלך זקן מאד ואבישג השונמית משרת את המלך"</note> that is, by the words "Bathsheba wiped herself," it is indicated that he [King David] touched her <insert>at that time</insert> thirteen times, and she wiped herself between each and every touch. And <insert>therefore</insert> there are thirteen words in this <insert>fifteenth</insert> verse <insert>in the Hebrew text, namely</insert>: *Vattávo Bathshéva el hammélech hachádrah vehammélech sakén meód vaabhíschag haschunámmith mescharáth eth hammélech* <note>original Hebrew: "And Bathsheba went in unto the king into the chamber; and the king was very old; and Abishag the Shunammite ministered unto the king."</note>: that is, **And Bathsheba went in unto the king into the chamber; and the king was very old: and Abishag the Shunammite ministered unto the king.** Is this not a subtle proof for such a gross and shameless lie?

<margin>Of Sisera and Jael.</margin>
In the fourth chapter of the Book of Judges, in the twenty-first verse, it is read how Jael drove a nail into Sisera’s temple and killed him. And in the fifth chapter, verse 27, it is written that Deborah spoke of it thus: **At her feet he bowed, he fell, he lay down: at her feet he bowed, he fell: where he bowed, there he fell down dead.** However, concerning these words, it is written in the Talmudic tractate *Nazir* <note>A tractate of the Talmud concerning the laws of the Nazirite vow.</note>, folio 23, column 2: <note>original: "אמר רבי יוחנן שבע בעילות בעל אותו רשע באותה שעה שנאמר בין רגליה כרע : נפל שכב"</note> that is, Rabbi Jochanan said that this same wicked man [Sisera] mixed himself carnally with Jael seven times in that hour, because it is said (in verse 27): **At her feet he bowed: he fell: he lay.** Furthermore, it is written in the *Tosaphoth* <note>Medieval commentaries on the Talmud, often printed on the outer margin of the page.</note>: <note>original: "שבע בעילות : בעל סיסרא דשבע פעמים כתיב כריעה נפילה ושכיבה"</note> that is, Sisera touched Jael seven times because the words "bowing," "falling," and "lying" are written seven times <insert>in the aforementioned 27th verse</insert>. Is this not once again an insane proof? When the nail was driven through Sisera’s temple, he bowed from great pain and fell down and died, as can be clearly seen in Judges 5:26–27; how then could a carnal union be understood through such bowing and falling? Rabbi David Kimchi <note>A famous medieval rabbi and grammarian (1160–1235), also known by the acronym Radak.</note> himself rejects such Talmudic folly in his commentary on the aforementioned passage of Judges 5:26–27, when he reports: <note>original: "כריעה שלא היתה לו תקומה וזהו שאמר כאשר כרע שם נפל שדוד. ויש בו דרש והיא רחוק כי יש בפסוק שבעה בין כרע ונפל ושכב ואמרו כי שבע בעילות בעל אותו רשע ליעל אותו היום ומה שכתבו למעלה במילת שמיכה מכחיש זה הדרש"</note> that is, "He bowed because he could not stand up again; and this is what it says, 'where he bowed, there he fell down dead.' And there is an interpretive midrash <note>A term for Rabbinic homiletic interpretation that often looks for hidden meanings beyond the literal text.</note> about this, but it is far-fetched; for there are seven instances in the verse of 'bowed,' 'fell,' and 'lay,' and they [the Sages] say that the wicked man had seven intercourses with Jael that day. But what they wrote above regarding the word 'covering' contradicts this midrash." That is: "He bowed because he could not stand up again..."

<margin>Of King Pharaoh.</margin>
It is also shamefully boasted in the Talmud by some regarding what great manhoods <note>The German word *Mannheit* here serves as a euphemism for the male anatomy</note> they possessed; and in the tractate *Moëd Katon*, folio 18, column 1, regarding the Egyptian King **Pharaoh**, who lived in the time of **Moses**, it is read as follows: <note>original: "Abitol the scribe said in the name of Rav Papa: Pharaoh who was in the days of Moses was one cubit tall; his beard was one cubit; his 'manhood' was one cubit and a span, to fulfill that which is said: 'And he sets up over it the lowliest of men.'"</note> That is, **Abitol**, the scribe, has said in the name of **Rav Papa**, that the Pharaoh who existed in the time of Moses was one **cubit** <term>cubit: an ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches (45 cm), based on the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger</term> tall, and had a beard that was one cubit long, and his manhood was one cubit and a span long, as is said (Daniel 4, verse 14, or according to others verse 17): **And he (namely God) sets the lowliest of men over it**—meaning over the kingdom.

<margin>Of Rabbi Ismael and Rabbi Jochanan.</margin>
Concerning **Rabbi Ismael** and **Rabbi Jochanan**, it is also written in the tractate *Báva Metzia*, folio 84, column 1: <note>original: "Rabbi Jochanan said: The organ of Rabbi Ismael was like a wine-skin of nine kabs. Rav Papa said: The organ of Rabbi Jochanan was like a wine-skin of five kabs."</note> That is, Rabbi Jochanan said that Rabbi Ismael's manhood was as large as a skin bag which holds nine **kabs** <term>kab: an ancient Hebrew unit of volume; the author provides a calculation based on eggshells to help the reader visualize the size</term>. (One kab, however, holds as much as fits into 24 chicken eggshells; thus nine kabs hold as much as 216 eggshells.) Rav Papa said that Rabbi Jochanan's manhood was as large as a skin bag that holds five kabs.

<margin>Of Balaam.</margin>
Concerning **Balaam**, the following shameful matter is written in the Talmudic tractate *Sanhedrin*, folio 105, column 1: <note>original: "Balaam was blind in one eye, as it is said: 'the man whose eye is closed.' He used to practice magic with his 'organ'; it is written here: 'falling down, but with opened eyes,' and it is written elsewhere: 'and Haman was falling upon the couch.' ... Mar Zutra said: He practiced magic with his 'organ.' Mar, son of Ravana, said: He had relations with his donkey..."</note> That is, Balaam was blind in one of his eyes, and this is what is said (Numbers 24:3, 15): **The man whose eye is closed.** He prophesied with his manhood. It is written here (Numbers 24:4, 16): **Who fell down, and had his eyes opened**; and (there in Esther 7:8) it is mentioned that **Mar Sutra** said he prophesied with his manhood, as we have reported. But according to the opinion of the one who said that he practiced **sodomy** <term>sodomy: here used to refer to bestiality, or sexual acts with animals</term> with his female donkey (this is proven from), because it is written here (Numbers 24:9): **He couched, he lay down**; and

# Of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked, Chapter VIII. #

there (Judges 5:27) it is written (of **Sisera** <note>A Canaanite general mentioned in the Book of Judges who was killed by Jael</note>): **He bowed at her feet, he fell, and he lay down.** Regarding these words, **Rabbi Salomon** <note>referring to Rashi, the preeminent medieval French commentator</note> writes in his commentary in this manner: <note>original: "מה כריעה דהתם דאית ביה נפילה בעילה אף כריעה דהכא דכתוב נופל בעילה היא שבא על בהמתו"</note> that is: Just as through the "bowing" there (Judges 5:27), where "falling down" was involved, a sexual touch <note>The author uses "Berührung" (touch) as a euphemism for sexual intercourse</note> is signified, so too is a sexual touch indicated by the "bowing" here (Numbers 24:9), where it is written (verse 4) that he (namely **Balaam**) had "fallen down," meaning that he had committed sodomy with his donkey. But is this not a devilish perversion of Holy Scripture? First, it is reported that Balaam was blind in one eye, and this is proven because in verses 3 and 15 he calls himself <term>Setúm haájin: a Hebrew phrase traditionally debated; it can mean "the one with the open eye" or "the one with the closed/hidden eye"</term>, which is falsely interpreted as **the one whose eye is shut or closed**; yet on the contrary it means **the one whose eyes are opened**, as **Ibn Ezra** <note>A celebrated 12th-century scholar and grammarian</note> interprets it, and as it is understood in the Chaldean translation of **Onkelos**; therefore in verses 4 and 16 it is clearly read: **To whom the eyes were opened.** Secondly, the words in verse 9, **He bowed and lay down**, are interpreted as referring to Balaam, even though they are said of the Israelite people and not of Balaam, as the text clearly demonstrates.

<margin>Of the people who lived at the time of the Great Flood.</margin>
In the Talmudic tractate *Sanhedrin*, folio 108, column 1, regarding the people who lived at the time of the Great Flood, it is written thus over the words of Genesis 6:12, **For all flesh had corrupted its way upon the earth**:
<note>original: "אמר רבי יוחנן מלמד שהרביעו בהמה על חיה וחיה על בהמה והכל על האדם והאדם על הכל"</note>
that is, **Rabbi Jochanan** said: this teaches us that they mated domestic cattle with wild animals, and wild animals with domestic cattle, and all these with humans, and humans with all these. This, however, is again a foolish interpretation of Scripture; for here, by "flesh," which in Hebrew is called *básar*, only humans are understood, just as in the Arabic language the word *báscharon* also signifies humans; and in such a sense the word *básar* or "flesh" is also used in Isaiah 40:6. And in the second column of this same folio 108, it is read: <note>original: "תנו רבנן שלשה שמשו בתיבה : וכולם לקו כלב ועורב וחם כלב נקשר עורב רק חם לקה בעורו"</note>
<margin>What Ham, the dog, and the raven did in Noah's Ark.</margin>
that is: Our Rabbis teach: three kinds [of beings] touched [their mates] <note>meaning they engaged in sexual intercourse</note> in the Ark (of **Noah**), and they were all struck (or punished) for it: the **dog**, the **raven**, and **Ham** <note>Noah's son</note>. The dog is tied (to his mate); the raven spits out (the seed); and Ham was punished in his skin, because the black **Cush** <note>Historically referring to the peoples of the upper Nile region/Africa; here the author references the "Curse of Ham" tradition to explain black skin</note> descended from him.

# Of the Talmud. #

<margin>
The seventh reason why the Talmud is not God's Word is because the Holy Scripture is perverted therein.
</margin>

The seventh reason why the Talmud is not **God’s** Word is this: because the Holy Scripture is therein often drawn into a false understanding, and one word is taken for another and it is said: "read it not so, but rather thus," so that only that which the Rabbis wish to assert may be proven. Therefore, in the Talmudic tractate *Berachoth, folio 32, column 1,* it is read thus: <note>original: אמר רבי אלעזר משה הטיח דברים כלפי מעלה שנ' ויתפלל משה אל י"י אל תקרי אל י"י אלא על י"י</note> that is: Rabbi Eliezer said that *Moses* let words fly against **God**, because (Numbers 11:2) it is reported: And *Moses* prayed *el Jehova* <note>original: אל יהוה</note>, that is, *to* the **Lord**; read not *el Jehova*, that is, *to* the **Lord**, but *al Jehova* <note>original: על יהוה</note>, that is, *against* the **Lord**. In the tractate *Shabbath*, on *folio 119, column 2*, the following also stands: <note>original: אמר ריש לקיש כל העונה אמן בכל כחו פותחין לו שערי גן עדן שנ' פתחו שערים ויבא גוי צדיק שומר אמונים אל תקרי שומר אמונים אלא שאומרין אמן</note> that is: *Resh Lakish* <note>A prominent 3rd-century Jewish scholar</note> said that for everyone who speaks the *Amen* with all his might, the gates of Paradise are opened, because (Isaiah 26:2) it is said: **Open the gates, that the righteous nation may enter**, *shomer emunim*, that is, which keeps the faith. Read not *shomer emunim*, that is, which keeps the faith, but *she-omerim Amen*, that is, those who say *Amen*. The same is also read in the tractate *Sanhedrin, folio 110, column 2*, regarding the word *emunim*. And in the tractate *Bava Bathra* on *folio 75, column 2*, it is written thus: <note>original: אמר ר' שמואל בר נחמני אמר ר' יוחנן שלשה נקראו על שמו של הקב"ה ואלו הן צדיקים ומשיח וירושלים צדיקים הא דאמרן. משיח דכתיב וזה שמו אשר יקראו ה' צדקנו וירושלים דכתיב סביב שמונה עשר אלף ושם העיר מיום ה' שמה אל תקרי שמה אלא שמה</note> that is: *Rabbi Samuel*, son of *Nachmani*, says that *Rabbi Jochanan* said: three are called by the name of the holy and blessed **God**, namely the righteous, the *Messiah*, and *Jerusalem*. Concerning the righteous, this is proven from what was said (from Isaiah 43:7). The *Messiah* (is called by the name of **God**, *Jehovah*) because (Jeremiah 23:6) it is written: **And this shall be his name, that he shall be called: Jehovah who is our righteousness.** *Jerusalem* (is called thus) because (Ezekiel 48:35) it is written: **Thus it shall have eighteen thousand rods round about, and then the city shall be named** *Jehovah shammah*, that is, the *Jehovah* is there: read not *shammah*, that is, "there," but *shemah*, that is, "her name"—meaning it shall be called *Jehovah*. In the tractate *Eruvin*, on *folio 19, column 1*, it is taught that the fire of Hell has no power over the godless *Israelites*, and this is given as the reason: <note>original: שמלאין מצוות כרימון שנ' כפלח הרימון רקתך ואלש"בל אל תקרי רקתך אלא ריקתיך שאפילו ריקנין שבך מלאין מצוות כרימון</note> because they are full of commandments like a pomegranate, as it is said (Song of Solomon 4:3): "Your temple [*raktékh*] is like a piece of pomegranate"; read not *raktékh*, your temple, but *reikatékh*, your empty ones; meaning that even the empty ones among you are as full of commandments as a pomegranate.
