# Of the Talmud. #

<margin>The seventh reason why the **Talmud** is not **God’s** Word is because the Holy Scripture is perverted therein.</margin>

The seventh reason why the **Talmud** is not **God’s** Word is this: because the Holy Scripture is often drawn into a false understanding within it; one word is substituted for another, and it is said, "read it not so, but rather thus," solely so that whatever the Rabbis wish to assert may be proven. Therefore, in the Talmudic tractate *Berachôth*, folio 32, column 1, it is read as follows: <note>original Hebrew: אמר רבי אלעזר משה הטיח דברים כלפי מעלה שנ' ויתפלל משה אל י"י: אל תקרי אל י"י אלא על י"י</note> that is: Rabbi Eliezer said that Moses let words fly against **God**, because (Numbers 11:2) it is reported: "And Moses prayed *el* **Jehovah**," <note>original: אל יהוה</note> that is, *to* the **Lord**; read not *el* **Jehovah**, that is, *to* the **Lord**, but *al* **Jehovah**, <note>original: על יהוה</note> that is, *against* the **Lord**. In the tractate *Shábbath*, folio 119, column 2, the following is also found: <note>original Hebrew: אמר ריש לקיש כל העונה אמן בכל כחו פותחין לו שערי גן עדן שנ' פתחו שערים ויבא גוי צדיק שומר אמונים אל תקרי שומר אמונים אלא שאומרין אמן</note> That is: Resch Lakisch <note>A prominent 3rd-century scholar (Amora) known for his physical strength and deep piety.</note> said, for every person who speaks the "Amen" with all his might, the gates of Paradise are opened, because (Isaiah 26:2) it is said:

> Open the gates, that the righteous nation may enter, *shomer emunim*, that is, which keeps the faith.

Read not *shomer emunim*, that is, "which keeps the faith," but *she-omerim Amen*, that is, "who say Amen." The same is also read in the tractate *Sanhedrin*, folio 110, column 2, regarding the word *emunim* <note>faithfulness/faiths</note>. And in the tractate *Bâva bâthra*, folio 75, column 2, it is written thus: <note>original Hebrew: אמר ר' שמואל בר נחמני אמר ר' יוחנן שלשה נקראו על שמו של הקב"ה ואלו הן צדיקים ומשיח וירושלים צדיקים הא דאמרן. משיח דכתיב וזה שמו אשר יקראו ה' צדקנו וירושלים דכתיב סביב שמונה עשר אלף ושם העיר מיום י"י שמה אל תקרי שמה אלא שמה</note> that is: Rabbi Samuel, son of Nachmani, says that Rabbi Jochanan said: three are called by the name of the Holy and Blessed **God**, namely: the Righteous, the **Messiah**, and **Jerusalem**. As for the Righteous, this is proven from what was said (from Isaiah 43:7). The **Messiah** (is called by the name of **God**, **Jehovah**,) because (Jeremiah 23:6) it is written: "And this shall be his name, that he shall be called: **Jehovah** our Righteousness." **Jerusalem** (is so called) because (Ezekiel 48:35) it is written: "It shall be eighteen thousand cubits round about, and then the city shall be named **Jehovah Shammah**," that is, "**Jehovah** is there": read not *shámma*, that is, "there," but *shemáh*, <note>Eisenmenger is noting a vowel change that alters the meaning to "her name."</note> that is, "her name"—meaning, her name shall be called **Jehovah**. In the tractate *Eeruvin*, folio 19, column 1, it is taught that the fires of Hell have no power over wicked Israelites, and this is given as the reason: <note>original Hebrew: שמלאין מצוות כרימון שנ' כפלח הרימון רקתך וארשב"ל אל תקרי רקתך אלא ריקניך שאפילו ריקנין שבך מלאין מצוות כרימון</note> because they are full of commandments like a pomegranate, as it is said (Song of Solomon 4:3), "Thy temples are like a piece of pomegranate," and Resch Lakisch said: read not "thy temples" <note>Hebrew: *rakatech*</note> but "thy empty ones," <note>Hebrew: *rekanim*</note> for even the empty ones among you are as full of commandments as a pomegranate.

# On the Jews’ Distorted Interpretation of Holy Scripture.

According to the 70 names of the Holy One, blessed be He <note>original: "נגד ע’ שמות של הקדוש ברוך הוא"</note>: that is, just as the holy, blessed **GOD** has seventy names, so the Law is interpreted in seventy ways, in regard to the seventy names of the holy, blessed **GOD**. That the Law is interpreted in seventy ways is proven by Rabbi Bechai in his commentary on the Five Books of Moses, in the <term>Parashah Mishpatim</term> <note>the weekly Torah portion covering Exodus 21:1–24:18, focused on civil laws</note>, folio 99, column 4, using the word *lehorótham* <note>original: "להורותם"</note>, which appears in Exodus 24:12 and means "to teach them." He interprets it in a ridiculous manner with these words: <note>original: "תמצא להורותם הלמ"ד והמ"ם שבעים ובאמצע תורה וזהו שבעים פנים לתורה"</note> <gloss>that is, You find in the word *lehorótham* the Lamed and the Mem (or the letters L and M, the former being the first and the latter being the last of the word), which numerically equal seventy, and in the middle *Torah* <note>original: "תורה"</note> (namely, between the two letters Lamed and Mem are the letters He, Vav, Resh, and Tau, which, when rearranged, form the word *Torah*, which means the Law); and this indicates that the Law is interpreted in seventy ways.</gloss> <note>In Hebrew numerology, Lamed is 30 and Mem is 40, totaling 70. The author considers this "letter-shuffling" to be an absurd basis for a theological claim.</note> Is this not a hair-splitting proof? In the <term>Yalkut Chadash</term> <note>a 17th-century collection of mystical and midrashic teachings</note>, folio 169, column 3, number 24, under the title *Torah*, from the book *Ziyoni*, folio 10, it is also written as follows: <note>original: "התורה נדרשת בשבעים פנים ולכך אינה נקודה בספר תורה שאו כל השבעים פנים בכח ובפועל אבל אילו היתה נקודה בס"ת לא היה לה רק על דרך הנקודה והקריאה"</note> <gloss>that is, The Law is interpreted in seventy ways; for this reason, there are no points (or vowels) in the Scroll of the Law, so that all seventy ways are present *potentially and actually* <note>original: "potestate & actu"</note>; but if the points or vowels were written in the Scroll of the Law, it could only be interpreted according to those points and the specific way it is read.</gloss> Concerning this, in Rabbi Bechai’s commentary on the Five Books of Moses, folio 197, column 1, in the <term>Parashah Va’etchanan</term>, the following is also written: <note>original: "התורה היא נדרשת לכמה טעמים עד שאפילו תיבה אחת היא מתפרשת לכמה ענינים לפי הנקוד"</note> <gloss>that is, The Law is explained in many different senses, so that even a single word is interpreted in various ways, according to how it is punctuated and which vowels are assigned to it.</gloss>

<margin>All interpretations of the Sages are also said to be **GOD’s** word, even when they are completely contradictory.</margin> For this reason, the Jews do not consider it at all absurd when the Rabbis interpret a matter in a completely contradictory manner—where one considers a thing pure and the other considers it impure, or one considers it permitted and the other considers it forbidden—but rather they are of the opinion that both are true and are **GOD’s** word. In Rabbi Menachem von Recanati’s commentary on the Five Books of Moses, folio 98, column 2, in the <term>Parashah Yitro</term> <note>original: "Vajischma Jethro"</note>, regarding the words of Exodus 20:1, **"And GOD spoke all these words,"** it is written as follows: <note>original: "אז"ל במסכת חגיגה בעלי אסופות אלו תלמידי חכמים שיושבין אסופות אסופות ועוסקין בתורה הללו מטהרין והללו מטמאין הללו מכשירין והללו פוסלין הללו מתירין והללו אוסרין"</note> <gloss>Our Sages, of blessed memory, said in the tractate <term>Chagigah</term>: "The masters of assemblies"—these are the disciples of the wise who sit in groups upon groups and occupy themselves with the Law; some declare a thing pure and others declare it impure; some declare it fit and others declare it unfit; some permit and others forbid...</gloss>

# On the Jews' Perverted Interpretation of the Holy Scripture.

(Deuteronomy 5, v. 22) it is said: "The Lord spoke all these words to your whole assembly." And for this reason, they (namely, our Sages) say: this and that is God’s word (that is, he who considers a thing pure, permitted, and right speaks God’s word just as much as he who perceives it as impure, forbidden, and wrong). # Chapter IX of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked

<page-num>458</page-num>
**[The Letter of the Law has] sixty times ten thousand forms, and sixty times ten thousand literal meanings.** And in the *New Yalkut* <note>original: *Jalkut chadasch*; a 17th-century collection of Kabbalistic midrashim</note>, on folio 155, column 1, number 34, under the title *Souls* <note>original: *Neschamoth*</note>, from the book *Intentions* <note>original: *Cavvanoth*</note>, folio 53, column 2, and folio 54, column 1, it reads as follows:

These sixty times ten thousand interpretations exist in the simple and literal sense; and there are corresponding numbers in the <term>Aggada</term> <note>homiletic or narrative traditions</note> and in the <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>the Jewish mystical tradition</note>.

<margin>The Law has as many interpretations as there are Israelite souls.</margin>
*That is, the sum of the souls consists of sixty times ten thousand (that is, six hundred thousand), and the Law is the foundation (or the origin) of the Israelite souls: and every <term>verse</term> <note>original: *Versickel*, from the Latin *versiculus*</note> that is in the Law has sixty times ten thousand interpretations. Thus, every soul is itself made from one interpretation, and in the future, everyone will read the Law according to the interpretation that concerns them, from which their soul was created. There are also many souls which comprise many interpretations within themselves, and our teacher Moses, peace be upon him, was comprised of all sixty times ten thousand together.*

<margin>The souls that are worthy of it ascend to heaven every night and read their interpretation there.</margin>
*Every night (also) when a person sleeps, if they are worthy of it, their soul ascends (into heaven) and reads there the interpretation that belongs to them in one verse, and on another night in another verse. ...to be seen on folio 180, column 1, under the title *The Gate of the World of Creation* <note>original: *Sha'ar Olam ha-Beriah*</note>, in the chapter called *The Gate of the Seven Lands* <note>original: *Sha'ar Sheva Aratzot*</note>—that is, the chapter concerning the seven earths—and the entire chapter, because it contains many foolish things about the seven earths which are said to exist, I will set down here as follows:

The holy worlds encompass one another, one below the other, down to the navel of the earth; the one called *Tebel* <note>The inhabited world; our Earth</note> is in the middle. Thus, there are seven encompassing heavens, as it is said: seven [heavens] and seven solidities. Just as the firmaments revolve above, so they revolve below; the firmaments are seven round spheres, and within them are seven earths. This secret was not given to the "dividers of boundaries" <note>A term for secular astronomers or geographers</note>, who are the experts of nature who divided the earth into seven climates or measures; rather, these are a great secret from the mysteries of the Torah. They were all created for the harsh punishment of the wicked, by means of <term>Shedim</term> <note>Malevolent demons or spirits</note>, spirits, and *Lilin* <note>Night-demons associated with Lilith</note>, who are the third class of demons; they multiply like humans, they eat and drink, and they die. These seven earths are one above the other, just like those seven heavens are one above the other. When Adam the first man was banished from the Garden of Eden, the Holy One, blessed be He, sent him to the lowest earth (*Eretz*), which is a place of darkness where no generation lives and nothing is of use; for the firmament there, called *Vilon* <note>The "Curtain," the lowest of the seven heavens</note>, is dark and serves no purpose because it contains no celestial lights, for the Moon has no light of its own. As soon as Adam entered there, great fear and dread fell upon him, along with a very great darkness. The "flaming sword which turns every way" was blazing on every side, and the opening of the earth was such that he had no place to hide himself. For he was driven out of Eden on the eve of the Sabbath, and he sat there all through the Sabbath day until the close of the Sabbath. He meditated on repentance, and the Holy One, blessed be He, raised him up to *Adamah* <note>The Second Earth</note>, which is the second from the bottom, as it is said: "The Lord God sent him forth from the Garden of Eden to till the *Adamah* [ground]." 

In this *Adamah*, there is a light that shines from its own firmament, and there are forms of stars and constellations there. In that place, there are forms of human beings, giants of tall stature, who were born of Adam during the one hundred and thirty years in which he fathered <term>Shedim</term>, spirits, and *Lilin*. Of all the seven mentioned earths, there is none where the inhabitants have bread, except for the people who are here, because Tebhel is the uppermost of all. There is also a brief summary of the likeness of those earths upon this earth Tebhel, and it has the same names as the seven earths, and the same nature, and various people dwell therein, as is said in Psalm 104:24: "O LORD, how manifold are thy works! In wisdom hast thou made them all." In the <term>Parascha Vajikra</term> <note>The weekly Torah portion "And He Called," opening the book of Leviticus</note>, the same author (namely, Rabbi Shimon ben Jochai, in the book Zohar) also says that between those (seven earths) lie Paradise and Hell, with their seven dwellings. And it is said that <term>Rav Hamnuna</term> <note>A prominent Babylonian teacher (Amora) mentioned frequently in the Talmud and Zohar</note> was punished because he would not believe this, as is reported in the same place (in the Zohar). These are the words of the book *Emeck Hammelech*, from which it can be seen how foolishly Holy Scripture is cited and interpreted therein.

# Chapter IX of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked.

The division of languages: The Holy One, blessed be He, created many kinds of <term>monstrous beings</term> <note>original Hebrew: *mistamdi*, likely a corruption of the Latin *monstruosi*</note>—so called in foreign tongues—in many places, and I shall mention some of them to you. In Africa, there are strange creatures who are androgynous <note>Possessing both male and female sex organs</note> and they have relations with one another. In the regions of Scythia <note>An ancient region in central Eurasia</note>, there are people who have only one eye in their foreheads. In India, there are those who have no mouth to eat and drink. In the mountains of India, there is a human species that has a tail and they do not follow human customs. And there is a species that has the body of a horse and the head of a ram, and on its forehead is a horn that shines brightly. And there is a species of man that has three rows of teeth, a human head, and the body of a lion. And there is a species of man that has only one leg and its foot is very wide, and they run very fast. And there is a species that has no throat and their eyes are on their backs. And there are those whose bodies are full of scales and their teeth are like those of a dog. In Scythia, there are those who have the form of a man but their legs are like a horse's, and they are called <term>Paturush</term> <note>Likely a phonetic rendering of Satyrs</note>. And there are people who do not walk on their feet, but rather they put their heads between their thighs and walk. In Ethiopia, there are those who have no nostrils. And there are those who have no ears, and some who have no mouth but only a small hole through which they drink with a straw. In the regions of the West, there are those whose ears are so large that they cover their entire bodies. In the regions of Arabia, there are very small people <note>Pygmies</note> whose women give birth at five years of age, and by the age of eight they are elderly; they have great wars with the <term>Norba</term> <note>Likely referring to the legendary battles between Pygmies and Cranes</note> who consume many of them. In Ethiopia, there is a species of man who lives in caves and they have no speech, only the voice of a cricket.

### Chapter IX of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked.

The division of languages: The Holy One, blessed be He, created many kinds of **monsters** <note>original Hebrew: "metstari," likely a corruption of the Latin "monstri" or Italian "mostri"</note> scattered in many places, and I will mention some of them to you.
In **Africa**, there are strange creatures who are **androgynous** <note>having both male and female characteristics</note> and they couple with one another. In the regions of **Scythia** <note>an ancient region in Central Eurasia</note>, there are people who have only **one eye** in their forehead. In **India**, there are those who have no mouth to eat or drink. In the mountains of **India**, there is a species that has a **tail** and they do not follow human customs. And there is a species that has the **body of a horse** and the head of a ram, and on its forehead is a horn that shines brightly. And there is a species of man that has **three rows of teeth**, a human head, and the body of a lion. And there is a species of man that has only **one leg** with a very broad foot, and they run very fast <note>These are the "Sciapods" or shadow-foots, legendary creatures said to use their single large foot as a sunshade</note>. And there are those who have no throat and their eyes are on their **shoulders** <note>original Hebrew: "ha-shurah," meaning the row or line</note>. And there are those whose bodies are full of **scales** and their teeth are like those of a dog. In **Scythia**, there are those who have the form of a man but their feet are like those of a horse, and they are called **Satyrs**. And there is a species of creatures who, in the summer time, turn into the shape of a **wolf**, and in the cold time, they return to the shape of a man; they worship the planet **Mars** and sacrifice people before him. In **Libya**, there are people who hate the sight of light and do not eat any living creature. And there are people who do not walk on their feet, but rather put their heads between their thighs and walk. In **Ethiopia**, there are those who have no **nostrils**. And there are those who have no ears, and some have no mouth but only a small hole through which they drink with a straw. In the regions of the **West**, there are those whose ears are so large that they cover their entire bodies. In the regions of **Arabia**, there are people who are very small, and their women give birth to daughters at **five years** of age; and when they are eight years old, they grow old; and they have wars with the species of **cranes** <note>original Hebrew: "ha-nurba," referring to the classical myth of the Pygmies' war against cranes</note> which destroy many of them. In **Ethiopia**, there is a species of humans who dwell in caves and have no mouth; they eat <unclear>nothing</unclear> but snakes, and they have no speech, only a sound like an **echo** <note>original Hebrew: "ha-kerrara"</note>.

...to him, and He took from Adam and gave to David; and concerning this, David said: "For You, Lord, have made me glad through Your work," etc. <note>Psalm 92:4</note>, meaning: Who caused me joy in this world to be alive? Your work—namely Adam the First—who is Your work and not the work of flesh and blood in the act of...

<margin>God showed Adam all the generations of mankind.</margin> That is, the holy and blessed God showed Adam all generations along with their preachers; He also let him see the kings whom He would set over Israel. But when He came to David, Adam saw that he was a dead lump <note>original: "todter Klumpen." This refers to a Midrashic legend where David was destined to be stillborn or die at birth</note>, and he said: "I will lend him some of my years (which I have to live)." Therefore, those years were taken from Adam and given to David. And because of this, David says: "For You, Lord, have made me glad through Your work," etc. That is: Who has caused me joy in this world, so that I am alive? Your work, namely the first man, is the one who is Your work and not a work of flesh and blood. I will rejoice in the work of Your hands, for he caused me joy by not living (the time that I now live, having gifted me such years from his own life).

<margin>Adam gave David some of his years.</margin> That God showed Adam all generations is also taught by the Talmud in the tractate *Sanhedrin*, folio 38, column 2, and in the tractate *Avoda Zara*, folio 5, column 1.

<margin>How many years he gave him.</margin> How many years Adam gave to David from his own is seen in the aforementioned *Yalkut Chadash* <note>original: ילקוט חדש, "The New Collection," a 17th-century compilation of Midrashic and Kabbalistic lore</note>, folio 7, column 1, number 92, where it is reported that they were seventy years <note>According to this legend, Adam was intended to live 1,000 years but lived only 930, giving 70 to King David</note>.

In Deuteronomy 20:19, it is forbidden to cut down any fruitful trees when a city is besieged, and the reason given is: "For the tree of the field is man's" <note>original Hebrew: כִּי הָאָדָם עֵץ הַשָּׂדֶה, *Ki ha-adam etz ha-sadeh*</note>. That is, as it is translated in the Zurich Bible: "Is such a tree of the field then a man (that he could do harm)?" or as Rabbi Joseph interprets it in his German-Hebrew Bible: "For the trees of the field are (or provide food) for man." However, in the *Midrash Koheleth* <note>A commentary on Ecclesiastes</note>, folio 329, column 1, it is cited as proof that even wolves and unfruitful trees must give an account on the Day of Judgment, where the words read as follows: "Rabbi Chama, the son of Gurion, said: Even the wolf, even the unfruitful trees are destined to give judgment and account. And the Rabbis derive this from the verse: 'For the tree of the field is man's.'" That is (as it is foolishly understood here): For as the man is, so is the tree of the field. Just as man must give an account, so also shall the unfruitful trees give an account.

<margin>The wolves and unfruitful trees shall give an account on the Last Day.</margin> In the prophet Hosea, chapter 4, verse 2, the murders committed by the people of Israel are held against them, and it is written there: "And blood touches blood."

### Of the Perverted Interpretation of the Holy Scripture by the Jews.

In the Talmudic tractate *Gittin*, however, on *folio 57, column 2*, the murders committed by *Nebuzaradan* <note>original: "Nebufar-Adan"</note>, the steward or captain of the *guards* <term>Trabanten; the personal bodyguards or elite soldiers of a monarch</term> of King *Nebuchadnezzar*, are interpreted with a great lie as follows:

> Rabbi Chiyya, the son of Abin, said that Rabbi Joshua, the son of Korcha, said: An old man from the inhabitants of Jerusalem told me that in this valley, Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guards, killed two hundred and eleven times ten thousand; and in Jerusalem he killed ninety-four times ten thousand upon one stone, until their blood flowed and touched the blood of Zechariah, to fulfill that which is said: **And blood touched blood.** <note>The quote "Blood touches blood" is from Hosea 4:2. The Zechariah mentioned here is traditionally identified as Zechariah son of Jehoiada, who was murdered in the Temple court (2 Chronicles 24:21)</note>

That is: Rabbi *Chiyya*, the son of *Abin*, said that Rabbi *Joshua*, the son of *Korcha*, said: An old man from among the inhabitants of *Jerusalem* told me— <margin>How many people *Nebuzaradan* killed.</margin> —that *Nebuzaradan*, the captain of the *guards*, killed two hundred and eleven times ten thousand (that is, two million and one hundred and ten thousand people) in the valley, and in *Jerusalem* he killed ninety-four times ten thousand (that is, nine hundred and forty thousand) upon one stone, so that their blood flowed and reached the blood of *Zechariah*, to confirm that which is said: **And blood touched blood.** This matter is described in the Talmudic tractate *Sanhedrin, folio 96, column 2*, with the following circumstances:

> He saw the blood of Zechariah, that it was seething. He said to them: "What is this?" They said to him: "It is the blood of sacrifices that was poured out." He said to them: "Bring some and I will see if it is the same as this blood." They brought some and it was not the same. He said to them: "Reveal it to me; if not, I will comb your flesh with iron combs." They said to him: "This was a priest and a prophet who prophesied to the Israelites concerning the destruction of Jerusalem, and they killed him." He said to them: "I will appease him." He brought the Rabbis and killed them over it, but it did not rest. He brought the schoolchildren and killed them over it, but it did not rest. He brought the young priests and killed them over it, but it did not rest, until he had killed ninety-four thousand over it, and yet it did not rest. He drew near to it and said: "Zechariah, Zechariah! I have destroyed the best among them; does it please you that I should kill them all?" Immediately it rested. At that moment, he thought of repentance in his heart and said: "If they, who only destroyed one soul, were treated thus, what will become of that man (himself)?" He fled, left his house to his family, and converted.

<margin>Why he did it.</margin> That is: When he (namely *Nebuzaradan*, of whom mention is made in *2 Kings 25:8*, after he had come into *Jerusalem*) saw the blood of *Zechariah*—that it was seething (and bubbling up as if it were boiling)—he asked them (namely the inhabitants of *Jerusalem*) what it was? And they answered him that it was blood from the sacrifice which had been poured out. Then he spoke to them: "Bring (livestock) here to me, so that I may (slaughter it and) test whether (the blood of the slaughtered animal) is similar to this (and seethes in the same way)." When he had slaughtered and it was not the same, he said to them: "Reveal it to me; if not, I will have your flesh combed with iron combs" <note>An ancient form of torture using metal-toothed instruments</note>. Then they spoke to him: "This man was a priest and a prophet, and because he prophesied the destruction of *Jerusalem* to the *Israelites*, they killed him." Thereupon he said to them: "I will appease him," and he had the *Rabbis* brought forth and killed them over the same blood, but it did not become still. ### Chapter IX of the First Part of *Judaism Unmasked*.

<margin>
Souls take on a body in heaven before they descend to the earth.
</margin>
In column 4, number 24, under the title <term>Neschamóth</term> <note>Hebrew for "Souls"</note>, it is proven that all souls, before they descend into the world, take on a body and present themselves in it before GOD; the words there read as follows: <note>original: "כל הנשמות קודם שירדו לעולם הזה מתלבשין בגוף ובדיוקן שעתיד לעמוד בע"הו..."</note> "Every soul, before it comes down into this world, clothes itself with a body; and with that very form in which it will exist in this world, it clothes itself above (in heaven) before it enters the world, and stands before God in that same body and that same form. And GOD adjures it <note>meaning the body along with the soul</note> that it shall not sin; and this is the meaning of the words: **Your eyes saw my unformed substance.** <note>Psalm 139:16</note> That is, Your eyes have seen my unformed substance, namely my body, as I stood before You."

In the first book of Moses <note>Genesis</note>, in the 33rd chapter, verse 4, we read: **But Esau ran to meet him (Jacob), and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him, and they wept.** By this, it is indicated that Esau, after a long-lasting enmity, loved his brother Jacob dearly once again. However, the Jews understand this quite differently, and it is written in <term>Bereshith rabba</term> <note>An ancient collection of Jewish homiletic interpretations (Midrash) on the Book of Genesis</note>, in the 78th <term>Parascha</term> <note>A weekly Torah portion or section</note>, folio 71, column 1, concerning the word <term>vajischakéhu</term> <note>Hebrew for "and he kissed him"</note>. This word is marked in the Hebrew text above with small dots in an extraordinary or unusual manner, and it is written thus: <note>original: "מלמד שלא בא לנשקו אלא לנשכו..."</note> "This <note>namely, that the word *vajischakéhu* is marked with dots above</note>

<margin>
How Esau bit Jacob, and why they both wept.
</margin>
teaches us that he did not come to kiss him, but rather to bite him. However, the neck of our father Jacob was turned into marble, and the teeth of that wicked man <note>Esau</note> were blunted (when he bit into the hard neck). What then does the word <term>vajifku</term> <note>Hebrew for "and they wept"</note> mean? It indicates that this one (Jacob) wept because of his neck (that it had been turned into marble), and the other (Esau) wept because of his teeth (which he had ruined by biting into Jacob’s hard neck)." On the neck of Moses.

# Chapter IX of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked. 474

<margin>
The Prophet Jeremiah is also said to have been accused of whoredom and adultery.
</margin>
In his commentary on this matter, <note>Likely referring to the medieval commentator Rashi or a similar authority cited in the previous context.</note> he prays thus: <note>original: "יצא חוץ שלא יחשדוהו עוד"</note> that is, "He went out (from the camp) so that they might no longer have any suspicion against him." Thus it is also read in the Talmudic tractate <term>Bava Kamma</term> <note>One of the foundational books of the Talmud, dealing primarily with civil matters and damages</note>, folio 140, column 2, concerning the prophet Jeremiah, that he was accused of whoredom or adultery; for regarding the words of Jeremiah 18, verse 22—*For they have dug a pit to take me, and laid snares for my feet*—it is written there as follows: <note>original: "רבי אליעזר אומר : שחשדוהו מזונה רבי שמואל בר נחמני אמר חשדוהו מאשת איש :"</note> that is, Rabbi Elieser says that they held him in suspicion regarding whoredom. Rabbi Samuel bar Nachmani said he was under suspicion regarding adultery <note>specifically with a married woman</note>.

<margin>
What took place between Joseph and Potiphar’s wife.
</margin>
Concerning Joseph, it is read in Genesis 39, verse 12, that when Potiphar’s wife wanted him to lie with her, he left the garment by which she had seized him in her hand, fled, and ran out of the house. However, in the Talmudic tractate <term>Sota</term> <note>A tractate concerning the 'Sotah' or woman suspected of adultery</note>, folio 36, column 2, it is read thus: <note>original: "תנא דבי ר' ישמעאל אותו היום יום אידם היה והלכו כולן לבית עבודת זרה שלהן..."</note> that is, Those of the house of Rabbi Ishmael teach that on that very day it was their (the Egyptians') festival day, and they had all gone to their idolatrous temple; and she (namely, Potiphar's wife) said to them (her household) that she was sick. But she thought: "I have no day on which Joseph might be intimate with me like this day" <note>because no one is at home</note>; and she seized him by his garment and said, "Sleep with me." In that very hour (as he lay down upon the bed and was about to fulfill her will), the form of his father appeared to him in the window and said to him: "Joseph, your brothers are destined to be written upon the stones of the <term>Ephod</term> <note>The ceremonial vestment of the High Priest</note>, and you among them; do you wish then for your name to be blotted out from among them and for you to be called a shepherd of harlots? As it is written (Proverbs 29, v. 3): *He who keeps company with harlots* (that is, adheres to harlots) *wastes his substance.*" Immediately following this <note>original: "אמר רבי יוחנן משום ר' מאיר ששככה קשתו לאיתנה..."</note> Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Meir: "His bow was appeased <note>a euphemism for the subsiding of his passion</note>, and he stuck his fingers into the ground, and semen came out from between his fingernails." Through the power of the Mighty One of Jacob, what caused him to be engraved upon the stones of the Ephod? Only the Mighty One of Jacob, from there he merited to become the Shepherd of the Stone of Israel, as it is said (Psalm 80:2): *Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel, you who lead Joseph like a flock.* It is taught: Joseph was worthy to have twelve tribes descend from him just as they descended from his father Jacob, as it is said: *These are the generations of Jacob, Joseph*; but because the semen came out from between his fingernails <note>representing a loss of potential offspring</note>, those tribes instead came from his brother Benjamin, yet they were all called by Joseph's name.

# On the Jews’ Perverted Interpretation of the Holy Scripture.

<margin>How Joab and David leaped over the wall.</margin>
When **David** said to the people of **Israel** that they should wage war against the **inhabitants** of the city of **Jebus** <note>Jebus is the ancient name for Jerusalem before it was fully conquered by David; see 1 Chronicles 11:3.</note> (concerning which one may read in **1 Chronicles** 11, verse 3, etc.), he began by saying: **Whoever strikes the Jebus (that is, the Jebusites) first shall be a chief and captain (or prince).** What did **Joab** do? He brought a green **fir tree** and placed it against the side of the **city wall** (into the earth) and bent its **treetop**, which was supple. **David** held the tree, and **Joab** leaped over **David’s head**, hung onto the **fir tree**, and leaped (from its top) onto the **city wall**. Then **David** spoke (the words of **Psalm** 141, verse 5): **Let the righteous smite me kindly and reprove me.** What did the holy, blessed **GOD** do? He made the **wall** shorter, and **David** climbed up after him, as it is said: **With my GOD I leap over walls.** <note>The author is quoting a Midrashic legend that combines military history with miraculous physical feats to explain David's conquest of Jerusalem.</note>

In the aforementioned second **Book of Samuel**, in the 15th **chapter**, verse 32, we read of **David**: **And David came** <term>עד הראש</term> <gloss>to the summit</gloss>, that is, **to the peak** (namely of the **Mount of Olives**, which is mentioned in verse 30) **that he might worship God there.** From this, it is clearly seen that **David’s** intent and purpose was to call upon **GOD** the **Lord** in his then-current distress.

<margin>The Talmud teaches that David intended to practice idolatry.</margin>
In the **Talmudic** tractate **Sanhedrin**, however, on folio 107, column 1, it is foolishly argued from these words that he intended to practice **idolatry** there. The text is written as follows: <note>original Hebrew: "אמר רב יהודה אמר רב בקש דוד לעבוד עבודה זרה..."</note> that is, **Rav Yehuda said that Rav said, David sought to commit idolatry, as it is said: And David came to the summit** (of the mountain, which is called <term>rosh</term>) **to worship** <term>לאלהים</term> <gloss>to God</gloss>, **that is, the gods (as the Talmud wishes it understood, namely the idols, which are also called Elohim, though here it must be interpreted as GOD). For "rosh" (which in the Hebrew language means a head, as well as a summit, peak, or height) signifies nothing other than an idol, as is said in Daniel 2, verse 32: The head of that image (in the Chaldean original text it is called "resheh," and in the Chaldean language the word "resh" means the same as "rosh" does for the Hebrews) was of fine gold. And behold, Hushai the Archite met him with a torn coat and earth upon his head, and said to David: "Shall it be said that a king such as you would practice idolatry?" But he answered...**

# On the Jews' Perverted Interpretation of the Holy Scripture.

### First Part

In the *Jalkut chádasch* <note>A 17th-century collection of Kabbalistic and Midrashic commentaries.</note>, on folio 143, column 2, number 54, under the title "Messiah," regarding the words of **Exodus 21:33**: **"And if a man shall open a pit, or if a man shall dig a pit, and not cover it, and an ox or a donkey fall therein,"** it is written in a foolish manner from the *Zohar* as follows: <margin>By the donkey, the Messiah is understood.</margin> <note>original: "כי יכרה איש בור וגו' ונפל שמה שור זה משיח בן יוסף או חמור זה משיח בן דוד ונפל שמה"</note> That is: **"When someone digs a pit etc. and an ox falls into it, this signifies the Messiah, the son of Joseph; or a donkey, this signifies the Messiah, the son of David"** (and it is said of him) *venafal*, that is, "and falls," because he is called *bar nifle* <term>son of the fallen</term> <note>A title for the Messiah found in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 96b), possibly derived from the "fallen tabernacle of David" in Amos 9:11, though some scholars suggest a connection to the Greek word for "clouds."</note> (from "falling," as can be seen in the Talmudic Tractate *Sanhedrin*, folio 96, column 2).

Likewise, in the aforementioned *Jalkut chádasch*, folio 91, column 2, number 157, under the title "Jacob," regarding the words of **Genesis 32:5**: **"And I have oxen, and donkeys, flocks, and menservants, and womenservants,"** it is written in the following manner: <note>original: "ויהי לי שור וחמור וגו' שור זה משיח מלחמה שנא' בכור שורו וגו' חמור זה מלך המשיח שנ' עני ורוכב על"</note> That is: **"And I have cattle or oxen, and donkeys, etc."** The word **ox** signifies the Anointed of War <note>The "Messiah of War" refers to a priest designated to address the troops before battle, as described in Deuteronomy 20.</note> (that is, that priest who, in war, proclaimed the words of **Deuteronomy 20:8**: **"What man is there that is fearful and fainthearted? let him go and return unto his house"**); as it is said (in **Deuteronomy 33:17**): **"His glory is like the firstling of his ox, etc."** The word **donkey** signifies the Messiah, as it is said (in **Zechariah 9:9**): **"Lowly, and riding upon a donkey."** The word **flocks** signifies Israel (as it is written in **Ezekiel 34:31**): **"And ye my flock, etc."** Something regarding this is also to be found in *Bereshith Rabbah* <note>The Great Genesis, a foundational Midrashic text on the first book of the Torah.</note>, folio 69, column 3, in the 75th *Parashah* <term>section</term>.

In the 139th Psalm <note>This citation likely refers to Psalm 129:3 in modern numbering.</note>, verse 3, it is read: **"The plowers plowed upon my back; they made long their furrows."** But what these words mean, according to the opinion of the Jews, is indicated by the Talmudic Tractate *Sota* <note>Tractate Sotah, folio 11, column 2.</note>, folio 11, column 2, with the following:

# Chapter IX of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked.

<margin>
How it fared with the children of the Israelites in Egypt, so that they were preserved alive.
</margin>
<note>original Hebrew: הק"בה על הים הם הכירוהו תחילה שנ' זה אלי ואנוהו</note>
The Holy One, blessed be He, was recognized by them [the children] first at the Sea, as it is said: "This is my God, and I will glorify Him" <note>Exodus 15:2. The Midrash suggests the infants recognized God because He had personally nursed them in the fields.</note>. That is: At the time when they (the Israelite women) went to draw water (for their husbands, who were in the heavy Egyptian servitude), the holy and blessed God caused small fish to enter their pitchers (or buckets). They drew them up, half water and half fish. Afterward, they set two pots (on the fire), one with water to warm it, and the other with the fish, which they cooked. They brought these to their husbands in the field, and they washed them, anointed them, and gave them to eat and drink. And they [the husbands] lay with them between the two pots (or hearth-stones), as it is said in **Psalm 68:14**: "Though ye have lien among the pots" (or as Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo itzhaki), the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> interprets it: "the ends or boundaries of the fields"). After they became pregnant, they returned to their houses. 

But when the time of birth approached, they went out into the field and gave birth under an apple tree, as it is said in **Song of Solomon 8:5**: "I raised thee up under the apple tree." And the holy, blessed God sent someone from the high heavens who cleansed the children and made them beautiful, just as a midwife makes a child beautiful, as is said in **Ezekiel 16:4**: "And as for thy nativity, in the day thou wast born thy navel was not cut, neither wast thou washed in water to supple thee," etc. 

And He gathered (or gave) them two spheres (or round stones), from one of which flowed oil, and from the other honey, as is said in **Deuteronomy 32:13**: "And he made him to suck honey out of the rock, and oil out of the flinty rock." But when the Egyptians became aware of this and came to kill them (the children), a miracle occurred for them: the earth swallowed them up (so that no harm should come to them). And the Egyptians brought oxen and plowed upon their backs, as is said in **Psalm 129:3**: "The plowers plowed upon my back." 

After the Egyptians had gone away, these same (children) grew up and came forth like the grass of the field, as is said in **Ezekiel 16:7**: "I have caused thee to multiply as the bud of the field." And when they were grown great, they came in throngs to their houses, as is said (in the same verse 7): "And thou hast increased and waxen great, and thou art come <term>ba'adi adajim</term> <note>original: בעדי עדיים</note>," that is, "with the ornament of ornaments." Do not read it as *ba'adi adajim*, "with the ornament of ornaments," but rather as <term>be'edre adarim</term> <note>original: בעדרי עדרים</note>, "with flocks of flocks" <note>This is a classic example of "Al Tikrei," a rabbinic interpretive technique where a word is playfully re-read with different vowels or similar letters to derive a new meaning—in this case, changing "ornaments" to "flocks" to support the story of children returning in groups.</note>.

When God also revealed Himself at the (Red) Sea, they (namely the aforementioned children) had recognized Him first, as it is said (**Exodus 15:2**): **This is my strong GOD, I will praise Him (or make Him a dwelling,)** namely, in which to serve Him. This fable is also found in the book **Zeéna ureéna** <note>The *Tze'enah U-Re'enah*, a popular Yiddish-language work for Jewish women, blending Torah commentary with legends (Midrashim).</note> folio 37, column 2, in the Portion **Shemót**, and in **Shemót Rabbáh** <note>Exodus Rabbah, a collection of homiletic interpretations of the Book of Exodus.</note>, folio 95, column 1, in the first Portion; as also in the small tractate **Sépher divré hayamim shel Moshé Rabbénu** <note>The Chronicle of Moses our Teacher, a medieval legendary biography of Moses.</note>, folio 2, column 1 and 2. <margin>What kind of prayers the Patriarchs established.</margin>
In the Talmudic tractate **Berachót** <note>The first tractate of the Talmud, dealing mostly with blessings and prayers.</note>, it is reported on folio 26, column 2, that the Patriarchs **Abraham, Isaac**, and **Jacob** established certain prayers, concerning which it is written there as follows:
<note>original Hebrew: אברהם תיקן תפילת שחרית שנ' וישכם אברהם בבוקר אל המקום אשר עמד שם ואין עמידה אלא תפילה שנ' ויעמוד פנחס ויתפלל . יצחק תקן תפילת מנחה שנ' ויצא יצחק לשוח בשדה לפנות ערב ואין שיחה אלא תפילה שנ' תפלה לעני כי יעטוף ולפני יי' ישפוך שיחו . יעקב תקן תפילת ערבית שנ' ויפגע במקום וילן שם ואין פגיעה אלא תפלה שנ' ואתה אל תתפלל בעד העם הזה ואל תשא בעדם רנה ותפלה ואל תפגע בי :</note>
Abraham established the morning prayer, as it is said: "And Abraham rose early in the morning to the place where he had stood." And "standing" is nothing other than prayer, as it is said: "Then Phinehas stood up and prayed." Isaac established the afternoon prayer, as it is said: "And Isaac went out to meditate in the field toward evening." And "meditating" is nothing other than prayer, as it is said: "A prayer of the afflicted when he is faint and pours out his meditation before the Lord." Jacob established the evening prayer, as it is said: "And he encountered the place and stayed there overnight." And "encountering" is nothing other than prayer, as it is said: "And as for you, do not pray for this people, nor lift up a cry or prayer for them, and do not encounter Me."

That is, **Abraham** ordered the **Morning Prayer**, as it is said (**Genesis 19:27**): **And Abraham rose early in the morning to the place where he had stood.** By "standing," however, nothing else is signified but prayer, as it is said (**Psalm 106:30**): **Then Phinehas stood up and prayed.** (As it is erroneously understood in the Talmud; for it actually means, "and executed judgment," or "practiced justice," since he stabbed an Israelite together with a Midianite woman while they were in the act of harlotry, as may be seen in **Numbers 25:7-8**, and thus he did not pray.) **Isaac** created the **Afternoon Prayer**, as it is said (**Genesis 24:63**): **And Isaac went out into the field to meditate when it began to be evening.** "Meditation," however, signifies nothing else than prayer, as it is said (**Psalm 102:1**): **A prayer of the afflicted, when he was troubled, and poured out his meditation before the Lord.** **Jacob** instituted the **Night Prayer**, as it is said (**Genesis 28:11**): **Vayifga**, etc., that is, **And he came to a place where he remained overnight.** This "coming" or "arriving" (which in Hebrew is called <term>Pegiah</term> <note>Pegiah (פגיעה) can mean to encounter, to strike, or to entreat/intercede.</note>) signifies nothing else than prayer, as it is said in **Jeremiah 7:16** (or according to others, verse 18): **And you shall not pray for this people, and shall not bring before them any lament or prayer, veal tifga**, that is, you shall also make no intercession. The very same is also found in the commentary of Rabbi **Menáchem of Recanati** on the five books of Moses, folio 52, column 3, in the Portion **Vayéra**; as also in the **Yalkút chadash** folio 49, column 1, number 47, under the title Galuth.

<margin>
What the Jews write concerning the manna which was eaten in the wilderness in former times.
</margin>
In the **Yalkut Shimoni** <note>A significant medieval collection of Jewish homiletic interpretations (Midrashim) on the Hebrew Bible.</note> on the five books of Moses, it is written in number 260, folio 74, column 3, concerning the manna—which, as we read in **Exodus 16:14**, God caused to rain from heaven as food for the children of Israel in the wilderness—that it lay so high that all the kings of the East and West <note>literally: "of the rising and setting [of the sun]"</note> were able to see it. This is proven in a foolish manner from **Psalm 23:5**; the words there read as follows:
<note>original Hebrew: אמר בן יהודה אומר מן שירד להן לישראל היה מתגבה ועולה עד שרואין אותו כל מלכי מזרח ומערב שנ' תערוך לפני שלחן נגד צוררי :</note>
That is: The son of Judah says: The manna that descended for the Israelites increased and rose to such a height that all the kings of the East and West saw it, as it is said (in **Psalm 23:5**): **You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies.** This fable is taken from the Talmudic tractate **Yoma** <note>The tractate of the Talmud dealing primarily with the rituals of the Day of Atonement, Yom Kippur.</note>, folio 76, column 1, where the same thing is found; and it is also reported there how high it lay, with these words:

<margin>
How high it was.
</margin>
<note>original Hebrew: מן שירד להן לישראל היה גבוה ששים אמה :</note>
That is: The manna which descended for the Israelites was sixty <term>cubits</term> <note>An ancient unit of length based on the forearm, roughly 18 to 22 inches.</note> high.

<margin>
Precious stones and pearls are also said to have fallen down with it.
</margin>
It is also claimed that magnificent precious stones fell down with the manna, as is found in the aforementioned tractate **Yoma**, folio 75, column 1, where it is argued in a subtle Jewish manner using the words of **Exodus 36:3**, **"And they brought their free-will offering to him every morning,"** as it is written there:
<note>original Hebrew: מאי בבקר בבקר א"ר שמואל בר נחמני א"ר יונתן מדבר שירד להם בבוקר בבוקר מלמד שירד להם לישראל אבנים טובות ומרגליות עם המן והנשיאים הביאו את אבני השהם תנא נשיאים ממש וכן הוא אומר נשיאים ורוח וגשם :</note>
That is: **What is the meaning of "every morning"?** Rabbi Samuel, the son of Nahmani, said that Rabbi Jonathan said: It [the Scripture] reports that it fell for them every morning; and this teaches us that precious stones and pearls came down to the Israelites with the manna. (So it is also written in **Exodus 35:27**: **And the Nesi'im** <note>original: והנשיאם / Vehannefiim</note>, that is, **the clouds** <note>A pun based on the Hebrew word *Nesi'im* (נְשִׂיאִים), which can mean "princes" or "leaders," but also "clouds" or "vapors," as in Proverbs 25:14.</note>, as it is understood here in the Talmud, though it usually means **the princes**; nevertheless, the word *Nesi'im* also signifies clouds elsewhere) brought onyx. We learn that they were actually clouds. In this sense, it is said in **Proverbs 25:14**: (Like) the clouds (which are also called *Nesi'im* here), the wind and rain, etc.

The many varieties of taste the manna had.
</margin>

<note>original Hebrew: הוריד להם המן שהיה בו מכל מיני טעמים והיה כל אחד מישראל טועם כל מה שהיה רוצה שכן כתיב זה ארבעים שנה יי" אלהיך עמך לא חסרת דבר מהו דבר כשהיה מתאוה לאכול דבר והיה אומר</note>
That is: He caused the manna to descend for them, in which were all kinds of tastes, and every individual of Israel tasted whatever he desired; for thus it is written (in **Deuteronomy 2:7**): **These forty years the LORD your God has been with you; you have lacked nothing.** What is the meaning of "nothing"? ### On the Jews’ perverted interpretation of Holy Scripture. 485

<note>original Hebrew: בפיו אלולי היה לי פטימא א' לאכול מיד היה נעשה לתוך פיו טעם פטימא דבר היה אומר וה"קבה היה עושה רצונו. א"ר אבא אף דבר לא היה אומר בפיו אלא חושב בלבו לומר מה שנפשו מתאוה היה ה"ב"ה עושה רצונו והיה טועם טעם מה שהיה מתאוה. תדע לך שכן אמר יחזקאל ולחמי אשר נתתי לך סולת ושמן ודבש האכלתיך:</note>
that is, **He (namely GOD) let the manna come down to them, which had all kinds of taste, and every Israelite experienced a taste in it just as he desired it; for it is written (Deuteronomy 2:7): "These forty years the Lord your God has been with you, and you have lacked nothing." What does "nothing" mean? When someone had a desire to eat something, and spoke with his mouth: "If only I had a fattened bird to eat"; then immediately the taste of a fattened bird was in his mouth. When someone said something, GOD did his will. Rabbi Abba said, even if a person had not spoken a thing with his mouth, but only thought in his mind what he desired, GOD fulfilled that longing, and he had the very taste that he craved. You must know that this is so, for as Ezekiel (chapter 16, verse 19) spoke: "My food, which I gave to you, fine flour and oil and honey, I gave you to eat."**

That the manna had all kinds of tastes, just as each person desired, can also be seen in the **Pesikta sotárta** <note>Also known as Lekach Tov, an 11th-century commentary on the Pentateuch and the Five Scrolls.</note> folio 45, column 2, in the **Parashah Behaalotecha** <note>The weekly Torah portion covering Numbers 8:1–12:16.</note>, where it is read: <note>original Hebrew: נשתנה להם לכל מיני תבשילין</note> that is, **It was transformed for them (namely the Israelites) into all kinds of cooked dishes.** And shortly thereafter it follows: <note>original Hebrew: נשתנה להם לכל דבר שמתלקט בשדה. כשהיה אדם מתאוה לאכול ענבים טועם ענבים תאנים גם כן וכן לכל דבר שבעולם :</note> i.e. **It was transformed for them into every thing that is gathered in the field. When a man wanted to eat grapes, it tasted like grapes; if he wanted figs, it also tasted so. And thus he could have everything that is in the world.**

<margin>As long as the Israelites ate the manna, they supposedly had no—saving your grace—bowel movements.</margin>
It is also said that the Israelites, in those forty years in which they ate the manna, had (to mention it with all due respect) no bowel movements; concerning which it is written in **Rabbi Bechai's** <note>Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century Spanish rabbi and kabbalist.</note> interpretation of the 5 Books of Moses, folio 83, column 1, in the **Parashah Beshallach** <note>The weekly Torah portion covering Exodus 13:17–17:16.</note>, regarding the words of Psalm 78:25, **They ate** <note>original Hebrew: לחם אבירים</note> **lechem abbirim**, **that is, bread of the mighty, or angels' bread, as follows:** <note>original Hebrew: לחם אבירים לחם שנבלע באברים ומזה דרשו רבותינו ז"ל מחופס בגימטריא רמ"ח אברים : ומכאן שלא היו צריכין לנקביהם שהרי מזונם היה נבלע ברמ"ח אברים שלהם שהיו אוכלים:</note> that is: **Bread of the angels, lechem shennibla ba-avarim, bread which was absorbed into the limbs; and therefore our Rabbis of blessed memory interpret the word** <note>original Hebrew: מחופס</note> **mechuspas** <note>Usually translated as "fine" or "flake-like" in Exodus 16:14, describing the manna.</note> **that is, "rounded," which by Gematria** <note>A system of Jewish numerology where letters of the alphabet correspond to numbers.</note> **equals the 248 limbs.** <note>The total numerical value of the Hebrew letters in 'mechuspas' (מחספס) equals 248, which corresponds to the traditional Jewish count of the number of organs/limbs in the human body.</note> **And from this it follows that they did not need their "outlets"** <note>A euphemism for the anus/excretory system.</note> **because their food was absorbed into their 248 limbs as they ate it.**

### Chapter IX of the First Part of *Judaism Unmasked*. 486

(which is said of the Manna in Exodus 16:14, that it was "round") they interpret it thus, and say that it amounts to two hundred and forty-eight through the **Gematria** <note>A Jewish system of numerology where letters of a word are added together to find a hidden meaning; here, the Hebrew word for "round" is linked to the number 248</note>, and it signifies the two hundred and forty-eight limbs of the human body: and from this it is proven that they had no bowel movements, because their food, which they ate, was absorbed into their two hundred and forty-eight limbs. The same is also to be found in **Pesikta Rabbetha** <note>A collection of homiletic Midrashim (interpretations)</note> folio 45, column 1, in the **Parashah Behaalotecha**. So it also stands in **Bammidbar Rabba** <note>Numbers Rabbah, a commentary on the Book of Numbers</note> folio 219, column 2, in the sixteenth **Parashah**, that God—when the Israelites called the Manna a "worthless" or "vile" food, as seen in Numbers 21:5—spoke thus: <note>original Hebrew: האכלתי להם מן מ' שנה ולא נצרך אחד מהם לנקביו אותו מ' שנה׃</note> That is: **I have given them Manna to eat for forty years, and not one of them had a need to go to the stool in those same forty years; rather, they ate the Manna, and it became flesh within them,** as it is said (Psalm 78:25): "They ate the bread of angels," and you provoke me to anger with it.

<margin>From the melted Manna, rivers and streams were created.</margin>
It is also said that from the Manna, when it was melted in the morning by the heat of the sun, rivers and streams arose; therefore, the words of Exodus 16:21 are thus translated in the **Chaldean Paraphrase** <note>The Targum, an Aramaic translation and expansion of the Hebrew Bible</note> of Jonathan: <note>original Aramaic: והוו מלקטין יתיה מן עדן צפרא עד ארבע שעין דיומא אינש לפום מיכליה ומן ארבע שעין ולהלא שחין שמשא עלוהי והוה שייח ומתעביד מבועין דמיין ונגידין עד ימא רבא ואתיין הינון דכיין ובעירן ושתין מניה והון בני ישראל צדין ואכלין יתהון׃</note> That is: **And they (namely the Israelites) gathered it from the time of the morning until the fourth hour of the day, each one as much as he could eat. After the fourth hour, however, and further on, the sun grew hot over it, and a trench was made in which springs of water arose, which flowed even to the Great Sea: and the clean animals and the cattle came and drank from it, and the children of Israel caught them through hunting and ate them.** But **Rabbi Salomon** <note>Better known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French commentator on the Torah and Talmud</note> writes in his commentary on this as follows: <note>original Hebrew: הנשאר בשדה נעשה נחלים ושותין ממנו איילים וצבאים ואומות העולם וצדין מהם וטועמים בהם טעם מן ויודעים מה שבחם של ישראל׃</note> That is: **What remained in the field (after the Israelites had taken as much as they needed) became streams, and the stags and gazelles drank from them; and the nations of the world caught them by hunting, and tasted in them the taste of Manna, and perceived wherein the excellence of the Israelites consisted.** This is also to be found in the book **Mechilta** <note>An ancient legal commentary on Exodus</note> folio 19, column 4, in the fifth **Parashah**. That streams arose from it after it had melted is also found in the **Jalkut**. <note>The Yalkut Shimoni, a major medieval compilation of Midrashic interpretations.</note>

# On the Jews' Perverted Interpretation of Holy Scripture.

*Jalkut Shimoni* <note>An extensive medieval midrashic anthology covering the entire Hebrew Bible</note> on the 5 Books of Moses, folio 73, column 4, number 258, may be seen / and there follows the following: <note>original Hebrew: כיון שהיה יורד בנחלים היו אומות העולם באים לשתות : ומיד מלוחו והוא נעשה בפיהם כמר כלענה שנאמר ושמו כזרע גד הוא אבל לישראל נעשה בחוץ כפי הטעם כדבש שנאמר וטעמו כצפיחית בדבש :</note> that is / When that same [Manna] flowed like streams / the nations of the world came / so that they might drink of it / and it became in their mouths as bitter as wormwood / as is said in (Exodus 16, v. 31): **And the Manna was like coriander seed.** <note>The author is highlighting a Jewish wordplay where the Hebrew word for coriander, *gad*, is linked to a word for "bitterness" for the Gentiles</note>. To the Israelites, however, it was in their mouths like honey / as is said (also in the mentioned 31st verse): **And its taste was like honey-cake.**

<margin>The children are said to have spoken with God from their mothers' wombs / and to have become guarantors for their parents.</margin>
Furthermore, the Jews teach / that / when God gave the Law / not only the children / but even those / who were still in their mothers' wombs / spoke with God / and became guarantors for Israel / that they would keep the Law / and such a thing is proven from Holy Scripture / according to their custom / in a foolish manner / of which it is written thus in the *Midrash Tillim* <note>A midrashic commentary on the Book of Psalms</note> folio 9, column 2, concerning the words of the eighth Psalm v. 3. **Out of the mouth of young children and sucklings hast thou ordained strength /**: <note>original Hebrew: בשעה שבקש הק"בה ליתן את התורה לישראל אמר להן תנו : לי ערבים שתקיימו את התורה אמרו לו הי אבות ערבים בנו אמר להן הק"בה חייבין הם לי ולואי שיעמדו בעצמם... </note> that is / At the time when God wanted to give the Law to the Israelites / he spoke to them; Provide me with guarantors / that you will keep the Law: Then they said / the fathers shall be guarantors for us. Thereupon God spoke to them / these same are indebted to me themselves / if only they might stand for themselves. This matter is like one / who went to borrow something / then they said to him / provide me a guarantor: Now when that same one had gone / and brought one / who was already indebted to him (that is, to the one who was the lender) / he spoke to the same / (who wanted to borrow /) if only he might stand for himself: bring me one / who is indebted to me for nothing. Thus God said to the Israelites / you have brought me guarantors / and how many debts do I have against them? Rather / give me guarantors who are indebted to me for nothing at all. And so it says / "The Lord made not this covenant with our fathers." They said to Him / who are they that are not indebted to you? He said to them / the infants. Immediately they brought him the infants from their mothers' breasts and from their wombs; and their mothers' bellies became like mirrors of glass / and they saw the Holy One, blessed be He, from within the bellies and spoke with Him / as it is said / "Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings," and it is written of infants that they "saw no light." The Holy One, blessed be He, said to them: "Are you guarantors for your fathers / so that if they do not keep the Law / you shall be held responsible for them?" They said to him / "Yes." He said to them / "I am the Lord your God." They said to him / "Yes." He said to them / "You shall have no other gods." They said to him / "Yes." And for every single word they answered Him / for a "no," No / and for a "yes," Yes. He said to them / "From your mouths I give the Law to them" / as it is said / "Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings you have ordained strength," and there is no "strength" but the Law / as it is said / "The Lord will give strength to His people." Therefore / when Israel neglects the Law / they [the children] are held responsible for them / as it is said / "My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge." <note>Hosea 4:6</note>: that is / At the time when God wanted to give the Law to the Israelites / he spoke to them; Provide me with guarantors / that you will keep the Law: Then they said / the fathers shall be guarantors for us. ### Chapter IX of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked.

The Israelites were told: "You have presented me with guarantors, but how many debts do I have to demand from them? Provide me with guarantors who owe me absolutely nothing." Thus it is said (Deuteronomy 5, v. 3): **The Lord made not this covenant with our fathers.** <note>The author uses this verse to suggest that the older generation was too burdened by sin to be the primary recipients or guarantors of the covenant</note>. They then asked him, "Who are those who owe you nothing?" and he answered them, "The children." Upon this, they immediately brought him the children from their mothers' breasts and their pregnant wives; the bellies of their mothers stood as clear as glass to look through, and they saw from within those wombs the holy and blessed God and spoke with him, as is said (Psalm 8, v. 3): **Out of the mouths of young children and sucklings.** And it is written (Job 3, v. 15 or according to others v. 16): **As the young children who have not seen the light.** <note>A legendary interpretation suggesting that the unborn were granted miraculous sight and speech to participate in the Sinai revelation</note>. Then God said to them, "Are you willing to provide surety for your fathers, so that in the event they do not keep the Law, you will be held liable for them?" and they answered, "Yes." Then he said to them: **I am the Lord thy God**, and they said, "Yes." Further, he said to them: **Thou shalt have no other God**, and they said, "Yes," answering him to every commandment with "Yes, yes" and to every prohibition with "No, no." He said further to them, "From your mouths I give them the Law," as is said (Psalm 8, v. 3): **Out of the mouths of young children and sucklings you have ordained power**; the word "power" <note>Original German: *Macht*. In Hebrew, the word *Oz* (strength/power) is frequently interpreted by the Rabbis as a synonym for the Torah</note> signifies nothing other than the Law, as is said (Psalm 29, v. 11): **The Lord will give power unto his people.** Therefore, when the Israelites destroy the Law, these same children are held liable on their account, as is said (Hosea 4, v. 6): **My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge.**

<margin>In the same way, Ben Sira is said to have spoken as soon as he was born, and Jeremiah while still in his mother’s womb.</margin>
Likewise, in the little book of *Ben Sira* <note>The *Alphabet of Ben Sira*, a medieval text containing various folk legends and proverbs</note> folio 2, column 2, it is read concerning the prophet Jeremiah's daughter that she became pregnant from her father—not through carnal union, but through another shameful deed which I do not wish to disclose <note>The author refers to a folk legend where Jeremiah was forced to release his seed in a bathhouse, and his daughter later conceived by it unintentionally; the author uses this to cast the story in a negative light</note>—and her child (who was named Ben Sira), as soon as he was born, spoke with his mother. And in folio 3, column 1 of the same work, it is also reported of the prophet Jeremiah himself that he spoke from his mother's womb and would not come out until he was told what his name should be. Furthermore, in folio 3, column 2 and folios 4 and 5 of that place, it is written that when Ben Sira was one year old, his mother led him to school, where he spoke with his teacher and displayed a great understanding, presenting him with all sorts of highly intellectual matters, of which something was already mentioned above on page 323.

And on folio 3, column 1, in the same place, it is also reported of the prophet Jeremiah himself that he spoke from his mother’s womb, and would not come out until he was told what his name should be. Furthermore, on folio 3, column 2, and folios 4 and 5, it is written there that when Ben Sira was one year old, his mother led him to the school, where he spoke with his teacher and displayed a great understanding, presenting all sorts of highly intellectual matters to him, of which something was already reported above on page 323.

That is, (**Our Rabbis**) have said that while **Jacob** and **Esau** were still in their mother’s womb, **Jacob** said to **Esau**: "My brother, we have two worlds before us: this world and the future one (that is, this temporal life and the future eternal life). You take this world, and I will take the future world," as is said in (**Genesis** 25, verse 31): **Sell me your birthright today.** (It is said) "today" because they were still in their mother’s womb. And some say even a change of place, as it is written: "And the Lord said to Abram: Go forth from your country... and I will make you into a great nation."

Rabbi Perez writes in his book *Maarécheth ha-Elahúth* <note>original: "Maarécheth haëlahúth" (The Order of Divinity), a 14th-century kabbalistic work.</note> (or *Maaréches ha-Elohús*) folio 59, column 2, as follows: "Every nation is drawn after its prince" <note>original: וז כל אומה ואומה היא נמשכת משר שלה (Ve-zeh kol umah ve-umah hi nimshekhet mi-sar shelah).</note>. ...read in the book **Chiffuk emuná** <note>original: *Hizzuk Emunah* ("Faith Fortified"), a 16th-century Karaite anti-Christian polemic by Isaac of Troki.</note>, page 53, with these words: <note>original: הראשון מהקיסרים הנכנס לאמונת ישו הוא הקיסר קוסטנטין שעזב אמונתו הראשונה וקבל אמונת ישו וחקק תורת הנוצרים אחר שלש מאות שנה למיתת ישו</note> "The first of the emperors who entered the faith of **Jesus** was the Emperor **Constantine**, who left his former faith and accepted the faith of **Jesus** and established the law of the **Nazarenes** <term>Nazarenes: A common Hebrew term for Christians (*Notzrim*).</term> three hundred years after the death of **Jesus**." <margin>Fourthly, it is called the Faith of the Hanged One.</margin>

if he wishes to lead another astray, he says: "by the nations' false faith" <note>original: "bey der Gójim schéker amón"; *Goyim* means nations/Gentiles, *sheker amon* refers to a false or lying trust.</note>. They claim this is far from their intent, and that they do not say it for the reasons indicated above, for they claim Christians uphold what is commanded of them. Wherever "nations" <note>original: "gójim"</note> is written, they argue it does not mean the Christians, but rather the heathens who serve "foreign worship" <note>original: "Avóda sára"; a standard Hebrew term for idolatry</note>. As for his claim that idolatrous peoples are meant by it, it will be incontrovertibly shown in the aforementioned 16th chapter that Christians are regarded by the Jews as great idolaters. Therefore, the excuse brought forward is worth nothing at all.

<margin>Seventhly, they call the same an error and a vanity.</margin>
Seventhly, they call the same an **Error** <note>original: "טעות Tatúa"</note>, and an **Error of Vanity** <note>original: "טעות הבל Tauth hével"</note>, or a vain error. <margin>How the Jews name the Roman Catholic, as well as the Reformed and Lutheran religion.</margin>

### Chapter 10 of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked. 500

<meta>Catchword: -chim</meta>

<margin>What the word Cumarim means.</margin>
In the Hebrew language, such priests are called כמרים *Kemarim* <note>original: *Kemarim*; a term often used in the Hebrew Bible for non-Levitical or idolatrous priests</note>. This word is read only three times in the Holy Scripture: in 2 Kings 23:5, Hosea 10:5, and Zephaniah 1:4. In these three places, the priests of Baal are called by this name.

<margin>Where it originates.</margin>
The word originates, however, from כמר *Camar*, or נכמר *Nichmar*, which means to be warm or burned, as well as to be brown, black, or shriveled. Among the Chaldeans, however, it means "to shut in." Idolatrous priests are called by this name either because they wore brown or black clothes, or because they appeared black and smoky from frequent sacrificing. It may also be because they were zealous and, as it were, "burning" in regard to their idolatrous service, or because they kept themselves enclosed and separated from the world <note>The author is suggesting these priests lived a lifestyle similar to cloistered monks</note>. In the Chaldean language, they are called כומרין *Cumarin*, and among the Rabbis they are called in the aforementioned manner כומרים *Cumarim*; it is always used to refer to idolatrous priests. In the Syriac language, however, even the true and righteous priests of God are called by this name. Thus, Christ the Lord is called in Hebrews 6:20 ܟܘܡܪܐ *Cumero* <note>original Syriac: *Cúmero*</note>, that is, a priest. In Hebrews 8:1 and 9:11, He is called ܪܒ ܟܘܡܪܐ *Raf cumere* <note>original Syriac: *Raf cúmere*</note>, that is, the High Priest; and in Hebrews 9:7, the High Priest is also called this, namely *Raf Cumere*. In Hebrews 9:6, all priests who attended to the divine service in the Temple at Jerusalem are called ܟܘܡܪܐ *Cumere*. However, among the Jews, the word is not used in a good sense, but in a bad one. That our clergy are called *Cumarim* can be seen in the Talmudic tractate *Avoda Sara* <note>a tractate concerning "Foreign Worship" or idolatry</note>, folio 2, column 1, in the *Tosephot* <note>medieval additions/commentaries on the Talmud</note>. There it is taught that a Jew may certainly lend money to Christians to offer in the church, and the reason given for this is: "For what they give to the *Gallachim* (that is, the Shaven Ones) and to the *Cumarim* is not actually for the sake of the idol, but for the necessity of their livelihood" <note>original Hebrew: *Ki mah she-hem notnim otam la-Gallachim ve-la-Cumarim eino mamash le-shem avoda zara ela le-tsorekh hanatam*</note>. Similarly, a prelate from Lindau is called ראש כומרים *Rosh Cumarim* <note>meaning "Head of Priests" or "Chief Priest"</note> in Rabbi Lipmann's *Book of Victory* <note>original: *Sepher Nizzachon*; a famous medieval polemical work</note> on page 159, number 290. Christian clergy are also called *Cumarim* three times in the book *Springs of Salvation* <note>original: *Majene jeshua*</note> on folio 91, column 2, and twice in the old *Nizzachon* on page 42, as well as in the little book *The Scepter of Judah* <note>original: *Shevet Jehuda*</note> on folio 4, column 1; folio 30, column 1; and folio 45, column 1. In the old *Nizzachon*, on page 82, regarding the words of Isaiah 5:11—"Woe to those who rise early in the morning to chase strong drink, and linger into the night until wine inflames them"—it is written: "These are the *Gallachim* and the *Cumarim* who rise early and stay late in their house of filth <note>A derogatory Jewish term for a church</note> for the sake of their portion which they call a prebend" <note>original Hebrew: *Alu ha-Gallachim ve-ha-Cumarim she-mashkimim u-maarivim be-veit tirfutam bi-shvil chokam she-korin prebenda*</note>. That is, these are the *Galla-chim*...

Whether it might mean as much as אֲבִי פְֿעוֹר *Afi Peor*, that is, the "Father of Peor," remains to be seen, because Christ is called *Baal Peor* <note>A reference to a pagan deity associated in polemics with shameful acts or excrement</note> by Abarbanel, as reported above on pages 78 and 79, and the Pope is the head of the Roman Catholic Church and is called "Father" by it. The slanderous minds of the Jews are unfathomable.

# Chapter XI.

### In which it is shown how the Jews name the churches of the Christians, and what else they write concerning them and the things found within them.

**R**abbi Bechai <note>Bahya ben Asher (1255–1340), a famous Spanish rabbi and biblical commentator.</note> writes in his commentary on the Five Books of Moses, folio 198, column 1, in the section *Eikev*, regarding the words of Deuteronomy 7:26, **"You shall utterly detest and abhor it"** (namely, idols), **in this manner:** <note>original Hebrew: למוד הכתוב שחייב האדם לשקץ עבודה זרה ולהזכירה בלשון גנאי</note> that is, **"The Scripture teaches you herewith that a person is duty-bound to have a loathing for an idol and to mention it with a mocking name."**

<margin>The Jews mockingly call a Christian church, specifically:</margin>
Because they now generally consider Christian churches to be houses of idolatry—as shall be shown in the following—they also give them shameful and mocking names, and call such a church:

<margin>1. Toëfa, that is, an abomination.</margin>
**First**, *Toëfa* <term>Toëfa: A Hebrew word for something disgusting or ritually "unclean," often translated as "abomination."</term>, which means an abomination; or more frequently in the plural, they call them *Toëfoth* (or *Toefos*). Regarding this, it is written in the German-Hebrew book called **Brandspiegel** <note>The *Brandspiegel* (Mirror of Fire) was a popular 16th-century Yiddish ethical guide for Jewish laypeople, especially women.</note>, in Chapter 18, folio 68, column 2: <note>The following is translated from the original Yiddish-influenced German dialect.</note> **"Those who keep maids to carry their children must take care that they do not carry the children among the Gentiles <term>Gojim: Literally "nations," used here to refer to Christians.</term>, lest they carry them before an 'Abomination' <note>Toëfa, meaning a church.</note> and go inside with them. For if the child were to see a painting and it pleased them, and they kissed the images and desired to go in again, such a habit in youth would lead them to all manner of evil."**

<margin>And a House of Abominations</margin>
They also call the same a *Beth toëfoth* (or *Bes toëfos*), **which means a House of Abominations.** Regarding this, it is mentioned in the booklet **Schévet Jehùda** <note>"The Scepter of Judah," a 16th-century history of Jewish persecutions by Solomon ibn Verga.</note>, folio 84, column 2, that once certain princes and prelates requested a Pope to expel the Jews, though they could not persuade him to do so. The words read as follows: <note>original Hebrew: אחר זה נתעצמו כל השרים והכמרים עד שאחד מההגמונים נתייעץ משרתו שיעלילו על היהודים מההגמונים ולא יכלו לנצח האפיפור עד שאחד מהם גנב צלם אחד של כסף מבית תועבות וגו</note> **"After this, all the princes and priests exerted themselves until one of the bishops counseled his servant that they should frame the Jews... and they could not prevail over the Pope until one of them stole a silver image from the House of Abominations, etc."**
