### How the Jews mock the Christian Church and what is within it.

"Brothers and friends, you Jews of the holy congregation in <term>Mainz</term> <note>original: Mayntz</note>; I have come to you, for I died in the holy congregation in <term>Cologne</term> <note>original: Cölln</note>, and I desire that you may bury me with my parents, who also lie in Mainz; and I wish you much happiness and long life; this is the request of <term>Amram</term>." Now, after the Jews had seen the letter, they all began to mourn and took the coffin out onto the land. Then the <term>Cutheans</term> <note>The author notes these are "Christians." In Jewish texts, "Cutheans" (Samaritans) was often used as a coded term for Christians to avoid censorship.</note> displayed great insolence, overpowered the Jews, and struck them. However, the Cutheans could not immediately move the coffin from its place, so the Bishop of Mainz ordered that the coffin be guarded right there, so that it would not be carried away by the Jews.

<margin>The coffin was carried away by the Christians, and a church was built over it, which is called the Emiranus Church <note>Saint Emmeram's Church.</note>.</margin>
And the Bishop had a <term>tifla</term> <note>A derogatory Hebrew term for a church, literally meaning "folly" or "insipidity," used as a parody of the word for "prayer."</note> built over it, which was immensely large. The Jews, however, applied great diligence and pleaded that they might take the coffin, but it was all for naught. And to this very day, such a <term>tifla</term> is still called <term>Tome Amram</term> <note>original Hebrew: טמא עמרם</note>, which means "Amram’s unclean (church)." And every night, Rabbi Amram came to his students in a dream and said to them, "Bury me with my parents."

<margin>The Jews, however, took Amram away by night and placed a thief in his spot.</margin>
When the students in Mainz heard this, they were very sorrowful. They went out of the city by night, took a thief from the gallows, dressed him in white clothes, and went and took Amram out of the coffin, laying the thief in his place. They then buried Rabbi Amram with his parents, and the holy blessed God rescued the Jews, and the matter remained a secret. These are the words of the <term>Ma'aseh-Book</term> <note>A famous collection of Jewish ethical tales and legends, often written in Yiddish.</note>, and the same are also found in the aforementioned manner in the book <term>Shalshelet Ha-Kabbalah</term> <note>The Chain of Tradition, a 16th-century historical work by Gedaliah ibn Yahya.</note>, folio 27, column 2, in the Hebrew language. Thus we see clearly from this that <term>Dieterich Schwabe</term> in his *Jewish Cover-up* <note>original: Jüdischen Deckmantel</note>, at the beginning of the 7th chapter of the first part, as well as <term>Johann Adrian</term> in his epistle, page 30, reported the pure truth when they wrote that the Jews call a Christian church a <term>tifla</term>.

<margin>V. They call it a "Shame-house" or a shameful thing.</margin>
Fifthly, they call a church <term>Beth hatturpa</term> <note>original Hebrew: בית התורפה</note>, that is, <term>house of turpitude</term> <note>original Latin: domum turpitudinis</note>, a shameful house, or "shame-house," or <term>Beth hatturpoth</term>, which is a house of shames; or even with just one word: <term>turpa</term>, which is a shame or a shameful thing; and in the <term>plural number</term> <note>original Latin: plurali numero</note>, <term>Batte turpoth</term> or simply <term>turpoth</term>. Regarding this, <term>Elias</term> writes in his <term>Tishbi</term> <note>A dictionary of Rabbinic Hebrew by Elias Levita, 1541.</note>, folio 87, column 2, under the root word <term>taraf</term> as follows: "Beth hatturpa: an explanation of a house of foreign worship, and they call it so in the language of mockery and derision." That is, <term>Beth hatturpa</term>, a shame-house, means as much as <term>Beth avoda zara</term>, that is, an idolatrous house.

### Chapter XI of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked.

And it is so named for the purpose of mockery and contempt. Rabbi <term>Moshe bar Maimon</term> <note>Also known as Maimonides, a preeminent medieval Jewish scholar.</note> also writes concerning this word in his commentary on the <term>Mishnah</term> <note>The first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions.</note>, in the Talmudic tractate *Avoda Zara*, folio 79, column 2 of the Amsterdam Talmud, as follows: <note>original Hebrew: הוא כינוי דרך ביזיון לבתי עבודה זרה שהולכין להם ולפיכך נקראו התועים ההולכים בתוכיהן</note> that is: "This is a nickname given out of contempt to the houses of idolatry into which they (namely the *Goyim*, meaning the Christians or heathens) go; therefore, such erring people are called *Hólechim betúrpoth*, that is, people who go into <term>houses of shame</term> <note>The Hebrew word *toreph* or *turpah* refers to indecency or even nakedness; Eisenmenger translates it as *Schand-Haus*.</note>." In the old *Nizzachon* <note>A famous medieval Jewish apologetic and polemical work.</note>, it is written on page 82 concerning the words of Isaiah 5, verse 11 ("Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them!") these words: <note>original Hebrew: אילו הגלחים והכומרים שמשכימים ומעריבים בבית תורפתם</note> that is: "This signifies the <term>Gallachim</term> <note>Literally 'the shaven ones,' a derogatory term for tonsured Christian monks and priests.</note>, and the <term>Cumarim</term> <note>A biblical term for priests of false gods.</note>, who sit early and late in their *Batte hatturpoth*, that is, their houses of shame."

And on page 134, the following is found in the same place: <note>original Hebrew: מה שאומרים כי הפסילים אשר בבתי תורפתם לפי שהם אלוהות לפיכך הם מכבדין אותם באלוהים הלא הוא אומר אני יי שמי וכבודי לאחר לא אתן ותהלתי לפסילים</note> that is: "As for what they (the Christians) say, that they honor the images which are in their *Batte hatturpoth* (houses of shame) as gods because they are their deities; surely God says (Isaiah 42:8), 'I am the **LORD**, that is my name; and my glory will I not give to another, nor my praise to graven images.'"

In the little book called *Sepher Serubabel* <note>An apocalyptic Hebrew text.</note>, a church is called *Beth hattoreph* (House of Shame), as can be seen from the words extracted below in the 11th chapter of the second part, where the subject of <term>Armillus</term> <note>A figure in Jewish eschatology, often described as an anti-Messiah or king who will conquer the world and be defeated by the true Messiah.</note> is treated; and this signifies the same as the previously mentioned eighth term, *Beth hatturpa*, namely, a house of shame. <margin>On houses built in the name of idols.</margin>
When the Israelites came into the Holy Land, the holy and blessed God wanted to keep us pure, to sanctify His land, and to prepare it for His Majesty, so that no <term>impurity<note>original: tuma; Hebrew term for ritual uncleanness.</note></term> should be therein. This means you should appoint your house for the Lord when you build it, and then you will not sin. And if one does not sanctify it for the Lord, it is immediately ready for the spirit of impurity to rest upon it; and how much more so for one whose intention is for the name of an idol, so that it receives filth, because the spirit of impurity dwells upon that house.

That is: In every single thing we do, we must mention at the beginning that it happens in the name of the **Lord**, so that the Holy Spirit may dwell upon it, and that same thing may be of the part of the blessed **God**.

# How the Jews Name the Christian Churches and what is therein.

...the book *The Generations of Adam and Eve* <note>original: *Toledoth Adam vechavva*; a 14th-century legal work by Rabbi Jeroham ben Meshullam.</note>, folio 104, columns 1 and 2, and in the book *New Light* <note>original: *Or chadasch*.</note>, folio 39, column 1; and it is taken from the Talmudic tractate *Berakhot* (or *Berochos*) <note>The first tractate of the Talmud, dealing with prayers and blessings.</note>, folio 58, column 2.

<margin>What they do when they see a Jewish synagogue.</margin>
When they see a Jewish synagogue standing, they say from Proverbs 15:25: **Blessed be He who establishes the border of the widow.** <note>original: *Baruch metziv gevul almanah*; a blessing used when seeing a rebuilt or standing Jewish settlement or synagogue.</note> But if it is destroyed, they say: **Blessed be the true Judge.** <note>original: *Baruch dayan ha-emeth*; the blessing said upon hearing bad news or witnessing tragedy.</note>

We see from this that Friedrich Samuel Brenz, in the second chapter of his *Shed Snakeskin* <note>original: *abgestreifften Schlangenbalgs*; a 1614 polemic written by Brenz, a convert from Judaism to Christianity, attacking his former faith.</note>, has once again written the truth when he reports: When a *Bar Israel* <term>Son of Israel; a Jew</term>, sees a ruined or destroyed *Toëfa* <term>Abomination; a derogatory term Eisenmenger claims Jews use for a church</term>, he shall immediately say the prayer for it: **Blessed be God, who has torn down the Toëfa, that is, the church, in this land or place.** Just as this church was destroyed, so shall all other *Toëfas*, that is, churches, be destroyed.

<margin>Rabbi Zalman Zevi indeed denies this.</margin>
The godless villain, Rabbi Zalman Zevi, intended to excuse this in his *Jewish Theriac* <note>original: *Jüdischen Theriack*; a 1615 work written to defend Judaism against the accusations made by Brenz in "The Shed Snakeskin."</note>, at the end of the second chapter, number 34, folio 16, column 1, when he reports:

There it stands plain and clear (that one should do such a thing) when one sees a *Beth avoda sara* <term>House of Foreign Worship; an idolatrous temple</term>, but not a church of the Christians, for we do not consider them a house of foreign worship.

<margin>But his statement is untrue.</margin>
But this is once again a reckless concealment of the truth, which Rabbi Zalman Zevi is accustomed to hiding everywhere; for indeed above on pages 509 and 510, it has been more than enough proven from the Jews' own books that they call a Christian church *Beth avoda sara*, that is, an idolatrous house; from which it follows that they also wish for their destruction whenever they catch sight of them.

<margin>They would destroy all our churches if they had the power to do so.</margin>
Yes, if the Jews had the power over our churches, they would destroy them all, as can be judged from Rabbi Moses ben Maimon's <note>Maimonides, the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note> *Sepher Mizvoth*, or *Book of Commandments*, folio 72, column 4, where it is taught thus:

> Commandment 185 is that He commanded us to destroy idolatry and all their houses with every kind of destruction and ruin: by breaking, burning, demolishing, and tearing down every kind in the most extreme and quickest manner of destruction.

<margin>Candlemas is called *Licht-misa*, that is, Light-death.</margin>
Because the Jews are also accustomed to calling everything by mocking names, and in the old *Nizzachon* <term>Nizzachon: Referring to the *Sefer Nizzachon Vetus*, a medieval Jewish polemical work written to counter Christian missionary arguments.</term>, page 7, Candlemas is called ליכט מיתה *Licht mitha*, or as the German Jews pronounce it, *Licht misa*, that is, Light-death, instead of Candlemas; for it is written there as follows: "And that day on which she (Mary) entered the Temple and brought her offering, they call that day *Misa*, which means Candlemas, *Licht-mitha* <note>original: "Licht-mitha" or "Licht-misa"</note> in their language." Because, I say, the Jews do this, there is no doubt that Friedrich Samuel Brenz <note>A Jewish convert to Christianity who wrote an anti-Jewish polemic in 1614.</note> also wrote the truth in the second chapter of his *The Jewish Sloughed-off Snake-skin*, when he reports that the Jews call a Mass vestment a *Miso*-garment, that is, a death-garment; for מיתה *Mitha*—and as the German and Polish Jews pronounce it, *Misa*—signifies death. Rabbi Salman Zevi <note>Salomon Zevi of Aufhausen, who wrote *Jüdischer Theriak* in 1615 as a point-by-point refutation of Brenz's book.</note> indeed wishes to excuse this in his *Jewish Theriac*, folio 13, column 1, in the second chapter, number 24, where he reports:

<margin>They call a Mass vestment a *Misa*-garment, that is, a death-garment.</margin>
<margin>Rabbi Salman Zevi denies this.</margin>

> And [the apostate] continues: "You call the Mass vestment a *Mitha*-vestment, which is a death-vestment." What drives the donkey to this lie? If he had left it at *Mes*-vestment, that already means "death-vestment" in German (since מת *Meth* or *Mes* <note>original: "Meth" or "Mes"</note> signifies a dead person). Why would we use another language? etc. We call it nothing other than *Messgewand* <note>original: "Meßgewand," meaning Mass vestment.</note>. Just as in German the word *kalt* <note>original: "kalt," meaning cold.</note> means fresh, but in Italian *calda* <note>original: "calda," meaning hot.</note> means warm.

That is: The apostate writes further that we call the Mass vestment מיתה גוואנט *Miso-Gewand*, which is supposedly a death-garment. What drives the donkey to such a lie? Had he simply called it a *Mes*-garment, that would already mean a "dead-man's garment" in German (for *Meth* or *Mes* means a corpse). Why should we call it anything other than what the Christians themselves call it? But that a word often has a contrary meaning in another language is nothing new. In German, the word *kalt* means "fresh," but in Italian *calda* means "warm." We call it nothing other than a Mass vestment. This is the excuse which Rabbi Salman Zevi puts forward; however, it is a worthless evasion.

<margin>But he deals in untruths.</margin>
That they call it not *Mes* but מיתה *Misa*-garment occurs without doubt because, in such a way, the contempt for it is made all the more clearly understood. For if one Jew were to say *Mes*-garment to another, the latter could not know whether the word *Mes* meant a corpse or the actual word "Mass" as used in the Roman Catholic Church. Thus, the godless are also called מתים *Methim* (or *Mesim*) <note>meaning "the dead."</note> by the Jews, as can be read in the book *Zerór hammór* <term>Zeror Hammor: "A Bundle of Myrrh," a Torah commentary by Rabbi Abraham Saba (15th century).</term>, folio 129, column 4, in the section *Elle Haddevarim*: "Since the wicked are called dead even while they are alive... etc. and their entire lives are not valued as even a single year."

### How the Jews name the Christian Churches and what is inside them. ###

...that is: Because the godless in their life are called *Methim* or *Mesim* <note>original Hebrew: *metim* (מֵתִים)</note>, that is, "the dead," their life is no life, even if they should live two thousand years; therefore, their entire life is to be regarded as no year at all. Since the Jews consider Christians to be godless people, and consequently to be dead, it is no wonder if they also call a Mass vestment a *Miso*-garment <note>A play on the German word *Messe* (Mass) and the Hebrew *mitah* (death), which in some dialects is pronounced *misa*.</note>, as they consider those who wear it to be dead.

<margin>From where the use of bells originates.</margin>
Regarding the bells, Rabbi Bahya <note>Bahya ben Asher (c. 1255–1340), a famous Spanish rabbi and commentator on the Torah.</note> writes in his commentary on the Five Books of Moses, folio 96, column 1, toward the end of the section *Mishpatim* <note>Exodus 21:1–24:18</note>, concerning their origin as follows: <note>The Hebrew text provided describes the pagan origins of bells in necromancy.</note> "It is reported in the books of sorcery that in the work of the spirit of divination, a woman stands by the grave at the head of the dead person, and a man at his feet, and in the middle a boy with a bell in his hand, and he rings it; and this was very common among the heathens in those times. From them, this was introduced into the Edomite kingdom <note>original: *Edomitische Reich*. "Edom" was a common Jewish rabbinic code word for Rome and, by extension, the Christian world.</note> (that is, Christendom, as will be proven below in the 16th chapter of this 1st part), among whom we live, who have bells with which they ring from their towers, and this is used by no other people. Thus they have this from this root (that is, from this origin), which is a root that bears poison <note>or "gall"</note> and wormwood."

In the old *Nizzachon* <term>Nizzachon: Referring to the *Sefer Nizzachon Vetus*, a medieval Jewish polemical work written to counter Christian missionary arguments.</term>, the words of Isaiah 5:18, "Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of vanity," are interpreted thus:
<margin>What the bell-ropes are called.</margin>
<note>The Hebrew text translates as: "These are the ropes with which they pull the bells in the house of their abominations for the service of their gods when they ring them."</note>
That is: These are the ropes with which they (the Christians) pull the bells in the house of their abominations (that is, in their churches) for the service of their God when they ring them. The convert Victor von Carben <note>A Jewish convert to Christianity (1422–1515) who wrote several works attacking his former faith.</note> also reports in the seventeenth chapter of his so-called "Jews' Booklet" that the Jews, when they hear the bells ringing, are accustomed to say:

<margin>What the Jews are said to say when they hear ringing.</margin>
*Moshech bachefel, yippol basefel, bachefel moshech, yippol bachoshech* <note>transliterated from the Hebrew provided</note>: that is, "He who pulls on the rope, may he fall into the filth; he who pulls on the rope, may he fall into the darkness" (that is, into the abyss of hell). And this may very well be true, just as that may also be true which Friedrich Samuel Brenz <note>A Jewish convert to Christianity who wrote an anti-Jewish polemic titled "The Jewish Sloughed-off Snake-skin" in 1614.</note> reports in his often-mentioned *The Jewish Sloughed-off Snake-skin*, in the

Erster Theil.

### The Eleventh Chapter of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked ###

<margin>
What they call the bells

...in the second chapter, page 9, he writes that the Jews, when they hear the bells ringing for prayer in the morning and evening, are accustomed to call the bells *Teréfa thólja* <note>original Hebrew: *Terefah tulyah* (טריפה תוליה)</note> bells—that is, "unclean gallows-bells." Rabbi Solomon Zvi <note>Solomon Zvi of Aufhausen, author of the *Jewish Theriac* (1615), a book written to refute anti-Jewish slanders.</note> wishes to deny this in the second chapter of his *Jewish Theriac*, folio 13, column 1, number 22, asking how the word *Teréfa* could possibly fit this context. I answer, however, that while it is true the word does not fit the nature of bells—for *teréfa* <term>Terefah: literally "torn," referring to meat from an animal killed by a predator or found to have physical defects, making it non-kosher</term> actually means meat torn by wild animals, as seen in Leviticus 17:15 and 22:8, as well as Ezekiel 4:14 and other places—among the Rabbis, it is used for any food coming from an animal that was sick or otherwise had a defect. Furthermore, Rabbi Solomon Zvi answers there and says that ringing is not wrong, whether one rings for it (as the Christians do) or knocks for it, as the Jews do. But if ringing is not wrong, why then do the Jews not also use a small bell instead of a wooden clapper <note>original: *hölzernen Klöppel*. They call the cross, which is marked with the hands, the "warp and the woof."

"Those who sanctify themselves"—these are the Edomites <note>original: *Edom* (אדום). In Rabbinic literature, "Edom" is a traditional code word for the Roman Empire and, by extension, the Christian world.</note> who are accustomed to move their fingers here and there (that is, to sanctify themselves with the sign of the cross). "Those who purify themselves"—these are the Ishmaelites <note>original: *Yishme'elim* (ישמעאלים). ## Chapter XI of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked ##

<margin>
What kinds of things the Jews are not allowed to sell to Christians.
</margin>

It is also forbidden for the Jews to sell incense, wax, and religious books to Christians, as is taught in the book *Col Bo* <note>The *Col Bo* ("Everything is in it") is a classic 14th-century work on Jewish law (Halakha).</note>, number 27, folio 104, column 1:

<note>original Hebrew: לבונה אסור למכור לגלח ולכומר דמידי דתקרובת הוא • וכן שעוה אסור • למכור לשום גוי ליום איד קנדלור שלהם ויום אחד שלפניו אבל שאר ימים שעה לשאר גוים מותר למכור • וכן גביעים שפגם הגוי ובטלם ואחר כך קנאם הישראל הרי הם אסור למכורן לגוים לפי שהגלח יעשה בו תפלה לעבודה זרה דבשביל פגם קטן לא יניח לעבוד הישראל ולפני עור לא תתן מכשול • וכן הספרים הפסולים אסור למכרן לגוים לפי שהגלח קורא בו ומזכיר ומשבח לע"ז ואפילו לגוי שאינו גלח אסור למכרן דודאי הגוי יתננו או ימכרנו לגלח :</note>
It is forbidden to sell incense to a *Gallach* <note>original: *Gallach* (גַלָּח) literally means "the shaven one," a derogatory reference to the tonsure of Catholic priests.</note> or to a *Cumar* <note>original: *Cumar* (כּוּמָר) is a biblical Hebrew term for an idolatrous priest.</note>, because it is something used for an offering. Likewise, it is forbidden to sell wax to any Gentile on their holiday of Candlemas and the day before it; but on other days, it is permitted to sell wax to other Gentiles. Similarly, regarding chalices that a Gentile has damaged and discarded, and then an Israelite has bought them: it is forbidden to sell them back to Gentiles because the *Gallach* would use them for prayer to an idol, for he would not cease his service because of a small blemish. And "you shall not put a stumbling block before the blind." Likewise, it is forbidden to sell "disqualified books" to Gentiles, because the *Gallach* reads them and mentions and praises the idol; and it is even forbidden to sell them to a Gentile who is not a *Gallach*, because the Gentile will certainly give or sell it to a *Gallach*.

It is forbidden to sell incense to a *Gallach*, that is, a "shaven one," or to a *Cumar*, that is, an idolatrous priest (by which two mocking names a Christian clergyman is understood, as was indicated above in Chapter 10, pages 500, 501, and 502), because it is something that is offered as a sacrifice. Likewise, it is also forbidden to sell wax to any *Goi* (or Christian) on their *jom ed* <note>original: *jom ed* (יוֹם אֵיד). While the Hebrew *Id* means "holiday," Eisenmenger interprets it through the lens of *Ed*, meaning "misfortune" or "destruction," suggesting the Jews use this pun to mock Christian festivals.</note>, that is, "day of destruction," on Candlemas (that is, on the holiday called Candlemas, which is here insultingly called a "day of destruction," about which more will be seen in the following thirteenth chapter) and on the day preceding it; but it is permitted to sell it to other *Gojim* (or Christians) on other days. The same applies to the chalices which a *Goi* (or Christian) has cracked and made useless (that is, removed from church use) and which an Israelite has subsequently bought: it is forbidden to sell them to the *Gojim* (that is, the Christians) because the *Gallach* or clergyman performs his prayer to the idol with them; for because of a small crack, that same (clergyman) will not refrain from performing his service with it (the chalice), and the Israelite (who sells such a chalice) violates the words of Leviticus 19:14:

> You shall not put a stumbling block before the blind.

Likewise, it is forbidden to sell the <term>Sepharim pesulim: literally "invalid books" or "unfit books"</term>, that is, the worthless books (by which the spiritual books used in the churches, and in particular the books of the New Testament, are understood, as can be explicitly read in the *Sepher Toledoth Adam ve-Chavva* folio 158, column 3 of the fifth part) to the *Gojim* (or Christians), because the *Gallach* reads from them and mentions the idol and praises the same. Indeed, it is even forbidden to sell them to a *Goi*, even if he is not a *Gallach*, because the *Goi* will surely give or sell (such a book) to the *Gallach*. Similar information can also be found in the *Sepher Agudda* folio 60, column 2, number 7, and in the *Sepher mizvoth gadol* <note>The *Sefer Mitzvot Gadol*, or "Smag," is a 13th-century codification of law by Rabbi Moses of Coucy.</note> of Rabbi Moshe of Coucy, folio 10, column 2, as well as in the *Sepher Toledoth Adam ve-Chavva* in the fifth part, folio 158, column 3.

<note>original Hebrew: נרות של שעוה שמדליקין לפני עבודה זרה מותרין לאחר שכבה אותן הגלח : אין לך בטול גדול מזה. וחתיכות של שעוה שהם של עבודה זרה מותרות בלא שום ביטול. ואותן ככרות של ע"ז שנותנין לכומרים שמקריבין לע"ז מותרין דאין נותנין אותו להאכיל לעבודה זרה ואם כן לא הוי תקרובת אלא נותנים לכומרים. והני מלבושים של גלחים שקורין שומ"י פל"ץ מותרין דאינן עשויין לנוי ע"ז אלא לנוי הכומרים. ואותן גביעין של ע"ז בעו ביטול משום דחשיבי כעבודה זרה עצמה. ואותן מחתות כמו כן הוא ממשמשי עבודה זרה וצריכין ביטול כך פירש רש"י ז"ל ע"כל :</note>

And those cakes of the idol that are given to the priests who offer them to the idol are permitted, for they do not give them to the idol to eat; and if so, it is not an offering but is given to the priests. And these garments of the priests which they call *surplice* <note>original: *shumi-peltz* (שומ"י פל"ץ), a Yiddish/Hebrew rendering of the Latin *superpellicium*.</note> are permitted, for they are not made for the beauty of the idol but for the beauty of the priests. And those chalices of the idol require nullification because they are considered as the idol itself. And those censers likewise are accessories of the idol and require nullification. This is how Rashi <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator, whom the author refers to as Rabbi Salomon Jarchi.</note> of blessed memory explained it; thus far his words.

That is: the wax candles which they (the Christians) light before the idol are permitted (to be bought) after the *Gallach* (that is, the shorn priest) has extinguished them, and there is no greater nullification <note>original: *Vernichtigung*. In this context, it refers to *bitul*, the legal process of "nullifying" an object's idolatrous status so it can be used for other purposes.</note> (by which they are removed from church use) than this. The pieces of wax, however, which come from the idolatrous service, are permitted without any nullification. Those idolatrous little cakes (meaning the wafers or hosts) also, which they give to the *Cumarim* <note>original: *Cumarim* (כּוּמָרִים), a biblical term for pagan or idolatrous priests.</note> (that is, the idolatrous priests) who use them for idolatry, are permitted; for they do not give them to the idol to eat: therefore they are not an offering, but are given to the *Cumarim*. Those clothes of the *Gallachim* (or shorn priests) also, which they call <term>Superpellicium</term> <note>A surplice; a white liturgical vestment worn by Christian clergy.</note>, are permitted, for they are not made for the decoration of the idol, but for the decoration of the *Cumarim*. Even the idolatrous cups (chalices) themselves require a nullification, because they are held in the same value as the idol itself. The censers also are likewise among the idolatrous vessels and require a nullification. This is how Rabbi Salomon Jarchi, of blessed memory, explained it, whose words go up to here. These are the words from the book *Col Bo*. The same is also taught in the book *Aguddah* <note>A 14th-century collection of legal decisions by Alexander Suslin.</note>, number 43, 63, columns 2 and 3.

# Chapter XI of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked.

<margin>Things which the Jews are not allowed to sell to Christians.</margin>

It is also forbidden for the Jews to sell incense, wax, and spiritual books to the Christians, concerning which it is taught in the book *Col Bo* <note>A 14th-century Hebrew work on Jewish law and ritual.</note>, number 27, folio 104, column 1, as follows:

<note>original Hebrew: לבונה אסור למכור לגלה ולכומר דמידי דתקרובת הוא • וכן שעוה אסור למכור לשום גוי ליום איד קנדלור שלהם ויום אחד שלפניו אבל שאר ימים פנוייה לשאר גוים מותר למכור • וכן גביעים שפגם הגוי ובטלם ואחר כך קנאם הישראל הרי הם אסור למכרן לגוים לפי שהגלה יעשה בו תפלה וזה דבשביל פגם קטן לא יניח לעבוד ויעבור הישראל ולפני עור לא תתן מכשול • וכן הספרים הפסולים אסור למכרן לגוים לפי שהגלה קורא בו ומזכיר שם ע"ז ואפילו לגוי שאינו גלח אסור למכרן משום דודאי יתננו או ימכרנו לגלה :</note>
It is forbidden to sell incense to a *Gallach* <note>original: *Gallach* (גַּלָּח), a derogatory term meaning "shorn one," referring to the tonsure of a Catholic priest.</note> or to a *Cumar* <note>original: *Cumar* (כומר), a term used in the Hebrew Bible for pagan priests, here applied to Christian clergy.</note>, for it is something used as an offering. Likewise, it is forbidden to sell wax to any *Goi* <note>Gentile/Christian</note> for their *jom ed* <note>literally "day of destruction," a polemical pun on the Hebrew word for "festival."</note>, their Candlemas, or the day before it; but on other days it is permitted to sell it to other Gentiles. Likewise, regarding chalices that a Gentile has damaged and nullified <note>meaning they were removed from sacred use</note>, and which an Israelite subsequently bought: it is forbidden to sell them back to the Gentiles because the priest will use them for prayer; for despite a small defect, he will not cease to perform his service with it, and the Israelite would then violate the command (Leviticus 19:14): "You shall not put a stumbling block before the blind." Similarly, it is forbidden to sell "invalid books" <note>original: *Sepharim Pesulim* (ספרים פסולים), referring to Christian liturgical books or the New Testament.</note> to Gentiles, because the priest reads from them and mentions the name of an idol and praises it. Indeed, it is even forbidden to sell them to a Gentile who is not a priest, because the Gentile will certainly give or sell it to a priest. That is:

It is forbidden to sell incense to a *Gallach*, that is, a "shorn one," or to a *Cúmar*, that is, an "idolatrous priest" (by which two mocking names a Christian clergyman is understood, as was indicated above in Chapter 10, pages 500, 501, and 502), because it is something that is offered. Thus, it is also forbidden to sell wax to any *Goi* (or Christian) on their *jom ed*, that is, "day of destruction," [which is] Candlemas (that is, on the holiday called Candlemas, which is here insultingly called a "day of destruction," about which more can be seen in the following thirteenth chapter) and on the day preceding it. However, it is permitted to sell it to other *Gojim* (or Christians) on other days. The same applies to the cups <note>chalices</note> which a *Goi* (or Christian) has cracked and made null (that is, removed from church use) and which an Israelite has afterwards purchased: it is forbidden to sell them to the *Gojim* (that is, to the Christians), because the *Gallach* or clergyman would perform his prayer to the idol with it; for on account of a small crack, the same (clergyman) will not refrain from performing his service with that (cup), and the Israelite (who sells such a cup) violates the words of Leviticus 19:14: "Thou shalt not set a stumbling block before the blind." Likewise, it is forbidden to sell the *Sepharím pesulím*, that is, the "worthless books" (by which the spiritual books used in the church, and especially the books of the New Testament—as can be expressly read in the *Sepher Toledóth Adam vechávva* <note>The Generations of Adam and Eve, a 14th-century work by Rabbi Jeroham ben Meshullam.</note> folio 158, column 3, of the fifth part—are understood) to the *Gojim* (or Christians), because the *Gallach* reads therein and makes mention of the idol and praises it. Indeed, it is also forbidden to sell them to a *Goi*, even if he is not a *Gallach*, because the *Goi* will certainly give or sell such a book to the *Gallach*. Similar statements are also to be found in the *Sépher Agúdda* folio 60, column 2, number 7, and in the *Sepher mizvóth* (or *mizvos*) *gadól* of Rabbi Mosche Mikkózi <note>The *Smag*, a 13th-century legal code.</note>, folio 10, column 2, as well as in the *Sepher Toledóth* (or *Tóledos*) *Adam vechávva* in the fifth part, folio 158, column 3.

Wax candles that are lit before an idol <note>A common Jewish polemical term for Christian images or the crucifix.</note> are permitted to be used after the *Gallach* <note>A derogatory term for a priest, meaning "shorn one."</note> has extinguished them; there is no greater nullification <note>original: *bittul*; a legal process where an object is stripped of its idolatrous status.</note> than this. Pieces of wax coming from idolatrous service are permitted without any nullification. Those garments of the *Gallachim* <note>plural of *Gallach*.</note> which are called surplices <note>original: *superpellicium*.</note> are permitted, for they are not made for the beauty of the idol, but for the beauty of the *Cumarim*. However, the idolatrous cups <note>the chalices used for wine.</note> require nullification because they are considered of the same status as the idol itself. The censers <note>vessels for burning incense.</note> likewise are among the vessels used for idolatry and require nullification. ### The Twelfth Chapter of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked.

...to show in a ready and wicked manner, [the names] which they are accustomed to use mockingly, and [so] they call the water of Holy Baptism:

<margin>The Water of Baptism / Water of Extermination.</margin>
Firstly, מי השמד <note>original Hebrew: *Me haschemed*</note> **Me haschemed** or **haschemad**, that is, **Water of Extermination** or of **Destruction**; and the word *Schemed* comes from the <term>root or stem-word שמד *Schamad*</term>, which in the conjugation called <term>Hiphil</term> <note>The causative active stem in Hebrew grammar.</note> means to destroy, disturb, and exterminate; but in the conjugation called <term>Niphal</term> <note>The passive or reflexive stem in Hebrew grammar.</note> it means to be destroyed and exterminated. In the Fifth Book of Moses <note>Deuteronomy</note>, chapter 9, verses 19 and 25, it is written: להשמיד אתכם <note>original Hebrew: *lehaschmid ethchem*</note> **lehaschmid ethchem**, that is, **to exterminate you**; and in the Book of Esther, chapter 3, verse 6, we read: להשמיד כל היהודים <note>original Hebrew: *lehaschmid kol hajehudim*</note> **lehaschmid kol hajehudim**, that is, **to exterminate all Jews**; and in chapter 8, verse 11 of the same book, it is written: להשמיד להרוג ולאבד <note>original Hebrew: *lehaschmid, laharog, uleabbed*</note> **lehaschmid, laharog, uleabbed**, that is, **to exterminate, to slay, and to perish**. One also reads in Proverbs 14, verse 11: The house of the wicked ישמד <note>original Hebrew: *jischamed*</note> **jischamed**, that is, **shall be destroyed**. From this it is clearly seen that both words *me haschemed* mean **Water of Extermination**; and the baptismal water is undoubtedly named thus because the Jews believe that those who are baptized are exterminated <note>meaning they are spiritually lost or cut off from the Jewish people</note> and have no salvation to expect. That it is called such can be seen in Rabbi Lipman’s <note>Yom-Tov Lipmann-Mühlhausen, a 14th-century Jewish apologist.</note> *Sefer Nizzachon* <note>The "Book of Victory," a famous polemical work defending Judaism against Christian critiques.</note>, number 218, where he writes as follows:

> והנה המה אומרים שמי השמד ניתנו תחת המילה :

that is: **Behold, they (the Christians) say that the *me haschemad* (the Water of Extermination) was established in place of circumcision.** And in number 289, the following is reported by the same author:

> אף הביאו הנוצרים ראייה על אמונתם / שמי השמד אינם מסריחים :
> והנה אם אמרו הדבר זה מחמת מלח שמערבים בו כי לכל שמד לוקחים מלח . וגם מחדשין
> אותו תמיד במים אחרים לפי שמתמעטין בהזאתו . גם ידעתי שיש מהם שמבשלים המים תחלה
> במלח ויש שלוקחים מי טל שאינם מסריחים לעולם ואין לגלות זאת להם שלא ילמדו הדבר
> אותם מי שאינן יודעין ויחזיקו בו טעותם :

that is: **The Christians also bring forth a proof for their faith (claiming it is the right one) because the *me haschemad* (the Water of Extermination, meaning the baptismal water) does not become foul-smelling. However, if this thing is true, it happens because of the salt which they mix into it; for they take salt for every *Schemad* (Extermination, by which baptism is understood). They also refresh it constantly with other water, because it is diminished by their sprinkling. I also know that some among them initially boil the water with salt; others, however, take dew-water, which never becomes foul. But one must not reveal this to them, lest they teach it to those who do not know it, and thereby strengthen them in their error.**

### How the Jews mockingly name the Holy Sacraments.

<margin>Baptism is called *schmadden*.</margin>
Since the water of Baptism is called **Me haschemed** <note>original Hebrew: *Me haschémed*, literally "Water of Extermination"</note>, it follows that the German Jews call the act of baptizing **schmadden**. When one of them is baptized, they are accustomed to say of him that he has "let himself be *schmadden*," which means to let oneself be exterminated or blotted out. However, when they write or speak in Hebrew, the act of being baptized is called **hishtammed** <note>original Hebrew: השתמד *hishtamméd*</note>, that is, to be corrupted or destroyed. This word *schmadden* is found in the 187th chapter of the **Maase-Buch** <note>A famous collection of Jewish legends and folktales, written in Yiddish for a general audience.</note>, where it is written that a Rabbi once lived in **Mainz** named **Rabbi Shimon the Great**, who had a young son named **Elchanan**. This child was taken away by a Christian woman who had been hired to heat the rooms on the Jewish Sabbath. It follows:

<margin>A Jewish child is said to have been stolen by a Christian woman, and later became the Pope in Rome.</margin>
"And this is what R.H. wrote: The **Cuthith** <note>original Yiddish/Hebrew: כותית *Cuthith*, literally "Samaritan woman," a term often used in these texts as a coded reference to a Christian woman to avoid censorship.</note> stole the child while everyone was in the synagogue. Her intention was to have the child baptized (*schmaden*). She took the child and it was soon after baptized (*schmaden*)." <note>The original Yiddish: *וזהו כתב ר"ח כותית דהט קינד אונ' זיין פֿיר גנבין אין דיא שול גיוווען: דאש מיינט זיא נון זיא העט קינד שמדן: זיא הויט קינד אונ' זי ווט קור פֿור גייטן האבן יים פֿל שמדן גהאלטן*</note> That is to say, the **Cuthith** or **Cutis** (meaning the Christian woman) took the child while everyone was in the synagogue, went away with him, and had him baptized (*schmadden*). She believed she had performed a meritorious deed <note>literally "brought an offering"</note>, for in those times, they placed great value on such conversions (*schmadden*). 

After this, it is reported that the **Galláchim** <note>original Hebrew: גלחים *galláchim*, literally "the shaven ones," a derogatory term referring to the tonsured heads of Catholic clergy</note> raised the boy. He became a very learned man, moving from one high school to another until he finally reached **Rome**. There, he became first a Cardinal and eventually even the **Pope**. However, because he knew well that he came from Jewish parents and that his father was a Rabbi in Mainz, he issued an order to the Bishop of Mainz to forbid the Jews from keeping the Sabbath, from "Jewish-ing" their children <note>German: *Judschen*, here meaning to circumcise</note>, and from allowing women to use the ritual baths. His goal was to force the Jews of Mainz to send his father to Rome to petition him to lift this harsh decree.

When his father was indeed sent to Rome for this reason, the Pope revealed his identity to him and assured him <margin>It is said the Pope became a Jew again.</margin> that he would write a book against the Christian religion and then return with him to Mainz to embrace the Jewish faith again. This is said to have happened: he brought a great fortune back to Mainz, and in Rome, no one knew where he had gone. His father, Rabbi Shimon the Great, composed a **Yotzer** <note>original Hebrew: יוצר *Józer*, a type of liturgical poem or prayer</note> for the New Year <note>Rosh Hashanah</note> based on this story. It begins: **Al tenúfeni nachalátho** (or *nachalóso*) **betáam lehischaféch** <note>original Hebrew: אל תנופני נחלתו בטעם להשפך, "Do not toss me, his inheritance, with the reason to be poured out."</note>. Much more regarding this can be read in the aforementioned place in the *Maase-Buch*.

In the 211th chapter of the same book, it is also reported concerning **Rabbi Amnon**—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the term "schmadden" (to be exterminated or baptized) by relating the famous legend of Rabbi Amnon of Mainz and explaining the derogatory language supposedly used by Jews regarding Christian baptism.</meta>

# The Twelfth Chapter of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked.

<margin>What occurred regarding Amnon in Mainz.</margin>
...should <note>Completing the sentence from the previous page's catchword "solte."</note> relates that a Bishop in **Mainz** urged him to let himself be **schmadden** <note>The term used by German Jews for baptism, derived from the Hebrew word for "destruction" or "extermination."</note>, whereupon he let it be known that he wished to consider it and would give an answer in three days. But when he did not appear again, and did not wish to declare his acceptance of the Christian religion, he requested that his tongue be cut out because he had wavered in his faith and had been willing to deny God by asking for three days' time to declare himself. Thereupon, the Bishop had his hands and feet cut off and sent him home in a bed. Shortly thereafter, he had himself carried into the synagogue, and after he had prayed a certain prayer which begins **Unetanneh Tokef** <note>original Hebrew: ונתנה תוקף *Unethánne tókef*, "Let us declare the power [of the day's holiness]," one of the most solemn prayers in the Jewish liturgy.</note>, which he himself had composed and requested that such a prayer be sent to all places where Jews reside, he disappeared, and God took him into Paradise. In memory of this, such a prayer was placed in the Jewish Prayer Book, which they are accustomed to pray every year on their New Year’s Day as well as on the Day of Atonement. Regarding this matter, which is said to have happened with **Rabbi Amnon**, one may also consult the book **Shalshelet HaKabbalah** <note>original: *Schalschéleth hakabbála*, "The Chain of Tradition," a 16th-century work of Jewish history and lore.</note>, folio 44, column 1, and the **Machsor** <note>A prayer book for festivals.</note> printed in folio at **Wilmersdorf** at the section for this prayer. But are these not foolish Jewish fables?

It is thus quite believable that what **Dieterich Schwabe** indicates in the eighth chapter of the first part of his *Jewish Cover-Cloak* <note>original title: *Jüdischer Deckmantel*, a 17th-century anti-Jewish polemic.</note>, page 64, is true when he reports: When they (namely the Jews) see a Christian child being carried into the church to receive the Holy Sacrament of Baptism, they must also use their unwashed mouths regarding it, then saying: "See, they are bathing the **Mamser** <note>original: *Mamser*, a Hebrew term for a child born of an illicit or incestuous union; a bastard.</note> in the **Tuma** <note>original: *Túma*, Hebrew for ritual impurity or uncleanness.</note> to **schmadden** him; see, they are carrying the child of a whore into the uncleanness (that is, the church) to be exterminated."

As for the mentioned word **Hishtammed** <note>original: השתמד *Hishtamméd*, "to be destroyed" or "to apostatize."</note>, which means "to be exterminated" and is used by them for "being baptized," it is found in Rabbi Lipmann’s **Sefer Nitzachon** <note>original: *Sepher Nizzachon*, "The Book of Victory," a medieval Jewish polemical work written to refute Christian arguments.</note>, number 21, where he writes as follows:

> <note>original Hebrew: הוכחתי להם שהם עושים שלא כדת שפוטיים איזה יהודים שחייבים מיתה כדי שישתמדו כי האמונה אינה תלויה במים שלהם אלא בלב ואלו היה אותו היהודי מאמין בלבו ככון אמונתם היה משתמד קודם שאנסוהו להשתמד :</note>
"I proved to them (the Christians) that they act contrary to the law of justice when they allow certain Jews who are guilty of death to go free so that they might let themselves be **schmadden** or exterminated (that is, baptized); for faith does not depend on their water, but rather in the heart. And if such a Jew believed in his heart according to their faith, he would have let himself be **schmadden** before they forced him to let himself be **schmadden**."

# The Twelfth Chapter of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked. 538

> <note>original Hebrew: שמעבור באותם המים לא תצא מתחת ידי כי כל נהרות העולם לא ישטפוך מתחת השגחתי :</note>
"That you pass through those waters, you shall not leave my hand; for all the rivers of the world shall not wash you away from my providence."

This has a meaning concerning <term>Mayim ha-zedonim</term> <note>original: *májim hasledónim*</note>, that is, the "arrogant waters"—meaning the people who are baptized when they accept their (namely the Christians') religion and faith. And God intends to say with this: "Even if you go through that same water (that is, you are baptized), you will still not leave my hand, for all the rivers of the world will not be able to overflow you so that you should be withdrawn from my providence." This same point is also found in the book **Mashmi'a Yeshu'ah** <note>original: *Maschmia jeschúa*, "The Herald of Salvation," a work by Isaac Abarbanel on messianic prophecies.</note>, folio 21, column 3; and in the same work on folio 2, column 3, the baptismal water is also named in this way.

<margin>III. They call it "Whore-Water" through a change of the word *Kedoshim* into *Kadeshim*.</margin>
Thirdly, they call it <term>Mayim kedeshim</term> <note>original: מים קדשים</note>, that is, "Whore-Water" <note>This refers to the Hebrew *kadesh*, which can mean a cultic prostitute; Eisenmenger interprets this as a derogatory pun on "Holy Water."</note>, through a malicious change of the words—a practice very common among them—instead of <term>Mayim kedoshim</term> <note>original: מים קדושים</note>, which means "Holy Water." Some examples can be found in Holy Scripture where a mocking name is given to a thing instead of its right name. For in the Second Book of Kings, chapter 23, verse 13, the Mount of Olives, instead of <term>Har ha-Mishchah</term> <note>original: הר המשחה</note>, which means "Mount of Anointing," is called <term>Har ha-Mashchit</term> <note>original: הר המשחית</note>, that is, "Mount of the Destroyer" or "Mount of Corruption." Concerning this, **Rabbi David Kimchi** <note>A famous 12th-13th century medieval French rabbi and grammarian, also known by the acronym Radak.</note> writes in his commentary as follows:

> <note>original Hebrew: הר הזיתים ונקרא הר המשחה ולגנאי מפני העבודה זרה שהיה שם קראו הר המשחית :</note>
"The Mount of Olives, which is called *Har ha-Mishchah* (the Mount of Anointing), was disgracefully called *Har ha-Mashchit* (the Mount of Corruption) because of the idolatry committed upon it (about which one may read in 1 Kings 11, verse 7)."

**Rabbi Solomon Jarchi** <note>Commonly known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator on the Torah and Talmud.</note> also indicates this same point in his commentary on the passage. Similarly, in Hosea 4, verse 15, the place **Bethel** <note>original: בית אל</note>, which means "House of God," is called **Beth-aven** <note>original: בית און</note>, that is, a "House of Vanity" and "Nothingness," because idolatry was practiced there with the golden calf that King Jeroboam set up, as can be seen in 1 Kings 12, verse 29. The aforementioned Rabbi David Kimchi writes the following in his commentary on it:

> <note>original Hebrew: בית און הוא בית אל שהיה שם אחד מן העגלים : ולגערען לכנות שמו לגנאי קורא אותו בית און :</note>
"Beth-aven is Bethel, where one of the services of the calves was located; but to diminish it and call it by a shameful name, he calls it Beth-aven."

The mentioned Rabbi David Kimchi also teaches concerning the words of Isaiah 22, verse 1, <term>Ge chizzayon</term> <note>original: גיא חזיון</note>, which means a "Valley of Vision" or a "Valley of Sight," as follows:

> <note>original Hebrew: נבואה זו נאמרה על ירושלם וקראה גיא חזיון לפי שהיא מקום הנבואה. ומה שקראה גיא והיא הר לכנותה לרעה לפי שהפילה יושביה לרעתם והשיבוה ההר אל בקעה ואינה ראיה שהיא שנקרא עתה הר אלא גיא :</note>
"This prophecy is spoken of Jerusalem, and it is called *Ge chizzayon* (the Valley of Vision) because it is the place of prophecy. As to why he calls it a valley when it is actually a mountain: this is to label it for evil, because its inhabitants fell into wickedness and they turned the mountain into a lowland; it is not seen as the mountain it is now called, but as a valley."

# How the Jews mockingly name the holy sacraments.
Yyy 3

...ways <note>likely referring to the scholar Christian Weise</note> wishes to claim that baptism is not called *Shemad* or *Shemed* <note>original: "Schémad oder Schémed"; Hebrew words implying destruction or apostasy</note> by the Jews, and that baptizing is not called *shmadden*.

<margin>II. It is called an impurity.</margin>
Secondly, the same is called *Tuma* <note>original: טומאה; meaning "ritual impurity" or "uncleanness"</note>, that is, an impurity; as can be seen in the old *Nizzachon* <note>The *Sefer Nizzachon Yashan*, a medieval Jewish handbook of counter-arguments against Christian missionaries</note> on page 36, where it is written concerning **Exodus chapter 14**: <note>original Hebrew: כאן אומרים המינים שכל ישראל נטבלו בים כמו שהם עושים בטומאתם</note> that is: "Here the heretics <note>meaning Christians</note> say that all Israelites were baptized in the sea, just as they do with their *Tuma*, that is, impurity (namely, their baptism)." And on page 55, columns 1 and 2 of the same book, concerning the words of **Deuteronomy 23, verse 13**, **"And you shall have a spade among your tools,"** the following is written: <note>original Hebrew: הפירוש אינכם יודעים כי יתר על אונך מצוה בשעה שתצורו למלחמה. אינמי יתר יהא לך בשיצא אחד מאחיו חוץ למחנה לבדל מן המחנה ויתפוש אמונה אחרת לערב יטבול מטומאתן דהיינו טניף שלהם ויכנס למחנה ישראל לכסות על זה</note> that is: "You do not know the interpretation (of these words), for the commandment is only to be observed during a time of war. Or rather, the meaning of the words 'you shall have a spade' is that if someone from among your brothers leaves the camp to separate himself from the camp (of the Jewish religion) and adopts another faith, he must wash himself of their (namely the Christians') *Tuma*, that is, impurity—by which their baptism is understood—and shall then enter the camp of the Israelites (or Jews) to cover this (impurity)."

<margin>III. They call it a shameful baptism.</margin>
Thirdly, the same is called *Shemez tevila* <note>original: שמץ טבילה; Eisenmenger writes "tefila" (prayer), but the context of the Hebrew refers to "tevila" (immersion/baptism). *Shemez* implies a "taint" or "whisper," used here as a derogatory pun</note>, that is, a "shame-baptism" or a shameful baptism; and this also appears in the old *Nizzachon* on page 70, concerning the words of **Jeremiah 31, verse 31**, **"I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah,"** where one reads: <note>original Hebrew: כאן פוקרין המינים ואומרים על ישו נתנבא שמשנולד נתן להם תורה חדשה ושמץ טבילתם תחת ברית מילה ויום ראשון שהוא זונטאג תחת השבת</note> that is: "Here the heretics teach erroneously and say that the prophet prophesied this concerning Jesus, who, after he was born, gave them a new law and established their *Shemez tevila*, that is, shameful baptism, in place of circumcision, as well as the first day (of the week), namely Sunday, in place of the Sabbath." And on page 192 of the said old *Nizzachon*, it is written: <note>original Hebrew: וכי שמץ טבילתם מה חטא : וטומאה דוחה</note> that is: "What then does their (the Christians') *Shemez tevila*, that is, shameful baptism, drive away but sin and impurity?" Likewise, on page 193, the words of **Psalm 144, verse 7**, **"Rescue me from great waters,"** and the words of **Psalm 69, verse 16**, **"Let not the flood of waters overflow me,"** are interpreted thus: <note>original Hebrew: אילו מי שמץ טבילתם</note> that is: "This signifies the water of their *Shemez tevila*, or their shameful baptism."

### Of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked, Chapter 12.

<margin>IV. They call the same an abomination-baptism.</margin>
**Fourthly**, the same is called *Schikkuz tefila* <note>Hebrew: שקוץ טבילה; meaning "abominable immersion"</note>, that is, an **abomination-baptism**; as can be read in the oft-mentioned old *Nizzachon* <note>The *Sefer Nizzachon Yashan*, a 13th-century Jewish handbook of counter-arguments against Christian missionaries</note>, page 64. There, concerning the words of **Jeremiah chapter 17, verse 13**, "**O Lord! You are the hope of Israel: all who forsake You must be put to shame: those who depart from Me must be written in the earth, for they forsake the Lord, the fountain of living water,**" it is written as follows: <note>original Hebrew: מקוה ישראל יי' קווי של ישראל זהו יי' : כל עוזביך יבושו שפנים מאחריו ללכת אחרי אלהים יכושו כשיבאו תשועת ישראל : יסורי' בארץ יכתבו כי עזבו מקור מים חיים את יי' ובבורות ודורשים במים מכונסים ומסורחים ר"ל בשיקוץ טבילתם שקורין טויף</note> *that is, O Lord! You are the hope of Israel, that is, You, O Lord, are the confidence of the Israelites. All who forsake You (meaning those who deviate from Him and follow other gods) must be put to shame when they see the salvation of Israel. Those who depart from Me must be written in the earth, for they forsake the Lord, the fountain of living water, and choose and seek for themselves gathered and stinking water—meaning their* Schikkuz tefila, *or abomination-baptism, which they call "Tauffe" (baptism).*

<margin>V. They call it a baptism of disgusting water.</margin>
**Fifthly**, it is called *Tibbul schékez májim* <note>Hebrew: טיבול שקץ מים; meaning "immersion in disgusting water"</note>, that is, a **baptism of disgusting water**; and this is likewise found in the old *Nizzachon*, page 62, where one reads: <note>original Hebrew: לפי דפריהם היה ירמיה מוכיח את ישראל על תורת ישו אלו עצמו למה לא היה מוכיח עליה ולמה לא הלך הוא בעצמו בתורתו : בטיבול שקץ מים ובימי אידיהם</note> *that is: According to their (namely the Christians') statement, Jeremiah rebuked the Israelites (in the 3rd chapter, verse 14, etc.) regarding the law of Jesus; but why did he not rebuke himself on that account? And for what reason did he not follow the same himself, and let himself be baptized with the* Tibbul schékez májim, *that is, the baptism of disgusting water, and celebrate the days of their downfall or destruction (meaning their festivals)?*

<margin>VI. They call it a filthy baptism.</margin>
**Sixthly**, it is also called *Tinnuf tefila* <note>Hebrew: טינוף טבילה; meaning "filthy immersion"</note>, that is, a **filthy baptism**; as can be seen in the frequently mentioned old *Nizzachon*, page 74, where it is read: <note>original Hebrew: כשייאמר לך וארחצך מים זהו נאמר על טינוף טבילתם וגו'</note> *that is: When a Christian says to you (that the words of Ezekiel chapter 16, verse 9), "And I bathed you with water," are said of their* Tinnuf tefila, *that is, their filthy baptism, etc.*

<margin>The Jews give no water from their houses for baptismal or holy water.</margin>
Furthermore, if a Christian wished to fetch water from a Jew's house for a baptism, or for holy water, and clearly stated that he intended to use it for that purpose, the Jew is forbidden from giving that person water, as is taught in the *Sepher Toledoth Adam ve-Chava* <note>The "Book of the Generations of Adam and Eve," a 14th-century legal code by Rabbi Jeroham ben Meshullam</note>, in the fifth part, folio 158, column 3.

<margin>How the Jews name the holy Lord's Supper: Unclean meal, water of impurity, unclean waters, unclean bread, unclean sacrifice, unclean and dead, meal of the unclean. <note>original Hebrew list: סעודה טמא מי טומאה מים טמאים לחם טמא זבח טמא טמא ומת סעודת טמא</note></margin>

Furthermore, they also call the bread in the holy Lord's Supper, or the host, <term>léchem tóme</term>, that is, **unclean bread**, or <term>sevach tóme</term>, that is, an **unclean sacrifice**, as will be proven in what follows. How then could it be too much for them to call the holy Lord's Supper *seüdá tóme*, or rather *seüdá teméa*, that is, an **unclean meal**? They might also call it <term>seüdath</term> (or *seüdás*) <term>tóme</term>, that is, the **meal of the unclean one** (because Christ the Lord is called by them <term>tamé uméth</term> or <term>tóme uméa</term>, that is, **the unclean and dead one**, as was proven above in Chapter 2, page 142, regarding the twenty-sixth name they give to our Savior). By this, they mean the meal in which the supposedly "unclean one" is eaten, because according to the teaching of the Roman Catholic Church, the host is transformed into the substantial body of Christ and is thus to be eaten.

### How the Jews mockingly name the Holy Sacrament.

The doctrine / that the Host, through the **Consecration** <note>The prayer or act that, in Catholic and some other Christian traditions, is believed to transform the bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ.</note> / is to be transformed into the essential body of Christ / and is then worshipped / is for this reason called *tome* <note>original: "tóme", from the Hebrew *tamei*</note>, that is / **unclean** / as can be judged from the commentary of **Rabbi Menachem of Recanati** <note>A 13th-century Italian kabbalist and halakhist.</note> on the Five Books of Moses, folio 124, column 4, in the section *Ki Tissa* / where it is written as follows: <gloss>What is the meaning of the words (Isaiah 42:8) **I will not give my glory to another**? Nor my praise to the *Pesilim* <note>original: "Pesilim", meaning idols or graven images.</note>, that is / to the idols / by which the powers of uncleanness are understood.</gloss>
<margin>A consecrated Host is called a bread-idol.</margin>

<margin>Refutation of Salman's statement.</margin>
These are the words of Rabbi Salman <note>Zalman Zvi of Aufhausen, author of the 1615 "Jewish Theriack," a defense of Judaism.</note>, in which he again reveals his frivolous, false, and deceitful spirit; and just as he tried to excuse it (as can be seen above in Chapter 11, pages 521 and 522) by saying that the Jews call a Christian church *Tuma* <note>original: "Tuma", meaning impurity or filth.</note> because, according to his statement, it is also called *Domo* <note>original: "Domo", referring to the Latin *Domus* or Italian *Duomo* (Cathedral).</note> in Latin; so he does here as well. In the Hebrew language, the *Radix* or root word is **Gaal**, meaning to redeem, deliver, save, or avenge; from this comes **Goël**, which signifies a redeemer (that is, a kinsman who has the right of redemption), a savior, or an avenger. In Ruth 4:1, 6, and 8, it is used for a redeemer or kinsman; in Isaiah 49:7 and 59:20 for a savior and deliverer; and in Numbers 35:19, 21, 24, and 25 for an avenger. However, the aforementioned root **Gaal** has an entirely different meaning in the second conjugation, which is called *Piel*; there, it is **Géel**, meaning to pollute or defile. And in the conjugation *Pual*, which is the passive of the *Piel* conjugation, it is **Goal**, meaning to be defiled; from this comes the participle **megóal**, which—as seen in Malachi 1:7 and 12—means "polluted" or "fouled."

<margin>Refutation of his worthless claim.</margin> To refute this frivolous evasion and reveal its worthlessness, one must know that in the Hebrew language, the <term>Radix</term> <note>The linguistic "root" of a word, usually consisting of three consonants.</note> or root *Sakal* means "to dwell," as seen in Genesis 30:20. From this comes the word <term>zebul</term> <note>original: "זבול sefül"</note>, which means a dwelling, as found in Isaiah 63:15, where it reads: "Look down from heaven, and see from the *zebul*, that is, the habitation of your holiness and glory." However, sometimes the <term>Schurek</term> <note>The Hebrew vowel for "u".</note> is removed, and in its place, the <term>Kibbutz</term> <note>Another Hebrew vowel for "u".</note> is placed under the letter *Beth* (b), and it is written as *zebyl* or *sefyl*, as can be seen in Psalm 49:15, 2 Chronicles 6:2, and 1 Kings 8:13. 

In the Chaldean <note>Aramaic.</note> language, however, as well as among the Rabbis and Talmudists, the root word *sakal* has a completely different meaning; in the second <term>conjugation</term> <note>The "Pahel" or "Piel" intensive form of the verb.</note> *zabbél* <note>original: "זבל sabbél"</note> means to dung or to fertilize with manure. This is also found in the Syriac as *sefal* <note>original: "ܙܒܠ"</note> and in the Arabic as *sabbala* <note>original: "زبل"</note>. Therefore, dung or filth is called *safal* <note>original: "זבל"</note> by the Chaldeans and Rabbis, *sefal* <note>original: "ܙܒܠ"</note> by the Syrians, and *Siblon* <note>original: "زبل"</note> by the Arabs. For this reason, Elias <note>Elijah Levita (1469–1549), a famous Hebrew grammarian.</note> writes in his book *Tishbi* <note>A dictionary of Talmudic and Rabbinic Hebrew.</note> on page 28, column 2: "dung and filth are called *Sefel*" <note>original: "זבל נקרא הצואה והרעי"</note>.

On column 2 of page 108 of the *Machsor* <note>A Jewish prayer book used for festivals.</note> printed in folio in Prague in the year 373 (that is, 1613 AD), but under the title *Yozer leyom sheni* <note>original: "Józer lejóm schení"; a specific liturgical poem for the second day of a festival.</note> in the edition printed here in Frankfurt am Main in the year 450 (that is, 1690 AD), the prayer beginning with *Itto mizvoth vechykkim* <note>original: "אתו מצוות וחוקים Ittó mizvóth vechykkím"; "With Him are commandments and statutes."</note> reads as follows:

"The idols of the uncircumcised nations stand deaf and do not speak; they are lifted upon shoulders and carried. They cannot benefit, help, or save in any way. Their feast days are despised and loathsome; their sacrifices are **abominable broths**, and their libations (or drink offerings) are *yain* or *yen tarelim* <note>original: "יין תרעלים jain oder jen tarèlim"</note>, that is, **wine of horror** or of trembling.

<margin>Refutation of the same vain pretext.</margin>
Through this, someone who does not understand the Hebrew language at all, and otherwise has no knowledge of the matter, could easily be persuaded that the Jews are being done a great injustice by being accused of such things. However, anyone who understands the Hebrew language even a little can very quickly notice the deceit. He shamelessly—and against his own conscience and better knowledge—pretends that the Jews call their holy vessels כליו *Keláv*, which is supposed to mean "vessels," even though in the Hebrew language vessels are not called כליו *Keláv*, but rather כלים *Kelím*. Furthermore, כליו *Keláv* means "his vessels" <note>original: "vasa ipsius"</note> in Latin, and "his vessels" in German, because the *av* at the end is the *suffixum Pronomen* <term>pronominal suffix: a grammatical ending attached to a noun to indicate possession</term> and means "his," just as דברים *devarím* means "words" and דבריו *devaráv* means "his words," or משפטים *mischpatím* means "judgments" and משפטיו *mischpatáv* means "his judgments." But because כליו *Keláv* sounds very similar in pronunciation to the word כלב *Kelef* <note>dog</note>, he wanted to give the Jews instructions in this manner on what sort of evasion they should use for their excuse against Christians who might confront them with this.

The same situation applies to the word כלך *Kelécha*, which, according to his deceptive claim, is also supposed to mean "vessels," whereas it actually means "your vessels," just as צרים *Zárim* means "enemies" and צרך *Zarécha* means "your enemies," or עינים *enájim* means "eyes" and עיניך *enécha* means "your eyes"; for the *écha* at the end is a *Pronomen suffixum pluralis numeri* <term>plural pronominal suffix</term> and means "your." How then does it make sense to call a chalice or beaker כליו *Keláv*, that is, "his vessels," or כלך *Kelécha*, that is, "your vessels"? Indeed, such a thing is a completely foolish excuse. That he reports it is not written with the letter *Beth* or 'b' at the end is a shameful lie; for not only do the aforementioned converted Jews indicate this, but it is also clearly and irrefutably confirmed in both of the cited passages of the old *Nizzáchon* <note>The *Sefer Nizzachon Yashar* is a medieval Jewish polemical work that responds to Christian interpretations of the Bible.</note>.

But as for Rabbi Salman Zevi daring to ask, "How does a dog come to a beaker?"—one can also ask: how does the word indicated above, מזבחים *meßabbechim*, which means "sacrificing," agree with מזבלים *meßábbelim*, which means "manuring/dunging"? Or how does חריא *Charja*, which (to speak with honor) means "excrement," agree with Maria? Or even פני מלך *Pené mélech*, which is the "face of a king," with פני כלב *pené kélef*, which is the "face of a dog"?

The word of Isaiah 1:14, "My soul is an enemy to your new moons and annual feasts," is interpreted and read as: <note>original: המועדים שבדאו מלכם שלא ייחדו י"י על זה נאמר חדשיכם ומועדיכם שנאה נפשי</note> that is: "Regarding their feast days, which they have invented out of their own minds and which God has not commanded, it is said: My soul is an enemy to your new moons and annual feasts." <note>Eisenmenger is quoting a Jewish commentary that repurposes a biblical rebuke of ancient Israel's hypocritical worship to apply it to Christian holidays.</note> And in the preceding twelfth chapter, on page 553, something was brought forward from the *Machsor* <note>A Jewish prayer book used for festivals.</note>, according to which it is written: <note>original: חגים מאוסים הגעלים</note> that is, "Their feast days are despised and loathsome." <margin>1. They call a holy or feast day *Ed*, that is, a downfall, misfortune, and ruin.</margin>

Firstly, *Ed* <note>original: איד</note>, that is, a misfortune, accident, ruin, and downfall; in the *plurali numero*, or plural number, *Edim* <note>original: אידים</note>, that is, downfalls or accidents, because they wish such things upon us on such a day. <margin>When and by whom Sunday was instituted as the Sabbath.</margin> Since Sunday is mentioned here, I cannot omit pointing out that Rabbi Joseph Albo, in his *Sepher Ikkarim* <note>The "Book of Principles," a 15th-century work of Jewish philosophy.</note>, in the 25th chapter, under the title *Maamar Shelishi*, folio 92, columns 1 and 2, claims that Sunday was instituted as the Sabbath in place of Saturday about five hundred years after Christ by a Pope. ### How the Jews Name the Christian Festival and Feast Days.

<margin>Jews are forbidden from fasting on our Sunday.</margin>
It is also forbidden for the Jews to fast on our Sunday because we celebrate that day; this is stated in the Talmudic tractate *Taanith* <note>A tractate concerning fast days.</note>, folio 27, column 2, with these words: <note>original: "בערב שבת לא היו מתענין מפני כבוד שבת ק"ו בשבת עצמו באחד בשבת מאי טעמא לא א"ר יוחנן מפני הנוצרים:"</note> that is: "On the eve of the Sabbath <note>Friday</note>, one did not fast out of honor for the Sabbath, and much less on the Sabbath itself. Why then did one not fast on the first day of the week <note>Sunday</note>? This happened because of the Christians."

<margin>Candlemas is also called *Ed*.</margin>
To return to the previously mentioned word *Ed* <note>The author interprets the Hebrew word "Ed" (אד) as "downfall" or "calamity," though in many contexts it simply refers to a "festival."</note>, the feast of **Candlemas** <note>The Feast of the Presentation of Jesus Christ, celebrated on February 2nd.</note> is likewise called by this name. During this time, Jews are also forbidden from selling goods to a Christian, as is taught in the *Sepher Mizvoth Gadol* <note>The "Great Book of Commandments," a 13th-century legal code by Moses of Coucy.</note> of Rabbi Moses of Coucy, folio 10, column 2: <note>original: "אסור למכור לבונה לגלח ולכומר דמידי דתקרובת הוא כן שעה אסור למכור לגוי ביום איד קנדליר שלהם אבל שאר ימים ולבונה לשאר גוים מותר למכור:"</note> that is: "It is forbidden to sell frankincense to a *Gallach* <term>Gallach: literally "shaved one," referring to the tonsure of a Catholic priest</term> and a *Cumar* <term>Cumar: a term used in the Hebrew Bible for idolatrous priests, here applied to Christian clergy</term>, because it is something used for an offering. Thus, it is also forbidden to sell goods to a *Goi* <note>literally "nation," but used here to mean a Gentile or Christian</note> on their *Yom Ed*, that is, the 'Day of Downfall' of their Candlemas. However, on other days, it is permitted to sell goods and frankincense to the other *Goyim* <note>Gentiles/Christians</note>." The same is found in the book *Agudda*, folio 60, column 2, number 7, and in the book *Kol Bo*, number 97, folio 104, column 1, the words of which were already cited above in the eleventh chapter, page 532.

<margin>Secondly, a festival or feast day is called a "Vanity."</margin>
Secondly, a Christian festival and feast day is called *Hefel* <note>Hebrew: הבל</note>, which means a "vanity" or "emptiness." This can be read in the commentary of **Maimonides** <note>Rabbi Moshe bar Maimon (1138–1204), a famous Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note> on the *Mishnah* of the Talmudic tractate *Avoda Sara* <note>The tractate on "Strange Worship" or "Idolatry."</note>, folio 78, column 3, of the Amsterdam Talmud: <note>original: "ואסור לקרותם אידיהם הבלייהם כנוי למועדיהם:"</note> that is: "Their *Edim* <note>downfalls, by which the feast days are understood, as mentioned</note> are their *Hafalim*, that is, vanities, which is a nickname for their feast days; and it is forbidden to call them *Moadim*, that is, 'festivals,' because in truth they are *Hefel*, that is, a vanity."

<margin>Thirdly, it is called *Chogga*, that is, a "Terror."</margin>
Thirdly, a Christian festival day is called *Chogga* <note>Hebrew: חגא</note>, a word that appears in Isaiah 19:17, where it is read: "The land of Judah shall be a *Chogga* to Egypt," that is, a "terror" (or trembling). This same word is interpreted by Rabbi **David Kimchi** <note>Known as Radak (1160–1235), a grammarian and biblical commentator.</note> as "a movement of fear and trembling," and by Rabbi **Solomon Yarchi** <note>Better known as Rashi (1040–1105).</note> as "a breaking, fear, and terror" in their commentaries. # Part I of Judaism Unveiled, Chapter XIII.

...because they wish that in such a time, fear and terror might overcome us, and that we be broken and brought to nothing. That a Christian festival is called *Chógga* <note>A polemical play on the Hebrew word *Chag* (festival). And thus it is also called *Ed* (אד), which is to say, a downfall or ruin. That we are, however, regarded as idolaters by the Jews will be proven in detail below in the 16th chapter of this first part.

Likewise, in the little tractate titled *Maase rûach* <note>The Story of a Spirit</note>, which tells the history of a spirit from *Nicolausburg* <note>Nikolsburg, now Mikulov in the Czech Republic. This refers to a famous 17th-century account of a dybbuk or possessing spirit.</note>, it is read on *folio 5, column 1*, that the spirit reported in his confession that he had been a Jew but became a Christian and committed many sins. Among other things, he is said to have said: <note>original: "חלפתי שמלותי ביום אדם"</note> *Chilläfti simlothäi bejóm edám*, which is there translated into German as: "I changed my clothes on *Chógga*"; however, it should mean on "their" (namely, the Christians') festival.

And on *folio 7, column 2*, it is reported there that the spirit gave no rest at all to the Jewish boy whom he had possessed, and it follows: <note>original: "אויף איין זונטאג האט ער קיין מנוחה גילאזין און מ'יחד לו און חגא האט ער אויך מנוחה גילאזין"</note> that is: "And on Sunday, as also at all times on the *Chógga*, he left him in peace." So it also stands there on *folio 8, column 2*: <note>original: "און גאנץ שבת האט ער איין ניט לאזין עסן און אן חגא האט ער אים ניקס גיטאן"</note> that is: "During the whole Sabbath he (namely, the spirit) did not let him (meaning the Jewish boy) eat; but on the *Chógga*, he did nothing to him."

Thus also in the German-Hebrew book *Masseóth Binjamin* <note>The Travels of Benjamin of Tudela, a famous 12th-century Jewish traveler.</note>, *folio 73, column 2*, a festival which the Egyptians are accustomed to keep is called *Chógga*. ...that became foolish / whereby without doubt the French word **Noël**, which means the Christ-festival / is considered / and alluded to / [but] named in a malicious way: and the word ניטול **Nittal**, which signifies a hanged one <note>The author argues that the Hebrew word *Nittal* is a derogatory play on the Latin *Natalis* (Birth), mockingly referring to Jesus as "the hanged one."</note> / is read in the old **Nizzáchon**, pages 7, 8, where it is written thus: <note>original: "כנגד אותן מ' ימים ששיהתה בנידה טומאתה מניטל ר"ל וזיין אוקמי עד לי"ט מע"ט כנגדן הם מתענין מ' יום שהרי כתוב אשה כי תזריע וילדה זכר וטמאה שבעת ימים ושלושים יום ושלושה ימים הרי מ' יום"</note> that is / In consideration of those forty days / in which she (namely Mary) remained in her impurity / from **Nital**, that is / from **Christmas** until **Candlemas** <note>Candlemas (Feb 2nd) marks the Feast of the Purification of the Virgin, 40 days after Christmas.</note> / they (the Christians) fast forty days / for see / it stands written (**Leviticus 12, v. 2**): When a woman has conceived seed / and borne a male child / then she shall be unclean seven days. that is: It is forbidden before the **Edim**, that is / the downfalls / (namely the feast days) of the **Cutheans** <note>Cutheans: Originally Samaritans; in polemical contexts, this was often used as a coded term for Christians to bypass censorship.</note> / to engage in trade with them etc. Samuel has said / in the *exilio* or misery [of the Diaspora] it is not forbidden / except on their **jom ed**, (that is / day of downfall) itself. **Rabbi Samuel**, the son of Meir / has explained it in the name of **Rabbi Solomon Jarchi** <note>Commonly known as Rashi, the preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator.</note> / that we now have no need of three days (to abstain from trade with Christians /) because we are in misery [the Diaspora] / and that only those feast days / which are celebrated on his account (that is / for the sake of Jesus /) such as קצח **Kézach**, that is / **Easter** (which is thus named disparagingly instead of פסח **Pésach** [Passover]) and ניטול **Nittal**, [Christmas] are to be forbidden: yet even such days are to be permitted because of **enmity** <note>A legal principle in Jewish law (*mipnei eivah*) allowing certain actions to maintain peaceful relations and avoid provoking hostility from the surrounding non-Jewish population.</note> (so that we do not make the Christians our enemies).

### Of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked, Chapter XIII.

...read from the Amsterdam edition. It is thus clear from this that Dieterich Schwab, in the 1st Chapter of the first part of his *Jewish Mantle* <note>Dieterich Schwab was a Jewish convert to Christianity; his book "Jüdischer Deckmantel" (The Jewish Mantle), published in 1611, was a polemical work exposing Jewish customs to a Christian audience.</note>, wrote the truth when he reports that the Jews call the Christmas festival *Nital*, that is, the Feast of the Hanged One <note>The author interprets the Hebrew word "Nital" as a derogatory play on the Latin "Natalis" (Birth), deriving it instead from a root meaning "to hang," referring to the Crucifixion.</note>.

The second word, ניטל **Nittal**, which signifies one who is taken away or removed from the midst, is found in the book *Shulchan Aruch* <term>Shulchan Aruch: The "Set Table," the most authoritative code of Jewish law, compiled in the 16th century.</term>, in the section *Yoreh Deah*, number 148, at the end, folio 119, column 1, where it is read: <note>original: "אם שולח דורון לעכו"ם בזמן הזה ביום ח' שאחר ני"טל שקורין ניי"א יאד וגו'"</note> "If one (namely a Jew) sends a gift to an idolater (meaning a Christian) at this time on the eighth day after **Nittal** (that is, Christmas), which they call New Year, etc." And so Christmas is also named in the *Sepher Mitzvoth Gadol* <term>Sefer Mitzvot Gadol: "The Great Book of Commandments," a 13th-century work by Rabbi Moses of Coucy.</term> of Rabbi Moses of Coucy, folio 10, column 2, as well as in the book *Terumah*, number 134.

The third word, נואל **Noal**, which signifies one who has become foolish, is found in the manuscript book *Etz Chaim* in the following words, as cited by the highly famous and learned Dr. Wagenseil <note>Johann Christoph Wagenseil (1633–1705) was a prominent Christian Hebraist who published Jewish texts to critique them.</note> in his book *Sota*, pages 775 and 776: <note>original: "ונוצרים שיום אידם יום ראשון אסור לשאת ולתת עמהם בארץ ישראל יום ה' ויום שבהם ו' שבכל שבת וכ"ש יום א' עצמו ובחוצה לארץ אין אסור לשאת ולתת רק ביום אידם בלבד פרש"בם בשם ר"י דווקא נואל וקמח שהם בשם התלוי ואפילו אותן יש להתיר"</note> "And as for the Christians, whose *yom ed* (that is, day of downfall) is the first day (of the week, namely Sunday), it is forbidden to trade with them in the Land of Israel (or in the Jewish land) on the fifth and sixth days of every week; how much more so then is it forbidden on the first day (that is, Sunday) itself. But outside the (Promised) Land, trade with them is only forbidden on their *yom ed*, that is, day of downfall. Rabbi Samuel, the son of Meir, explains this in the name of Rabbi Isaac specifically as referring to **Noal** (that is, the Christmas festival) and **Kefach** (that is, the Easter festival), which are established because of the Hanged One (that is, Jesus), but which are nonetheless permitted."
