### How the Jews name the Christian Feast and Holy Days. 563

...prayers and thanksgivings with reading and singing to God, because on that same night the *Alma* <note>original: "Alma" — Hebrew for a young woman or virgin, referring to the prophecy in Isaiah 7:14.</note> (that is, the Virgin), according to the declaration of Isaiah, gave birth to Christ, our Messiah. When you Jews then hear the bells ringing, you speak with quite terrifying words: "Now the *Mamser* <term>Mamser: A Hebrew term for a child born of an illicit or adulterous relationship; used here as a derogatory slur against Jesus.</term> crawls through all <term>מושבים</term> <gloss>moschovim</gloss>," that is, now the illegitimate child must go through all the sewers and secret chambers. These are the words of Ernst Ferdinand Hessen; with which Dieterich Schwab also entirely agrees in his *Jewish Mantle*, in the first chapter of the first part, pages 30 and 31; as well as Friedrich Samuel Brenz in the first chapter of his *Stripped Snake-skin*, page 7; along with Johann Adrian in his *Epistle*, page 29. <margin>The Jews are allowed neither to study nor pray on the Christmas festival, and why this happens.</margin>
Furthermore, the aforementioned Dieterich Schwab writes in the last-mentioned place as follows: They are also permitted neither to study nor pray during the time of Christmas, which they call *Nital* <note>As noted previously, a pun on "Natalis" (Birth) interpreted as "The Hanged One."</note> (that is, the Feast of the Hanged One). The reason is that they believe Christ is in great hellish pain on that night, and they wish him to have no rest or refreshment; for they do nothing else then but curse, spit upon, and revile Christ. Regarding this, the mentioned Johann Adrian, in the last-cited place of his *Epistle*, also addresses the Jews thus: On Ascension (he meant to say, Christmas) Day you do not study, and you claim that our Lord Christ must do penance, and as punishment must crawl through all the disgusting privies and secret places that same night, and has no rest unless he hears you studying. But because you do not grant him such rest, you refuse to study. You also say to your children at that time, "See to it that the <term>תלו</term> <gloss>Tolui</gloss> (that is, the Hanged One) does not pull you in." So also writes Friedrich Samuel Brenz in the last-mentioned place: On the said Christmas night the Jews are very merry; they play, feast, and drink, claiming that in whichever house they were to read and pray, the *Tolui* would have all the more rest, and would not have to crawl through the corners in those same houses.

### The Thirteenth Chapter of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked. 564

<margin>
The damned in hell are said to have rest when the Jews pray.
</margin>
That this B. Kehrten <note>Likely a reference to a specific source or convert mentioned in the preceding text.</note> wrote the truth, I do not doubt at all, for I know from experience that the Jews do not study at that same time. They also believe that the damned have rest from their torment during the time of their prayer, of which it is written in the book *Megalleh Amukkot* <note>original: *Megallé amykkôth*; a Kabbalistic work by Nathan Nata Spira, the title meaning "Revealer of Depths."</note>, folio 41, column 3, in the 127th *Ofan* <term>Ofan: A "wheel" or section within this specific Kabbalistic text.</term>, as follows:

"It is found in the Zohar, Portion Noah, page 49, that every day at the time of prayer, there is rest for the wicked in Gehenna <note>The Hebrew term for the place of spiritual purification or punishment, often translated as Hell.</note> during every prayer for an hour and a half. It follows from this that every day, during the three prayers (namely the morning, afternoon, and evening prayers), the wicked in Gehenna have four and a half hours of rest. This makes six times four and a half hours in the six days of the week, which is twenty-seven hours that the wicked have in Gehenna during the six workdays. Likewise, the twenty-four hours of the Sabbath make fifty-one hours in each week that the wicked have rest in Gehenna." <note>This calculation reflects a Kabbalistic tradition that the sanctity of prayer and the Sabbath temporarily suspends the punishments of the afterlife.</note>

More on this can be found below in the 22nd <note>original: "aa ten," a 17th-century way of writing 22nd.</note> chapter of the second part. Since, according to their opinion, the damned have rest during the time of prayer, but they are sworn enemies of Christ the <term>Lord</term>, it is easy to imagine that they will omit nothing that they believe to be contrary to Him.

<margin>
The Jews are accustomed to reading the cursed little book *Toledot Yeshu* on Christmas Eve.
</margin>
The aforementioned Friedrich Samuel Brenz also reports in his *Stripped Jewish Snakeskin* <note>A 1614 polemical work by a Jewish convert to Christianity, titled *Jüdischer Schlangenbalg*.</note>, in the first chapter, page 2, that the Jews read the devilish book of slander—which is called *Ma'aseh Talui* <note>original: *Máase Talúi*; literally "The Story of the Hanged One."</note>, that is, the history of the one who was hanged, but is otherwise also called *Toledot Yeshu*, that is, the *Birth of Jesus*—quite secretly in their houses on Christmas Eve, to the greatest insult of Christ. This is quite easy to believe; for as I mentioned shortly before, when I was once at a Rabbi's house here in Frankfurt in the Jewish Lane <note>The *Judengasse*, the compulsory Jewish ghetto in Frankfurt.</note> on a Christmas Eve, a Jewish student who did not know me came in and asked the Rabbi to lend him that *Sepher* <term>Sepher: The Hebrew word for "book."</term> which was customary to be read on that same night. However, because I was standing there, the Rabbi did not answer him, as he was embarrassed in my presence. It was certainly no other than this cursed, hellish little book; and it were to be wished that all such and similar godless books were taken from the Jews.

### How the Jews Name the Christian Feast and Holy Days. 565

<margin>
How the Easter festival is mockingly named.
</margin>
Regarding the Christian Easter festival, which in the Hebrew language is called **פסח** *Pésach* <note>original: *Pésach*; the Jewish festival of Passover</note>, it is named by them, through a common malicious distortion, almost mockingly as **כסח** *Késach* <note>original: *Késach*</note>, that is, a "cutting off" or a "hewing out," from **כסח** *Casach* <note>original: *Kasach*</note>, which means to cut off and hew out. They do this because they believe that the Christians, during such a festival, shall be rooted out by their supposed Messiah and all be put to death, as will be shown more extensively below in the 14th Chapter of the second part. However, so that their malice might not be noticed, they often used to write, instead of **כסח** *Késach* with the letter *Caph*, **קסה** *Késach* with the letter *Koph*, which means nothing, or even **קנח** *Kézach* <note>original: *Kézach*</note>, which signifies Roman coriander <note>likely *Nigella sativa* or black cumin</note> or, according to others, vetches. The word **כסח** *Késach* with the letter *Caph* is read in Rabbi Lipmann’s *Sepher Nizzáchon* <note>The "Book of Victory," a famous 14th-century Jewish apologetic and polemic work</note>, number 240, page 134, where **ביום הכסח** *bejóm hakkésach*, that is, "on the day of Késach," is written instead of *Pésach*. Thus it is also taught in the *Piske Toséphoth* <note>Decisions of the Tosafists, medieval commentators on the Talmud</note> of the Talmudic tractate *Avoda sára* <term>Avoda Zarah: A tractate concerning "Foreign Worship" or idolatry</term>, number 1, folio 77, column 1 of the Amsterdam Talmud: **מותר לרון אפילו בכסה וניתל** that is, "It is permitted for us (to trade with the Christians) even on their *Késach* and *Nital* <note>Nital is a traditional Jewish term for Christmas, likely derived from the Latin *Natalis*</note>," and this is also found in the words cited above on page 561 from the book *Col bo*. I have often seen the word **קסה** *Késach* with the letter *Koph* in their calendars, and the same also stands in the *Sepher mizvóth gadól* <note>The "Great Book of Commandments" by Moses ben Jacob of Coucy</note> of Rabbi Moshe Mikkózi, folio 10, column 2, with these words: **דווקא ניטל וקסה ושנה עיקר אידם וראש יראתם אסור :** "Specifically *Nital* (that is, the Christ-festival) and *Késach* (that is, the Easter festival), both of which are their main festivals and the most prominent work of their idol, are forbidden (to trade with them)." It is also read this way in the written book *Ez chájim* <note>Tree of Life</note>, as can be seen in the *Sóta* of the highly esteemed Doctor Wagenseil <note>Johann Christoph Wagenseil (1633–1705), a Christian Hebraist</note>, page 776. The word **קנח** *Kézach*, however, stands above in the words cited on page 561 from folio 59, column 3 of the book *Agúdda*, as well as in the book *Terúma* of Rabbi Baruch, number 134.

<margin>
How the Jews are to behave toward Christians on Christian feast days.
</margin>
How the Jews should behave toward Christians on Christian feast days is sufficiently shown in their books; they are forbidden from going into a Christian’s house on his feast day and from greeting him, as can be found in the Talmudic tractate *Gittin* <term>Gittin: A Talmudic tractate primarily concerning divorce, but also containing various social laws</term>, folio 62, column 1, where it is written: **לא יכנס אדם לביתו של נכרי ביום אידו ויתן לו שלום מצאו : בשוק נותן לו בשפה רפה ובכובד ראש :** that is, "A man shall not enter the house of a stranger (understand: a Christian) on the day of his *Ed* <note>original: *Ed*; a term used in the Talmud for a pagan festival, interpreted by the author as "downfall" or "calamity"</note> (that is, his ruin; namely, on his feast day) and greet him. If he finds him on the street (or in the market), he greets him with a low voice and with a bowed head." Exactly the same stands also in the book *Col bo*, number 108, as well as in the book *Schylchan áruch*, in the part *Jore déa* <note>Yoreh De'ah: A section of the Shulchan Aruch, the standard code of Jewish law</note>.

# Of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked, Chapter 13.

<margin>
The damned in Hell are said to have rest when the Jews pray.
</margin>

But that these converts <note>Referring to Jewish people who converted to Christianity and then wrote accounts of Jewish life</note> have written the truth, I do not doubt at all, for I know from experience that the Jews do not study at that same time. For they also hold that the damned have rest from their torment during the time of their prayer, of which it is written in the book *Megallé Amukkôth* <note>original: *Megallé amukkôth*, meaning "Revealer of Depths," a Kabbalistic work by Nathan Nata Spira</note>, folio 41, column 3, in the 127th *Ofan*, as follows:

<note>Translation of the Hebrew/Aramaic text:</note>
It is found in the Zohar, portion Noah, page 49, that every day, during each of the three prayers, the wicked in Gehenna <note>The place of punishment or purification in the afterlife</note> have rest for an hour and a half during each prayer. It is found, according to this, that every day during the three prayers, the wicked in Gehenna have four and a half hours of rest. Thus, in the six days of the week, six times four and a half makes twenty-seven hours that the wicked in Gehenna have during the six working days; and likewise twenty-four hours on the Sabbath; which together makes fifty-one hours in every week that the wicked in Hell have rest.

That is, it stands in the Zohar <note>The foundational work of Jewish mysticism</note>, in the portion of Noah, in the 49th column, that the godless have rest in Hell every day at the time of prayer, and at each prayer, for one and a half hours. It is therefore found, according to this, that the godless in Hell have four and a half hours of rest every day during the three prayers (namely, the morning, afternoon, and evening prayers), which in the six days of the week, six times four and a half hours, makes twenty-seven hours in the six workdays in Hell; and likewise twenty-four hours on the Sabbath, which together makes fifty-one hours in each week in which the godless have rest in Hell. More concerning this can be found below in the eighth chapter of the second part. Now, because in their opinion the damned have rest at the time of prayer, and yet they are mortal enemies of Christ the Lord, it is easy to imagine that they will omit nothing which they believe to be contrary to Him.

<margin>
The Jews are accustomed to reading the cursed booklet *Toledoth Yeshu* on Christmas Night.
</margin>

The aforementioned Friedrich Samuel Brenz also reports in his *The Stripped-off Jewish Snake-skin* <note>A common title for polemical works by converts, suggesting they have shed their former "Jewish" nature</note>, in the first chapter, page 2, that the Jews read that devilish book of slander, which is called <term>מעשה תלוי</term> <gloss>Ma'aseh Talui</gloss> (the History of the Hanged One) or *Toledoth Yeshu* <note>The "Generations" or "Life" of Jesus; a medieval Jewish parody of the Gospel stories</note>—that is, the birth of Jesus—quite secretly on Christmas Night in their houses, to the greatest insult of Christ. This is very easy to believe; for when I was once, as mentioned shortly before, at a Rabbi's house here in Frankfurt in the Jewish Quarter on a Christmas Eve, a Jewish student came in who did not know me and addressed the Rabbi, asking if he would lend him that *Sepher* <note>original: *Sepher*; book</note> which was accustomed to be read on that same night. Whereupon the Rabbi, because I was standing there, did not answer him, as he was wary of me. But it was certainly no other than this cursed, hellish booklet; and it would be wished that all such and similar godless booklets were taken from the Jews.

## The XIV Chapter.

### In which it is shown how much the Jews boast, and elevate themselves above all the nations of the world.

<margin>The Jews are a proud and boastful people.</margin>
Since I intend to report in the following fifteenth chapter how the Jews despise and hate all nations found outside of Judaism—especially the Christians—I have deemed it not unhelpful to first set before your eyes their pride and great boastfulness in this chapter. This is so one can see how these wretched people foolishly elevate themselves in their vain imaginations above all other nations, even though the righteous wrath and curse of God is upon them. Because of their poor condition—being a people cast out and rejected by the Most High—they should rightly be brought to humbler thoughts and to the recognition of their unhappy state. 

<margin>For although they have been rejected by God,</margin>
It is true that in olden times they were the chosen people of God, for which reason Moses addresses them in *Deuteronomy* 7:6 thus: **You are a holy people to the Lord your God; the Lord your God has chosen you to be a people of His own possession, out of all the peoples who are on the face of the earth.** 

<margin>And the Kingdom of God has been taken from them.</margin>
The like of this can also be read in the same book, chapter 10:15 and 14:2. However, because of their ungodly nature, *the Kingdom of God*—as *Jesus* prophesied to them in *Matthew* 21:43 <note>The source text cites verse 4, but the prophecy of the kingdom being taken and given to another nation is found in Matthew 21:43</note>—has been taken from them and given to the Gentiles. Regarding this, it is also written in the **<term>Midrash Tehillim</term>** <note>A rabbinic commentary on the Book of Psalms, likely compiled between the 4th and 13th centuries</note>, folio 35, column 1, concerning the words of *Psalm* 75:10, **I will break all the horns of the wicked/** as follows:

## How the Jews boast and exalt themselves above all nations.

is/ The purpose of the creation of the world was solely for the sake of *Israel*; although all this is clear, one must nevertheless consider these words and taste them with the palate <note>An idiomatic way of saying "to contemplate deeply."</note>, for it is known that when the Law <note>The Torah</note> was given, all *Israelites* attained all perfections which the nations of the world lack, because they did not want to accept the Law. And in the book *Schené luchóth habberith* <note>meaning "The Two Tablets of the Covenant," a major work of Jewish law and mysticism by Isaiah Horowitz, 17th century</note> (or *lúchos hábberis*) it is read on folio 145, column 3: <note>original: "בריאת העולם היה בשביל ישראל והם הפרי ושאר האומות הקליפות להם נמצא שבאמת אין שום עם אלא ישראל ושאר האומות הם קליפה להם"</note> that is: **The world was created for the sake of the *Israelites*, and they are the fruit, while the remaining nations are their shells.** <note>The word "shells" refers to the "Kelipot," a kabbalistic term for the forces of evil or impurity that surround the "holy spark."</note> We find, therefore, that in truth there is no other people but *Israel*, and the remaining nations are their shells.

*Abarbenel* <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a famous 15th-century Jewish statesman and philosopher</note> also teaches in his commentary on the Prophet *Isaiah*, folio 63, column 4, regarding chapter 41, verse 16, thus: <note>original: "ישראל הם תכלית העולם השפל והם בעין החטה והאומות בערך הקש"</note> that is: **The *Israelites* are the purpose of the lower world, and they are compared to the wheat, but the nations are compared to the straw.**

And in *Bammidbar rabba* <note>A collection of ancient rabbinic homilies on the Book of Numbers</note> it is read on folio 171, column 1, in the Portion *Bammidbar*: <note>original: "נמשלו ישראל כערימה של חטים מה החטים הללו נכנסות לאוצר במנין כך אמר הק"בה שיהו ישראל נמנים בכל שעה לכך נאמר פטנך ערימות חטים אבל התבן והקש אינן נמנים ולא נמדדים כך עכ"ום נמשלו כתבן וקש שנ' כקש לפני רוח : וכן ובית עשו לקש : למה שאין להק"בה הנייה מהם שנ' כל הגוים כאין נגדו . אבל ישראל יש להק"בה הנייה מהם קורין שמע מתפללין ומברכין שמו של מלך הק"בה בכל יום לפיכך הן נמנין בכל שעה לכך נמשלו בחטים שנ' בטנך ערימת חטים:"</note> that is: **The *Israelites* are like a heap of wheat: just as the wheat is brought into the treasure-house (or the granary) by number (that is, counted by the bushel and measure), so God says the *Israelites* shall be counted every hour; therefore it is said (*Canticles* 7, v. 3):**

**Israelites are beloved, for they are called friends** <note>original: "חביבים ישראל שנקראו רעים"</note> (of God), as it is said (Psalm 122, verse 8): **For the sake of my brothers and friends.** So also writes Rabbi Bechai <term>Rabbi Bechai: Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century Spanish scholar and commentator on the Torah</term> in his commentary on the Five Books of Moses, in the section *Mishpatim*, folio 96, column 4, thus: **It is known that the Israelites are called God’s friends** <note>original: "ידוע כי ישראל נקראו רעים למקום"</note> **as it is said (Psalm 122, verse 8): For the sake of my friends and brothers.**

They also claim that they are all children of kings; for in the Talmudic tractate *Shabbath*, folio 67, column 1, and folio 128, column 1, it is written: **All Israelites are children of kings** <note>original: "כל ישראל בני מלכים"</note>. This is also found in the book *Emek Hammelech* <term>Emek Hammelech: "The King's Valley," a 17th-century Kabbalistic work by Naphtali Herz ben Jacob Elhanan</term>, folio 27, column 3, in the 48th chapter under the title *Sha’ar Olam Hatohu* <note>The Gate of the World of Confusion</note>.

<margin>For this reason, they thank God daily that He has made them Jews.</margin>
Because of the aforementioned conceits <note>original: "Einbildungen"; the author views these religious claims as arrogant delusions</note> which they have about themselves, they thank God every morning that He made them Jews and not Heathens or Christians; and each one speaks: **Blessed art Thou, Lord our God, King of the Universe, who has not made me a Goy or Heathen.** <note>original: "ברוך אתה יי' אלהינו מלך העולם שלא עשני גוי"</note> In some copies, however, it stands: **Who has made me an Israelite.** <note>original: "שעשני ישראל"</note> In others, however, it is read: **Who has made me a Jew.** <note>original: "שעשני יהודי"</note>

<margin>No Jew may call another a servant.</margin>
And because they come from such a high lineage, no Jew may call another a servant—under penalty of excommunication—as can be seen in the book *Shulchan Aruch* <term>Shulchan Aruch: "The Set Table," the most authoritative legal code in Judaism</term>, in the part *Yoreh De'ah*, number 334, paragraph 40, folio 306, column 1. There, those who are to be excommunicated are mentioned, among whom is **he who calls his companion a servant** <note>original: "הקורא לחבירו עבד"</note>. This is also found in the *Sefer Hasidim* <term>Sefer Hasidim: "The Book of the Pious," a primary work of the medieval German-Jewish Pietists</term>, number 43, folio 11, column 1. Thus, out of a ridiculous pride, they do not wish to be considered servants, even though they are under the yoke of other nations; therefore they also say every morning: **Blessed art Thou, Lord our God, and King of the Universe, who has not made me a servant.** <note>original: "ברוך אתה יי' אלהינו מלך העולם שלא עשני עבד"</note>

<margin>In contrast, they consider Christians to be their servants.</margin>
On the other hand, in a mocking and contemptuous manner, they consider Christians to be their servants, as can be seen in their *Selichoth* (or *Selichos*) <term>Selichoth: Prayers for forgiveness, often recited during the High Holy Day season</term>. On the first day of the New Year, in the prayer beginning **"Le-enenu Asheku"** <note>Before our eyes they have oppressed us</note>, they lament and quote from Lamentations 5, verse 8: **Servants rule over us** <note>original: "עבדים משלו בנו"</note>. By this, all those nations are understood under whose yoke they have been and still are, as is found in *Echa Rabbathi* <term>Echa Rabbathi: A Midrash (homiletic interpretation) on the Book of Lamentations</term>, folio 309, column 1, where it is read: **The words "servants rule over us" signify the kingdoms or the monarchies.** <note>original: "עבדים משלו בנו אלו מלכויות"</note> And in the mentioned *Selichoth*, they pray in a prayer which begins—

### Chapter 14 of the First Part of Judaism Unveiled ###

An interpretation of the Five Books of Moses is read on folio 81, column 2, in the Portion <term>Parashah: The weekly section of the Torah read in the synagogue</term> of *Beshallach*: **"All who rise up against Israel, it is as if they rose up against the Divine Majesty"** <note>original: "כל הקמים על ישראל כאלו הם קמים כנגד השכינה Kol ha-kamim al Yisrael k'ilu hem kamim k'neged ha-Shekhinah"</note>; that is, all those who rebel against Israel do as much as if they rebelled against the Divine Majesty <term>Shekhinah: The dwelling or settling of the divine presence of God</term>. Thus it is also seen written in the book *Zeror Hammor* <term>Zeror Hammor: A 15th-century Torah commentary by Abraham Saba</term>, folio 66, column 1, in the Portion of *Shemot*: **"Whoever causes harm to the Israelites does not depart in peace"** <note>original: "מי שמזיק לישראל אינו יוצא לשלום Mi she-mazik le-Yisrael eino yotze le-shalom"</note>; that is, whoever inflicts damage upon the Israelites does not come to a fortunate end. And in the Talmudic tractate *Sanhedrin*, folio 58, column 2, it is read: **"A Gentile who strikes an Israelite is guilty of death"** <note>original: "גוי שהכה את ישראל חייב מיתה Goi she-hikkah et Yisrael chayav mitah"</note>; that is, a *Goi* (that is, a Christian or a Heathen) who strikes an Israelite is worthy of death. This can also be found in the book *Yad Hazakah* <term>Yad Hazakah: Also known as the Mishneh Torah, a comprehensive code of Jewish law compiled by Maimonides</term>, in the second part, folio 43, column 1, in the fifth chapter, § 3, under the title *Hilkhot Chovel u-Mazzik* <term>Hilkhot Chovel u-Mazzik: Laws concerning wounding and damaging</term>. And immediately following in the aforementioned tractate *Sanhedrin*, folio 58, column 2: **"Whoever strikes an Israelite on the cheek, it is as if he strikes the cheek of the Divine Majesty"** <note>original: "הסטור לועו של ישראל כאלו סוטר לועו של שכינה Ha-soter lo'o shel Yisrael k'ilu soter lo'o shel Shekhinah"</note>; that is, whoever gives an Israelite a slap on the cheek (or a box on the ear) does as much as if he gave a slap on the cheek to the Divine Majesty.

Kol ha-m'kayyem nefesh achat mi-Yisrael..."</note>; that is, for every person who kills a soul from Israel, it is held by the Scripture as if he had killed a world full; but for every person who preserves an Israelite soul, it is received by the Scripture as if he had preserved a world full. Such is also found in the *Yalkut Shimoni* <term>Yalkut Shimoni: A major medieval compilation of Midrashic interpretations of the Hebrew Bible</term> on the Five Books of Moses, folio 4, column 4, and in the *Midrash Mishle* <term>Midrash Mishle: A homiletic commentary on the Book of Proverbs</term>, folio 65, column 3, as well as in the book *Pirke Rabbi Eliezer* in the 48th chapter. In the book *Pesikta Zutarta* <note>original: "Pesikta fotárta," likely an archaic variant or transcription error for Pesikta Zutarta, a 12th-century Midrash</note>, folio 44, column 4, in the Portion of *Behaalotekha*, the following is also read: **"Everyone who hates Israel, it is as if he hates Him who spoke and the world was, etc.; and everyone who helps Israel, it is as if he helps Him who spoke and the world was"** <note>original: "כל מי ששונא ישראל כאלו שונא למי שאמר והיה העולם וגו' : וכל העוזר לישראל כאלו עוזר למי שאמר והיה העולם"</note>; that is, everyone who hates an Israelite does as much as if he hated the one who said that the world should be (that is, God), etc. And everyone who helps an Israelite does as much as if he helped the one who said that the world should be. ### Chapter 14 of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked ###

Why does Israel pray in this world and yet they are not answered? It is because they do not know the Explicit Name <term>Shem HaMephorash: The "Explicit Name" of God, referring to the Tetragrammaton or other secret, multi-lettered names of God in Jewish mysticism. It was believed that speaking the correct name with perfect intention could affect the physical and spiritual worlds.</term>. But in the time to come, the Holy One, blessed be He, will make it known to them, as it is said (Isaiah 52:6): *Therefore my people shall know my name.* At that time, they will pray and be answered, as it is said (Psalm 91:15): *He shall call upon me, and I will answer him.* **That is: Rabbi Joshua, the son of Levi, said in the name of Rabbi Phinehas, the son of Jair: Why do the Israelites pray in this world (that is, at this time) and are not heard? Because they do not know the *Shem HaMephorash*. In the future, however, the holy and blessed God will make it known to them; for it is said (Isaiah 52:6): *Therefore my people shall know my name.* At that same time, they will pray and be heard; for it is said (Psalm 91:15): *He shall call upon me, and I will answer him.***

<margin>
Another reason why the prayer of the Jews is not heard by God.
</margin>
In the commentary of **Rabbi Menachem of Recanati** <note>A prominent 13th-century Italian kabbalist who integrated mystical philosophy into his Torah commentary.</note> on the Five Books of Moses, on folio 64, column 4, and folio 65, column 1, in the *Parashah Vayishlach Yaakov* <term>Parashah: The weekly portion of the Torah read in the synagogue; Vayishlach covers Genesis 32:4–36:43.</term>, the reason why the prayers of the Jews are not heard by God today is presented differently, and the words there read as follows: <note>original: "דע והבן..." — Eisenmenger is quoting a Hebrew passage from Recanati that explains the necessity of "Kavanah" (intention) and the specific use of Divine Names in prayer.</note> Know and understand that the devotion of the petitioner must be directed according to the request and the "place" from which the request emanates. As our Rabbis of blessed memory said: "Why is Israel not answered? Because they do not know how to pray using the [Divine] Name." The wise **Rabbi (Aben) Ezra** <note>original: "רבי עזרא"; likely referring to the kabbalist Ezra of Gerona, whose ideas were often cited in Recanati's work.</note>, of blessed memory, explained this correctly: it refers to the Name appropriate for that specific matter, provided that the thought is focused on the unity of all. Understand this well: for every matter, there is a Name that governs it. There is one appointed over forgiveness, prayer, and mercy; one over tears; one over plagues and troubles; one over the petition for children; one over sustenance; one over might; and one over kindness. If a man does not know how to focus his prayer on that specific Name appointed over what he needs, what causes him to fail in his desire? His own ignorance and lack of attention. He might then harbor the evil thought that God, may He be exalted, has denied him his wish, when it is actually nothing but his own ignorance—as it is said (Proverbs 19:3): *The foolishness of man perverteth his way,* etc. and (Jeremiah 5:25): *Your sins have withholden good things from you.* However, when one is expert in these Names and needs to bring a request before God, and directs his mind and intention toward the Name appointed over his request, he will not only fulfill his desire but will be beloved above and cherished below. It is like a treasure house full of all good things, containing many rooms, each dedicated to one thing. In this room is food, in this one gold, in this one pearls, in this one clothing. When a man needs to eat but does not know which room holds the food, he may die of hunger even though the rooms are full of goods—not because his request was denied, but because he did not know where to find the thing he needed. **That is: Know and understand that the devotion (or the purpose) of the one praying must be directed according to the request and the place from which the request has its influence (or from which the thing requested is granted), just as our Rabbis of blessed memory have said: Why are the Israelites not answered (in their prayer)? Because they do not know how to pray by the Name. The wise Rabbi (Aben) Ezra, of blessed memory, has interpreted this correctly: that it is to be understood as that Name which is suitable for the specific matter (which is desired), and that the thoughts do not deviate from the unification of everything (that belongs to it). Therefore, note this well: that in every matter there is a Name—**

# Chapter XIV of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked #

"An iron wall is between you and the city." <note>original Hebrew: קיר ברזל בינך ובין העיר</note> That is: From the day that the Temple was destroyed, an iron wall has been placed between Israel and their Father who is in heaven (by which they are separated from one another), as is said in (Ezekiel 4:1, 3): "And you, son of man, take an iron plate, and set it for an iron wall between you and the city."

<margin>Why the Jews turn their faces toward Jerusalem when they pray.</margin>
Since we are dealing here with the prayers of the Jews, I must also show the reason why they are accustomed to turning their faces toward Jerusalem when they perform their prayers. In the book *Sha'are Zedek* <note>translated as "Gates of Righteousness," a Kabbalistic work</note>, folio 22, column 1, it is written thus:

"The prayer which takes place outside the Land [of Israel] does not ascend by the straight path until it goes into the Land of Israel (or the Promised Land), and from there to Jerusalem, and from there into the Temple, as it is written in the prayer of Solomon, upon whom be peace (1 Kings 8:30): 'And when it arrives at the Temple, then it ascends.' For this reason, the Israelites who are in exile or misery pray around Jerusalem from the four corners of the earth, and Jerusalem is in the middle. Therefore, all those in exile who live toward the sunset <note>the West</note> pray toward the sunrise <note>the East</note>; and likewise those who live toward the sunrise pray toward the sunset; similarly, those who stay toward midnight <note>the North</note> turn their faces toward midday <note>the South</note>. Thus it is found that all Israelites send their prayers toward Jerusalem and into the Temple, because from there the prayers ascend to blessed God."

<margin>From whence it comes that the Jews move from one side to another when they pray or read.</margin>
<margin>The first opinion.</margin>
The Jews also have the custom, when they read or pray, of moving themselves from one side to the other <note>this rhythmic swaying is known as "shuckling"</note>. Regarding why this happens, I find two opinions. The first is in the second part of the book *Kuzari* <note>an influential 12th-century philosophical work by Judah Halevi</note>, numbers 79 and 80, pages 141 and 142, in these words:

"The Khazar said: I ask you, do you know why the Jews move about while reading the Hebrew [language]? The Rabbi replied: Some say it is on account of the stirring of natural heat; but I do not think it is for any other reason than the matter we are discussing—because many of them were able to read at once, it could happen that ten or more would gather over a single book. Because of this, our books were large, and each of the ten needed to lean in at all times to see the word and then move back; and so he was constantly leaning and returning, etc."

<summary>This page explains two physical aspects of Jewish prayer: the requirement to face Jerusalem so that prayers can "route" through the site of the destroyed Temple, and the origin of swaying during study and prayer, which the Kuzari attributes to the practical need for multiple students to share a single large book.</summary>

# How the Jews Boast and Elevate Themselves Above All Nations #

<note>original Hebrew: שֶׁהוּסְפַּר בְּאֶרֶץ וְהוֹדּוּ זֶה הַסִּבָּה הָרִאשׁוֹנָה... — this Hebrew passage is the source for the German translation that follows, taken from the "Kuzari," a 12th-century philosophical work by Judah Halevi.</note>
"It was recounted in the land, and they confessed that this was the first cause. Afterward, it became a habit because of the constant looking and seeing during their wandering, and to resemble those they saw, as is the nature of human beings. Others read each one in his own book and bring it close to his eyes, or he approaches it as he wishes, without being crowded by his companion, and he does not need to turn and return." 

That is: **The Kuzari** <note>The King of the Khazars, a character in Judah Halevi’s dialogue who seeks the true religion</note> has said (to the Jewish Rabbi): "I ask you, are you also aware why the Jews move when they read Hebrew?" 
The Jewish Master or **Rabbi** has answered: "It is said that this happens to awaken the natural heat <note>A medieval medical belief that physical motion stimulated the body's internal 'fire' or energy</note>. I, however, hold that it happens solely because of the matter we are discussing. Because many of them had to read together (from a single book), it was possible that ten or more of them gathered around a single book. For this reason, our books were also large, and each of the ten needed to constantly turn to see the words and then step back again (to make room for others), so that he had to continually bend and go back because the book was on the ground; and this was the first cause. 

After this, a habit arose from this practice of looking, as they were always moving, so that they might make themselves equal to those they saw, as is the nature of men. Among other (peoples), however, each person reads in his own book and holds it close to his eyes, or he goes close to it according to his pleasure, so that no one is burdensome (or obstructive) to him, and he has no need to turn and go back."

The other opinion is read in the *Jalkut Chadash* <note>original: "Jalkut chádasch," a 17th-century collection of Kabbalistic and Midrashic teachings</note>, where on folio 103, column 4, number 24, under the title "Israel," it is written thus:

"Why do the Israelites move when they learn <note>study Torah</note>, while the nations of the world do not move? Because the souls of Israel are a light from above, as it is written (Proverbs 20:27): 'The lamp of the Lord is the soul of man.' And behold, the nature of the lamp is always that it hovers and moves around the wick and never rests. So too is Israel, whose souls are emanated and attached to the lamp of the Lord above; therefore they move always when they occupy themselves with the light of the Torah. But the nations, whose souls are not from the lamp of the Lord, therefore they do not move." 

That is: Why do the Israelites move when they learn, and the peoples of the world do not move? Because the souls of the Israelites are from the higher light, as is written (Proverbs 20:27): "The soul of man is a light of the Lord." And behold, the nature of light is always that it hovers around the wick and moves, and never stands still: thus also do the Israelites move, whose souls come from the highest light of the Lord and are attached to the same forever, whenever they study in the light of the Law <note>the Torah</note>. The peoples, however, whose souls do not come from the light of the Lord, do not move. Concerning this, it is also written in the book *Zeror Hammor* <note>original: "Zerór hammôr," a popular 15th-century Torah commentary by Abraham Saba</note>...

# The 14th Chapter of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked #

**An iron wall between you and the city** <note>original Hebrew: קיר ברזל בינך ובין העיר</note>: that is, **From the day the Temple was destroyed, an iron wall has been placed between Israel and their Father who is in Heaven** (by which they are separated from one another), as it is said in Ezekiel 4:1-3: **And you, son of man, take an iron plate and set it as an iron wall between you and the city.**

<margin>Why the Jews turn their faces toward Jerusalem when they pray.</margin>
Since we are dealing here with the prayer of the Jews, I must also indicate the reason why they are accustomed to turning their faces toward Jerusalem when they perform their prayers. It is written regarding this in the book *Sha’are Tzedek* <note>Gates of Righteousness, a classic Jewish ethical or mystical text</note>, folio 22, column 1, as follows:

> The prayer of those outside the Land does not ascend directly upward until it goes to the Land of Israel, and from there to Jerusalem, and from there to the Temple, as it is written in the prayer of Solomon, peace be upon him. And when it reaches the Temple, then it ascends on high. Therefore, the Israelites who are in exile <note>original Hebrew: בגלות (*ba-galut*)</note> pray surrounding Jerusalem from the four corners of the earth, with Jerusalem in the middle. Therefore, all those in exile in the West shall pray toward the East; likewise, those on the Eastern side shall pray toward the West. Likewise, those on the Northern side shall turn their faces and pray toward the South. Thus it is found that all Israelites direct their prayers toward Jerusalem and the Temple, because from there the prayers ascend to God, may He be blessed.

That is: **(Israel’s prayer) does not ascend the straight path until it comes into the Land of Israel (or the Promised Land), and from there to Jerusalem, and from there into the Temple, as it stands written in the prayer of Solomon, upon whom be peace (1 Kings 8:30): And when it arrives in the Temple, then it ascends. Therefore, the Israelites who are in exile or misery pray all around Jerusalem, in the four corners of the world, and Jerusalem is in the middle. For this reason, all those who live in misery <note>Eisenmenger translates the Hebrew *Galut* (Exile) as *Elend* (misery/hardship), reflecting the historical German term for being far from home</note> toward the West pray toward the East: and likewise, those who live toward the East pray toward the West: similarly, those who reside toward the North turn their faces toward the South; it is thus found that all Israelites let their prayer go toward Jerusalem and into the Temple, because from there the prayers ascend to the blessed God.**

<margin>Where it comes from that the Jews move from one side to another when they pray or read.</margin>
The Jews are also accustomed, when they read or pray, to move from one side to the other: but as to why this happens, I find two different opinions. The first is found in the second part of the book *Kuzari* <note>A famous work by Judah Halevi defending Judaism</note>, numbers 79 and 80, pages 141 and 142, with these words:

<margin>The first opinion.</margin>
The Kuzari said: I will ask you, do you know why the Jews move while reading Hebrew? The Rabbi <note>original Hebrew: החבר (*He-Chaver*), the Jewish scholar in the dialogue</note> said: They say it is because of the awakening of the natural heat, but I do not think it is for any reason other than the matter we are discussing—because many of them could read as one. It was possible that ten or more would gather over a single book, and for this reason our books were large, and it was necessary for each of the ten to lean in at every moment to see the word, and then return, and return again, constantly bending...

# How the Jews boast and exalt themselves above all nations. #

<note>original Hebrew: שהספר בארץ והיה זה הסבה הראשונה. ואחר כן שב מנהג מפני ההסתכלות והראיה בנורדם תדיר ולהדמות למי שרואים אותם כאשר הוא בטבעי בני אדם. וזולתינו קורא כל אחד בספרו ומקרבו אל עיניו או יקרב הוא אליו כפי רצונו מבלי שיצר עליו חבירו ואיננו צריך שיטה וישוב:</note>

I, however, hold that it happens solely because of the matter we are discussing. For because many of them were able to read at once (from a single book), it could happen that ten or more of them gathered around a single book. For this reason, our books were also large, and each of the ten needed to constantly turn to see the words and then move back again (to make room for others), so that he had to continually lean in and pull back, since the book was on the ground; and this was the first cause. After this, because of the habit of looking in while they were constantly moving, a custom arose from it, so that one might be like those whom one saw, as is the nature of men. Among other (nations), however, each person reads from his own book and holds it near his eyes, or he goes close to it according to his pleasure, so that no one is burdensome (or an obstacle) to him, and he has no need to turn and move back.

<margin>The second opinion.</margin>
The other opinion is read in the *Yalkut Chadash* <note>The *Yalkut Chadash* (New Collection) is a 17th-century compendium of Jewish midrashic and mystical traditions</note>, where on folio 103, column 4, number 24, under the title *Israel*, it is written as follows:

<note>The Hebrew text above is translated as follows: Why do the Israelites move when they learn, while the nations of the world do not move? Because the souls of the Israelites are from the light above, as it is written (Proverbs 20:27): "The soul of man is the lamp of the LORD." And behold, the nature of the lamp is always to flicker and move around the wick, never resting. So too are the Israelites, whose souls emanate from and cling to the lamp of the LORD on high; therefore they move constantly when they occupy themselves with the light of the Law. But the nations, whose souls do not come from the lamp of the LORD, therefore do not move.</note>

**That is:** Why do the *Israelites* move when they learn, and the nations of the world do not move? Because the souls of the *Israelites* are from the upper light, as it is written (*Proverbs 20:27*): **The soul of man is a light of the LORD**; and behold, the nature of light is always to hover around the wick, and move, and never stand still. Thus also do the *Israelites* move, whose souls come from the highest light of the **LORD** and cling to the same forever, whenever they study in the light of the Law <note>The "Law" here refers to the Torah</note>. But the nations, whose souls do not come from the light of the **LORD**, do not move. Regarding this, it is also written in the book *Tzeror HaMor* <note>A 15th-century Torah commentary by Abraham Saba</note>...

**That is:** Regarding the matter of swaying, it demonstrates the excellence of the Israelites, for they originate from the power of fire. And it is written (Proverbs 20:27): **The soul of man is a lamp of God.** The flame of a lamp moves constantly and rises upward; likewise, the Israelites move from the power of fire, as it is written (Isaiah 62:6): **You who remind the Lord, do not stand still** <note>The Hebrew word *dami* is usually translated as "be silent," but the author interprets it here as "stay still" to support the custom of swaying.</note>. It is also written (Psalm 83:2): **O God, do not stay still** (or, do not be silent). But the nations of the world are extinguished and silent, like a bone in a fire that lies still and does not move. This practice has remained with the Israelites since the time the Law was given, as it is written (Exodus 20:18): **And the people saw it, and they moved.** <note>The verse refers to the people trembling at Mount Sinai; here it is used to justify the swaying motion during study.</note> Regarding all of the above, one may also read in the book *Nishmat Chayim* <note>A work on the soul by the famous rabbi Menasseh ben Israel, published in 1651.</note>, folio 96, column 2, and folio 97, column 1, in the first chapter of the third part.

Returning to the privilege they believe they hold over other nations, they maintain that God proceeds much more leniently in His judgment toward them than toward other nations. That is: When the holy and blessed God judges the nations, it is a joy to Him, as it is said (Deuteronomy 32:36 and Psalm 135:14): **For He will judge His people.** <note>The interpretation here plays on the word "judge," suggesting that when God judges other nations, it results in his people being vindicated.</note> But when God judges the Israelites, it brings Him regret, as it were, as is said (in the aforementioned passage of Deuteronomy 32:36): **And He will have compassion on His servants.** For the word *nechama* <note>Hebrew for comfort or compassion.</note> means nothing other than a feeling of regret. <margin>And that He judges them by day, but others by night.</margin>

...them when they study the Law <term>Law: referring to the Torah or the body of Jewish religious instruction</term>. <note>original Hebrew: בשעה שהקב"ה דן את ישראל דן אותן מעומד מקצר בדין ומופשר בדין אבל כשהוא דן את העכו"ם דן מיושב מדקדק בדין ומאריך בדין:</note>

That is: At the time when the Holy One, blessed be He, judges the Israelites, He judges them standing, and makes the judgment short and mild. But when He judges the idolaters <note>The original uses the acronym "Akum," standing for "worshippers of stars and planets," a term often used in these texts to refer to non-Jews or heathens.</note>, He judges them sitting, examines them closely, and takes a long time with it.

<margin>They are also of the opinion that God provides for them alone directly; the others, however, in an indirect manner.</margin>
They also hold that God provides for the Jews more directly, but provides for the other nations in an indirect manner, about which it is taught in the book *Mashmia Jeshua* <note>"The Announcer of Salvation," a work by Isaac Abarbanel.</note> folio 25, column 2: <note>original Hebrew: האל משגיח בכל האומות על ידי אמצעיים ומשגיח בישראל בעצמו מבלי אמצעי ולכן נקרא בעיני האומות אלהי האלהים כי הוא אלוה על האלהים המנהיגים אותם:</note> that is, GOD provides for all nations through intermediaries <note>Referring to angels or celestial powers assigned to govern different peoples.</note>, but the Israelites He provides for without an intermediary; therefore, in the eyes of the nations, He is called a "God of gods," because He is a God over the gods who rule them.

<margin>Also, that God regards all nations except them as nothing at all.</margin>
Indeed, in the book *Shir HaShirim Rabbah* <note>An ancient commentary on the Song of Solomon.</note> it is taught on folio 273, column 3, that God pays attention to and cares for the Jews alone, but regards the other nations as nothing at all, where the words read thus: <note>original Hebrew: כשם שאין בעל הבית משגיח לא על הקש ולא על התבן ולא על המופלחות של תבן ולא על המוץ למה שאין נחשבים לכלום כך אין הקב"ה משגיח על עכ"ם למה שאינן כלום שנ' כל הגוים כאין נגדו וגו' ועל מי הוא משגיח על ישראל שנ' כי תשא את ראש בני ישראל וגו' שאו את ראש כל עדת בני ישראל:</note> that is: Just as a householder does not look at the baskets into which one puts dung and straw, nor at the stubble or chaff, because they are worth nothing: so too the Holy and Blessed God regards the idolaters as nothing, because they are nothing, as it is said (Isaiah 40:17): **All nations are as nothing before Him**, etc. Whom does He regard then? The Israelites, as it is said (Exodus 30:12): **When you take the census of the children of Israel**, etc. (and in Numbers 1:2 it stands): **Take a census of the whole congregation of the children of Israel.** And in the book *Kad HaKemach* <note>"The Flour Jar," a work on Jewish ethics and philosophy by Bahya ben Asher.</note> it is taught on folio 46, column 1, regarding the words of Isaiah 40:15, "Behold, the nations are regarded as a drop from a bucket, and as a speck of dust that remains in the balance," as follows: <note>original Hebrew: כל האומות אין נחשבין כלום לפני ישראל כשם שאין הטיפה נחשבת כלום כשנפלה מן הדלי ובעל הדלי לא יחשוב אותה כלל כי מי הדלי הם עיקר וגו' :</note> that is: All nations are regarded as nothing compared to the Israelites, just as a drop is regarded as nothing when it falls from the bucket, which the one to whom the bucket belongs does not regard at all, because the water in the bucket is the main thing, etc. The like is also to be found in the book *Mashmia Jeshua* folio 21, column 1. <margin>Whether the soul is called *adám*, that is, Man.</margin>
...comes from *adamá*, which is the word for Earth; and man is called *adám* in the Hebrew language because he was created from the earth. This is taught by Rabbi Salomon ben Melech in his book *Michlál jóphi* <note>A 16th-century Hebrew grammar and commentary titled "The Perfection of Beauty."</note> on folio 3, column 2, regarding the words of Genesis 5:2, **And he called their name Adam, that is, Man.** There he writes: <note>original Hebrew: נקרא כן על שם האדמה אשר לוקח משם</note> that is, "He (namely Adam, the man) was so named because of the *adamá*, that is, the earth, from which he was taken." It is also written in *Bereshíth rábba* <note>An ancient collection of Jewish legends and interpretations regarding the Book of Genesis.</note> on folio 17, column 1, in the 17th *Parashah* <note>A section or chapter of the Torah.</note>, that Adam gave names to all things. When God asked him what his own name should be, he replied: <note>original Hebrew: אני נאה להקרא אדם שנבראתי מן האדמה</note> that is, "It is very fitting that I be called Adam, because I was created from the *adamá*, that is, the earth." Therefore, the soul alone cannot be called *adám*, or Man; rather, this name properly belongs to the body because of the matter from which it was created. Nevertheless, the whole human being—consisting of both body and soul—is called by this name, particularly on account of the earthly body.

# 606 Chapter 15 of the First Part of Revealed Judaism.

(Deuteronomy 12:30) it is said: "Take heed to yourself that you be not snared by following them." All of this has a specific meaning, and (the Scripture) warns that one should not consider oneself equal to them, and that an Israelite should be distinguished from them; he should be recognized by his clothing and his other works, just as he is separated from them in his knowledge and his opinions. Therefore He (namely God, in Leviticus 20:26) says: "And I have severed you from the people." He shall not put on any garment which is made according to their own fashion, nor let the locks of hair on his head grow long like their locks, nor shave the sides of his head while leaving the hair in the middle, as they do—which is called <term>belurith</term> <note>original: "בלורית." Nor shall he cut the hair across his face from one ear to the other while leaving the hair long in the back, as those people do; nor build places according to the architecture of idolatrous churches so that many may enter, as they do. On the occasion of the distinction which they make between themselves and us—whereby they also imagine that they are a holy and pure people, but we are an ungodly and impure people; they are the true humans, but we are only to be considered as cattle, as has been proven in the preceding pages—I must also point out here that when they mention Christians (or another nation) and Jews at the same time, they are accustomed to add the word <term>lehavdil</term> <note>original Hebrew: "להבדיל." Meaning "to separate" or "to make a distinction."</note>, which signifies: *A distinction is to be made.* By this they want to give it to be understood that although the Christians (or another nation) and the Jews are placed together and mentioned at the same time, yet a

# On the Jews' Hatred Toward All Nations, and Their Hypocrisy.

<note>original Hebrew: "נראה בירושלמי וכן אנו נוהגים בזה התר עכשו . אבל הרמ"בן ז"ל כתב בעל נפש צריך לפרוש"</note> It appears in the Jerusalem Talmud, and thus we currently follow this permission. But Nachmanides, of blessed memory, wrote that a pious soul must abstain. That is: Therefore our Sages, of blessed memory, have taught based on a weak method of proof, that it is forbidden to rent one’s house to a <term>Goi</term> <note>A Hebrew term for a non-Jew, used here polemically to refer to Christians.</note> or Christian as a dwelling-place, because the <term>Goi</term> brings an idol into it; and an Israelite who rents it out violates (this commandment): for look, through a lease the lessee does not acquire the ownership of the ground and soil, and the ground is not the <term>Goi’s</term>, but the Israelite’s; therefore he violates (such a commandment) thereby. However, we find some of our doctors, of blessed memory, who have written that this is only to be observed in the Land of Israel, where the main concern of <term>Abgötterey</term> <note>Idolatry; the author reflects the Jewish legal view that Christianity was a form of "foreign worship" due to the use of icons or the doctrine of the Trinity.</note> is to be observed (and where one must especially guard against it); and so it appears in the Jerusalem Talmud: Thus we are accustomed to allow it in the present time. But Rabbi Moses bar Nachman <note>Also known as Nachmanides or Ramban, a leading medieval Sephardic scholar.</note>, of blessed memory, has written that a courageous or pious person should abstain from renting (a house to a <term>Goi</term>), even outside the Land of Israel. Concerning this, one may also look in the book <term>Kol Bo</term> <note>A 14th-century Hebrew work on Jewish ritual and civil law.</note>, folio 108, column 2, number 97, under the title <term>Avoda Zara</term> <note>Literally "Foreign Worship," the Talmudic tractate dealing with idolatry.</note>; and in the <term>Sefer Mitzvot Gadol</term> <note>The "Great Book of Commandments" by Moses ben Jacob of Coucy.</note>, folio 10, column 4, as well as in the Talmudic tractate <term>Avoda Zara</term> folio 15, column 1, and folio 20, column 2, as well as folio 21, column 1.

<margin>But the high authorities have much more reason to forbid any Jew from renting a house.</margin>
Since, in this manner, it is forbidden to the administration of the Jews by their rabbis to rent a house to a Christian, the Christian authorities would have much more reason to forbid it to the Christians, so that they should not rent any house to a Jew, because the same [Jew] blasphemes Christ the **Lord** therein, and curses and scorns the Christians, and also despises everything that is Christian.

<margin>The Jews are also forbidden from letting any idolatrous person dwell in their land.</margin>

# Chapter XV of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked.

<margin>Sarah is said to have nursed the children of many pagan kings.</margin>
"...And He exalted the low tree; this is our father Abraham. And He withered the green tree; this signifies the women of the nations of the world. And He made the dry tree flourish; this signifies our mother Sarah." <note>This is a midrashic interpretation of Ezekiel 17:24, common in rabbinic literature to explain the miracle of Isaac’s birth.</note> And they all brought their children to Sarah, and she nursed them, as it is said (Genesis 21:7): **Sarah has suckled children.**

<margin>Brief refutation of this fable.</margin>
However, this is a foolish proof for the claim that Sarah nursed many children, simply because it is written: "And Sarah has suckled children," and not "a child." For it is common among the Hebrews that the *pluralis numerus* <note>Latin: "plural number"</note> is used for the *singularem*, that is, the plural is used instead of the singular. Thus, we read in Genesis 46:7 that Jacob took his "daughters" and "granddaughters" with him into Egypt, even though he had only one daughter, namely Dinah (as seen in verse 15 of the same chapter), and only one granddaughter, namely Serah (as seen in verse 17). A similar example is found in verse 23 of the same chapter, where we read: **The children (or sons) of Dan: Hushim,** <note>Original Hebrew: *Bnei Dan Hushim*</note> though Dan had only one son, namely Hushim. The same can be seen in Numbers 26:8. Thus, it is also said here that Sarah suckled "children," even though she had and nursed only one son.

<margin>A Jewish midwife is not readily permitted to serve a Christian woman, and why.</margin>
A Jewish midwife is also not permitted to serve a Christian woman; therefore, it is written in the book *Agguda* <note>Original: *Aggúda*, referring to the *Sefer Ha-Agudah*, a 14th-century legal compendium by Alexander Susslin Ha-Kohen.</note> folio 60, column 4, number 17: **A daughter of Israel shall not deliver the child of a foreign woman, because she is delivering a child into idolatry.** <note>Original Hebrew: *Bat Yisrael lo tayaléd le-nochrit mipnei she-meyaledet ben le-avodat elilim.* The author translates the Hebrew *nochrit* (foreign woman) as "Christian."</note> And in the Talmudic tractate *Avoda sara* <note>Original: *Avóda sara*, the tractate "Avodah Zarah" which deals with "Foreign Worship" or "Idolatry."</note> we read on folio 26, column 1:
<margin>Likewise, no Christian woman should be a midwife to a Jewish woman.</margin>
**A foreign woman (understand a Christian woman, or another woman who is outside of Judaism) shall not serve as a midwife to a daughter of Israel, because they are suspected of bloodshed (and it is feared that they might kill the child).** <note>Original Hebrew: *Nochrit lo tayaléd et bat Yisrael mipnei she-chashudan al shefikhut damim.*</note>

<margin>Yet some Rabbis allow it to avoid all enmity.</margin>
However, some Rabbis do permit this to be done so that Christians do not become hostile toward the Jews for that reason; therefore, it is written in the *Sepher mizvoth gadol* <note>Original: *Sepher mizvóth gadól* (The Great Book of Commandments, abbreviated as the SMaG), a 13th-century code by Isaac of Corbeil.</note> folio 10, column 2, and in the book *Col bo* <note>Original: *Col bo*, a collection of Jewish rituals and laws from the 14th century.</note> folio 108, column 2, number 97: **A daughter of Israel shall not let herself be used as a midwife for a foreign woman, because she causes a child to be born into idolatry. Regarding the Law <note>The Torah</note>, the situation is as our Rabbis of blessed memory have said: **A son of Noah (that is, one who is not a Jew, for all people outside of Judaism are called "Children of Noah" by the Jews) who studies the Law is guilty of death, etc.** <term>Children of Noah: also known as Noahides; in Jewish law, non-Jews are obligated to follow seven basic moral laws, but traditional Rabbinic views often restricted them from deeper study of the Mosaic Law.</term> Regarding almsgiving, it is as stated in Proverbs 14:34: **"Almsgiving exalts a nation"**; and our Rabbis of blessed memory have interpreted this to mean it refers to the Israelites. But how can it be said here that a Jew's prayer is heard, when—as shown above on pages 581 and 582—by their own admission they are not heard by God because they do not know the *Shem HaMephorash*? <term>Shem HaMephorash: The hidden, explicit, or Ineffable Name of God, which was said to hold great power but was lost to common knowledge after the destruction of the Temple.</term>

<margin>They also do not consider Christians worthy enough to accept alms from them.</margin>

If a king or a gentile prince sends money to an Israelite for charity, one does not return it for the sake of the 'peace of the kingdom,' but rather takes it from him and gives it to the poor of the idolaters secretly so that the king does not find out."</note>
That is: **"It is forbidden for an Israelite to take alms from an idolatrous person publicly; however, if he cannot survive on the alms of the Israelites and cannot obtain it from the idolaters secretly, it is permitted to him. # On the Jews' Hatred toward all Nations and their Hypocrisy. 619

<margin>
All the good that the Jews do toward Christians is done out of hypocrisy.
</margin>
...[recognized?] and that everything they do happens out of pure hypocrisy, so that they may obtain the favor of Christians or other people.

<margin>
What the Jews may object in response when they are accused of hypocrisy.
</margin>
In response to this, the Jews might argue that I do them an injustice by accusing them of hypocrisy, since hypocrisy is so strictly forbidden among them. For in the book *Reshith Chokhma* <term>Reshith Chokhma: "The Beginning of Wisdom," a 16th-century kabbalistic work on morality</term> it is written on folio 412, column 1, in the 16th chapter, under the title *Or Olam* [Eternal Light], from the Talmudic tractate *Sota* <term>Sota: A volume of the Talmud dealing with rituals, which also contains many moral teachings</term>, folio 41, column 2: <note>original Hebrew: "כל אדם שיש בו חנופה נופל בגיהנם"</note> **Every person in whom there is hypocrisy falls into Hell.** Furthermore, it is written there: <note>original Hebrew: "לעולם יפרוש אדם מן החנופה לפי שהיא שקולה כנגד עבודה זרה וגלוי עריות ושפיכות דמים"</note> **A person should always distance himself from hypocrisy, because it is considered equal to idolatry, unchastity, and the shedding of blood.** A similar passage is found in the book *Sefer Ha-Yirah* <note>OCR reads "Lefär je," likely a corruption of this title</note> folio 78, column 2. And in the book *Brandspiegel* <term>Brandspiegel: "The Burning Mirror," a famous Yiddish book of ethical instruction often aimed at women</term>, in the 52nd chapter, folio 189, column 2, we read: <note>original Yiddish/Hebrew: "ועון חזן לזון חציפות טרייבט וגא"</note> **It is a great sin when one practices hypocrisy toward people.** Likewise, in the aforementioned place in the tractate *Sota*, folio 41, column 2, it is taught: <note>original Hebrew: "כל אדם שיש בו חנופה אפילו עוברין שבמעי אמן מקללין אותו"</note> **A hypocritical person is cursed even by the children who are still in their mothers' wombs.** More of the same is reported there, as well as on folio 42, column 1. And in the *Yalkut Shimoni* <term>Yalkut Shimoni: A major medieval collection of interpretations on the Hebrew Bible</term> regarding the book of Job, on folio 149, column 3, number 906, it is taught: <note>original Hebrew: "ארבע כתות אין מקבלין פני שכינה כת החנפים וכת השקרנים וכת הלצים וכת מספרי לשון הרע"</note> **Four groups do not come before the face of the Divine Presence: the group of hypocrites, the group of liars, the group of scoffers, and the group of those who speak evil gossip.** In addition to the above, we read in the *Sefer Mitzvot Gadol* <term>Sefer Mitzvot Gadol: "The Great Book of Commandments," a 13th-century legal code</term>, folio 58, column 3, under the title *Hilkhot Genefa u-Gezela* [Laws of Deception and Robbery]: **We learn in the seventh chapter of the Talmudic tractate *Chullin* (folio 49, column 1) that Rabbi Samuel said it is forbidden to "steal the mind" of people, even the mind of the *Goyim* <note>original: "Gójim" — a Hebrew term for non-Jews or nations</note> or heathens.** This "stealing of the mind" means to make them believe this or that which is not actually true, as hypocrites are accustomed to do.

<margin>
Answer to these objections and their refutation.
</margin>
To this, however, I answer that this prohibition of hypocrisy is only to be understood as meaning that no Jew should show himself hypocritical toward another Jew. Consequently, it is not taught at all that one must also behave sincerely toward Christians. I prove this by the fact that hypocrisy toward Christians and other nations is permitted to them; for in the book *Ir Gibborim* <term>Ir Gibborim: "City of Heroes," a commentary on the Torah by Shlomo Ephraim of Luntschitz</term>, folio 36, column 1, number 55, it is written as follows: <note>original Hebrew: "מותר להחניף לרשע מפני היראה כדאיתא בפרקי דרבי אלעזר אמר יעקב לעשו כה אמר עבדך יעקב"</note> **It is permitted to be hypocritical toward the wicked <note>The author interprets "the wicked" here as referring to non-Jews</note> out of fear, as it is found in the *Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer*: Jacob said to Esau, "Thus says your servant Jacob."**

> <note>original: "אמר הק"בה ליעקב עשית קודש חול אמר לו מחניף אני לרשע שלא יהרגני מכאן אמרו מחניפים לרשעים בעולם הזה מפני דרכי שלום. ואמר ר' שמעון מותר להחניף לרשעים בעולם הזה שנ' לא יאמר עוד לנבל נדיב ולכילי לא יאמר שוע מכלל דבעולם הזה שרי:"</note>

*That is:* It is permitted to act hypocritically toward a godless person because of the fear one has of him, as is written in the "Chapters of Rabbi Eliezer" <term>Pirke De-Rabbi Eliezer: An 8th-century collection of Jewish ethical and aggadic (narrative) teachings</term> in the 37th *chapter*. When Jacob said to Esau (Genesis 32:4): "Thus spoke your servant Jacob," the Holy Blessed God said to Jacob: "You have made a holy thing out of an unholy thing" (*that is:* you have defiled yourself, who are holy, by calling yourself Esau’s servant). Jacob answered Him: "I only flatter the godless man so that he does not kill me." Therefore it is said: One may be hypocritical toward the godless in this world for the sake of peace. Rabbi Simeon also said: It is permitted in this world to practice hypocrisy against the godless, as it is said (Isaiah 32:5): "A fool shall no more be called a prince, nor a miser be called mild (or generous)." This is also discussed by Rabbi Bechai <term>Bahya ben Asher: A 13th-century Spanish rabbi and biblical commentator</term> in his book *Cad hakkémach* <term>Kad Ha-Kemach: "The Jar of Flour," a work on Jewish ethics and philosophy</term>, folio 30, column 1, as follows:

> <note>original: "מצינו חנופה שהיא מותרת בענין אחד והוא שיתנהג אדם עם הרשע בדרך מוסר ויכבדנו ויעמוד מפניו ויאמר לו שהוא אוהב אותו וזה מצינו שהוא מותר כשהוא צריך אליו ומפני היראה שכן מצינו ביעקב שאמר לעשו הרשע כי על כן ראיתי פניך וגו' ואמר רבי יוחנן אמר מותר להחניף את הרשעים בעולם הזה שנ' כי על כן ראיתי פניך וגו' :"</note>

We find this is permitted when he has need of him and because of fear. And Rabbi Jochanan said: "It is permitted to flatter the wicked in this world, as it is said (Genesis 33:10): 'For I have seen your face,' etc."

*That is:* We find that hypocrisy is permitted in one way, such that a person presents himself politely to a godless man, honors him, stands up before him, and says to him that he loves him. This we find to be permitted when one has need of him or is afraid (of him). For we find this in Jacob, who said to the godless Esau (as may be read in Genesis 33:10): "For I saw your face as the face of God." Rabbi Jochanan said: It is permitted to be hypocritical to the godless in this world, as it is said (Genesis 33:10): "For I saw your face," etc. Similar things are also found in the same author's commentary on the five books of Moses, folio 42, column 2, in the *Parashah Vayishlach* <term>Parashah: The weekly portion of the Torah read in the synagogue; "Vayishlach" covers Genesis 32:4–36:43</term>, and in the *Jalkut Shimon* <term>Yalkut Shimoni: A massive 13th-century compilation of Jewish midrash (scriptural interpretation)</term> on Isaiah, folio 47, column 3, number 302, and in the book *Zeror Hammor* <term>Zeror Ha-Mor: "A Bundle of Myrrh," a 15th-century Torah commentary</term>, folio 21, column 2, in the *Parashah Vayera*, and in the book *Orchot Tzaddikim* <term>Orchot Tzaddikim: "The Ways of the Righteous," an anonymous 15th-century work on Jewish ethics</term> folio 15, column 2, in the 24th *chapter*, as well as in the Talmudic tractate *Sota*, folio 41, column 2.

### On the Hatred of the Jews toward all Peoples/ and their Hypocrisy. 621

<note>original: "רשעים מחמת דרך שלום לא ידבר טוב הרשע ולא יתנהג בכבודו על דרך שיתחשבו בני אדם שהוא נכבד בעיניו ואין לחלוק לו כבוד אלא כדרך בני אדם המכבדים העשירים בעבור כי צלחה דרכם ולא מפני שהן ערכם ואף בזה יש חטא ואשמה כי לא הותר לכבד הרשעים אלא מחמת מורא שירא שיזיק לו הרשע ויגרום לו הפסד בזמן שיד הרשעים תקיפה על כן הותר לו לכבדו כדרך שמכבדין בני אדם בעלי זרוע אך לא יחשבנו לא ידבר עליו טוב בפני בני אדם :"</note>

The wicked: For the sake of the **way of peace** <term>Derech Shalom: A Jewish legal principle prioritizing social harmony and the avoidance of conflict with non-Jewish neighbors</term>, one should not speak well of the wicked man, nor should one behave with such honor toward him that people might think he is truly respected in one’s own eyes. One should not grant him honor except in the manner that people honor the wealthy simply because their path has prospered, and not because of their intrinsic worth. Even in this, there is sin and guilt, for it is only permitted to honor the wicked out of fear—fearing that the wicked man might cause harm or loss at a time when the power of the wicked is strong. Therefore, it is permitted to honor him in the way that people usually honor those who possess power; but one should not truly esteem him, nor speak well of him in the presence of others.

That is: He who honors the **godless** <term>Gottlosen: Here referring to the "wicked" mentioned in the Hebrew text, which the author identifies as non-Jews/Christians</term> for the sake of peace, shall speak nothing good of the godless one, and shall conduct himself in the honor he shows him in such a way that people do not think that the person is held in high esteem by him. He shall also show him no honor other than in the manner that one honors the rich because they are fortunate, but not because they are otherwise worthy. Although even in this a sin is committed, for it is not permitted to honor the godless except out of fear—fearing that the godless person will do him harm and cause some loss when the godless have the upper hand. For this reason, it is permitted to honor them, just as people are accustomed to honoring those who are powerful. However, he shall not speak anything good of such a godless person in the presence of others.

Since Christians are now considered by the Jews to be idolatrous and godless people (as will be clearly proven below in the 16th chapter of this first part), they are also permitted to use **hypocrisy** against them, and to honor them only with forced gestures and words. They know how to practice this so masterfully against those whom they need or whom they must fear, that many a Christian considers such a Jew—who gives him the smoothest words and knows how to show himself very humble and polite—to be an honest and fine man. However, he is certainly shamefully deceived in his opinion; for although the Jew's false tongue gives smooth words, and the outward gestures indicate nothing but good, yet in the heart nothing but poison and irreconcilable hatred is hidden. Of them it can be said from *Jeremiah 12:6*:

> Trust them not, even though they speak kindly with you.

And from *Psalm 55:22*:

> Their mouth is smoother than butter, yet they have war in their mind; their words are softer than oil, yet they are drawn swords.

These last words can be very appropriately applied to them, for they wish to make war against all Christians at the arrival of their supposed **Messiah** and want to shed their blood, as can be seen in detail below in the 14th chapter of the second part. How can one then expect anything from such **arch-enemies**, who have a daily, longing desire to defile their godless hands with the innocent blood of Christians, an—

->### The Fifteenth Chapter of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked.<-

...anything good to expect, or hope for a sincere and upright heart, even if they act quite friendly and show the sheep's clothing outwardly, while they are inwardly **ravening wolves** <note>A reference to Matthew 7:15; Eisenmenger frequently uses New Testament imagery to characterize the Jewish subjects of his study.</note>, and are called a **hypocritical nation** in Isaiah 10, v. 6? Furthermore, their Talmud permits them to deceive someone with flattering words, as it is written in the Tractate *Bava Batra*, folio 123, column 1: <note>original: "ומי שרי להו לצדיקי לסגויי ברמאותא"</note> that is, **"Is it then permitted for the righteous to deal deceitfully (with the godless)?"** "Yes, certainly" (for it stands written in 2 Samuel 22, v. 27:) <note>original: "עם נבר תתבר ועם עקש תתפל"</note> **"With the pure you show yourself pure, and with the crooked you show yourself crooked."**

<margin>What is to be thought of the Jewish greeting.</margin>
Since it is now evident from the preceding that Jews are permitted to act hypocritically toward Christians, we must also see what is to be thought of the **greeting** which they are accustomed to give them. In the Talmudic Tractate *Berachot*, folio 17, column 1, it is written: <note>original: "מרגלא בפומיה : דאביי לעולם יהא אדם ערום ביראה מענה רך משיב חמה ומרבה שלום עם אחיו ועם קרוביו ועם כל אדם ואפילו עם נכרי בשוק כדי שיהא אהוב למעלה ונחמד למטה ויהא מקובל על הבריות"</note> that is, **"It was a pearl in the mouth of Abaye"** (when he spoke:) **"A man should always be shrewd in the fear (of God)** (because Proverbs 15, v. 1 is written:) **'A soft answer turns away wrath,' and he should increase peace with his brothers and relatives, and with all men, even with a stranger"** (that is, one who is not a Jew) **"in the marketplace, so that he may be beloved above (in Heaven) and esteemed below (on Earth), and also be acceptable to all creatures."** It is said of Rabbi Jochanan, the son of Zakkai, that no man—not even a stranger—ever greeted him first in the street. Likewise, in the fourth chapter of the *Pirkei Avot* <term>Pirkei Avot: "Ethics of the Fathers," a compilation of ethical teachings and maxims from the Mishnaic period</term>, one reads: <note>original: "ר' מתיא בן חרש אומר הוי מקדים בשלום כל אדם"</note> that is, **"Rabbi Mathja, the son of Charash, says: Be the first to greet every man."**

From this, one might surmise that the Jews are commanded to greet Christians and other peoples with a sincere heart; however, the matter is of a completely different nature. For their greeting does not come from a good heart, but happens solely for the end that they may maintain the favor of the Christians, and live peacefully with them, so that nothing adverse might befall them from the same. *The Districts of the Land of Israel* <note>original: *gelilôth érez Jisraël*, a 16th-century geographical and hagiographical work</note> is found / where on the sixth page / column 1. it is written / that the grave of **Ezra** <note>Ezra the Scribe, the biblical leader who led the second wave of Judean exiles back from Babylon</note> was broken in ancient times / and when a shepherd laid himself upon it to sleep / it occurred to him in a dream / that **Ezra** said to him: I, **Ezra** the scribe, lie buried here / go to the Jews / so that they may take me away from this place / and lay me in another place; and if the prince of the city will not suffer it / then tell him / that the whole city will perish <note>original: *auspegern*; Eisenmenger highlights this term as a derogatory way to describe dying, similar to "to die like a beast"</note>. Then the shepherd went to the Jews / and told them / and they went with him to the prince / then the shepherd told the prince / how it had happened to him / but he would not let him be led out of his land. Soon thereafter a plague came into the place / and nearly half of the idolatrous people were swept away <note>original: *weg gepegert*</note>. Otherwise, the Jews use such a word for cattle when they die; therefore it stands in the *Maase Buch* <note>A collection of Yiddish folk tales and ethical stories</note> / in the 155th Chapter: I had a sheep that had a young lamb / and the sheep perished <note>original: *gepgrt*</note> immediately.

But some say (from **Isaiah** 26. verse 14.) "They are dead, and shall not live; they are deceased, and shall not rise again" &c. # Chapter XVI.

## In which it is shown how the Jews are accustomed to calling the Christians, and what mostly mocking names they give them.

Since the great hatred which the Jews bear toward Christians was sufficiently proven in the previous chapter, one can easily judge from this that they also give them very contemptuous and mocking names. However, so that the favorable reader may know all the names by which they are accustomed to calling us, I will show both the good and the bad. Thus, if one of these names appears either in the conversation of the Jews or in their books, one may know for certain whether we are meant by it or not. Without further digression, to proceed to the matter itself, they call us:

<margin>The Jews call us 1. *Nazarenes*.</margin>
Firstly, נוצרים *Nozerim*, that is, *Nazarenes*. Rabbi **Abraham Perizol** also writes about this in his book *The Shield of Abraham* <note>original: *Maggen Abraham*</note>, in the 59th chapter: <note>original: "It is clear that this nation is called Nazarenes after the name of Jesus the Nazarene."</note> "It is clear that this nation is called *Nazarenes* after the name of Jesus the *Nazarene*." We can well tolerate being called thus, for the Christians in the time of the holy Apostles were already called by this name, as can be seen in Acts 24:5.

And because the Romans were conquerors of kingdoms and destroyers of lands, he called them *Nozerim*, meaning destroyers. Furthermore, the prophet foresaw through the Holy Spirit that the Romans would in the future believe in Jesus the Nazarene and would because of this be called Nazarenes."</note> "Why did he (namely the prophet) call the Romans *Nozerim*?
