This is also read in folio 243, column 3, of the same work.

# How Christians are named by the Jews.

written one under another, the four outermost letters, when read crosswise, also form "Sammael," while the four inner letters form "Edom" <note>Edom is the biblical kingdom associated with Esau; in medieval Jewish literature, it became a standard code name for Rome and, by extension, the Christian Church.</note>. By this, it is signified that Esau was marked for Sammael. Therefore, in the little book **Schechéchat léket** <note>A collection of various midrashic and Kabbalistic sayings.</note> at number 8, under the title **Jacob**, regarding the words of **Jacob in Genesis 33:10, "For I have seen your face as though I had seen the face of God," it is read:** <note>original: "חמי באנפין דעשו כדיוקנא דאתחזי ליה סמאל ממש"</note> that is: **"He saw in the face of Esau the very same form as if Sammael had actually appeared to him." This Sammael, as seen in the book Maarécheth haëlahúth <note>The "Order of Divinity," a 14th-century Kabbalistic manual.</note> folio 213, column 2, is called** <note>original: "אל אחר"</note> **El ácher, that is, the other god; and in the book Zerôr hammór <note>"A Bundle of Myrrh," a Torah commentary by Abraham Saba.</note> folio 141, column 1, he is called** <note>original: "אל נכר"</note> **El néchar, that is, the foreign god.**

<margin>Many shameful names are given to Esau by the Jews, and he is hated by them.</margin>
Since Esau, as previously mentioned, has drawn into himself all the impurity which the supreme devil Sammael is said to have cast into Eve, and also carried the image of the same at his side, the Jews give him all kinds of shameful names which belong to the devil, as if he were the devil himself; and they call him:

<margin>I. Sammael.</margin>
**First,** סמאל Sammaël, as may be seen in the book **Megallé amykkóth** <note>"Revealer of Depths," a work by Nathan Nata Spira.</note> folio 165, in the 191st **Ofan** <note>A section or "wheel" of mystical interpretation.</note>, where it is read: <note>original: "יוֹסף הוּא שִׂטְנוֹ שֶׁל עֵשׂוֹ שֶׁהוּא סמאל"</note> that is: **"Joseph is an adversary of Esau, who is Sammael."** And in the book **Emek hammélech** <note>"The King's Valley," a Kabbalistic work by Naphtali Herz ben Jacob Elhanan.</note> it is written on folio 18, column 4, in the 9th **chapter**, under the title **Scháar tikkúne hatteſchúva** <note>"Gate of the Reparations of Repentance."</note> regarding **Proverbs 30:21–22**: <note>original: "תחת שלש אלה רגזה ארץ העליונה תחת עבד כי ימלוך הוא סמאל שנ' ואת אחיך תעבוד וגו'"</note> That is: **"The upper land is moved by these three things: by a servant when he reigns; this is Sammael, as is said (of Esau in Genesis 27:40): 'You shall serve your brother,' etc."**

<margin>II. Satan.</margin>
**Secondly,** he is called שטן Satan, as is found in the book **Zerôr hammór** folio 11 and 29, column 4, in the <term>Parashah Toledot</term> <note>The weekly Torah portion covering the generations of Isaac.</note>, where concerning the words of **Genesis 27:1, "And he called Esau his elder son,"** it is written: <note>original: "הוּא שטן הוּא נחש הוּא הולך לשׁוּט בארץ"</note> that is: **"This (elder son) is Satan; he is the serpent that wanders upon the earth."** And on folio 109, column 3, in the <term>Parashah Naso</term>, it is read: <note>original: "אמר בעשו שׁהוּא שטן הלעִיטֵנִי מן האדום הזה כי אין תאותו אלא הלעטה ואכילה ושתית היין"</note> that is: **"Of Esau, who is Satan, the Scripture mentions (Genesis 25:30) that he said: 'Let me swallow of the red, red'; for his desire was only swallowing, eating, and drinking wine."**

<margin>III. The Old Serpent.</margin>
**Thirdly,** he is called נחש הקדמוני **Náchasch hakkadmóni**, that is, **the old serpent**. Thus it is written in the aforementioned book **Zerôr hammór** folio 27, column 2, in the <term>Parashah Toledot</term>: <note>original: "יצחק יצא ממנו עשו הוא סמאל הוא נחש הקדמוני"</note> that is: **"From Isaac came forth Esau, who is Sammael, who is the Old Serpent..."**

# Chapter XVI of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked.
<meta>catchword: Seven-</meta>

From Isaac came Esau, who is Sammael and <term>Nachash hakkadmoni</term> <note>original: "נחש הקדמוני"</note>, that is, the ancient serpent. He is also simply called <note>original: "נחש"</note> *Nachash*, that is, a serpent; therefore, in the **Jalkut chádasch** <note>A 17th-century collection of Kabbalistic midrashim.</note>, folio 109, column 3, number 76, under the title *Keschafim* (Sorceries), we read as follows:

<note>original Hebrew: "עשו הרשע נקרא אדם רע וגם נקרא נחש וז"ש הצילני נ"א נוטריקון נחש אדם"</note> That is: The wicked Esau is called the evil man; he is also called a serpent; and this is what (Jacob in Genesis 32:11) meant when he said: "Deliver me <note>original: "נא"</note> *na*," that is, "now." (And he forms the little word *na* through <term>Notarikon</term> <note>A system of Hebrew shorthand where each letter of a word stands for another word.</note>, where each letter signifies a separate word), namely: <note>original: "נחש"</note> *Nachash*, that is, a serpent, and <note>original: "אדם"</note> *Adam*, that is, a man. By this, it is given to be understood that the man Esau is a serpent. Exactly the same is also found in the great **Jalkut Rubéni** <note>A major collection of Kabbalistic commentaries on the Torah by Reuben Hoeshke.</note>, folio 59, column 4, in the section *Vajischlach*.

<margin>IV. A Devil-man.</margin>
Fourthly, in **Bereschith Rabba** <note>A classic Jewish commentary on Genesis, likely referencing a specific sub-commentary here.</note> folio 59, on the first page, in the commentary *Mattenoth Kehunna*, he is called <note>original: "גבר שדין"</note> *Gefer shedin*, that is, a Devil-man. This is also read in the **Jalkut Shimoni** <note>A medieval midrashic anthology covering the whole Hebrew Bible.</note> regarding the books of Moses, folio 33, column 3, number 114, at the end, where he is also called in the margin <note>original: "בעל שדים"</note> *Baal Shedim*, which likewise signifies a Devil-man. This occurs in both places because, as is read in Genesis 27:11, Jacob said to his mother: "Behold, my brother Esau is <note>original: "איש שעיר"</note> *isch sair*, that is, a rough (or hairy) man." According to the opinion of the Jews, the word *Sair* here means a devil, just as it is used in Isaiah 13:21 <note>The text cites v. 20, but the passage regarding "satyrs" or "dancing goats" is usually v. 21.</note>, where it is written: "And the <note>original: "שעירים"</note> *Seirim*, that is, field-spirits or devils, shall dance there." Thus, it is clearly to be seen from all this that when the Jews call us "Esau's children," it is the same as if they called us children of the devil.

<margin>V. The Raven.</margin>
Otherwise, fifthly, he is also called <note>original: "עורב"</note> *oref*, that is, a Raven, in the book **Megalle Amykkoth** <note>"Revealer of Depths," a Kabbalistic work by Nathan Nata Spira.</note>, folio 10, column 3, in the fortieth *Ofan* (section), as well as in the **Jalkut chádasch**, folio 109, column 2, number 73, under the title *Keschafim*; and

<margin>VI. The Pig and Wild Boar.</margin>
Sixthly, <note>original: "חזיר"</note> *Chasir*, that is, a Pig, as can be seen in number 79 of the aforementioned title *Keschafim*; or <note>original: "חזיר מיער"</note> *Chasir mijaar*, that is, a wild boar. Regarding this last name, it is written in the book **Shene Luchoth Habberith** <note>"The Two Tablets of the Covenant," a major work of Jewish ethics and mysticism by Isaiah Horowitz.</note>, folio 265, column 2: <note>original Hebrew: "עשו נקרא חזיר מיער כי הוא פושט טלפיו להראות שיש בו סימן טהרה והוא נחש מכננותו של סמאל"</note> That is: "Esau is called a wild boar, for he stretches out his (cloven) hooves to show that there is a sign of purity upon him." (For in Leviticus 11:3, animals that have cloven hooves and chew the cud are considered clean). But he is Esau; he is the serpent from the school of Sammael.

<margin>VII. The Goat</margin>
*Seventhly*, he is called שעיר <note>original: "Sair"</note> **Sair**, that is, a **Goat**; as found in **Bechai's** <note>Rabbi Bahya ben Asher (13th century), a famous Torah commentator.</note> commentary on the five books of Moses, folio 36, column 2, in the section <term>Toledot</term> <note>The weekly Torah portion covering Genesis 25:19–28:9.</note>, and in the **Yalkut Shimoni** <note>An influential medieval compilation of midrashic interpretations.</note> on the said books of Moses, folio 33, column 3, number 115. Furthermore, in the great **Yalkut Reuveni**, it is written on folio 60, column 1, in the section <term>Vayishlach</term> <note>The Torah portion covering Genesis 32:4–36:43.</note> regarding the words of **Genesis 33:16**: *So Esau returned that day on his way unto Seir*, it is written as follows: <note>original Hebrew: "הוא שעיר שנתנו לעזאזל"</note> *He is the Sair or Goat which was given to Azazel*, of which mention is made in **Leviticus 16:8**. <note>This refers to the "scapegoat" ritual of Yom Kippur, where one goat was sent into the wilderness for "Azazel."</note> He is also called a goat in the first part of the **Prague Machzor** <note>A festival prayer book.</note> folio 57, column 2, under the title *Musaf shel rosh hashaná yom shéni* <note>Additional service for the second day of the New Year.</note>, where in a prayer beginning *Ahallelâ Elohai, ashira ysso*, it is written: <note>original Hebrew: "שעיר החניף להורתו בצידו"</note> *The goat (or the hairy one) practiced hypocrisy toward his parent with his game (venison)*; and the **Commentary** on this states: <note>original Hebrew: "הוא שעיר זה עשו"</note> *This goat (or hairy one) is Esau.*

<margin>VIII. The Ox prone to goring.</margin>
*Eighthly*, he is called שור המועד <note>original: "Schor hammúad"</note> **Schor hammuad**, that is, the **ox prone to goring**; as can be read in the book **Emek hammelech** <note>"The King's Valley," a 17th-century Kabbalistic work.</note> folio 8, column 1, at the end of the 41st chapter, under the title *Shaar Shaashue hammelech*, and folio 77, column 4, in the 41st chapter, under the title *Shaar Abba veéma*, as well as in the great **Yalkut Reuveni** folio 59, column 1, in the section *Vayishlach*. <note>In Jewish law, a "Muad" ox is one that has gored three times and whose owner is now fully liable for damages; it signifies a known danger.</note>

<margin>IX. The apostate Israelite.</margin>
*Ninthly*, he is called ישראל משומד <note>original: "Jiſraël meſchúmmad"</note> **Yisrael meshummad**, that is, the **apostate Israelite**; concerning which it is written in the aforementioned commentary by Rabbi **Bechai** on the five books of Moses, folio 56, column 1: <note>original Hebrew: "קרא התלמוד לעשו ישראל משומד"</note> *The Talmud called Esau the apostate Israelite*; and such a name is also to be found in the book **Sera Abraham** folio 37, columns 2 and 3.

<margin>X. A Fool.</margin>
*Tenthly*, he is called נבל <note>original: "Nábhal"</note> **Naval**, that is, a **Fool** or a simpleton; and concerning this, it is written in the book **Midrash Tillim** <note>A midrashic commentary on the Psalms.</note>, folio 12, column 4, regarding the words of **Psalm 14:1**, *The fool says in his heart*, as follows: <note>original Hebrew: "אמר נבל זה עשו הרשע: שהוא אומר אחד בפה ואחד בלב וגו': ד\"א אמר נבל בכאבו זה עשו הרשע ולמה נקרא שמו נבל רבי יהודה בשם רבי שמואל אומר על שמלא כל העולם כולו נבלה"</note> That is: (Through the words) *"the fool says,"* the **wicked Esau** is meant, who speaks one thing with his mouth and thinks another in his heart, etc. In another way, the words *"the fool says in his heart"* are interpreted to mean the wicked Esau. But why is he called a fool? Rabbi **Yehuda** says in the name of Rabbi **Samuel** that it is because he has **filled the entire world with folly** (or defilement).

### Chapter XVI of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked.

From Isaac came Esau, who is <term>Sammaël</term> <note>In Jewish lore, a major archangel who often takes on a demonic or accusatory role.</note> and the <term>Nachash hakkadmoni</term> <note>original: "Nachash hakkadmoni," meaning the "Ancient Serpent" of Eden.</note>, that is, the ancient serpent. He is also simply called **Nachash** <note>Hebrew: נחש</note>, that is, a **Serpent**; for this reason, in the book **Yalkut Chadash** <note>The "New Anthology," a 17th-century compilation of Midrashic and Kabbalistic lore.</note>, folio 109, column 3, number 76, under the title *Keshaphim* <note>Sorceries</note>, it is read as follows: <note>original Hebrew: "עשו הרשע נקרא אדם רע וגם נקרא נחש וז"ש הצילני נ"א נוטריקון נחש אדם"</note> *The godless Esau is called the evil man; he is also called a serpent; and this is what (Jacob, in Genesis 32:11) said: "Deliver me, na"* <note>Hebrew: נא, usually meaning "now" or "I pray."</note>, *and through <term>Notarikon</term>* <note>A system of interpretation where each letter of a word stands for another word.</note> *(when each letter represents a separate word), he makes the little word **na** into **Nachash** <note>serpent</note> and **Adam** <note>man</note>.* By this, it is meant to be understood that the man Esau is a serpent. The very same can be found in the great **Yalkut Reuveni**, folio 59, column 4, in the section <term>Vayishlach</term> <note>The weekly Torah portion covering Genesis 32:4–36:43.</note>.

<margin>
IV. A Devil-Man.
</margin>

Fourthly, in **Bereshith Rabba** <note>Genesis Rabbah, an ancient commentary on Genesis.</note> folio 59, on the first page, in the commentary **Mattenoth Kehunna** <note>"Gifts of the Priesthood," a standard commentary on the Midrash.</note>, he is called **Gepher shedin** <note>Hebrew: גבר שדין</note>, that is, a **Devil-Man**; this is also read in the **Yalkut Shimoni** on the books of Moses, folio 33, column 3, number 114, at the end, where he is also called **Baal Shedim** <note>Hebrew: בעל שדים</note> in the margin, which likewise means a **Devil-Man**. This occurs in both places because, as can be read in Genesis 27:11, Jacob said to his mother: "Behold, my brother Esau is an **ish sair**" <note>Hebrew: איש שעיר</note>, that is, a rough (or hairy) man; and here, according to the opinion of the Jews, the word **Sair** means a **devil**, as it is used in Isaiah 13:21, where it is written: *And the Seirim (field-spirits or devils) shall dance there.* It is therefore clearly to be seen from all this that when the Jews call us "Esau’s children," it is the same as if they called us "children of the devil."

Sixthly, **Chazir** <note>Hebrew: חזיר</note>, that is, a **Pig**, as seen in number 79 of the aforementioned title *Keshaphim*; or **Chazir mi-yaar** <note>Hebrew: חזיר מיער</note>, that is, a **wild boar**, of which latter name it is written in the book **Shene Luchoth Habberith** <note>The "Two Tablets of the Covenant," an influential work of Jewish ethics and mysticism.</note> folio 265, column 2: <note>original Hebrew: "עשו נקרא חזיר מיער כי הוא פושט טלפיו להראות שיש בו סימן טהרה והוא נחש מכננותו של סמאל"</note> *Esau is called a wild boar, for he stretches out his (cloven) hooves to show that there is a sign of purity in him* (for in Leviticus 11:3, animals that have cloven hooves and chew the cud are considered clean). *But he is Esau; he is the serpent, from the mastery of Sammaël.* <note>The author points out a traditional Jewish metaphor: the pig is seen as the ultimate hypocrite because it displays its cloven hooves (a sign of being kosher) while lacking the internal sign (chewing the cud), representing those who are outwardly holy but inwardly corrupt.</note>

</margin>

Seventhly, he is called **שעיר Sair**, that is, a **Goat** <note>The Hebrew word *Sair* can mean both "hairy" and "goat," a pun on Esau being described as hairy in Genesis.</note>, as found in **Rabbi Bahya's** <note>Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century Spanish commentator.</note> commentary on the five books of Moses, folio 36, column 2, in the portion <term>Toledot</term> <note>The weekly Torah portion covering Genesis 25:19–28:9.</note>, and in the **Yalkut Shimoni** <note>A major medieval compilation of Midrash (Jewish homiletic teachings).</note> on the aforementioned books of Moses, folio 33, column 3, number 115. In the great **Yalkut Reuveni**, it is written on folio 60, column 1, in the portion <term>Vayishlach</term> concerning the words of Genesis 33:16, **"So Esau returned that day on his way to Seir,"** as follows: **הוא שעיר שנתנו לעזאזל** <note>original: "Hu Sair she-natnu le-Azazel"</note>—that is, **"He is the Sair [Goat] who was given to Azazel,"** regarding which Leviticus 16:8 may be consulted <note>Azazel is the destination for the "scapegoat" in the rituals for the Day of Atonement.</note>. He is also called a goat in the first part of the **Prague Machzor** <note>A prayer book for the Jewish High Holidays.</note>, folio 57, column 2, under the title *Musaph shel Rosh Hashanah yom sheni* <note>The additional service for the second day of the Jewish New Year.</note>, where in a prayer beginning *Ahallela Elohai, ashira yffo*, it is written: **שעיר החניף להורו בצדו**—that is, **"The Goat [or Hairy One] practiced hypocrisy against his father with his venison,"** and the commentary on it states: **הוא שעיר זה הוא עשו**—that is, **"This goat [or hairy one] is Esau."**

<margin>
VIII. The Ox Prone to Goring.
</margin>

Eighthly, he is called **שור המועד Schor hammu'ad**, that is, the **Ox Prone to Goring** <note>In Jewish law, a "mu'ad" ox is one that has gored three times and whose owner is now fully liable for its damages.</note>, as may be read in the book **Emek Hammelech** <note>The "Valley of the King," a 17th-century Kabbalistic work.</note>, folio 8, column 1, at the end of the 41st chapter, under the title *Sha'ar Sha'ashu'e Hammelech*, and folio 77, column 4, in the 41st chapter, under the title *Sha'ar Abba ve'Imma*, as well as in the great **Yalkut Reuveni**, folio 59, column 1, in the portion *Vayishlach*.

<margin>
IX. The Apostate Israelite.
</margin>

Ninthly, he is called **ישראל משומד Yisrael meshummad**, that is, the **Apostate Israelite**, about which it is written in the aforementioned commentary by **Rabbi Bahya** on the five books of Moses, folio 56, column 1: **קראו התלמוד לעשו ישראל משומד**—that is, **"The Talmud called Esau an apostate Israelite."** This name is also to be found in the book **Zera Abraham** <note>"Seed of Abraham."</note>, folio 37, columns 2 and 3.

<margin>
X. A Fool
</margin>

Tenthly, he is called **נבל Naval**, that is, a **Fool** or a **Simpleton**. Concerning this, in the book **Midrash Tehillim** <note>An ancient commentary on the Psalms.</note>, folio 12, column 4, regarding the words of Psalm 14:1, **"The fool says in his heart,"** it is written: **אמר נבל זה עשו הרשע שהוא אומר אחד בפה ואחד בלב וגו' : ד"א אמר נבל בלבו זה עשו הרשע ולמה נקרא שמו נבל לפי שהו' ר' יהודה בשם רבי שמואל אומר על שמלא כל העולם כלו נבלה :**—that is, **"By the words 'the fool says,' the godless Esau is meant, who says one thing with his mouth and thinks another in his heart, etc."** In another way, the words **"the fool says in his heart"** are interpreted to mean the godless Esau. But why is he called a fool? Rabbi Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Samuel that it is because he has filled the entire world with folly <note>The Hebrew *nevalah* can mean folly, but also disgrace or vileness.</note>.

First Part.

### Of the First Part of *Judaism Unmasked*, Chapter 16.

<margin>
XI. The Red or Reddish one.
</margin>
Finally, eleventhly, he is called **אדמוני Admoni**, that is, the red or reddish one, because it is written of him in Genesis 25:25: **The first that came out was reddish.**

<margin>
Why Esau was reddish.
</margin>
The reason why he was reddish is found in the <term>Yalkut Chadash</term> <note>A 17th-century compilation of Midrashic and Kabbalistic teachings.</note>, folio 91, column 3, number 167, and in the great <term>Yalkut Reuveni</term> <note>A collection of Kabbalistic commentaries by Reuben Hoeshke (d. 1673).</note>, folio 50, column 1, in the portion <term>Toledot</term> <note>The weekly Torah portion "Generations," covering Genesis 25:19–28:9.</note>, with these words: ויצא הראשון אדמוני ששתה במי נדה אמר דם נדתה <note>original: "Va-yetze ha-rishon admoni she-shata be-mei niddah amar dam niddatah"</note>: That is, **He came out reddish for this reason: because while in his mother’s womb, he drank the blood of her monthly impurity.** <note>The author highlights a polemical Jewish tradition regarding Esau’s gestation.</note> However, <term>Rabbi Solomon Jarchi</term> <note>Better known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> teaches in his commentary on Genesis 25:27 that he was called reddish because he would become a shedder of blood. In the commentary of <term>Menachem von Recanati</term> <note>An Italian Kabbalist of the 13th and 14th centuries.</note> on the five books of <term>Moses</term>, yet another reason is brought forward on folio 57, column 4, in the portion <term>Toledot</term>: עשו הרשע נמשך אחרי פעולת הדין וזהו סוד ועל חרבך תחיה ועל כן היה אדמוני <note>original: "Esau ha-rasha nimshach acharei peulat ha-din..."</note>: That is, **The godless Esau followed after the works of Judgment** <note>In Kabbalah, "Judgment" (Din) is associated with the left side, severity, and the color red.</note>, **and this is the secret** (of the words in Genesis 27:40) **"By your sword you shall live"; for this reason, he was reddish.** But <term>Abarbanel</term> <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a Jewish statesman and philosopher.</note> sets forth another reason in his commentary on Isaiah, chapter 35, folio 54, column 4, stating that he was reddish because he was born under the planet **Mars**, and his words read as follows: אמרו בבראשית רבה ויצא הראשון אדמוני כתיב מדוע אדום בלבושך הוא אדום ותבשילו אדום וארצו אדומה וגבוריו אדומים לבושיהם אדומים ופורע ממנו אדום בלבוש אדום: הוא אדום שנאמר ויצא הראשון אדמוני. תבשילו אדום שנאמר הלעיטני נא מן האדום. ארצו אדומה שנא' ארצה שעיר שדה אדום. גבוריו אדומים שנ' מגן גבורהו מאדם. לבושיהם אדומים שנאמר אנשי חיל מתולעים: ופורע ממנו אדום שנאמר דודי צח ואדום בלבוש אדום מדוע אדום ללבושך. העירו בזה הבחינות אשר בעבורם נקרא עשו וכל הנקראים בשמו אדום והוא לפי שהיה מושל עליו מאדים ולכן נולד אדמוני ונפשו מאדם תאוה כי המזון ראוי שידמה לניזון והארץ אשר גר בה היתה תחת מאדים וגם אחר כך הגבורים אשר יצאו ממנו ומלכו באיטלי' כולם היו ממשלת מאדים כל הורג נפש וכל נוגע בחלל והם מלכי איטליא וקיסרי רומי לבושי תולעת שנ' כי כן היה מנהגם ברומי עד היום הזה <note>original: "Amru be-Bereshit Rabba..."</note>: that is, (**Our Sages**) **have said in <term>Bereshit Rabba</term>** (folio 57, column 2, in the 63rd <term>Parasha</term>) **concerning Genesis 25:25: "And the first came out reddish" (and from Isaiah 63:2) where it is written: "Why is your clothing red?" He (Esau) was red, his food was red, his land was red, his heroes were red, their clothes were red, and the one who will take vengeance on him (Esau) is red, with a red garment. He (namely Esau) was red, for it is said (Gen 25:25): "And the first came out reddish." His food was red, for it is said (Gen 25:30): "Let me swallow some of that red stuff." His land was red, for it is said (Gen 32:3): "Into the land of Seir, the field of Edom." His heroes were red** <note>The Hebrew text continues by quoting Nahum 2:3 and Song of Solomon 5:10, linking Esau's descendants—identified here with the Roman Empire and Italy—to the planet Mars and the color red, which Abarbanel notes is still reflected in the scarlet robes of Roman officials.</note>

<margin>Esau’s children are said to have been bastards</margin>
<gloss>He defiled a betrothed maiden, and killed a soul, and denied the resurrection of the dead, and denied the Root, and despised the birthright, etc.</gloss> <note>original: "המאורסה והרג את הנפש וכפר בתחיית המתים וכפר בעיקר ושט את הבכורה וגו׳"</note> That is: Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, teach that this same wicked man (namely Esau) committed five sins in a single day; that he slept with a betrothed maiden, murdered a man, denied the resurrection of the dead, denied the Foundation (of the faith) <note>Refers to the existence of God or the core principles of religion.</note>, and despised the right of the firstborn. This can also be found in Jonathan’s <gloss>Chaldean (Aramaic) translation</gloss> <note>The Targum Pseudo-Jonathan, an Aramaic translation and expansion of the Torah.</note> of Genesis 25, verse 29, and in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>An ancient commentary on the Psalms.</note>, folio 10, column 1, as well as in the Talmudic tractate *Bava Batra*, folio 16, column 2. It is also claimed that all of his children were bastards, about which it is written in the book *Mattat-Yah* <note>A commentary on the Midrash.</note>, folio 17, column 2, in the <term>Parashah Vayeshev</term> <note>The weekly Torah portion "And he dwelt," Genesis 37:1–40:23.</note>, as follows: <gloss>The excellence of Jacob was on account of his children, who were proper and honest; but the children of Esau were bastards.</gloss> <note>original: "מעלתו של יעקב היה מצד בניו שהיו כשרים : ובניו של עשו היו ממזרים :"</note> That is: Jacob’s glory consisted in his children, who were upright and honorable, but Esau’s children were bastards.

<margin>He is also said to have been devoted to idolatry even in his mother’s womb.</margin>
Furthermore, he is said to have been devoted to idolatry even while in his mother’s womb, about which it is written in the *Bereshit Rabbah* <note>A major rabbinic commentary on the book of Genesis.</note>, folio 56, column 2, in the 63rd <term>Parashah</term> concerning the words of Genesis 25, verse 22: *And the children struggled together within her womb*, as follows: <gloss>Whenever she stood near synagogues or houses of study, Jacob struggled to come out, as it is written (Jeremiah 1:5): "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you." But whenever she passed by houses of idolatry (or temples), Esau moved and struggled to come out, as it is written (Psalm 58:3): "The wicked are estranged from the womb."</gloss> <note>original: "בשעה שהיתה עומדת על ב״כ ובתי מדרשות ויעקב מפרכס לצאת... וכשהיה עוברת על בתי ע״ז עשו דץ ומפרכס לצאת..."</note> That is: at the time when she (namely Rebecca) stood by the synagogues or by the schools, Jacob twitched and wanted to get out, and this is what is written in Jeremiah 1, verse 5: **I knew you before I prepared you in your mother’s womb.** But when she passed before the idolatrous houses (or temples), Esau moved and twitched to get out; and this is what is written in Psalm 58, verse 4 <note>In most English Bibles, this is verse 3.</note>: **The wicked have gone astray (or become estranged) from the mother’s womb.** The very same thing is found in the *Yalkut Shimoni* <note>A compilation of rabbinic myths and teachings on the Hebrew Bible.</note> regarding the five books of Moses, folio 32, column 2, number 110, and in the often-mentioned interpretation of Rabbi Bechai <note>Bahya ben Asher.</note>, folio 34, column 3, in the <term>Parashah Toledot</term>.

<margin>What kind of clothing he had.</margin>
Since Esau is mentioned here, we shall also investigate what kind of clothing he is said to have possessed, which are mentioned in Genesis 27, verse 15, and which his mother put upon Jacob. In the book *Tze'enah u-Re'enah* <note>A popular Yiddish-language work for women, summarizing the Torah and its legends.</note>, it is read in folio 5, column 1, in the <term>Parashah Bereshit</term>, that it was the very same coat which God made for Adam, as can be read in Genesis 3, verse 21, upon which all the wild beasts and birds of the world were embroidered and sewn. Regarding this, it is written in the book *Tzeror ha-Mor* <note>A commentary by Abraham Saba (15th century).</note>, folio 28, column 3, in the <term>Parashah Toledot</term>: <gloss>Our Sages, of blessed memory, have already said that these were the garments of the first Adam, and upon them were depicted all the beasts and birds as if they were alive, and they came into the hands of Nimrod; therefore, Nimrod was called a mighty hunter, because all the beasts...</gloss> <note>original: "כבר אמרו חכמים ז״ל שהיו אלה הבגדים של אדם הראשון ובהם היו מצויירים כל החיות והעופות כאלו היו חיים ובאו לידי נמרוד ולכן נקרא נמרוד גבור ציד לפי שכל החיות"</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Esau’s character, focusing on the legendary "garments of Adam" that he allegedly stole from Nimrod. It also explores the rabbinic reasoning for Isaac’s love for Esau and the tradition regarding Esau’s death in the Cave of Machpelah.</meta>

# How the Christians are named by the Jews.

<gloss>The beasts and the birds would come of their own accord to the garments, and Nimrod would hunt them. Esau the Wicked saw them, killed Nimrod, and robbed them from him. Therefore, he [Esau] was also called a "skilled hunter." On that day, God <note>The Hebrew OCR reads "השט," which may be a fragment of "The Adversary" (Satan) or a typo for "The Name" (God); the German text translates this as God.</note> caused him not to wear them, and he was delayed in the hunt, so that Jacob might receive the blessings.</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: "החיות והעופות היו באים מעצמם אצל הבגדים וצד אותם נמרוד והמדם עשו הרשע והרג לנמרוד וגזלם ממנו ולכן נקרא איש יודע ציד גם כן ואותו היום סבב השט שלא לבשם ונתאחר בצידה בענין שיקבל יעקב הברכות׃"</note> That is: Our Sages of blessed memory have said that these same clothes belonged to the first man, **Adam**, and that upon them all the wild beasts and birds were depicted as if they were alive. Because of this, these garments came into the hands of **Nimrod**, which is why **Nimrod** (Genesis 10:9) is called a "mighty hunter," because all the wild animals and birds came to these clothes of their own accord, and **Nimrod** captured them. However, after the wicked **Esau** developed a desire for them, he killed **Nimrod** and stole them from him; for this reason, he is also called a "skilled hunter" (Genesis 25:27). On that same day (when his mother dressed **Jacob** in his clothes), <term>God</term> caused him [Esau] not to put them on, and he remained a long time out on the hunt, so that **Jacob** might receive the blessings. Similar accounts can be found in the <term>Zohar</term> <note>The foundational work of Jewish mysticism.</note> printed in Sulzbach, in the <term>Parashah Toldot</term> <note>The weekly Torah portion "Generations," Genesis 25:19–28:9.</note>, in the 333rd column; and in the large <term>Yalkut Reuveni</term> <note>A 17th-century collection of Kabbalistic midrashim.</note>, folio 52, column 1, in the aforementioned <term>Parashah</term>; and in the oft-mentioned commentary of <term>Rabbi Bahya</term>, folio 14, column 1, in the <term>Parashah Bereshit</term> <note>The first Torah portion, Genesis 1:1–6:8.</note>; and in the book <term>Netzach Yisrael</term> <note>"The Eternity of Israel," a work by the Maharal of Prague.</note>, folio 26, columns 2 and 3, in the 16th chapter; as well as in the 24th chapter of the *Chapters of **Rabbi Eliezer***.

<margin>Why *Isaac* loved *Esau*.</margin>
Otherwise, we read in Genesis 25:28 that **Isaac** loved **Esau**; but why this was supposed to have happened can be seen in the small <term>Yalkut Reuveni</term>, number 11, under the title <term>Gehinnom</term> <note>The place of spiritual purification or punishment in Jewish tradition, often translated as Hell.</note>, and in the large <term>Yalkut Reuveni</term>, folio 51, column 4. It is stated there that **Isaac** foresaw that his children would sin against <term>God</term>, and that their sins were to be atoned for through the *exilium* <note>Latin: "exile."</note> or the captivity under the children of **Esau**; therefore, he rejoiced and loved **Esau**, because the <term>Israelites</term> are freed from Hell in such a manner.

<margin>How *Esau* died.</margin>
Regarding the death of **Esau**, it is found in the <term>Midrash Tehillim</term> <note>An ancient commentary on the Psalms.</note>, folio 17, column 4, regarding the 18th Psalm, as well as in the <term>Yalkut Shimoni</term> regarding the Books of *Samuel*, folio 25, column 4, number 163, that when **Isaac** was buried in the "double cave" mentioned in Genesis 23:19 <note>The Cave of Machpelah in Hebron.</note>, **Esau** was also present at the burial. And as the sons of **Jacob** left the cave and left their father [Jacob] standing alone, as he was weeping, **Esau** crept in toward him. Thereupon **Judah** immediately followed him so that he might not murder his father, and he found that he [Esau] intended to kill his father; therefore, he [Judah] struck him from behind.

-># The Sixteenth Chapter of the First Part of Revealed Judaism.<-

<note>original Hebrew: "המאורסה והרג את הנפש וכפר בתחיית המתים וכפר בעיקר ושט את הבכורה וגו׳"</note> This means: Our Rabbinic Sages, of blessed memory, teach that this same godless man (namely Esau) committed five sins in a single day: he lay with a betrothed young woman, he murdered a man, he denied the resurrection of the dead, he rejected the foundation (of the faith), and he despised the right of the firstborn. This can also be found in the <term>Chaldean Translation</term> <note>This refers to the Targum, an Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible.</note> of Genesis 25:29, and in the <term>Midrash Tehillim</term> <note>A rabbinic commentary on the Psalms.</note> (folio 10, column 1), as well as in the Talmudic tractate <term>Bava Batra</term> (folio 16, column 2). It is also said that all of his children were illegitimate, about which it is written in the book *Mattath-jah* (folio 17, column 2) in the portion *Vayeshev*: <note>original Hebrew: "מעלתו של יעקב היה מצד בניו שהיו כשרים : ובניו של עשו היו ממזרים"</note> That is: The glory of Jacob consisted in the regard of his children, who were upright and honest; but the children of Esau were bastards.

<margin>Esau’s children are said to have been bastards.</margin>

<margin>He is said to have been devoted to idolatry even in his mother’s womb.</margin>
Furthermore, he is said to have been devoted to idolatry even while in his mother’s womb, regarding which it is written in the <term>Bereshith Rabbah</term> <note>A collection of ancient rabbinic interpretations of the book of Genesis.</note> (folio 56, column 2) in the 63rd portion concerning the words of Genesis 25:22—*And the children struggled together within her*—as follows: <note>original Hebrew: "בשעה שהיתה עומדת על ב"כ ובתי מדרשות ויעקב מפרכס לצאת ה"ה וזרז בטרם אצירך בבטן ידעתיך : וכשעה שהיא עוברת על בתי ע"ז עשו רץ ומפרכס לצאת ה"ה זורו רשעים מרחם :"</note> That is: whenever she (namely Rebecca) stood by the synagogues or the houses of study, Jacob would struggle and try to come out; and this is what is written (Jeremiah 1:5): *Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee.* But whenever she passed by the houses of idolatry (or temples), Esau would move and struggle to get out: and this is what is written (Psalm 58:4): *The wicked are estranged from the womb.* The same is found in the *Yalkut Shimoni* on the five books of Moses (folio 32, column 2, number 110) and in the frequently mentioned commentary of Rabbi Bechai (folio 34, column 3) in the portion *Toledot*.

<margin>Regarding the clothes he possessed.</margin>
Since Esau is mentioned here, we shall also look into what kind of clothes he is said to have possessed, which are mentioned in Genesis 27:15, and which his mother put upon Jacob. In the book *Ze’enah U-Re’enah*, it is read (folio 5, column 1) in the portion *Bereshit* that it was the same coat which God made for Adam, as read in Genesis 3:21, upon which all the wild beasts and birds of the world were embroidered and sewn. Regarding this, it is written in the book *Zeror Hammor* (folio 28, column 3) in the portion *Toledot*: <note>original Hebrew: "כבר אמרו חכמים ז"ל שהיו אלה הבגדים של אדם הראשון וגם היו מצויירים כל החיות והעופות כאלו היו חיים ובאו לידי נמרוד ולכן נקרא נמרוד גבור ציד לפי שכל"</note> That is: Our Sages, of blessed memory, have already said that these were the clothes of the first man, **Adam**, and also that all the animals and birds were depicted on them as if they were alive, and they came into the hands of **Nimrod**; and therefore **Nimrod** was called a "mighty hunter," because all...

<meta>catchword: the animals</meta>

<summary>This page details rabbinic traditions characterizing Esau as a lifelong sinner—from committing five major crimes in one day to exhibiting an inclination toward idolatry while still in the womb. It also introduces the legend of the "garments of Adam," miraculous clothes embroidered with living animals that passed from Adam to Nimrod and eventually to Esau.</summary>

<note>original Hebrew: הַחַיּוֹת וְהָעוֹפוֹת הָיוּ בָּאִים מֵעַצְמָם אֵצֶל הַבְּגָדִים וְצַד אוֹתָם נִמְרוֹד וְחָמַד עֵשָׂו הָרָשָׁע וְהָרַג לְנִמְרוֹד וּגְזָלָם מִמֶּנּוּ וְלָכֵן נִקְרָא אִישׁ יוֹדֵעַ צַיִד גַּם כֵּן וְאוֹתוֹ הַיּוֹם סָבַב הַשֵּׁם שֶׁלֹּא לְבָשָׁם וְנִתְאַחֵר בַּצִידָה בְּעִנְיָן שֶׁיְּקַבֵּל יַעֲקֹב הַבְּרָכוֹת׃</note>

This means: Our Sages of blessed memory have said that these same garments belonged to the first **man, Adam**, and that all wild **animals** and **birds** were depicted upon them as if they were alive; and that these came into the **hands** of **Nimrod**, for which reason **Nimrod** (**Genesis 10:9**) is called a mighty **hunter**, because all wild **animals** and **birds** came to such garments of their own accord, and **Nimrod** captured them. However, after the godless **Esau** developed a **desire** for them, he killed **Nimrod** and robbed them from him; therefore he is also called (**Genesis 25:27**) a **man skilled** in the **hunt**. But on that same day (in which his mother dressed **Jacob** in his clothes), **God** caused him [Esau] not to put them on, and he remained long at the **hunt**, so that **Jacob** might receive the blessings. Similar accounts of this can be found in the **Zohar** <note>The primary work of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah).</note> printed in **Sulzbach**, in the portion <term>Toldot</term> <note>The weekly Torah portion covering Genesis 25:19–28:9.</note>, in the 333rd column; and in the great **Yalkut Reubeni**, folio 52, column 1, in the aforementioned portion; and in the often-cited commentary of **Rabbi Bechai** <note>Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century Spanish rabbi and scholar.</note>, folio 14, column 1, in the portion <term>Bereshit</term> <note>The first portion of Genesis.</note>; and in the book **Netzach Yisrael** <note>The "Eternity of Israel" by Rabbi Judah Loew of Prague.</note>, folio 26, columns 2 and 3, in the 16th chapter; as well as in the 24th chapter of the <term>Chapters of Rabbi Eliezer</term> <note>Pirke De-Rabbi Eliezer, an 8th-century midrashic work.</note>.

<margin>Why Isaac loved Esau.</margin>
Otherwise, it is read in **Genesis 25:28** that **Isaac** loved **Esau**. But why such a thing should have happened is to be seen in the small **Yalkut Reubeni**, number 11, under the **heading Gehenna** <note>The place of spiritual purification or punishment in Jewish tradition.</note>, and in the great **Yalkut Reubeni**, folio 51, column 4, where it is reported that **Isaac** foresaw that his children would sin against **God**, and that their sins should be atoned for through the exile or captivity under the children of **Esau**; for this reason, he rejoiced and loved **Esau**, because in this way the **Israelites** would be freed from Hell.

<margin>How Esau died.</margin>
Regarding **Esau's** death, it is found in the **Midrash Tillim** <note>Midrash Tehillim, a rabbinic commentary on the Psalms.</note>, folio 17, column 4, on the 18th Psalm, as well as in the **Yalkut Shimoni** on the books of **Samuel**, folio 25, column 4, number 163, that when **Isaac** was buried in the double cave <note>The Cave of Machpelah, the traditional burial site of the Patriarchs.</note>, of which mention is made in **Genesis 23:19**, **Esau** also attended the burial. And as the **sons of Jacob** went out of the cave and had left their father [Jacob], who was weeping, standing alone, **Esau** sneaked in to him; thereupon **Judah** immediately followed him so that he might not kill his father, and found that he [Esau] intended to kill his father; for this reason, he [Judah] struck him from behind...

<margin>VI. They also call us the generations of Seir, and the descendants of Seir.</margin>
Sixthly, they call us *Toledot Seir* <note>original Hebrew: תולדות שעיר</note>, that is, the generations of **Seir**; and *Ummat* or *Ummas Seir* <note>original Hebrew: אומת שעיר</note>, that is, the people of **Seir**; as well as *Nechde Seir* <note>original Hebrew: נכדי שעיר</note>, that is, the descendants of **Seir**, because the land in which **Esau** lived was called **Seir**, as can be seen in **Genesis 32:3** and **Deuteronomy 2:12**; and *Seirim* <note>original Hebrew: שעירים</note>, that is, those of **Seir**. The name *Toledot Seir*, that is, the generation of **Seir**, is found in the first part of the **Prague Mahzor** <note>A prayer book for Jewish festivals</note>, folio 142, column 1, under the title *Yotzer le-yom rishon shel Sukkot* <note>A prayer for the first day of the Feast of Tabernacles</note>, in the prayer which begins *Kosht Sheinat ez*, with these words: "Destroy the generations of **Seir**" <note>original Hebrew: תאבד תולדות שעיר</note>. Regarding this, in the **Mahzor** printed here in **Frankfurt** in the year 1690, it is read: "Destroy the generations of your enemies" <note>original Hebrew: תאבד תולדות אויבך</note>. However, both terms refer to the **Christians**, for they are held by the Jews to be enemies of **God**, as was proven above in the 15th chapter, page 604. The name *Ummat Seir*, that is, the people of **Seir**, is found in the book *Magen Avraham* <note>"Shield of Abraham," a commentary on Jewish law</note>, in the second chapter, where it is read: "The people of **Seir** is **Edom**" <note>original Hebrew: אומת שעיר היא אדום</note>. The name *Nechde Seir*, however, is found in the second part of the **Prague Mahzor**, folio 86, column 1, in the prayer which begins *Shem yikare bi-khtifato*, where it is written: "When He (namely **God**) strikes the descendants of **Seir** (and carries out the aforementioned bloodbath), He will take His vengeance on His enemies" <note>original Hebrew: נכדי שעיר בכוחו באויביו יתן נקמתו</note>. However, these words were entirely omitted from the aforementioned **Mahzor** printed here in **Frankfurt** out of fear <note>Eisenmenger suggests the text was censored by Jews to avoid provoking Christian authorities</note>. The name *Seirim*, that is, those of **Seir**, is found in the second part of the **Prague Mahzor**, folio 52, column 2, under the title *Yotzer le-yom rishon shel Pesach* <note>A prayer for the first day of Passover</note>, in the prayer which begins *Shelachayich Pardes* etc. <note>original Hebrew: שלחך פרדס וגו׳</note> with these words: "I sleep (that is, I am in exile or misery for so long) until I come into the city (Jerusalem) from the *Seirim* (that is, from those of **Seir**)" <note>original Hebrew: אני ישנה ביאת עיר משעירים</note>.

<margin>The two names Esau and Amalek are used interchangeably and both signify the Christians.</margin>

### How the Christians are named by the Jews.

<margin>Amalek’s People and Amalekites.</margin>
as well as <term>Amalekites</term> <note>original Hebrew: עמלקים, Amalékim</note>. The name <term>Children of Amalek</term> <note>original Hebrew: Bené Amaleck</note> is read in the *Mahzor* <note>a Jewish festival prayer book</note> printed in folio in Venice, on folio 60, column 2, in a prayer that begins <term>They spoke with weeping</term> <note>original Hebrew: Amárer bischí</note>, under the title <term>For the Ninth of Av</term> <note>original Hebrew: Letischā beāf; a day of mourning for the destruction of the Temple</note>. Likewise, the name <term>Seed of Amalek</term> <note>original Hebrew: Séra Amalek</note> is found in the second part of the Wilmersdorf *Mahzor*, folio 60, in the commentary where it is written: <term>In the future, the Holy and Blessed God will sound the trumpet three times: once for the resurrection of the dead; the second time to root out the seed of Amalek; and the third time to gather the Jews who are in captivity.</term> <note>original Hebrew: עתיד הק"בה לתקוע שלש תקיעות אחת לתחיית המתים ואחת להכרית זרעו של עמלק ואחת לקבץ גלויות</note> However, instead of the words <term>to root out the seed of Amalek</term>, the Prague *Mahzor* in the first part, folio 17, column 2, says <term>to root out the seed of Esau</term> <note>original Hebrew: להכרית זרעו של עשו</note>, because these two names are taken to have the same meaning. Furthermore, such a name is found in the aforementioned Venice *Mahzor*, in the first part, under the title <term>Evening prayer for the departure of the Sabbath</term> <note>original Hebrew: Arafith lemozāë Schabbáth</note>, on the last leaf of that title; and in the second part of the Prague *Mahzor*, folio 16, column 2, in the commentary under the title <term>Liturgical poem for the portion ‘Remember’</term> <note>original Hebrew: Józer leparascháth sechór; referring to the Sabbath before Purim</note>, as well as in the book *Pesikta Rabbati*, folio 19, column 4. # How the Christians are Named by the Jews.

But [the Christians] will have no part with the rest of the nations who shall remain, nor shall they be remembered any longer. This is what is written in **Obadiah 1:18**: **"And there shall be no survivor of the house of Esau."** The explanation of this verse consists in this: that while some of the other nations will remain to serve the Lord, none from the seed of Esau shall remain; rather, they shall be exterminated from the world, just as it is written in **Exodus 17:14**: **"For I will utterly blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven."** And then the Name and the Throne (of God) shall be perfect; for the three letters *Aleph*, *He*, and *Vav* make the Throne and the Name complete. <note>In Jewish mysticism, the "Throne" and "Name" of God are considered "incomplete" as long as evil (symbolized by Amalek/Esau) exists in the world. The author is explaining a Kabbalistic wordplay where the Hebrew words for throne and God's name are spelled in a shortened form in certain biblical verses.</note> All of this can also be found in the book *Ze’enah u-Re’enah* <note>A famous Yiddish-language commentary on the Torah, traditionally read by women</note>, folio 45, column 1, at the end of the *Parashah* <term>Parashah: a weekly portion of the Torah read in the synagogue</term> *Beshallach*. Then, instead of *Kes*, it shall be said *Kisse*, and instead of *Yah*, it shall be said *Jehovah*.

Since both the name "Amalek" and "Esau" are understood to mean the descendants of Esau and the Christians, Rabbi Menachem of Recanati <note>A 13th-century Italian Kabbalist and biblical commentator</note> writes in his commentary on the Five Books of Moses, folio 96, column 1, in the *Parashah Vayishlach Jethro*, in the following manner: **In the days of the Messiah, the seed of Esau and Amalek will be wiped out because of the power of Israel, which will prevail above (that is, in heaven), etc.** <note>original Hebrew: בימות המשיח ימחה זרעו של עשו ושל עמלק מפני כחן של ישראל שיגבר למעלה וגו׳</note>. Likewise, in the aforementioned book *Ze’enah u-Re’enah*, folio 45, column 2, in the said *Parashah Vayishlach Jethro*, the following is read: **It is well known that Esau has been a wicked man toward Israel in all generations, as indicated by the first war of Amalek; for no man had waged war with Israel before Esau—that is, Amalek—who was the first to begin. Likewise, the final war will be with Esau in the days of the Messiah.** <note>The original text here is in Yiddish: עס איז וויסיג דס עשו איז גוועזן איין רשע צו ישראל אין אלע דורות...</note> That is to say: It is known that Esau has shown himself godless toward Israel in all generations and at all times, whether it be in the first war of Amalek (of which one reads in Exodus 17:8) or otherwise; for no man ever waged war with Israel for the first time except Esau, that is, Amalek, who started it first. # Chapter 16 of the First Part of Judaism Unveiled.

<margin>
Called foreigners by us as well.
</margin>
**Strangers** <note>original Hebrew: זרים, *zârim*</note>; but a single one is called **Foreigner** <note>original Hebrew: נכרי, *Nóchri*</note>, or **Foreignness** <note>original Hebrew: נכר, *Néchar*</note>, or **Son of a foreigner** <note>original Hebrew: בן נכר, *Ben néchar*</note>, or **Stranger** <note>original Hebrew: זר, *Sar*</note>. What the word *Nochri* signifies is taught by Rabbi Abraham Perizol <note>A 15th-16th century Italian Jewish scholar and geographer</note> in his book *Maggen Abraham* <note>The Shield of Abraham</note>, in the 72nd chapter, when he reports: **"The word *nochri* is the opposite of 'brother,' for he (namely the foreigner) does not keep the covenant of brotherhood, nor does he hold the same opinions; his law is set apart and distinct in beliefs and faith. The primary meaning of the word *nochri* is one who is uncircumcised; for the uncircumcised is called *nochri* and *nechar*, as it is said (Ezekiel 44:9): 'No foreigner, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, shall enter my sanctuary.'"** <note>original Hebrew: מלת נכרי היא היפך האח שאינו שומר ברית אחוה ולא שומר דעות ותורתו נבדלה ונפרשה ובאמונות והעיקר במלת נכרי הנה שאינו בלתי נימול שהערל נקרא נכרי ונכר כאמרו כל בן נכר ערל לב וערל בשר לא יבא אל מקדשי;</note> That is: The word *Nochri* or Foreigner is the opposite of the word Brother, for he (the foreigner) does not maintain the bond of brotherhood and does not share his brother’s beliefs. Likewise, his law is separate and different in its views and faith. And the word *Nochri*, or Foreigner, mainly signifies one who is not circumcised; for an uncircumcised person is named *Nóchri* and *Néchar*, that is, a foreigner, as it is said in Ezekiel 44, verse 9: No *ben néchar*, that is, a foreigner of an uncircumcised heart and uncircumcised flesh, shall come into my sanctuary. Similarly, in the old *Nizzachon* <note>A medieval Jewish polemical work written to defend Judaism against Christian arguments</note>, page 139, we read: **"It is written: 'You shall not charge interest to your brother,' but to the *nochri*—that is, one who is not circumcised—you may charge interest."** <note>original Hebrew: כתיב לאחיך לא תשיך אבל לנכרי ר"ל שאינו נימול תשיך</note> That is: It stands written in Deuteronomy 23:19–20: You shall not charge interest to your brother, but from the *Nóchri*, that is, the foreigner who is not circumcised, you shall charge interest. From this we see that an uncircumcised person is called *Nóchri* or a foreigner; therefore, every Christian is so named by the Jews because he is not circumcised. In the Talmudic tractate *Berachoth*, folio 47, column 2, it is reported regarding a <term>proselyte: a convert to Judaism</term>: **"He is never a convert until he is circumcised and immersed; as long as he has not immersed, he is a *nochri*."** <note>original Hebrew: לעולם אינו גר עד שימול ויטבול וכמה דלא טבל נכרי הוא;</note> That is: He is never a Jewish associate until he is circumcised and washed <note>Referring to the ritual bath or Mikveh</note>; but as long as he is not washed, he is a *Nóchri*, that is, a foreigner.

<margin>
What the word "foreigner" signifies.
</margin>
Rabbi Bechai <note>Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century Spanish rabbi and biblical commentator</note> also wrote in his commentary on the Five Books of Moses, folio 207, column 3, in the portion *Shophetim* <note>The weekly Torah reading "Judges"</note> regarding the words of Deuteronomy 17:15, "You shall set one from among your brothers as king over you," in this manner: **"From here one may learn that whoever is not your brother is not an Israelite, and whoever is not an Israelite is called a foreigner."** <note>original Hebrew: מכאן יש ללמוד שכל מי שאינו אחיך אינו ישראל וכל מי שאינו ישראל נקרא נכר;</note> That is: From this it is to be learned that everyone who is not your brother is not an Israelite, and everyone who is not an Israelite is called a foreigner. Thus, according to Rabbi Bechai’s teaching, the foreigner is placed in opposition to an Israelite, so that an Israelite is not a foreigner, and a foreigner is not an Israelite. For this reason, he also teaches on folio 213, column 4, in the aforementioned book, in the portion *Ki Tetze*: **"To the foreigner you may charge interest, but not to the Israelite."** <note>original Hebrew: לנכרי תשיך ולא לישראל;</note> The same is also to be found in the *Sepher Chasidim* <note>The Book of the Pious, a foundational work of German-Jewish ethics and law from the 12th/13th century</note>, numbers 1014, 1017, and 1018, where **Jews** <note>original Hebrew: יהודים, *Jehúdim*</note> and **foreigners** <note>original Hebrew: נכרים, *nóchrim*</note>, as well as **foreigner** <note>original Hebrew: נכרי, *nóchri*</note> and **Israelite** <note>original Hebrew: ישראל, *Jisrael*</note>, are set against one another.

Response to the objection and proof that the Jews do regard us as foreigners.

<meta>This page continues the author's argument against Jewish interpretations of the word "nokhri" (stranger). On the previous page, Eisenmenger quoted the scholar Abravanel claiming Christians are "brothers," but here he argues this was merely a diplomatic deception to avoid persecution.</meta>

-> ### How Christians Are Named by the Jews. <-

It is read in *Shevet Yehuda* <note>original: "Schévet Jehuda" (The Scepter of Judah), a 16th-century historical work by Solomon ibn Verga</note> fol. 7, col. 2, that a man named Thomas held a conversation with a King of Spain named **Alfonso**, and said to him: <note>original Hebrew: ויכוח היה לי בזה עם שר אחד מבני אברבניל... "I had a disputation concerning this with a prince of the sons of Abravanel, who came from Seville, his birthplace, and he said that for one who knows the Hebrew language, it is not difficult to understand that there is a difference between the term 'foreigner' (nokhri), 'Christian' (notzri), or 'Gentile' (goi)..."</note> that is: I had a disputation regarding this (namely, regarding an ox belonging to a Jew which kills the ox of a *nokhri* <note>stranger or foreigner</note>) with a prince from the house of **Abravanel**, who had come from Seville, his fatherland. He said to me that for one who understands the Hebrew language, it is not difficult to see that there is a distinction between the word *nokhri* (stranger), the word *notzri* (Christian), or *Goi* (Gentile). For he is called *nokhri* or a stranger who behaves as a stranger toward his Creator and does not believe in the fundamental articles of religion; but a Christian is not called *nokhri* or a stranger because he believes in the creation of the world, the miracles, as well as the (Divine) **Providence** or oversight. 

Even though, I say, this appears in the little book *Shevet Yehuda*, it was not said in earnest by one of the sons of Abravanel, but only out of hypocrisy and flattery for the sake of living in peace and to avoid the enmity of the Christians—just as has happened with many other things mentioned in the aforementioned book *Shevet Yehuda* which I have pointed out in this work.

<margin>
Further proof that Christians are regarded as foreigners.
</margin>

The truth of my statement can also be easily gathered from the fact that in 1 Kings 8:41, someone who was not an Israelite is called *nokhri*, that is, a stranger. There, the word *nokhri* is translated in the Chaldean <note>Aramaic Targum</note> version as *bar ammin* <note>original: בר עממין</note>, meaning a "son of the nations" (of which there are said to be seventy in the world besides the Jews). How then could one of Abravanel’s sons have understood it in earnest any differently than it is used in the Holy Scriptures? 

Likewise, both words, *nokhri* and *Goi*, are often used interchangeably. In the Talmudic tractate *Gittin* <note>A volume of the Talmud dealing with legal contracts and divorce</note>, fol. 70, col. 1, it is written: <note>original Hebrew: רב שימי בר אשי עבד ליה לההוא נכרי</note> That is: Rav Shimi, the son of Ashi, did this for a certain *nokhri*, meaning he healed a stranger. In the Talmudic tractate *Avoda Zara* <note>A volume dealing with "strange worship" or idolatry</note>, on fol. 26, col. 2, in the *Tosefot* <note>Medieval additions and commentaries to the Talmud</note>, where the same matter is repeated, the word *Goi* is found instead of the word *nokhri*. And in **Doctor Wagenseil’s** <note>Johann Christoph Wagenseil, a contemporary Christian scholar of Hebrew</note> rebuttal of the Lipmannian poem, page 600, it is read from the written book *Etz Chayim* <note>The Tree of Life</note>: <note>original Hebrew: מצות עשה להשיך לגוי שנ׳ לנכרי תשך</note> "It is a positive commandment to lend with interest to a *Goy*, as it is said [in Deuteronomy 23:20]: To a *nokhri* <note>stranger</note> you shall lend with interest."

<margin>IX. Ninth naming: they call us *Goyim*, that is, Heathens.</margin>
Ninthly, they call us *Goyim* <note>original: גוים</note>, that is, **Heathens**; and one individual alone is called a *Goi* <note>original: גוי</note>, that is, a **Heathen**; a female person, however, is called a *Goya* <note>original: גויה</note>, that is, a **female Heathen**; and two or more female persons are called *Goyoth* or *Goyos* <note>original: גויות</note>, that is, **female Heathens**. In the Hebrew text of the Old Testament, the word *Goi* means "a nation," and is read as referring to both the Jewish and the Heathen people; for it is said of the former in Exodus 19, verse 6, Joshua 5, verse 8, 2 Samuel 7, verse 23, and Ezekiel 37, verse 22, as well as in many other places. <margin>What the word *Goyim* signifies in Holy Scripture.</margin>

### Chapter 16 of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked.

Rabbi Salman Zevi <note>Solomon Zvi Aufhausen, author of the *Jüdischer Theriak* (1615), a famous defense of Judaism against Christian accusations</note> indeed wants to claim in his *Jewish Theriac*, in the second chapter, number 31, folio 15, column 2, that the word *Goi* <note>original: "Goi"</note> or *Gojim* <note>original: "Gojim"; the plural form meaning nations or Gentiles</note> signifies nothing evil and that no one should be ashamed of it; however, this is yet another of his false maneuvers. Tenthly, they call us *Bené Adina* <note>original: בני עדינה</note>, which means **Children of the Voluptuous.** The Babylonian Empire is called *Adina* in Isaiah 47:8—meaning one who is given over to pleasures; however, the Jews call Christendom by this name as well. Therefore, in the *Selichoth* <note>Selichot: Penitential prayers recited during the High Holy Days</note>, in the prayer which begins *Elle eskerá venáfschi* <note>original: אלה אזכרה ונפשי וגו'; "These things I remember and pour out my soul"</note>, under the title for the eve of the 12th and 13th days <note>original: לערב י"ב ולערב י"ג</note> before Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, folio 39, column 1, in the old Prague edition, it reads as follows: <note>original Hebrew: יתמונו בני עדינה להלחמה הרעו לנו מכל מלכי ארמיה</note> which means, **"The *Bené Adina*, or Children of the Voluptuous, have broken us by waging war; they have done more evil to us than all the kings on earth."** In the Frankfurt edition from the year 425 <note>Jewish calendar year 5425</note>—that is, according to our calendar, the year 1665—instead of the word "to war" <note>original: להלחמה; lehillachamá</note>, the word *Schoméma* <note>original: שוממה; meaning "desolate" or "devastating"</note> stands. The Jewish-German translation of this, which was printed in Amsterdam in the year 430 (our year 1670), folio 30, column 2, reads as follows: **"They** (the Edomites) **have broken us, those who are called the gentle (that is, the tender and voluptuous); those same ones now devastate us."** Here we see clearly that in this translation, the words *Bené Adina* are explained as Edom, which among the Jews signifies Christendom <note>In medieval Jewish literature, "Edom"—the biblical kingdom of Esau—became a standard coded term for the Roman Empire and, by extension, the Christian Church</note>.

Thus it is also read in the second part of the Prague *Machsor* <note>A prayer book for Jewish festivals</note>, folio 77, column 2, under the title *Yotzer for the Sabbath of the intermediate days of the festival*, in the prayer which begins <note>original: ברח דודי וגו׳</note> *Flee, my beloved*, etc.: <note>original: הנה אכלונו בכל פה מדיקינו</note> **Behold, those who crush us eat us with a full mouth.** That the Christians are understood by this is to be seen in the *Commentary* thereon, where it is explained thus: <note>original: זו מלכות אדום הרשעה שנ׳ אכלה ומדקה ושארא ברגלה רפסה פירוש שאוכלים ממונינו עד שנשארנו ריקים ודקים ומה שאינו שוה להם ליקח להנאתם רופסים ברגלם</note> **This (*Maddikim* or crushers) signifies the godless Edomite Empire (understand: Christendom), as it is said in Daniel 7:7: 'It devoured and crushed, and the rest it trampled with its feet': that is, they (the Christians) devour our property so that we become empty and thin; but what is not suitable for them to take for their benefit, they trample with their feet.** One must, however, turn the matter around and say that the Jews devour the property of the Christians, in that through their godless extortions, usury, and deceptions, they pinch away the property of the poor Christians, so that the same become entirely thin and empty and fall into the greatest poverty.

<margin>XII. They also call us *Zorim*, that is, those from *Zor*.</margin>
Twelfthly, they call us <note>original: צורים</note> *Zorim*, that is, those from *Zor*. In the Holy Scriptures, *Zor* <note>original: צר</note> signifies the city of *Tyre*, as seen in Joshua 19:29 and 2 Samuel 24:7 and other places. The Jews, however, also call Christendom *Zor*, as is to be seen in the book *Cad ha-Kemach* <note>original: כד הקמח; "The Jar of Flour," a work by the 14th-century scholar Bahya ben Asher</note>, folio 48, column 1, where, regarding the word *Zor* which is read in Isaiah 23:5, it is written: <note>original: הרי צור מלכות אדום היא</note> **Behold, *Zor* signifies the Edomite Empire (that is, Christendom).** Thus also teaches Rabbi *Jacob de Mercado* <note>A 17th-century Jewish scholar and commentator</note> in his interpretation of the *Psalms*, regarding the words of Psalm 45:13, **"The daughter of Tyre,"** thus: <note>original: כנוי לעם אדום</note> **This is a surname for the Edomite (or Christian) people**, regarding which more is to be found below in the following 17th Chapter. Therefore, from the word *Zor*, the Christians are also called *Zorim*, that is, those from *Zor*, as is to be read in the second part of the Prague *Machsor*, folio 70, column 1, under the title *Yotzer for the second day of Passover*, in the prayer which begins <note>original: קמי קהלך קצצת וגו׳</note> *Those who rose against your congregation, you cut down*, etc., where the plagues that came upon *Egypt* are commemorated, and there follows: <note>original: ראה יראו בן צורים</note> **Behold, the sons of the Zorim shall see**, that is—

<margin>xv. They call us Arélim, that is, uncircumcised.</margin>
Fifteenthly, they call us <term>Arélim</term> <note>original: ערלים</note>, that is, **Uncircumcised**; a single person, however, is called <term>Arel</term> or <term>Erel</term>, that is, an uncircumcised one; and I have heard this many hundreds of times from the Jews. Thus it is also written in the book *Chizzuk Emunah* <note>original: "Chiffuk emuna"; a famous 16th-century Karaite polemic titled "Faith Strengthened"</note>, on page 211, regarding the words of Isaiah 52:13, **"Behold, my servant shall deal prudently,"** etc.: <note>original Hebrew: הרצון בו הנה ישכיל עבדי ישראל בצאתו מגלות אדום וישמעאל הנקראים בשם: ערל וטמא</note> that is: By this it is signified: behold, my servant **Israel** shall have good fortune when he departs from the captivity of **Edom** <note>In Jewish literature of this period, "Edom" was a common coded term for Rome or Christendom</note> and **Ishmael** <note>A coded term for the Islamic world or the Turks</note>, who are called by the names **uncircumcised** and **unclean**. <margin>What a shameful thing the foreskin is said to be.</margin>
It is true that the name "uncircumcised" was held as a term of mockery in Holy Scripture, as can be seen in 1 Samuel 14:6, 17:26, and 31:4. However, so that one may rightly know how much we are despised by the Jews through this name, one must consider what they write concerning the foreskin and the uncircumcised. Regarding the foreskin, Rabbi Menachem of Recanati <note>A 13th-century Italian kabbalist</note> teaches in his commentary on the Five Books of Moses, folio 47, column 1, in the portion *Lech Lecha* <note>The Torah portion Genesis 12:1–17:27</note>: <note>original Hebrew: הערלה מאוסה וטמאה מכל טומאות שבעולם</note> that is, **"The foreskin is loathsome and more unclean than all the impurities that exist in the world."** And shortly thereafter follows: <note>original Hebrew: הערלה רומזת לכחות הטומאה</note> that is, **"The foreskin signifies the powers of impurity (that is, the unclean spirits)."** In the book *Akedat Yitzchak* <note>A 15th-century philosophical and homiletic work by Isaac Arama</note>, it is written on folio 47, column 1, from the Talmudic tractate *Nedarim* <note>The volume of the Talmud concerning vows</note>, folio 31, column 2, the following: <note>original Hebrew: מאוסה הערלה שנתגנו בה רשעים שנ' כי כל הגוים ערלים</note> that is, **"The foreskin is loathsome, for the godless are dishonored (or shamed) by it, as is said (Jeremiah 9:26): For all the heathens are uncircumcised."** Further, in the same book *Akedat Yitzchak*, folio 47, column 2, we read: <note>original Hebrew: הערלה עצמה כטבור או איזה דבר שרוע שנולד ממותרי החומר שהוא גנאי באדם</note> that is, **"The foreskin itself is like a navel, or some other superfluous thing which is produced from the excess matter of the body, and is a disgrace to man."** Furthermore, it stands written there: <note>original Hebrew: הערלה מום גדול בגוף האדם אשר בעמדה בו אי אפשר להגיע אל שלמותו המיוחדות שלא תשרה שכינה עליו בשלמות</note> that is, **"The foreskin** is a great defect in the human body, and as long as it remains upon him, it is impossible for him to reach his unique perfection, so that the <term>Shekhinah</term> <note>The Divine Presence of God</note> does not rest upon him in perfection."

# How the Christians are named by the Jews. #

The foreskin is a great defect (or blemish) on the body of man: as long as it is upon him, he cannot attain his proper perfection, and the Divine Majesty will not dwell fully upon him. In the book *Pirke Rabbi Elieser* <note>original: "Pirke Rabbi Elieser"; an 8th-century midrashic work. The text cites chapter 92, though standard editions have fewer chapters; this likely refers to chapter 29</note>, it is also written in the 92nd chapter as follows: <note>original Hebrew: שנ' הערלה טומאה מכל הטומאות :לא יוסיף יבא בך עוד ערל וטמא</note> that is, "The foreskin is an impurity above all impurities, as it is said (Isaiah 52:1): 'Henceforth there shall no more come into thee the uncircumcised and the unclean'; for the foreskin is a blemish above all blemishes." Thus it is read in *Bammidbar Rabba* <note>Numbers Rabbah, a homiletic commentary on the Book of Numbers</note>, folio 203, column 2, in the 12th *Parashah* <note>term: Parashah; a section of the Torah read weekly in the synagogue</note>: <note>original Hebrew: הערלה מום היא בגוף</note> that is, "The foreskin is a blemish on the body." And in the Talmudic tractate *Pesachim* <note>The tractate concerning the laws of Passover</note> is found on folio 92, column 1: <note>original Hebrew: הפורש מן הערלה כפורש מן הקבר</note> that is, "He who separates himself from the foreskin does as much as if he separated himself from a grave (wherein lies an unclean corpse)." In the small *Jalkut Rubeni* <note>A 17th-century Kabbalistic anthology by Reuben Hoeschke</note> it stands under the title *Orla* <note>term: Orla; Hebrew for "foreskin"</note>, number 2, from the book *Sha'are Orah* <note>Gates of Light, a foundational Kabbalistic text by Joseph Gikatilla</note>, folio 41, that when God had said to Abraham, "Walk before me and be perfect," Abraham asked him: "O Lord of the world! How shall I then be perfect?" God gave him this answer: <note>original Hebrew: בשעה שתכרית הערלה שבגופך שהוא חלק עכ"ום</note> that is, "When you cut away the foreskin from your body, which is the portion of the idolatrous people <note>original Hebrew: עכ"ום (Akum); an acronym for "worshipers of stars and constellations," used to refer to heathens or non-Jews</note>, then you shall be perfect." From this it is to be seen that only the idolatrous people are meant to be uncircumcised.

<margin>The same is said to be the Devil's portion.</margin>
In the great *Jalkut Rubeni* it is read on folio 58, column 2, in the *Parashah Vayeze*, from the book *Gale Rasya*, that God said to the chief devil Sammael <note>In Jewish lore, Sammael is the accuser, seducer, and destroying angel, often equated with Satan</note>: <note>original Hebrew: החלק שלך יהיה הערלות</note> that is, "Thy portion shall be the foreskins"; which is also to be found in the small *Jalkut Rubeni*, under the title *Mila* <note>term: Mila; circumcision</note>, number 34, and in the booklet *Tuf Ha'aretz*, folio 32, columns 3 and 4, in a conversation between God and Sammael. Indeed, the aforementioned devil Sammael is himself called *Orla*, that is, the foreskin, as it stands in the book *Emek Hammelech* <note>Valley of the King, a 17th-century work on Lurianic Kabbalah</note>, folio 37, column 2: <note>original Hebrew: הערלה היא קליפת אדום</note> that is, "The *Orla* is the *Kelifa* or rind of Edom." <note>term: Kelifa; literally "husk" or "shell," representing the forces of evil or impurity that surround the holiness in Kabbalah. Edom is a common rabbinic code for Rome and, by extension, the Christian world.</note> For the mentioned Sammael is called the *Kelifa* of Edom, as shall be proven below in the 18th chapter of this first part. But if the foreskins are given as a portion to the devil, how does that harmonize with what is read in *Shir Hashirim Rabba* <note>A midrashic commentary on the Song of Solomon</note>, folio 266, column 2, that God took such great pleasure in the scent of the same? For it is written there: <note>original Hebrew: בשעה שמל אברהם אבינו את עצמו ובני ביתו עשרה ערלותיהן גבעה וזרחה עליהן החמה והתליעו ועלה ריחן לפני הק"בה כריח קטורת הסמים וכריח קומץ הלבונה שעל גבי האישים ואמר הק"בה לכשיבאו בניו של זה לידי עבירות ומעשים רעים אני נזכר להם זה הריח ואתמלא רחמים עליהם והופך להם מדת הדין</note> "When our father Abraham circumcised himself and the men of his house, he made a heap of their foreskins; and the sun shone upon them, and they became wormy, and their scent rose before the Holy One, blessed be He, like the scent of spicy incense and like the scent of the handful of frankincense upon the altar-fires. And the Holy One, blessed be He, said: 'When the children of this man fall into transgressions and evil deeds, I will remember this scent for them, and I will be filled with mercy toward them, and I will turn the attribute of strict judgment for them [into the attribute of mercy].'"

<margin>Nevertheless, the smell of foreskins in which worms had grown is said to have been very pleasing to God.</margin>
The judgment leads to the attribute of mercy; <note>original: "Ha-din le-middat rachamim"</note> that is: at the time when our father Abraham had circumcised himself and his household, he placed their foreskins in a heap. But when the sun shone upon them, worms grew within them, and their scent rose up before the Holy and Blessed God like the scent of spice smoke, and like the scent of a handful of incense upon the fire-offerings. And God said: "Whenever his children sin and perform evil deeds, I will remember this scent on their behalf and be filled with mercy toward them, and I will transform the attribute of judgment into the attribute of mercy." This same account is also found in *Genesis Rabbah* <note>term: Bereshit Rabbah; a homiletic midrash (commentary) on the Book of Genesis</note>, folio 42, column 4, in the 47th *Parashah* <note>term: Parashah; a section of the Torah read in the weekly synagogue service</note>; and even more of such things can be found in the *Song of Songs Rabbah* <note>midrashic commentary on the Song of Songs</note> immediately following the previous section. Should God then have taken such great delight in the scent of that which belongs to the Devil? These foolish Jews should be ashamed to write such a thing, as it redounds to God's great dishonor.

<margin>How greatly the uncircumcised are despised.</margin>
Since the foreskin is said to be such an unclean and shameful thing, it is easy to imagine how greatly the uncircumcised must be despised by the Jews. Therefore, Rabbi Elieser also writes in his aforementioned 29th chapter:

> Whoever eats with an uncircumcised person does as much as if he ate with a dog: just as a dog is not circumcised, so is the one who has a foreskin not circumcised. Also, whoever touches an uncircumcised person does as much as if he touched a corpse. Whoever washes with him does as much as if he washed with a leper; for in their lives they are as if dead; and when they die, they are like the carrion of the field, and their prayer does not come before God. Of them it is also said (Psalm 115:17): "The dead shall not praise the Lord."

Likewise, in the great *Yalkut Reuveni* <note>term: Jalkut Rubenî; a 17th-century Kabbalistic anthology</note>, folio 37, column 2, in the portion *Lech Lecha* <note>term: Lech Lecha; the Torah portion (Genesis 12:1–17:27) where Abraham is commanded to undergo circumcision</note>, it is written from the *Zohar* <note>term: Sóhar; the foundational work of Jewish mysticism</note>, concerning the words of Genesis 15:1 ("After these things it happened that the word of the Lord came to Abraham in a *machaseh*," that is, a vision):

> There is a difference between the words *mareh* and *machaseh*. *Mareh* is the "holy tongue" (Hebrew), but *machaseh* is the translation (Aramaic). Therefore, regarding Abraham before he was circumcised, the word of the Lord came to Abram in a *machaseh*, so that the angels would not know that the Holy and Blessed God was speaking with an uncircumcised man, for the angels do not pay attention to the Aramaic translation. But after Abraham was circumcised, God spoke with him [directly].

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the mystical and theological significance of circumcision in Jewish thought, specifically focusing on its role in securing a place in the afterlife and its use as a mark of divine identity.</meta>

### Chapter XVI of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked. ###

<margin>Jacob was circumcised in his mother's womb.</margin>
"...and we shall have no part in the world to come" <note>original Hebrew: ולא יהיה לנו חלק עולם הבא</note>: this means that the man who is circumcised is marked with the name *Shaddai* <note>term: *Shaddai*; a Hebrew name for God usually translated as "The Almighty." As noted on the previous page, the letter *Yod* is thought to complete this divine name on the person's body</note>. Because of this, the two brothers, Jacob and Esau, fought with one another over the inheritance of the two worlds—namely, this world and the world to come—as Rabbi Salomon Jarchi <note>term: *Rabbi Salomon Jarchi*; better known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator on the Torah and Talmud</note> explained in his commentary on the Torah portion *Toledot Isaac* <note>term: *Toledot*; the section of Genesis beginning at 25:19</note> (specifically on Genesis 25:22). For Jacob was already circumcised while in his mother's womb, according to what our sages of blessed memory interpreted regarding the words (Genesis 25:27), "Jacob was an upright man." They explain that he was marked with the letter *Yod* from the name *Shaddai*—which is the letter representing circumcision—and thus he wished to possess the future world, which was also created through the letter *Yod*. Esau, however, said, "Neither I nor you shall have it" (meaning the future world, or eternal life). For this reason, we always find that the idolaters issued decrees or rulings against the Israelites, forbidding them from being circumcised.

<margin>Why the Jews were forbidden from circumcising their children.</margin>
But why did they issue decrees against this commandment more than the other commandments found in the Law? The reason is what we have already stated: because circumcision brings about eternal life. For the living God, who is our portion, commanded us to save our dear children from destruction through circumcision, for the sake of His covenant which He makes in our flesh. Therefore, the heathens issue decrees or commands that they should not be circumcised, so that they might share the same portion in Hell and have no part in eternal life. As for who specifically forbade circumcision, this can be seen in the Talmudic tractate *Rosh Hashanah*, folio 19, column 1, where it is read that the Roman Empire—by which Christendom is understood <note>Eisenmenger often interprets "Rome" or "Edom" in Jewish texts as coded references to the Christian Church</note>—did this.

<margin>Why the Jews circumcise their uncircumcised infant sons after their death.</margin>
Since the Jews believe that they achieve salvation through circumcision, they also practice the custom of circumcising their infant sons who die before they can be circumcised. Concerning this, in the aforementioned work of Rabbi Bechai <note>term: *Rabbi Bechai*; Bachya ben Asher, a 13th-century Spanish scholar</note>, folio 26, column 1, the following is read shortly after the preceding passage: "Therefore, all Israel has the custom regarding a dead child who did not reach the days for the commandment of circumcision, that they circumcise him at the grave, etc." <note>original Hebrew: על כן נהגו כל ישראל : לנער המת שלא הגיע ימי למצות מילה שממלהין אותו בקבר וגו'</note>.

We see from all the above that Rabbi Salman Zevi <note>term: *Salman Zevi*; Zalman Tzvi of Aufhausen, who wrote the *Jewish Theriac* in 1615 to defend Judaism against Christian attacks</note>, in the fourth chapter of his *Jewish Theriac*, number 5, folio 24, column 1, once again...
