Thus we place a vessel with dust during the time of circumcision to put the foreskin there..."</note> (This was said to show that the serpent caused Adam to sin, and thereby caused him to die and be forced to return to dust, as it is written in **Genesis 3:19**: **"For you are dust," etc.** For this reason, the serpent was punished in such a way that "like was repaid with like," and it must eat dust, as is written in **Isaiah 65:25**: **"And the serpent shall eat dust."** For this reason, we set out a vessel with dust at a circumcision, in order to place the foreskin, which has been cut off, into it. This is proven by an *argumentum a pari* <note>a Latin logical term meaning an "argument from analogy" or "by the same token"</note>, or a proof from similar cases; for it is written of the foreskins of the Philistines in **1 Samuel 18:27**: **"And they gave them in full number to the king"** <note>The German text clarifies this as delivering the full count of foreskins</note>; and in **Genesis 26:15**, it is written: **"And they filled them with earth."** The reason for this is that God commanded the foreskin to be cut off so that this specific member would be weakened, and the power of the serpent's impurity would be exhausted. Thus it is also written in **Proverbs 25:21**: **"If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat"** (or food). Therefore, we set out dust, which is the serpent's food.) Regarding this, one may also read in the aforementioned book <term>Zeror ha-Mor</term> <note>original: "Zerór hammór"; a 15th-century Torah commentary by Abraham Saba</note>, folio 19, column 1, in the <term>Parashah</term> <note>the weekly Torah portion</note> *Lech Lecha*, and folio 143, column 1, in the <term>Parashah</term> *Ki Tetze*; as well as in the <term>Yalkut Chadash</term> <note>original: "Jalkut chadaſch"; a 17th-century collection of mystical midrashim</note>, folio 121, column 3 and 4, numbers 10 and 16. It also appears in the <term>Zohar</term> <note>the foundational work of Jewish mysticism</note> regarding *Bamidbar* (the Fourth Book of Moses), in the 421st column, in the <term>Parashah</term> *Pinchas*: <note>original Hebrew: תקינו לשויה ערלה במנא דעפרא...; "They [the Sages] ordained that the foreskin be placed in a vessel of dust to fulfill: 'And the serpent’s food shall be dust.'"</note> That is: (Our Sages) have ordained that the foreskin should be placed in a vessel with dust, in order to confirm (the words of Isaiah 65:25) **"The serpent shall eat dust."**

<margin>Why the Jews are accustomed to set out a chair for Elijah at every circumcision.</margin>
Whenever a circumcision takes place among the Jews, they are also accustomed to always set out a chair for the Prophet Elijah so that he may sit upon it, and they say aloud: **"This is the chair of the Prophet Elijah."** Why this occurs is written in the 29th chapter of the <term>Chapters of Rabbi Eliezer</term> <note>original: "Capiteln des Rabbi Eliéſers," also known as Pirkei De-Rabbi Eliezer</note> as follows: <note>original Hebrew: עמד אליהו וברח...; "Elijah arose and fled, escaping from the Land of Israel... He replied: 'I have been very zealous [for the Lord God of Hosts, for the children of Israel have forsaken Your covenant]...' The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: 'You are always zealous...'"</note>

# How Christians are named by the Jews.

<margin>
Refutation of Rabbi Salman Zevi.

...that the aforementioned Brenz <note>Johannes Brenz, a 16th-century German Reformer</note> must have understood the words *Meám sar* <note>original: מעם זר; meaning "from a foreign people"</note> to mean *Mamzer* <note>A Hebrew term for a child born of an illicit relationship</note>. But this is a flippant and cunning malice from Rabbi Salman <note>Zalman Zvi of Aufhausen, a Jewish author who wrote a defense against anti-Semitic charges in 1615</note>, who, according to his habit, has sought all kinds of crafty excuses to gloss over and defend the Jews' malicious pieces. Thus, he also denied in that same place that *Mamzer* signifies a child of a harlot, and pretended instead that it means a foreigner. He attempted to prove this from Zechariah 9, verse 6, where it is read: "And a *Mamzer* shall dwell in Ashdod," where the word *Mamzer*, according to the opinion of some interpreters, means "foreigner." However, Rabbi Aben Esra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a 12th-century scholar</note> writes in his commentary on it as follows: "Rabbi Jehuda, the son of Bileam, said that it is the name of a nation; but in my opinion, it signifies a *Mamzer* born from forbidden unions" <note>original Hebrew: אמר ר' יהודה בן בלעם כי הוא שם לגוי ולפי דעתי שהוא ממזר מהעריות וגו'</note>. Likewise, Rabbi Levi ben Gersom <note>Also known as Gersonides, a 14th-century philosopher and commentator</note> writes in his interpretation of the Five Books of Moses, folio 332, column 4, in the section *Teze* <note>Parashat Ki Teitzei, a weekly Torah portion</note>, concerning the words of Deuteronomy 23, verse 2—"No *Mamzer* (that is, a child of a harlot) shall enter the assembly of the LORD"—in the following manner: "It is known that the offspring a man has from his wife is his child and is called a son. But whoever he has from a person with whom he has no marriage in any way is called a *Mamzer*, that is, a bastard" <note>original Hebrew: ידוע כי הולד שיהיה לאיש מאשתו הוא בנו והוא נקרא בן ואמנם מי שיש לו מבני שאין לו אישות בה בשום פנים הוא הנקרא ממזר</note>. So too teaches Rabbi Bechai <note>Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century Spanish scholar</note> in his frequently mentioned interpretation, folio 213, column 3, in the section *Ki Teze*: "The term *Mamzer* refers to one who is born from forbidden unions" <note>original Hebrew: לשון ממזר הוא מי שנולד מן העריות</note>. How then can Rabbi Salman Zevi deny that *Mamzer* means a child of a harlot?

### The Sixteenth Chapter of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked.

<note>original Hebrew: הרשעה באומרו הנה בימים הקדומים בהתחלת ענייניך לא היית מולך בכל העולם כי קטון נתתיך בגוים וגו'</note> ...the wicked one, saying: "Behold, in the days of old at the beginning of your affairs, you did not rule over the whole world, for I made you small among the nations," and so on. <margin>
XVIII. They call us the cursed people.

->Eighteenthly, they call us *ummah ha-mekulalah* <note>original: אומה המקוללה</note>, that<-
is, the **cursed people**, or *am ha-mekullal* <note>original: עם המקולל</note>, which has the exact same meaning. The first is found in **Abravanel’s** <note>Isaac Abravanel, a prominent 15th-century statesman and philosopher</note> book *Mashmia Jeshua* <note>The Announcer of Salvation</note>, folio 30, column 2, where the following is written concerning God’s vengeance against Christendom: <note>original Hebrew: תהיה נקמת השם יותר באומת אדום מבשאר האומות ולא תזכה אותה אומה המקוללת אל מה שיזכו האומות האחרות</note>—that is, the vengeance of God will come more upon the Edomite people than upon other peoples, and that cursed nation <note>original: ummah ha-mekulleleth</note> will not be worthy of that which other nations shall be worthy. # How the Christians are named by the Jews.
<note>Signature mark: SSSS 2</note>

16. verse 22 teaches: "If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be cursed." <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 16:22</note> So too, Rabbi Isaac Karo confesses in his interpretation of the Five Books of Moses, which is titled *Toledoth Jizchak* <note>original: "Toledoth Jizchak" means 'The Generations of Isaac'; Karo was a 15th-century Spanish scholar</note>, folio 109, column 2, in the portion *Ki Tavo* <note>The section of Deuteronomy containing the blessings and curses</note>, that all the curses of the Law have come upon the Jews, as he writes thus: <note>original Hebrew: לפי שנתארך הגלות הזה כל כך באו עליהם כל הקללות : והם שממנה תורה</note>—that is, "Because this captivity (among the Christians) has lasted so very long, all those curses which stand in the Fifth Book of Moses <note>Deuteronomy</note> have come upon them (namely, the Jews)."

<margin>XIX. They also call us Heretics.</margin>
Nineteenthly, they call us *Minim*, that is, **Heretics**; a single one, however, is called a *Min*. Concerning the origin of this name, Elias writes in his *Tishbi* <note>Elias Levita (1469–1549), a renowned Hebrew grammarian; his "Tishbi" was a dictionary of rabbinic Hebrew terms</note>, folio 53, column 2, as follows: <note>original Hebrew: נמצא בספרי היונים שהיה אדם אחד :</note>—"It is found in the books of the Greeks that there was a certain man who was called Manes <note>Mani, the 3rd-century founder of Manichaeism</note>, and had no religion, and all those who follow him are called *Minim* or Manichaeans (that is, heretics) after his name." The book *Ammude Golah* <note>“Pillars of the Exile,” a 13th-century legal code by Isaac of Corbeil</note>, folio 123, can also be consulted on this. And in the booklet *Michlam le-David*, on folio 81, column 2, it is read: <note>original Hebrew: ראש המינים שהיה כופר באחדות השם'ת' היה נקרא בשמו : מנו ועל שם אותו מנו קראו כל מי שכופר באחדות השם יתברך מין :</note>—that is, "The arch-heretic who denied the unity of the blessed God was called Manes, and after the name of this Manes, every person who denies the unity of the blessed God is called a *Min*."

<margin>On the various types of Heretics.</margin>
Rabbi Lipmann, however, teaches in his *Sepher Nizzachon* <note>"The Book of Victory," a famous 14th-century polemical work written to defend Judaism against Christian arguments</note>, number 76, page 46, how many types of *Minim* or heretics there are, and reports: <note>original Hebrew: אלו הן חמשה מיני מינים האחד אומר שאין נמצא אלוה ואין לעולם מנהיג : והשני אומר שישנו מנהיג אלא שישנו יותר על אחד : והשלישי שאומר שיש אחד אלא שהוא גוף ובעל תמונה : הרביעי שאומר שאינו לבדו ראשון וצור לכל : החמישי העובד אלהות זולתו להיות מליץ בינו ובין אדון כל :</note>—that is, "These are the five types of heretics. The first (type) says that there is no God and that no one rules the world. The second (type) says that there is indeed someone who rules, but that there are more than one. The third reports that there is indeed only one who rules, but that He has a body and a form. The fourth says that He alone is not the first and the rock of all things. The fifth, however, is the one who serves another deity so that the same might be an intercessor <note>A "mediator" or "advocate"; the author implies this category is used by Jewish writers to target the Christian belief in Jesus as mediator</note> between him and the Lord of all things."

<margin>Proof that we are called Heretics.</margin>
That we, however, are called *Minim* or heretics can be seen in the aforementioned book of Rabbi Lipmann, page 7, number 4, where he writes as follows concerning the words of Genesis 1, verse 1, "**In the beginning God created**": <note>original Hebrew: כאזני המינים לזכור בראשית</note>—"In the ears of the heretics, to mention 'In the beginning'..."

# Chapter 16 of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked.
<note>Heading: Des I. Theils des entdeckten Judenthums XVI. Capittel.</note>

<note>original Hebrew: וזהו ה"ש הנקרא ראשון והוא ברא אלהים ומפרשים הדבר על ישו הנוצרי</note> — "And this is the Name called 'First,' and He created God; and they interpret this matter as referring to Jesus the Nazarene." That is: Here the **Minim** <term>Minim: a Hebrew term for heretics, often used in rabbinic literature to refer to early Jewish-Christians or Gnostics</term> or heretics err, [believing] that by "the Beginning" <note>Referring to Genesis 1:1, "In the beginning..."</note> God is understood, who is called the First, and that He created God; which they interpret as referring to Jesus the Nazarene. So it is also written in the *Medrash Tillim* <note>A rabbinic commentary on the Psalms, also known as Midrash Tehillim</note>, folio 4, column 3, concerning the words of Psalm 2, verse 7 ("You are my son"): <note>original Hebrew: מכאן תשובה למינים שהם אומרים יש לו בן וגו'</note> — "From here is an answer against the **Minim**, that is, the heretics, who say that He (namely, God) has a son, etc."

The scholar Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a Jewish statesman and philosopher</note> also writes in his book *Markéveth hammishneh* <note>A commentary on Deuteronomy; the title means "The Second Chariot"</note>, folio 110, column 3, in the portion *Haazinu* <note>The "Song of Moses" in Deuteronomy 32</note>, regarding the words of Deuteronomy 32, verse 21 ("I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation"), in the following manner: <note>original Hebrew: כבר כתב : רבינו משה בר נחמן שזה נאמר על עשו שהיה נבל ולא זכר ברית אחים ויותר נראה לפרש נבל שהוא מין ואפיקורוס וזהו קראו הרומיים גוי נבל רוצה לומר גוי מין ונבל באמונתו שמאמין האלהות בבשר ודם : וכן דרשו בספרי בלא עם אלו הכותיים . וכן הוא אומר וישמעו צרי יהודה : בגוי נבל אלו המינים וכן הוא אומר אמר נבל בלבו אין אלהים :</note> — That is: "Our teacher Rabbi Moses bar Nachman <note>Nachmanides (1194–1270), also known as Ramban</note> has already written that this was said of Esau, who was a fool <note>Hebrew: 'Nabal'</note> and did not remember the brotherly covenant. But it seems to me more correct that the word 'foolish' should be interpreted as a **Min**, that is, a heretic, and an **Epicurus** <term>Epicurus: originally referring to the Greek philosopher, in Jewish usage it denotes a freethinker or one who denies divine revelation</term>; and in such a way the Romans (that is, the Christians) are called a foolish nation, meaning a heretical and foolish nation in their faith, who believe that the Godhead is flesh and blood (that is, a man). Likewise, in the book *Siphre* <note>An ancient legal commentary on Numbers and Deuteronomy</note>, the words 'By those who are not a people' are interpreted as the Cutheans <note>Samaritans</note>, according to what is said (Ezra 4, verse 1), 'Now when the adversaries of Judah heard.' But the words 'by a foolish nation' are understood to be the heretics, as it is said (Psalm 14, verse 1): 'The fools say in their heart, there is no God.'" These are the words of Abarbanel.

In the old *Nizzachon* <note>Sefer Nizzachon Yashar, a 13th-century anti-Christian polemical text</note>, it is also written concerning the words of Genesis 14, verse 18 ("And Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine, and he was a priest of God Most High"): <note>original Hebrew: אומרים המינים שהוא רמז לישו</note> — "The heretics say that it has a significance referring to Jesus." Similar things are found on pages 12, 17, 24, 37, 83, 116, and 126 in the aforementioned old *Nizzachon*; and on page 146, we are even called **Minim arúrim**, that is, **cursed heretics**, within that same book.

<margin>In particular, converted Jews are called heretics.</margin>

Specifically, those Jews who leave their religion are called **Minim**; for this reason, in the Talmudic tractate *Avoda sara* <note>"Foreign Worship," dealing with idolatry</note>, folio 26, column 2, in the *Tosephoth* <note>Medieval commentaries on the Talmud</note>, it is read: <note>original Hebrew: איזהו מין זה העובר ע"ז משמע דישראל משומד ל"ע נקרא מין :</note> — "Who is a **Min**? He who practices foreign worship; this implies that an Israelite who becomes an apostate <note>Hebrew: 'Meshumad'</note> is called a **Min**."

<note>Header: Wie die Christen von den Juden genennet werden.</note>

—that is: Who is a **Min** <term>Min: (plural Minim) a Hebrew term for a heretic or sectarian; in this context, the author notes it is applied specifically to those who "practice idolatry"</term> or heretic? The one who practices idolatry. This teaches us that an Israelite who has fallen away into idolatry is called a **Min**, regarding which more can be found in that same place. For this reason, the convert Nicolaus, in the disputation he held with Rabbi Jechiel, on pages 6, 8, 17, and 22, is called a **Min**, that is, a heretic; this name is also given to the convert Paul in the disputation he held with Rabbi Nachman <note>Referring to Nachmanides, a leading medieval Jewish scholar, in the Disputation of Barcelona (1263)</note>, on pages 42, 44, 49, and 60. And even though it is read in the aforementioned tractate *Avodah Zarah* <note>The Talmudic tractate dealing with "Strange Worship" or idolatry</note>, folio 26, column 2, in the *Tosephot* <note>Medieval commentaries on the Talmud</note>, as well as in the tractate *Chullin*, folio 13, column 2: <note>original Hebrew: אין מינים באומות</note> — "Among the nations (those living outside of Judaism) there are no **Minim**, or heretics"—one must not be misled by this, for they consider us all to be **Minim**, as has been clearly enough proven in the preceding pages.

<margin>20. They also call us **Copherim**, that is, Deniers</margin>
Twentiethly, they call us **Copherim** <term>Copherim: from the Hebrew 'Kofer,' meaning an infidel or one who denies a fundamental truth of faith</term>, that is, deniers—namely, of God and of the Divine Law. Rabbi Lipmann teaches in his *Sefer Nizzachon* <note>The "Book of Victory," a 15th-century Jewish polemical work intended to provide arguments against Christian claims</note>, number 76, page 46, how many kinds of **Copherim** there are, and writes as follows: <note>original Hebrew: חמשה מיני כופרים הן הא' כופר בתורה אפילו תיבה אחת : השני הכופר בפירושה והיא התורה שבעל פה כמו צדוק וביתוס : השלישי כמו הכותיים והישמעאלים : הרביעי הכופר בתחיית המתים : החמישי הכופר בביאת הגואל</note> — That is: There are five

<margin>How many kinds of deniers there are.</margin>
kinds of **Copherim**, or deniers. The first kind consists of those who deny the Law, even a single word of it. To the second kind belongs the one who denies the interpretation of the Law, that is, the Oral Law (which is contained in the Talmud), as Zadok and Boethus <note>Historical figures associated with the Sadducees, who rejected the Rabbinic Oral Law</note> did. The third kind consists of such people as the **Cutheans** <note>Historically the Samaritans; here the author claims it refers to Christians</note> and the **Ishmaelites** <note>Historically the Muslims</note> are (who teach that the Law of Moses has come to an end and another must be given in its place). To the fourth kind belongs the one who denies the resurrection of the dead. To the fifth, however, belongs the one who does not acknowledge the coming of the Redeemer (namely, the Messiah). We see from this, therefore, that we are held to be **Copherim** because we teach that the Old Testament has been abolished and the New Testament has been given in its place. It is also read in the old *Nizzachon*, page 181, that we are deniers of God because we believe that Christ the Lord is God; it stands there as follows: <note>original Hebrew: הם אומרים כי אלהים הוא אם כן הם כופרים בי' : שהרי כתוב בתורה ראו עתה כי אני אני הוא ואין אלהים עמדי אני אמית ואחיה מחצתי ואני ארפא</note> — that is: They (the Christians) say that he (namely, Christ) is God; but herewith they deny God, for behold, it stands written in the Law (Deuteronomy 32:39): "See now that I, even I, am he, and there is no god beside me. I kill, and I make alive; I wound, and I heal."

### Chapter 16 of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked.

They also consider us to be **Copherim** <term>Copherim: derived from the Hebrew root 'kafar,' meaning to deny or disavow; it refers to apostates or those who deny the foundational truths of the faith</term>, because—according to their teaching—we are devoted to idolatry. This is taught in the book *Markéveth hammiſchneh* <note>A commentary on the Mishneh Torah, likely by Isaac Abrabanel or a similar authority</note> on folio 43, column 3, in the Section *Re'eh* <note>The weekly Torah portion Deuteronomy 11:26–16:17</note>: <note>original Hebrew: העובד עבודה זרה ככופר בכל התורה כולה</note> that is, **"Whoever practices idolatry acts as if he denied the entire Law."** The same can be found in Rabbi Bachya's commentary on the Five Books of Moses, folio 198, column 2, in the Section *Ekev* <note>Deuteronomy 7:12–11:25</note>. In the aforementioned Rabbi Lipmann’s *Sepher Nizzáchon* <note>A famous 14th-century polemical work titled "The Book of Victory," written to refute Christian arguments</note>, one also reads concerning the words of Genesis 1:1, **"In the beginning God created:"** <note>original Hebrew: טעו הכופרים לדקדק אל ה: יחיד ומעתה אלהים לשון רבים</note> that is, **"The Copherim (namely, the Christians) err when they attempt to argue in a subtle manner that the word El (which means God) is singular or the individual number, but the word Elohím (which also means God, and is used in the cited place) is the pluralis numerus, or the multiple number."** <note>Christians often argued that the plural name for God, 'Elohim,' was proof of the Trinity; Lipmann argues here that this is a grammatical misunderstanding or a "denial" of God's unity.</note>

And on page 35, number 56, the said Rabbi Lipmann reports on the words of Genesis 15:2 <note>The author likely refers to Exodus 15:25 regarding the "wood" at Marah, though he cites Genesis</note>, **"And the Lord showed him a piece of wood,"** that the Christians say it was a cross, and he writes concerning it: <note>original Hebrew: והכופרים סמכו לדבריהם עץ בגימטריא צלם</note> that is, "And the **Copherim**, or Deniers, prove their statement because the word **Etz** <note>original: עץ</note> (which means wood) through Gematria <term>Gematria: A Kabbalistic method of interpreting Hebrew words by calculating the numerical value of their letters</term> makes **Zelem** <note>original: צלם</note> (which means an image or a cross); for each of them amounts to the number 160." In the same way, we are named in the first part of the Prague *Machzor* <note>A prayer book for festivals</note>, folio 34, column 1, in the commentary, where it is taught: <note>original Hebrew: כופרים היינו : אומה הרשעה</note> that is, **"The Copherim are the godless nation,"** by which the Christians are meant, as was reported above on page 689 regarding the seventeenth name they give us.

In addition to the above, it is also written in the book *Cad hakkémach* <note>"The Flour Jar," a work on ethics by Bachya ben Asher</note>, folio 78, column 2, concerning the words of Song of Solomon 7:11, **"Nalína bakkepharím,"** that is, **"Let us remain in the villages overnight,"** as follows: <note>original Hebrew: אל תקרי בכפרים אלא בכופרים אראך בני עשו שהשפעת להם טובה וכפרו בך</note> that is, **"Do not read 'bakkepharim,' that is, 'in the villages,' but rather 'bakkopherim,' that is, 'among the deniers.' I will show you the children of Esau <note>In rabbinic literature, 'Esau' or 'Edom' is the standard coding for the Roman Empire and, by extension, the Christian Church</note>, upon whom you have poured out good things, yet they deny you."** This is also found in the book *Avodáth hakkódeſch*, in the fourth part, in the 1st chapter, folio 121, column 4, and it is taken from the Talmudic tractate *Erúvin*, folio 21, column 2.

...and those who follow them are called **Minim** or **Minæans** <term>Minim: a Hebrew term for heretics or sectarians, frequently used in the Talmud to refer to early Judeo-Christians</term> and **Epicureans** <term>Epicurer/Apikoros: while derived from the Greek philosopher Epicurus, in Jewish law it refers to a heretic who treats the Torah or its scholars with contempt</term>. Isaac Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508) was a famous Portuguese Jewish statesman, philosopher, and biblical commentator</note>, however, teaches regarding this in his book *Rosh Amanah* <note>The Pinnacle of Faith</note>, folio 5, column 1, after he has presented the thirteen articles of faith of the Jewish religion: <note>original Hebrew: אם לא יאמין האדם אלה העקרים כלם כראוי : כבר יצא מן הכלל וכפר בעקר ונקרא מין ואפיקורוס וקוצץ בנטיעות וחייב אדם לשנאתו ולמאסו בו ולאבדו ועליו נאמר הלא משנאיך יי' אשנא</note> that is, **"If a person does not believe all these fundamental principles as is proper, he has already departed from the community [of Israel] and denied the root principle; he is called a Min (that is, a heretic) and an Epicurus (that is, an Epicurean), as well as 'one who cuts the plantings' <note>This is a Hebrew idiom for an apostate who causes damage within the 'garden' of faith; it is famously used in the Talmud regarding the sage Elisha ben Abuyah</note> (concerning which idiom and its meaning, one may read Rabbi Bachya in his commentary on the Five Books of Moses, folio 12, column 1, in the section *Bereshith*, and folio 111, column 1 and 2). One is also obligated to hate him, to despise him, and to remove him from our midst."** Of such a person it is also said (Psalm 139:21): **"Do I not hate those, O Lord, who hate You?"**

Rabbi Moses bar Maimon <note>Better known as Maimonides or Rambam (1138–1204)</note> agrees with this in his book *Pirkei Moshe* <note>The OCR reads "Báb o Mófe," likely a corruption of "Pirkei Moshe" (Aphorisms of Moses) or a specific chapter title</note>, page 169, and also reports on it in his book *Yad Chazakah* <note>The Strong Hand, also known as the Mishneh Torah</note>, in the fourth part, in the tractate *Mamrim* <term>Mamrim: the section of Jewish law dealing with "Rebels" or those who defy the authority of the high court</term>, chapter 3, section 1, folio 269, column 1, as follows: <note>original Hebrew: כי שאינו מודה בתורה שבעל פה אינו זקן ממרה האמור בתורה אלא הרי הוא בכלל האפיקורוסין</note> that is, **"He who does not acknowledge the Oral Law is not the 'rebellious elder' mentioned in the Law, but is instead included in the number of the Epicureans."** There are, however, said to be two kinds of Epicureans, as may be read in the *Talmudic tractate Sanhedrin*, folio 38, column 2, namely **a Gentile Epicurean** <note>original Hebrew: אפיקורוס גוי</note> **and an Israelite Epicurean** <note>original Hebrew: אפיקורוס ישראל</note>.

That we [Christians] are also named thus can be seen in the old *Nizzachon* <note>A Jewish polemical work written to defend Judaism against Christian missionary arguments</note>, where on page 186 it is written: <note>original Hebrew: הוי שקוד ללמוד תורה כדי שתשיב לאפיקורוס</note> that is, **"Be diligent to study the Law, so that you may answer the Epicurean,"** which words are taken from the previously mentioned place in the tractate *Sanhedrin*, namely folio 38, column 2. Who is meant by this is clearly shown by the words that follow, in which arguments are made against the Christians. Something similar is also found in the book *Chizzuk Emunah* <note>"Faith Strengthened," a 16th-century polemical work by Isaac ben Abraham of Troki</note>, page 9. Thus also Rabbi Lipmann begins his poem or song, which he calls *Sichron Sepher Nizzachon* <note>A Memorial of the Book of Victory</note>, and which he composed against the Christian religion, with these words: <note>original Hebrew: מה אשיב לאפיקורוס הבא : להאביד ולהרוס תורת שומרי אמונים ועל הייחוד מדבר גבוהים</note> that is, **"What shall I answer the Epicurean who comes to destroy and to demolish the Law of those who keep the faith (that is, the Jews), and speaks loftily against the Unity [of God]?"**

These (wicked) are the **Edomites**, as it is said (Malachi 1:4):

The same [people] mock the Israelites daily because of the tribulations that come upon them, etc. But God will repay them like for like, as it is said (Obadiah 1:15):

<margin>XXVI. They also call us the Erring.</margin>
**Twenty-sixthly, they call us** *Toim* <note>original Hebrew: תועים *Tóim*, meaning those who have gone astray or are lost</note>, **that is, the Erring;** as can be read in the book *Maggen Abraham* <note>The "Shield of Abraham," a polemical work by Abraham Farissol</note>, in the 73rd chapter, where it is written concerning the words of Isaiah 52:13, **"Behold, my servant shall deal prudently,"** as follows: **The Erring have interpreted this (Parasha) <note>A section of the Torah or prophetic books</note> as referring to their Messiah, etc. But Rabbi Joseph ben Caspi <note>A 14th-century philosopher and biblical commentator</note> dared to say that those who interpret this Parasha as referring to the King Messiah (who may come soon and in our days) are the cause of the Erring explaining the same as referring to Jesus.** Thus we are also named in the written commentary of Rabbi David Kimchi <note>A significant medieval grammarian and commentator, often called Radak</note> on Micah 5:2, as can be seen in the late Doctor Pococke's <note>Edward Pococke, a famous 17th-century English scholar of Oriental languages</note> *Miscellaneous Notes*, page 431, following Rabbi Moshe bar Maimon's <note>The great philosopher Maimonides</note> book *Babo Mose*. Beyond this, we are also called *Toe ruach* <note>original Hebrew: תועי רוח *Toë ruach*</note>, that is, **the Erring in Spirit**, in Abraham ibn Ezra's <note>A leading medieval scholar and astronomer</note> interpretation of Genesis 18 at the beginning, in the old Venetian edition, where it is read: **The erring in spirit say that God consists of three persons, that He is one and three, and that (the three) are not separated (or divided) from one another.** And in the same scholar's interpretation of Genesis 37:35, the Latin translator, who is called the *Vulgatus Interpres* <note>The Vulgate Translator, St. Jerome</note>, is named **The translator of the *Toim*, or the Erring.** <note>original Hebrew: המתרוגם לתועים *ha-meturgam la-to'im*</note>

<margin>XXVII. They also call us Scoffers.</margin>

> It is already known that the Gentile, while he is alive, is unclean and causes impurity because of the impurity <note>referring to an impure spirit</note> that dwells in him. For this is a foundation among us: that the graves of the *Goyim* <note>plural of Goy</note> (that is, of Christians or heathens) do not defile in a tent, because (in the mentioned passage of Numbers 19:14) it is said: 'When a man dies,' but the nations of the world are not called 'men.' For this reason, it is customary to guard the bodies of the dead so that no evil spirit may enter them; for these (evil spirits) desire to make their creation complete, in that they wish to become holy and thus perfect in the body in which a holy spirit has been. # How the Christians are named by the Jews.

<margin>
The Jews call a pig "another thing" and do not like to name it.
</margin>

Since a pig is supposed to be such a foul and unclean animal, even the Rabbis do not like to mention it even once by its proper name, but instead sometimes call it only *dávar ácher* <term>dávar ácher: Hebrew for "another thing"</term>. Therefore, in the Talmudic tractate *Berachoth*, folio 43, column 2, it is written: <note>original Aramaic: "תלה ליה קורא לדבר אחר ואיהו דידיה עביד"</note> that is, **Hang the tip of a palm branch upon the *dávar ácher*, that is, the other thing (namely the pig), and it will still do its own thing, namely wallow in the filth.** Elias <note>Elijah Levita (1469–1549), a famous Jewish scholar and lexicographer</note> writes in his *Tishbi*, folio 19, columns 1 and 2, regarding the word *dávar* <term>dávar: thing or word</term>, these words: <note>original Hebrew: "קורין לחזיר דבר אחר ונראה לי הטעם כדי שלא לזכור שמו בפני התינוקות וידרשו וישאלו עליו ויבאו לידי אכילה כמו שאין זוכרין שם לחם בפסח מטעם זה:"</note> that is, **A pig is called *dávar ácher*, and it seems to me that this is the reason: so that one does not mention its name in front of children, lest they ask about it and thereby come to eat of it; just as for this reason one makes no mention of bread during the Passover festival.** Thus, leprosy is also called *dávar ácher*, that is, the other thing, in the Talmudic tractate *Gittin*, folio 70, column 1. Otherwise, a pig is also called *othó* (or *ofó*) *min* <term>othó min: Hebrew for "that species" or "that kind"</term>, and it is read in the *Midrash Koheleth* <note>A rabbinic commentary on the Book of Ecclesiastes</note>, folio 326, column 4: <note>original Aramaic: "אכלין מן ההוא מינא"</note> that is, **They ate of that species.** This is explained in the commentary upon it, which is called *Mattenoth Kehunnah* <note>A widely used 16th-century commentary on the Midrash Rabbah by Issachar Berman ben Naphtali Ha-Kohen</note>, as follows: <note>original Hebrew: "אכלים מן אותו מין כלומר מבשר חזיר כמו שקורין אותו דבר אחר כן קורא אותו ההוא מין:"</note> that is, **They ate of *otho min*, that is, of that species, namely of pig's meat. Just as the pig is called *dávar ácher*, so it is also called *hahú min*, that is, that species.**

Swine's flesh is said to have been permitted in ancient times; it is permitted to Jews who go to war, and will also be permitted in the future.
</margin>

# How Christians are Named by the Jews.

...sets the bound (or captives) free; as it is written: <note>original Hebrew: מהו מתיר אסורים יש אומרים כל הבהמה שנטמאת בעולם הזה מטהר אותה הק"בה לעתיד לבא</note> that is, **What do the words "He sets the bound free" <term>Mattir asurim: A phrase from the daily Jewish liturgy; Eisenmenger interprets it here as "permitting things that were previously forbidden."</term> mean? Since pigs are mentioned here, I must also point out that the Prophet Daniel, according to the teachings of the Talmud, is said to have bought pigs in Egypt for King Nebuchadnezzar and brought them to Babylon. Concerning this, it is written in the Treatise *Sanhedrin*, folio 93, column 1: <note>original Hebrew: מעשה דעשו אלו אנשים שהיה להם מופת הוי אומר זה חנניה מישאל ועזריה. ודניאל להיכא אזל אמר רב למיברא נהרא רבא בטביריא ושמואל אמר לאיתויי ביזרא דאספסתא. ורבי יוחנן אמר לאיתויי חזירי דאלכסנדריא של מצרים איני והתניא חזוס הרופא אמר אין פרה וחזירה יוצאה מאלכסנדריא של מצרים שאין חותכין האם שלה בשביל שלא תלד. וטרי אייתי בלא דעתיה</note> that is: **Who are those men for whom a miracle occurred? Samuel said he had gone to fetch seeds (of a certain herb) for fodder (for the cattle). Rabbi Jochanan said (he had traveled) to bring pigs from Alexandria, which is in Egypt. How so? We have indeed learned in the Barajetha <term>Barajetha: A tradition from the Jewish oral law not incorporated in the Mishnah.</term> that Thodos the physician said that no cow or sow ever left Alexandria in Egypt without them cutting out its womb so that it could not give birth.** (To this, one must answer:) **He brought small pigs so that they (namely, the Egyptians) did not know it, and thus he led them away in secret.** If the pious and holy Prophet Daniel dealt with pigs in such a manner, then they surely cannot be such shameful and unclean animals as they are described and held to be by the Jews; otherwise, he would have had nothing to do with them. However, this is also one of the Talmudic untruths, for Daniel was not employed for such things.

<margin>Refutation of this accusation.</margin>
How can the foolish Jews consider *Christ* to be a dead God / since he suffered and died not according to his Divine / but according to his human nature / as was prophesied in *Isaiah chapter 53* / and the Godhead can neither suffer nor die? Beyond the above, more can be read concerning the idolatry of which Christians are accused by the Jews / in Abarbanel’s <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508) was a celebrated Jewish statesman, philosopher, and Bible commentator.</note> commentary on the prophet *Habakkuk, chapter 2, folio 272, column 4* / and in his book *Markéveth hammischne* <note>The Second Chariot, a commentary on Deuteronomy.</note>, *folio 21, column 1* / in the section *Vaethchannán* <note>The weekly Torah portion "And I besought".</note>, and *folio 77, column 2, 3* / in the section *Távo*, as well as in the old *Nizzáchon* <note>The *Sefer Nizzachon Yashar*, a medieval Jewish apologetic work written to refute Christian arguments.</note>, *page 135*.

<margin>Exposure of the deceitful statement of Rabbi Salman Zevi and its refutation.</margin>
We see thus from all this / how light-handedly the godless villain / *Rabbi Salman Zevi* <note>Zalman Zvi of Aufhausen, who wrote the "Jewish Theriac" in 1615 to defend Judaism against the attacks of the convert Samuel Friedrich Brenz.</note> in his *Jewish Theriac* <note>A "theriac" was a medicinal ointment or antidote; here it refers to a book meant to "cure" the "poison" of anti-Jewish accusations.</note> / in the second chapter / *number 31, folio 14, column 2* / has again denied the truth according to his custom / when he reports / that all Jewish legal scholars write / that Christians are not idolatrous people / in that they teach: <term>the Gentiles in this time are not idolaters</term> <note>original: גוים בזמן הזה לאו עובדי ע"ז הנה</note> : that is / the *Goyim* <note>A Hebrew term for "nations," often used to refer to non-Jews.</note> are not idolatrous at this time. It is indeed true / that such is written by the Rabbis / for which reason it is also read in the commentary of *Rabbi Menachem of Recanati* <note>A 13th-14th century Italian rabbi and kabbalist.</note> on the five books of Moses / *folio 203, column 1, 2* / in the section *Re'eh*: <term>Our Rabbis of blessed memory say, that the Goyim who are outside the (Holy) Land are not idolaters</term> <note>original: אמרו רז"ל גוים שבחוצה לארץ לאו עובדי ע"ז הן</note> : that is / Our Rabbis / of blessed memory / say / that the *Goyim*, who are outside the (promised) Land / are not idolatrous people. The same is found in the book *Col bo* <note>The *Kol Bo* is a large collection of Jewish ritual laws and customs from the medieval period.</note>, *folio 104, column 2, number 96* / under the title *Hilkhoth* (or Hilchos) *yen nesech* <note>Laws regarding wine used for libations or handled by non-Jews.</note>, and in the Talmudic tractate *Avoda Zara* <note>The tractate concerning "Foreign Worship" or idolatry.</note>, *folio 2, column 1* / in the *Tosafot* <note>Medieval commentaries on the Talmud.</note>, and *folio 81, column 4* / in Rabbi Asher’s commentary / as well as in the *Sefer Toledoth Adam ve-Chavva* <note>"The Generations of Adam and Eve," a legal work by Jeroham ben Meshullam.</note> *folio 158* / under the title *Nathif schifa asar, chelek chamischi*. ### Chapter XVI of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked.

(namely the Christian) Kingdom is described by the name "Dogs," it is because—as is well known—when many dogs pursue a man, and he is afraid of them and tries to flee, they will not leave him, but will cling to him. However, if he wishes to be freed from them, he must stand bravely still before them; then they will immediately leave him. So also does this Kingdom act; for all their desire and longing is directed toward making me stand against them and act according to their works; then they will not bark at me through their decrees. But because I turn away from them and flee from their ways, they surround me. **Abarnenel** <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a prominent Jewish statesman and theologian.</note> also gives us this title in his book *Majene jeschúa* <note>original Hebrew: מעייני הישועה *Ma'ayenei ha-Yeshu'ah*, meaning "Springs of Salvation," a commentary on the Book of Daniel.</note> folio 5, column 2, in the preface, where he reports that the Promised Land was once in the power of the **Edomites** <note>In medieval Jewish polemics, "Edom" was a common coded term for Rome and, by extension, the Christian Church.</note>—that is, the Christians—and another time in the power of the **Ishmaelites**—or the Turks <note>A common term for Muslims in early modern European texts.</note>—and writes thereupon: "They are all dumb dogs." <note>original Hebrew: כלה כלבים אלמים *Kullan kelavim illemim* (Isaiah 56:10).</note> We are likewise called "dogs" in the *Sépher hachájim* <note>The "Book of Life," a work on ethics and mourning.</note> of **Rabbi Chajim ben Bezaleel**, in the first part, in the second chapter, § 6.

<margin>

...found in the phrase <note>original: *Al hare béter* (הרי בחר), likely referring to "On the mountains of separation" from the Song of Solomon 2:17</note>, in which the destruction of four kinds of animals—namely bears, leopards, lions, and pigs—is prayed for, and in the **commentary** on it, it is written: <note>original: הם ד' מלכיות דוכים זה : פרס נמרים יון , אריות בבל , חזירים אדום</note> **That is: These (four types of animals) signify the four kingdoms (or monarchies). # Of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked, XVI. Chapter.

<note>original Hebrew: ונשותיהן שרץ ועל בנותיהן הוא אומר ארור שוכב עם כל בהמה</note> "And their wives are vermin <note>original: *Sheretz* (שרץ), meaning swarming creatures or insects</note>, and of their daughters He says: 'Cursed be he who lies with any animal.'" That is, they are a *Shekez*—an abomination—and their wives are vermin; of their daughters it is also said (in *Deuteronomy 27, v. 21*): **Cursed be he who lies with any kind of beast.** Most Jews, however, are *idiots* <note>In the 17th century, "idiot" referred to an unlearned or common person, rather than its modern clinical definition</note> and have not studied; for this reason, for the most part, they are to be considered abominations.

<margin>XXXVIII. They also sometimes call us "others."</margin>
Thirty-eighthly: they sometimes call us in their books by the word **אחרים** *acherim*, that is, "others"; this happens when they are hesitant to make explicit mention of Christians. An example of this is found in a small book printed in Amsterdam in the year 439 according to the Jewish reckoning—that is, the year 1679 according to our reckoning—called *Sepher Minhagim* <note>The "Book of Customs," a popular guide to Jewish rituals</note>. In this book, on folio 10, column 1, whenever the moon is addressed during the New Moon <note>This refers to *Kiddush Levanah*, the Sanctification of the Moon</note>, it is spoken to thus: <note>original Hebrew: ברוך יוצריך ברוך עושיך ברוך קוניך ברוך בוראיך כשם שאני מרקד כנגדיך ואיני יכול ליגע ביך כך אם ירקדו אחרים כנגדי לא יוכלו ליגע בי וגו'</note> **"Blessed be your Former, blessed be your Maker, blessed be your Possessor, blessed be your Creator. Just as I dance toward you and cannot reach you, so if *acherim*—that is, others—dance against me, they shall not be able to reach me, etc."** 

This same word *acherim* is also read in the Amsterdam Talmud in *Massecheth Sopherim* <note>Tractate Sopherim (Scribes), one of the minor tractates of the Talmud</note>, folio 14, column 2, at the beginning of the twentieth chapter. However, in many prayer books, in its place stands **כל אויבי** *col oyefai*, that is, "all my enemies," by which they mean the Christians, whom they consider their enemies, as was proven above in Chapter 15. Furthermore, in the Talmudic tractate *Sanhedrin* <note>The tractate dealing with legal procedures and capital crimes</note>, on folio 52, column 2, concerning the words in *Leviticus 20, v. 10*: **"A man (or one) who commits adultery with a man's wife, who commits adultery with his neighbor's wife, shall surely be put to death,"** it is taught thus: <note>original Hebrew: תנו רבנן איש פרט לקטן : אשר ינאף את אשת איש פרט לאשת קטון אשת רעהו פרט לאשת אחרים</note> **"Our Rabbis teach: (Through the word) 'A man,' a minor is excluded. (And through the words) 'who commits adultery with a man's wife,' the wife of a minor is excluded. (Through the words) 'With his neighbor's wife,' a wife of the *acherim*—that is, of the 'others'—is excluded."**

### Chapter XVI of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked.

...mistress, the godless **Lilith** (or Lilis) <note>In Jewish folklore, Lilith is a demonic figure, often depicted as the first wife of Adam who became a bringer of disease and a threat to children</note> in his heart, who with her foreskin hides and covers the holy covenant <note>The "holy covenant" refers to the *Brit Milah* or circumcision; the author is interpreting mystical texts to suggest that the "uncircumcised" nature of Christians is spiritually demonic</note>, according to the secret of the words in Proverbs 30:23: *And a maidservant when she becomes heir to her mistress.* (As also the words of verse 22): *A servant when he becomes king.* And this is the mystery of that which is written in Psalm 137:7: *Lord, remember the children of Edom on the day of Jerusalem, who said, "Lay it bare, lay it bare," (namely the city of Jerusalem) even to its foundation.* The meaning of these words consists in this: that the **Messiah, the son of Joseph** <note>In Jewish eschatology, the *Mashiach ben Yosef* is a precursor to the final Messiah; he is expected to lead the armies of Israel in a great war and die in battle</note>—who is to be the first Messiah—will, out of divine zeal, lead a mighty war against the **Edomites** <note>The "Edomites" in this context is a common code in medieval Jewish literature for the Roman Empire and the Christian world</note>, that is, the Christians, who have inflicted all suffering upon them and persecuted them like **Haman** <note>The villain of the Book of Esther who sought to exterminate the Jewish people</note>. **This name** <note>original Hebrew: זה השם, *zeh ha-shem*</note> that is / This word is derived from (that which is written in Esther 7:4 /) **le-hashmid** <note>original Hebrew: להשמיד</note>, that is / **to destroy** / **le-harog** <note>original Hebrew: להרוג</note> **to kill** / **u-le-abbed** <note>original Hebrew: ולאבד</note> **and to cause to perish**. This term historically refers to an apostate, often specifically one who converted under duress, though Eisenmenger emphasizes the meaning of "one who is destroyed."</note> (that is / **one destroyed** / from the preceding word *hashmid*, which means to destroy /) because actually those who fell away began [to be called so] at the time of the **Shemad**, i.e., persecution (or destruction). They (the apostates), however, have been called **Meshummadim** (or *Meshummodim*) / which means as much as / they have changed (their religion) at the time of the **Shemad** or persecution: (whereby it is intended to indicate / that they have been called *Meshummadim* because of the *Shemad*, that is / the persecution or destruction.) ### How Christians are named by the Jews. 727

However, <term>Rabbi Saadia</term> <note>Saadia Gaon (882–942), a foundational figure in medieval Jewish philosophy.</note> teaches in his *Book of Beliefs and Opinions* <note>original: "Sèpher haëmúnoth vehadeóth"</note>, folio 29, column 2, that even someone who—in just one single commandment—always and intentionally disagrees with others, is called a <term>Meshummad</term>, stating: <term>An apostate is one who has made it a rule for himself to always dispute even a single commandment, and our ancients call him a Meshummad.</term> <note>original Hebrew: המומר הוא מי ששם לעצמו חוק לחלוק על מצוה אחת תמיד וקדמונינו קוראים אותו משומד</note> That is / a defiant person is one who has taken it upon himself as a custom (or law) to be constantly in conflict with a commandment: our elders, however, call such a person a <term>Meshummad</term>. Thus, the word <term>Meshummad</term> does not only signify one who has entirely left the Jewish religion and accepted another, but also one who is still a Jew but acts against the Jewish faith in one or more points, as can be seen in what follows.

### How Christendom is Named by the Jews. 735

"The children of Edom, who proceed from the arm of Esau" <note>original: *Bnei Edom ha-yotzim mi-zro'o shel Esau*</note>: That is, [Targum] Jonathan <note>The Targum Jonathan is an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Prophets.</note> has everywhere translated the words "Mount Seir"—wherever they are written in the prophecies—as "the great city of Esau." It is without doubt true that this refers to Rome, the princess of provinces, which is in the power of the children of Edom (that is, the Christians), who descend from the seed of Esau.

<margin>She is also called Nineveh.</margin>Furthermore, she is also called Nineveh, and it is written in the booklet called the *Book of Zerubbabel* <note>An apocalyptic Hebrew text likely written in the 7th century.</note> that Zerubbabel said: "And a wind carried me between the heaven and the earth and brought me to Nineveh, the city of blood, etc. And I asked the man (namely, the angel Metatron <note>A powerful angel in Jewish mystical tradition who acts as a celestial scribe and guide.</note>, who spoke with me) what the name of this place was; and he said to me: 'This is Great Rome.'" <note>original: *Va-tissa'eni ruach bein ha-shamayim u-vein ha-aretz va-tevi'eni le-Ninueh ir ha-damim... va-eshal le-ish mah shem ha-makom ha-zeh, va-yomer elai zot hi Roma rabbata.*</note> In what follows, one further reads: "This city is Nineveh, the city of blood, and it is Great Rome." <note>original: *Ha-kerach ha-zeh hu Ninueh ir ha-damim ve-hi Roma rabbata.*</note>

<margin>Thus she is also called the godless or wicked Rome.</margin>Finally, she is also called *Romi ha-resha'ah*, that is, "the godless Rome," or *Romi chayaveth*, that is, "the wicked Rome." The name *Romi ha-resha'ah* is found in the book *Pesikta Rabbati* (or *Rabbesa*), folio 63, column 1; where, concerning the words of Isaiah 61:10—"I will greatly rejoice" <note>original: *Sus asis*</note>, meaning I will rejoice exceedingly—it is written: "I will rejoice in the days of the Messiah; I will rejoice over the fall of *Romi ha-resha'ah*," that is, of godless Rome. <note>original: *Sus be-yemot ha-Mashiach asis be-mappaltah shel Romi ha-resha'ah.*</note> And in the book *Kad Ha-Kemach* <note>A work on Jewish ethics by Bahya ben Asher.</note>, regarding the words of Isaiah 33:23—"Thy tacklings are loosed"—it is read: "This is said concerning the godless Rome." <note>original: *Zeh ne'emar al Romi ha-resha'ah.*</note> She is also called by this name in the book *Mayene Yeshuah*, folio 52, column 3 (in the ninth *Mayan*, second *Tamar*), and in the Prague *Machzor* <note>A prayer book for Jewish holidays.</note>, in the first part, folio 34, column 2, in the commentary. However, in the book *Emek Ha-Melech*, she is called *Gapim ha-resha'ah* (the godless Gapim) three times on folio 49, column 4, and four times on folio 40, column 1. The word *Gapim* (גפ"ם), through the swapping of letters according to the *Atbash* alphabet <note>A substitution cipher where the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet is replaced by the last, the second by the second-to-last, and so on.</note> mentioned previously, signifies the same as *Romi*, that is, Rome. ### 756 Part I of Judaism Unmasked, Chapter XVII.

When he reached it, he took water from the Euphrates and mixed it with clay, and they built them, and they stood. From that time on, it was a proverb: Any province that does not have an Abba Kolon does not deserve the name of a province. And they called it Rome Babylon." <note>original: *Romi Bablon*</note>. This means: Rabbi Levi said: In the same day that Solomon took Pharaoh Necho's daughter as a wife, Michael, the great prince, came down from heaven and stuck a large reed into the sea, and moisture (or a moist silt) rose up on all sides of it, through which it became like a forest; and that was the place of Rome (where this city was built). Then the Despised One, the *Malchuth Esav*—that is, the Kingdom of Esau—rose up in its place, as it is said (in Obadiah 1, verse 2, regarding Edom): 'You are greatly despised.' For the Romans took the kingdom from the Greeks."

# The 17th Chapter of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked. #

<margin>
For this reason they also call their present misery the Esauite Misery.
</margin>
Misery <note>original: גלות *Galúth* (or *Gólus*)</note> of Esau, that is, the Esauite Misery, as can be seen in the small *Yalkut Reuveni* <note>A 17th-century collection of Kabbalistic midrashim</note>, number 11, under the heading *Gehinnom* <note>the Rabbinic term for Hell or Purgatory</note>, where the words read as follows: <note>original: יצחק אבינו ע״ה היה צופה כל העתיד לבא וראה בני יעקב חוטאים וירשו גיהנם וכשראה יצחק ישראל בגלות עשו שמח ואמר גלות מכפרת עון וגו׳</note> that is, "Our father Isaac, peace be upon him <note>original: ע״ה (*a.h.*), an abbreviation for *alav ha-shalom*</note>, foresaw everything that was to happen in the future and saw that the children of Jacob would sin and inherit Hell. But when Isaac saw the Israelites in the *Galuth Esav* or Esauite Misery, he rejoiced and said: 'The misery <note>or exile</note> atones for the sin,' etc." Something similar can also be found in the aforementioned *Yalkut*, number 7, under the title *Olam ve-olam habba* <note>This world and the world to come</note>.

<margin>
What reasons the Jews bring forward for being in exile or misery.
</margin>
Since the Jewish misery is mentioned here, I must also indicate what reasons they write for it, and various ones are found. In the *Yalkut Chadash* <note>A 17th-century compendium of Midrashic literature</note>, folio 84, column 2, number 16, it says that the Jews had to come into misery under Esau's descendants because Jacob said to Esau (as seen in Genesis 32:4), **"Your servant Jacob:"** and there it is written as follows: <note>original: כשאמר יעקב לעשו עבדך יעקב אמר הק״בה לא דייך שעשית עצמך קודש חול אלא אני אמרתי ורב יעבוד צעיר אתה אומר עבדך יעקב חייך כדבריך יהיה הוא ימשול בך בע״הז ואתה תמשול בו לעולם הבא</note> that is: When Jacob said to Esau, **"Your servant Jacob,"** then the Holy One, blessed be He <note>original: הק״בה (*hakadosh baruch hu*)</note>, spoke to him: "Is it not enough for you that you made yourself, who are holy, unholy <note>or profane</note>? I said, **'The elder shall serve the younger'** (as read in Genesis 25:23), and yet you say to Esau, **'Your servant Jacob.'** I swear by your life that it shall go according to your words: he will rule over you in this world, but you shall have dominion over him in the world to come."

In the following number 19, another reason is shown, namely, because Jacob acted deceitfully with Esau, and the words read as follows: <note>original: כמה יש לו לאדם לילך בדרך ישרה שהרי יעקב ע״י שנטל הבכורה מעשו ברמיאות לכך לא ניתן רשות לשום אומה להשתעבד בזרעו כי אם זרעו של עשו</note> that is: "How much should a man strive to walk the right path (that is, to act uprightly), for see, because Jacob took the right of the firstborn from Esau through deceit, no nation has been given the power to bring his (Jacob’s) descendants into servitude except for the seed (or descendants) of Esau."

In the aforementioned *Yalkut Chadash*, folio 47, column 3, number 19, under the title *Galuth* <note>Exile</note>, the same is attributed to the selling of Joseph into Egypt.

# Chapter 17 of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked.

...Edomite Captivity. The words **"And a flame of fire"** signify *Galúth Edom*, that is, the Edomite Captivity. The same can be read on folio 37, column 3, in the *Parashah* <note>the weekly Torah portion</note> *Vayéze*, in the aforementioned book *Zerór hammôr* <note>"A Bundle of Myrrh," a 15th-century commentary by Abraham Saba</note>. And in Abarbenel’s <note>Don Isaac Abarbenel, a prominent 15th-century statesman and philosopher</note> commentary on the prophet Obadiah, it is taught on folio 256, column 1: <note>original Hebrew: "Kol Yisrael she-hem hayom beyedei ha-Yishme’elim ve-ha-Notzrim le-galut Romi ve-Edom yehashevu."</note> that is, **All Israelites who are today under the power of the Turks <note>original Hebrew: "Ishmaelites"</note> and the Christians <note>original Hebrew: "Nazarenes"</note> are counted as belonging to the Roman and Edomite captivity.** Likewise, in the same author's commentary on Isaiah, folio 38, column 1, regarding Isaiah 21, verse 11, the following is written: <note>original Hebrew: "Hineh ha-nevu’ah ha-zot efshar le-farshah kefi derekh Hazal al zeh ha-galut she-anachnu bo she-hu galut Edom ve-kara’o Dumah lefi she-anachnu bo domemim ve-shotekim ki lo neda mati ketz ha-pela’ot."</note> that is: **Behold, one can interpret this prophecy according to the manner of our Sages (of blessed memory) as referring to this captivity in which we now find ourselves, which is the Edomite Captivity. However, the prophet called the same "Duma" (which means a silence), because we remain silent within it, for we do not know the end of the wonders <note>meaning the time when the promised miracles of redemption will occur</note>.**

<margin>
VI. They also call Christendom "The Red One."
</margin>
Sixthly, they call Christendom *Admon*, that is, **the Red One**, and this is for the reason that Esau—from whom the Christians are said to descend—is called *Admóni*, that is, **the Ruddy** or **the Red**, as was indicated above on page 649. That they are named in this way can be seen in the prayer found in the *Machsor* <note>a festival prayer book</note> under the title *Músaph lejom ríschon schel rosch haschána* <note>the additional service for the first day of the New Year</note>, which begins *Essa deï bezédek*. In this prayer, the Jews call upon GOD to *leröea Admon*, that is, **to break the Red One**. In the Prague *Machsor*, in the first part, folio 36, column 2, the word *Admon* is explained in the commentary as: <note>original Hebrew: "Esau she-nikra Admoni"</note> that is, **Esau, who is called Admóni, the Red.** By Esau, however, Christendom is understood, as was indicated above on pages 739 and 740.

<margin>
VII. They call the same the Kingdom of Edom and Amalek, or even just Amalek.
</margin>
Seventhly, it is called *Malchúth Edom ve-Amalek*, that is, **the Kingdom of Edom and Amalek**, or the Edomite and Amalekite Kingdom; or even simply **Amalek**. The name *Malchúth Edom ve-Amalek* is read in the *Sépher ha-Emunóth* <note>"The Book of Beliefs" by Shem-Tov ben Shem-Tov</note> on folio 78, column 2, in the fifth chapter of the seventh *Sháar* <note>section or "gate"</note>, where it is written: <note>original Hebrew: "Hineh Yonadav ben Rechav keshe-ra’ah hurban ha-mikdash ve-ha-galut u-memshelet ha-malkhuyot ve-atid lavo ve-lakum malkhut Edom ve-Amalek tzivah et banav ki lo yeshvu rak be-ohalim dirat arai."</note> that is: **Behold, when Jonadab the son of Rechab (of whom mention is made in Jeremiah 35, verses 6 and 7) saw the destruction of the Temple, the captivity, and the dominion of the kingdoms, and that in the future the Kingdom of Edom and Amalek would come and arise, he commanded his sons that they should only dwell in tents, as a temporary dwelling.**

# Chapter XVII of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked.

...future war / as it is written in (Zechariah 14, v. 3): **But the Lord will go out / and fight against those same heathens / just as he is accustomed to fight / at the time of battle / against Amalek.** <note>The author cites Zechariah to link historical battles against Amalek with a predicted final battle against the "heathen" nations.</note> But to point toward the future war / it (namely the Scripture) says here: **Against Vaheb in Supha.** <note>A difficult phrase from Numbers 21:14. Furthermore, in the aforementioned book *Zerór hammór* <note>original: "Bundle of Myrrh," a late 15th-century Torah commentary by Rabbi Abraham Saba.</note> folio 123, columns 2 and 3, in the Torah portion *Vayera Balak* <note>The section of the Pentateuch beginning at Numbers 22:2, containing the story of the prophet Balaam.</note>, the following is read regarding the previously mentioned war:

Because Amalek was the chief of the adversaries and waged war against Israel when they went out from Egypt, and is destined to wage war in the end of days, it says: "And he looked on Amalek, and he took up his parable, and said, Amalek was the first of the nations; but his latter end shall be that he perish everlastingly" <note>Numbers 24:20</note>. This means his end will reach until that time when the King Messiah shall come; then that which is written shall be fulfilled: "The destructions of the enemy are come to a perpetual end" <note>Psalm 9:7</note>, referring to that eternity described by the prophets. "Thou hast destroyed cities"—this refers to that which is said: "And he shall destroy the remnant from the city" <note>Numbers 24:19</note>. "Their memorial is perished with them"—this refers to what is written here: "And his end is to perish everlastingly," in the sense that their memory shall vanish and their fame shall cease, from man to woman, from the older children to the infants, so that everything shall be rooted out and destroyed.

That is: Because Amalek was the chief enemy / and waged war against Israel / when they marched out of Egypt / and will also wage war (against them) in the last days / so the Scripture says (*Numbers* 24, verse 20): **And when he** (namely Balaam) **saw the Amalekites / he began his proverb / and said: Amalek is the first among the heathens / but his end is to destruction.** That is / his descendants will survive until that time / in which the King Messiah shall come / then that which is written (*Psalm* 9, verse 7) shall be completed: **The destructions of the enemy have an end in eternity** / which is to be understood as that eternity / which is described by the prophets. **You have overturned the cities** / this is (that which is said in *Numbers* 24, verse 19:) **And what remains of the cities / he shall kill.** (Furthermore follows *Psalm* 9, verse 7:) **Their memory is perished along with them;** this aims at that which is written (in the aforementioned place *Numbers* 24, verse 20): **But his end is to destruction** / in that their memory shall pass away / and their reputation / from the man to the woman / and from the older children to the infants / shall come to an end / so that everything shall be rooted out and annihilated.

We see thus from the above words of the book *Zerór hammór*, that the war / which shall be waged in the latter times / by the supposed Messiah against Christendom / is the very same war / which shall be waged against Amalek and Edom / from which it is reasonably to be concluded / that by Amalek, Christendom is understood. <note>The author argues that when Jewish texts speak of destroying "Amalek" at the end of time, they are using it as a coded reference to the Christian world.</note>

Thus far reaches the Edomite exile and the redemption of Israel.

# How Christendom is named by the Jews.

—but none of the seed of <term>Esau</term> <note>In Jewish tradition, Esau, the brother of Jacob, is viewed as the ancestor of the Roman Empire and, subsequently, the Christian world.</note> shall remain among them; instead, they shall be wiped out from the world, according to what is written (Exodus 17, v. 14): **For I will utterly blot out the remembrance of Amalek.** All of this clearly shows that in the final war, which will be waged against Esau—that is, against Christendom—the memory of <term>Amalek</term> <note>The Amalekites were the biblical archetypal enemies of Israel; here, the author argues that Jewish writers use "Amalek" as a coded reference to Christians.</note> shall be blotted out, and through the total extermination of the Christians, Amalek shall be rooted out. From this, it necessarily follows that Christendom is understood by the name Amalek: something regarding this can also be found in <term>Rabbi Moshe bar Nachman’s</term> <note>Also known as Nachmanides (1194–1270), a leading medieval Jewish scholar and philosopher.</note> commentary on the five books of Moses, folio 56, column 3, in the Torah portion <term>Beshallach</term>.

Beyond this, Christendom is called *Adina* by the Jews, which means "the Voluptuous," as can be seen later in this chapter under the twenty-fourth name they give to it. In the Prague <term>Machsor</term> <note>A prayer book used by Jews for the High Holy Days and festivals.</note> however, in the second part, folio 11, column 1, the words *shachach shem Adina*, that is: "Make the name of Adina to be forgotten," are explained in the commentary as follows: <note>original Hebrew: שכח שם עמלק מן העולם והוא נקרא עדינה על שם שמתעדנת מן ממון ישראל</note> that is: "Cause the name of Amalek to be forgotten from the world; he is called Adina because he indulges in luxury and pleasure using the wealth of the Israelites." Similarly, the chief devil <term>Sammaël</term>, who—as indicated in the 18th Chapter of this first part—is said to rule over Christendom, is not only called *Sar Esau*, that is, the Prince Esau, and *Sar Edom*, that is, the Prince of Edom, as well as *Saro shel Romi*, that is, the Prince of Rome, or the Prince of the Roman Empire, but is also called *Sar Amalek*, that is, the Prince of Amalek, as is indicated in the aforementioned 18th chapter of this first part. Furthermore, in the book *Lefarjeh*, folio 52, column 4, the *Chajath kane*, that is, the "beast in the reeds" or "beast of the marsh" (by which Christendom is understood, as can be seen below under the twenty-eighth name in this chapter), is also called Amalek, and the words there read as follows:

In the tractate *Berachóth* (or *Beróchos*) <note>A volume of the Talmud dealing with blessings and prayers.</note> folio 61, column 2, it is to be read, where the words go as follows: <note>original Hebrew: פעם אחת גזרה מלכות הרשעה שלא יעסקו ישראל בתורה בא פפוס בן יהודה ומצאו : לרבי עקיבא שהיה מקהיל קהלות ברבים ועוסק בתורה א"ל עקיבא אי אתה מתירא מפני מלכות הרשעה וגו'</note> that is, "Once the <term>Malchúth harescháa</term> <note>The Wicked Kingdom.</note> or godless Empire, had issued a decree that the Israelites should not study the Law. Then <term>Papus ben Jehúda</term> came and found <term>Rabbi Akkíva</term> <note>A famous 2nd-century Jewish sage.</note> holding public gatherings and studying the Law. He said to him: 'Akiva, are you not afraid of the *Malchúth harescháa*—that is, the godless Empire?'" And in the tractate *Schabbath* (or *Schábbas*) <note>The Talmudic tractate concerning the Sabbath.</note> it is written on folio 16, column 1: <note>original Hebrew: ק"פ שנה עד שלא חרב הבית פשטה מלכות הרשעה על ישראל</note> that is: "One hundred and eighty years before the Temple was destroyed, the *Malchúth harescháa*, or godless Empire, spread over **Israel**." This means, as <term>Rabbi Salomon Jarchi</term> <note>Commonly known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator on the Bible and Talmud.</note> explains in his commentary, that it began to subjugate the Israelites. 

But so that one may know what kind of empire is understood by the "godless Empire," the aforementioned Rabbi Solomon writes in his cited commentary: <note>original Hebrew: מלכות הרשעה רומי</note> "The godless Empire signifies **Rome**, or the Roman Empire." All of this is also found in the tractate *Avóda fára* <note>The tractate concerning "Strange Worship" or idolatry.</note> folio 8, column 2, in both the text and the commentary. Likewise, this name is found on folio 9, column 1 of the same tractate *Avóda fára*; in the tractate *Pesachím* folio 118, column 2; in the book *Nèzach Jifraèl* folio 31, columns 1 and 2, in the 21st chapter; and in *Pesíkta rábbertha* (or *rábbesa*) folio 28, column 2; as well as in the *Jalkut Schimóni* regarding the five books of **Moses**, folio 2, column 4. And in the Talmudic tractate *Gittín* <note>The tractate concerning divorce and legal documents.</note> it stands on folio 57, column 2, as follows: <note>original Hebrew: ידי עשו זו מלכות הרשעה שהחריבה את ביתנו ושרפה את היכלנו והגלתנו מארצנו</note> that is (referring to the words of Genesis 27:22): "But the hands are **Esau's** hands; these signify the *Malchúth harescháa*, that is, the godless Empire, which destroyed our House, burned our Temple, and led us from our land into captivity."

The name <term>Malchús marsháas</term> <note>The evilly-acting or wicked kingdom.</note> appears in the *Benschbuch* <note>A book containing the "Birkat Hamazon" or Grace After Meals, along with other prayers and songs.</note> folio 20, column 1, under the title *Semiróth lemozáe schabbath* <note>Songs for the departure of the Sabbath.</note>, in a prayer that begins <term>Afai májim schetafúni</term> <note>original: אזי מים שטפוני; "Then the waters overwhelmed me."</note>, with these words: <note>original Hebrew: רבולי ימי לוחצי ביד מלכות מרשעת כואן עוד מנוח קצי. והפרות לא נוערה</note> that is: "The days of my oppressors last long in the power of the *Malchúth marsháas*, that is, the godless or wickedly acting Empire, so that I can no longer count (or calculate) my end (meaning the end of my misery); and the redemption is unknown, as to when it shall occur."

As for the name <term>Malchús chajéves</term> <note>The Guilty Kingdom.</note>, it is found in the book *Cad hakkémach* <note>A work on Jewish ethics and philosophy by Bahya ben Asher (13th century).</note> folio 7, column 2, where the words read as follows: "No man knows what..."

that is: **"The gold signifies Babylon"** (or the Babylonian Empire), for in Daniel 2:32 it is said: **"The head of this image [was of fine gold]..."**

# Chapter XVII of the First Part of Judaism Unveiled.

<margin>Called the Kingdom and the Haughty Dominion.</margin>
*Memsheleth zadon* <note>original: "ממשלת זדון"</note> (or *Memsheles zodon*), that is, the **haughty dominion**, or the **proud rule**. The name *Malkhuth zadon* <note>original: "מלכות זדון"</note> [Haughty Kingdom] is found in the book *Tzeror ha-Mor* <note>A Torah commentary by Abraham Saba, a 15th-century scholar who experienced the expulsions from Spain and Portugal.</note>, Cracow edition (for in the Venice edition, an empty space was left for it <note>This suggests censorship or caution by the printers in Venice regarding anti-Christian content.</note>) folio 4, column 1, regarding the words of David in Psalm 124, verses 2, 3, 4, and 5, where it is written as follows:

<note>original Hebrew: רמז המשורר אלו המלכיות במקום אחר כאומרו לולי ה' שהיה לנו בקום עלינו אדם זה רמז לגלות בבל וגו' : אזי חיים בלעונו בחרות אפם בנו כנגד גלות מדי וגו' : אזי המים שטפונו כנגד גלות יון וגומר : אזי עבר על נפשנו המים הזדונים כנגד מלכות אדום שהיא מלכות זדון כאומרו בו כי זדון לבך השיאך וזהו המים הזדונים ואמר גם כן אזי עבר על נפשנו לפי שדעתם גם כן להעבירנו על דת ולצור נפשותינו כמו שראינו בעינינו בגירוש פורטוגל :</note>

That is: The Psalmist alluded to these four kingdoms in another place when he said (Psalm 124:2): **"If it had not been the Lord who was on our side, when men rose up against us;"** this alludes to the Babylonian captivity, etc. (The following words in verse 3): **"Then they would have swallowed us up alive, when their wrath was kindled against us;"** these refer to the Median captivity, etc. (And the words in verse 4): **"Then the waters would have overwhelmed us;"** these aim at the Greek captivity, etc. (The following words, however, in verse 5): **"Then the proud waters would have gone over our soul;"** these concern the Edomite kingdom <note>In this context, "Edom" is a common rabbinic code for the Roman Empire and, by extension, Christendom.</note>, which is the *Malkhuth zadon*, that is, the **haughty kingdom**, as it is said of it (Obadiah 1:3): **"The pride of your heart has deceived you;"** and this is the "proud water." Thus he also says (namely David in the cited verse 5), that it would have "gone over our soul," because their (meaning the Christians') intention is also to make us fall away from our religion and to trap our souls, as we saw with our own eyes in the expulsion from Portugal <note>Referring to the forced conversions and expulsion of Jews from Portugal in 1497.</note>.

<margin>Further proof that Christendom is called the haughty kingdom.</margin>

<note>original Hebrew: א"ל שאת זו בבל וגו' ספחת זו מלכות מדי וגו' בהרת זה יון וגו' והיה בעור בשרו לנגע זו מלכות זדון שהשם יתברך מלקה אותו בצרעת ואת השר שלו שנאמר מדוע אביריך נסחף בחחף כמו נספח :</note>

That is: Our (Sages), of blessed memory, say: the "rising" signifies Babylon (that is, the Babylonian Empire), etc. The "scab" signifies the Median Empire, etc. The "bright spot" signifies Greece (or the Greek Empire). ...will be lacking, and what remains is <note>original: ע״ש וישב — an abbreviation related to the phrase "and he dwelt"</note> that is: In the last days, the **Malchúth Achum** <term>Malchúth Achum: "Kingdom of the Worshipers of Stars and Planets," a coded term often used in Jewish texts to refer to the Christian world to avoid censorship</term>, that is, the Kingdom of those who worship the stars and planets (or the worshipers of Christ and Mary), shall be completely rooted out. And just as Jacob's hand held the heel of **Esau** (as can be read in **Genesis** 25:26, which signifies the letter *Vau* <note>The letter "V" or "W" in the Hebrew alphabet</note> in the name of **Esau** <note>original: עשו</note>), so shall the name **Jaacob** <note>Jacob</note> be made perfect (and written as **Jaacób** <note>original: יעקוב</note> with the *Vau Cholem*), while the name **Esav** <note>Esau</note> will be left lacking. It will remain only as **Asch** <note>original: עש</note> (which means a moth that eats away at clothing, instead of **Esav**) and a rotting remnant.

And in the **Bereschith Rabba** <note>A classic collection of ancient Jewish interpretations of the book of Genesis, likely compiled around 400–600 AD.</note>, on folio 3, column 3, in the second section regarding the words of **Genesis** 1:2—**And the earth was waste and void, and it was dark upon the deep**—it is written as follows: <note>original: רבי שמעון בן לקיש פתר קרא במלכיות : והארץ היתה תהו זו מלכות בבל וגו׳ : ובהו זו מלכות מדי וגו׳ : וחשך זו מלכות יון וגו׳ : על פני תהום זו מלכות עכ״ם שאין לה חקר וגו׳</note> that is: **Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish** interpreted this verse as referring to the various kingdoms (or world powers) and said: The words **"And the earth was waste"** signify the **Babylonian Empire**, etc. The words **"And void"** point to the **Median Empire**, etc. The words **"And it was dark"** have a meaning pointing to the **Greek Empire**, etc. The words **"Upon the deep"** signify the **Malchus Achum** <note>The Kingdom of the Star-Worshipers, i.e., Christendom</note>, which is unfathomable and cannot be fully explored, etc. 

However, in **Rabbi Nachman's** disputation with **Brother Paulo** <note>Refers to the famous Disputation of Barcelona in 1263 between the Jewish scholar Nahmanides and the Christian convert Pablo Christiani.</note>, on page 56, where this foolish interpretation of Scripture also appears, the term **Malchus Edom ha-resha'ah** <note>original: מלכות אדום הרשעה</note> is used instead of **Malchúth Achum**, meaning "The wicked Edomite Kingdom." Furthermore, in the **Jalkut Chadasch** <note>A 17th-century compilation of Jewish mystical and midrashic lore.</note>, folio 49, column 1, number 48, it is read as **Malchus ha-resha'ah**, that is, "The wicked kingdom."

It is also written in the aforementioned **Bereschith Rabba**, folio 59, column 1, in the 65th section: <note>original: אין אדם יודע מה בלבו של חבירו דכתיב אני י״י חוקר לב וגו׳ ומלכות עכ״ם אימתי היא נופלת דכתיב כי יום נקם בלבי</note> that is: No man knows what is in his companion’s (or fellow human's) heart, as it is written in **Jeremiah** 17:10: **I the Lord search the heart**, etc. Similarly, no one knows when the **Malchus Achum** <note>The Kingdom of the Star-Worshipers</note> shall fall, as it is written in **Isaiah** 63:4: **For the day of vengeance was in my heart.** This can also be found in the **Medrasch Kohéleth** <note>A traditional commentary on the book of Ecclesiastes.</note>, folio 335, column 2.

The name **Achum** alone appears in the stated **Bereschith Rabba**, folio 91, column 3, in the 99th section, with these words: <note>original: רבי פנחס בשם רבי שמואל בר נחמן אמר מסורת היא שאין עכ״ם נופלת אלא ביד בניה של רחל הה״ד אם לא יסחבום צעירי הצאן</note> that is: **Rabbi Pinchas** said in the name of

**Sixteenthly**, they also call it המים הזדונים *Hammájim hašſedónim*, that is, the arrogant water, as can be read in the book *Cad hakkémach* <term>Kad HaKemach: "The Flour Jar," a work on Jewish ethics by Bahya ben Asher</term>, folio 62, column 2, where concerning the words (Psalm 124:5) **Then the proud water would have gone over our souls,** it is written thus: <note>original: מלכות אדום המים הזדונים לפי שעיקר אמונתם הוא שהם נטבלים במים</note> [The Kingdom of Edom is the "arrogant water" because the core of their faith consists in the fact that they are immersed in water.]

King **David** called the **Edomite** kingdom *Hammájim hašſedónim*, that is, the arrogant water, because the main practice of their faith consists in being baptized with water. And such a name is found in the book *Zerór hammór* <term>Tzeror HaMor: "A Bundle of Myrrh," a Torah commentary by Abraham Saba</term>, folio 4, column 1, and in **Rabbi Moshe de Mirçado's** interpretation of the Psalms, folio 103, column 4, regarding Psalm 124:4, as can be seen under the previous fifteenth name, where the words from both of these books are to be found.

XVII. They also call it the Kingdom of the worshipers or servants of the stars and planets.
</margin>

**Seventeenthly**, it is called by them מלכות עכו"ם *Malchúth* (or *Málchus*) *Achum* (which word *Achum* is an abbreviation <note>original: עובדי כוכבים ומזלות — óvede cochavím umaššalóth</note> meaning "worshipers of stars and planets"), that is, the Kingdom of the servants (or worshipers) of the stars and the planets. Although they know that we do not worship stars, yet because the idolatrous heathens of old were so named, we—being regarded by them as idolatrous people—must also bear this name. They use this name frequently so that a Christian reading the material may not know that Christendom is meant by it. Or else (since the abbreviation עכ"ם *Achum*, according to the highly learned Doctor **Wagenseil’s** <note>Johann Christoph Wagenseil was a 17th-century Christian Hebraist who sought to expose Jewish polemics.</note> indication on page 120 in his **Refutation of Rabbi Lipmann's Carmen or Poem**, is said to mean עובדי כריסטוס ומרים / *Ovedé Chrístus u-Mír-jam*, that is, worshipers of **Christ and Mary**, as was already indicated above in Chapter 16, page 713, under the thirty-third name they give to Christians) *Malchúth óvede Chrístus u-Mír-jam*, that is, the Kingdom of the worshipers of **Christ and Mary.** It is also called simply עכ"ם *Achum*, omitting the word *Malchúth* <note>Kingdom</note> usually placed before it.

Concerning the name *Malchúth Achum*, the same is read in the book *Lef árjeh* <term>Lev Aryeh: "The Heart of the Lion," a work by Judah Leib Hanau</term>, folio 17, column 4, and it is written there as follows: <note>original: באחרית הימים תעקר מלכות העכ"ם לגמרי וידו אוחזת בעקב עשו בי"ו של עשו שיעק"ב יהיה מלא ועשו</note> [In the end of days, the kingdom of the heathens shall be completely uprooted; and his hand holds the heel of Esau, by the "V" of Esau, so that Jacob will be full and Esau...]
