# Chapter XVIII of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked.

<margin>
Michael is said to be the Prince of the Jews.
</margin>
We must now also see what kind of prince the Jews, according to their teaching, are supposed to have. It is important to know that, although in the aforementioned book <term>Avodáth hakkódesch</term> <note>Hebrew: "Holy Service," a 16th-century Kabbalistic work by Meir ben Gabbai</note>, in the 4th chapter of the first part, folio 10, column 3, it is read: <note>original Hebrew: ישראלים אינם נמסרים לשום כח ולשום שר ואל כלל כי אם לי' לבדו ומענין כי</note> *that is: Behold, the Israelites are handed over to no power, and to no prince or god at all, except to the Lord alone, according to the content (of that which is read in Leviticus 25:55: ) For the children of Israel are my servants, etc. (as also that which stands in Deuteronomy 32:9: ) For the Lord's portion is his people.* Nevertheless, they teach that the Angel Michael is their prince. Therefore, it is written in the book <term>Shaáre óra</term> <note>Hebrew: "Gates of Light," a foundational Kabbalistic text by Joseph Gikatilla</note>, folio 60, column 3, as follows: <note>original Hebrew: מיכאל הכהן הגדול שהוא נושא דגל יי' יתברך מסר אותו לו לישראל</note> *that is: The blessed Lord has given the High Priest Michael, who carries the banner, to the Israelites (as their prince), about which more is to be found in the book Zijóni folio 31, column 4, and folio 53, column 2.* Thus also teaches Rabbi Joseph ben David Jachjah <note>A 16th-century Jewish philosopher and commentator from Italy</note> in his exposition on the Prophet Daniel, concerning the words in chapter 12, verse 1: **At that time the great prince Michael, who stands for the children of your people, shall arise,** saying the following: <note>original Hebrew: כי אומות יש להם בשמים ע' שרים וכן לישראל יש שר אחד והוא מיכאל ואמנם יתחלף שר ישראל בהנהגתו עמו מהנהגת שאר השרים לאומותיהם כי שרי העמים הם אלהיהם ויפעלו בהם באלוהות ולא ישגחו מזולת שריהם ואמנם ישראל הם מושגחים מה' ואם מיכאל יפעל בם יהיה במצות קונו ולא יעשה קטנה או גדולה בלי רשות</note> *that is: The seventy nations have seventy princes in heaven; likewise Israel also has a prince, namely Michael. However, there is a difference between the Prince of Israel and his governance of his people, and the governance of the other princes over their nations: for the princes of the nations are their gods, and they deal with them as gods; they are also cared for by no one else but their princes. The Israelites, however, are cared for by the Lord: and although Michael rules over them, this happens by the command of his Creator; and he does nothing, whether small or great, without permission.*

<margin>

Why? Likewise, in the **Talmudic** tractate **Shabbath, folio 30, column 2**, the following is read concerning **King David**:

<note>original: "יומא דשבתא הוה יתיב וגריס כולי יומא ההוא יומא דבעי מיתח נפשיה קם מלאך המות קמיה ולא יכיל ליה דלא הוה פסק פומיה מגירסא אמר מאי עביד ליה הוה ליה בוסתנא אחורי ביתיה אתא מלאך המות סליק ובחיש באילני נפק למחזי הוה סליק בדרגא איפחית דרגא מתותיה אישתיק ונח נפשיה:"</note>

Now, he (namely King David) had a garden behind his house, and as the Angel of Death climbed into the trees and shook them, David went out to see (who was doing such a thing) and climbed up a ladder; but the ladder broke under him, and he fell silent and died.**

# What the Jews teach about the Angel of Death and the Dead #

The interpretation of Rabbi Solomon Jarchi <note>Known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator on the Bible and Talmud.</note> signifies that they lacked no good thing. **Moses**, **Aaron**, and **Miriam**, of whom it is written (**Deuteronomy 34:5 and Numbers 33:38**): **By the mouth of the Lord.** Rabbi Eliezer has said that **Miriam** also died by a kiss, which is proven by the fact that the little word *Sham* <note>original: שם (*Sham*), meaning "there." The argument relies on a Jewish interpretive method called *Gezerah Shavah*, where identical words in different verses link the laws or circumstances of those verses.</note> is read for both **Miriam** and **Moses** (for of **Moses** it is said in **Deuteronomy 34:5**: **So Moses the servant of the Lord died there:** And of **Miriam** it is reported in **Numbers 20:1**: **And Miriam died there.**) But why is it not said of her: **By the mouth of the Lord?** Because it would be an unseemly thing to say <note>The author suggests the Jewish sages found it inappropriate to describe God "kissing" a woman.</note> (that God should have kissed her, just as he allowed **Moses** and **Aaron** to die by a kiss). But are these not foolish proofs, through which the Holy Scripture is maliciously pulled into a perverted meaning?

<margin>Nine are said to have entered Paradise alive</margin>
It is also read by some that they did not die at all, but rather entered into Paradise alive, regarding which it is written in the book **Avodáh hakkódesch folio 37, column 4** <note>Hebrew: *Avodat HaKodesh* ("Holy Service"), a work on Kabbalistic theology by Meir ibn Gabbai.</note> in the **19th Chapter** of the second part, which is called **Chélek haavóda** <note>The "Part on Service."</note>, as follows: <note>original: "תשעה נכנסו בחייהם לגן עדן ולא טעמו טעם מיתה : בנימין בן יעקב כלאב בן דוד . סרח בת אשר . בתיה בת פרעה . אליעזר עבד אברהם . עבד מלך הכושי . ומשיח . ואליהו . ויעבץ בנו של רבי יהודה הנשיא . ויש אומרים אף רבי יהושע בן לוי :"</note> that is, **Nine have entered into Paradise during their lifetime and have not tasted the flavor of death: Benjamin the son of Jacob, Kelab the son of David, Serach the daughter of Asher, Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh, Eliezer the servant of Abraham, Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, and the Messiah, and Elijah, and Jabez the son of Rabbi Judah the Prince. Some say also Rabbi Joshua ben Levi.** In the **Jalkut chádasch** <note>A 17th-century collection of midrashic and kabbalistic traditions.</note> this stands on **folio 57, column 2, number 48** under the title **Gan Eden** <note>The Garden of Eden or Paradise.</note>, somewhat changed, in this manner: <note>original: "תשעה נכנסו חיים לגן עדן חנוך אליהו משיח אליעזר עבד אברהם עבד מלך כושי חירם מלך צור ויעבץ בן בנו של רבי יהודה הנשיא סרח בת אשר בתיה בת פרעה ויש אומרים הוציא חירם מלך צור והכניס במקומו רבי יהושע בן לוי :"</note> that is, **Nine entered into Paradise alive: Enoch, Elijah, the Messiah, Eliezer the servant of Abraham, Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, Hiram the King of Tyre, and Jabez the grandson of Rabbi Judah the Prince, Serach the daughter of Asher, Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh. But there are some who say: remove Hiram the King of Tyre and put Rabbi Joshua ben Levi in his place.** Regarding this, the Talmud in **Tractate Derech Eretz Zuta, folio 20, column 3** can also be opened.

<note>original Hebrew: במדרש אחר איתא שחורם לא טעם מיתה וי"ג היו שלא טעמו טעם מיתה : ה"ג חנוך אליעזר עבד אברהם מתושלח חירם מלך צור עבד מלך הכושי שהציל את ירמיה הנביא מן הבור בתיה בת פרעה סרח בת אשר ג' בני קרח ואליהו ז"ל ומשיח ורבי יהושע בן לוי :</note>
In another Midrash <note>A form of rabbinic biblical interpretation or commentary.</note> it is stated that Hiram did not taste death, and that there were thirteen who did not taste the flavor of death: namely, **Enoch**; **Eliezer**, the servant of Abraham; **Methuselah**; **Hiram**, the King of Tyre; **Ebed-Melech** the Ethiopian <note>original: *Kushi*</note>, who rescued the prophet Jeremiah from the pit; **Bithiah**, the daughter of Pharaoh; **Serah**, the daughter of Asher; the **three sons of Korah** (who are mentioned in **Exodus 6, verse 24**); and **Elijah** (of blessed memory); and the **Messiah**; as well as **Rabbi Joshua ben Levi**.

In the little book of *Ben Sira* <note>Refers to the *Alphabet of Ben Sira*, a medieval text containing various legends and folklore.</note>, this is recorded on folio 15, column 2, and folio 16, column 1, with some variations, and the reasons are provided as to why they did not die. It is read there that King Nebuchadnezzar asked Ben Sira why the Angel of Death has power over all creatures except for the race of the bird *Mileham* <note>original: מלחם</note>, which is the **Phoenix** (about which something was also noted in the preceding 18th Chapter, page 829). Following this, it is written that Ben Sira answered him thus:

<note>original Hebrew: לאדורו של מלחם העוף בלבד אין מלאך המות שולט בם אף דורו של יודב ויש אומרים אנשים מבני אדם נכנסו בחיים בגן עדן. אמר לו מי הם. אמר לו חנוך וסרח בת אשר. ובתיה בת פרעה. חירם מלך צור. ואליעזר עבד אברהם. ועבד מלך הכושי. ועבדו של רבי יהודה. ויעבץ. ורבי יהושע בן לוי. וכל זרע יונדב. והעוף מלחם העוף. אמר לו ספר לי למה נמלטו אלה ממלאך המות. אמר לו אני אספר לך. חנוך לפי שהיה צדיק בדורו שלא היה כמוהו והוא חי בגן עדן. אליעזר עבד אברהם הוא בנו של חם בן נח וכששמע קללת אביו מסר עצמו לאברהם והיה צדיק והוא בגן עדן. סרח בת אשר בעבור שאמרה ליעקב יוסף חי. אמר לה יוסף זה הפרה שבשרני עלי יוסף שהוא חי לא יטעום טעם מות. בתיה בת פרעה לפי שגדלה משה רבינו מקטנותו שלא יאמרו ומה זה עבדה לכך. ועבד מלך הכושי שהציל את ירמיהו מבור הטיט. ועבדו של רבי יהודה הנשיא על שהיה צדיק עני ושפל רוח. ויעבץ גם הוא בגן עדן לפי שהיה צדיק מכל דורו. ורבי יהושע בן לוי שהיה גם הוא צדיק גמור ואהוב למלאך המות. פעם אחת אמר למלאך המות הראני גן עדן. אמר לו בשמחה לך עמי. בדרך אמר לו מפחד אני ממך שמא תהרגני בחרבך שלא ברצונך. אם תאהבני ותרצה שאליך עמך תן לי חרבך בידי עד שאלך עמך ותראני גן עדן כטוב עד שאסתכל וחזרינו מן השער. אמר לו בטוב. מיד הוליך אותו. מה עשה רבי יהושע עמד בפתח גן עדן עד שהתחיל לראות וקפץ פתאום ונכנס לגן עדן. גם היה סכינו של מלאך המות בידו והיה בידו שבע שנים עד שאמר לו הקב"ה יהושע בן לוי דבר גדול עשית השב למלאך המות סכינו וכשקפץ שלפני מלאך המות ונכנס לגן עדן צעק מלאך המות צעקה גדולה ורצה להחריב העולם ושתקו אל לאחר שבע שנים החזירה לו. חירם מלך צור הכניסו הקב"ה לגן עדן שבנה בית המקדש והיה בתחילה</note>

Not only the generation of the bird *Mileham* is beyond the control of the Angel of Death, but also the generation of Jonadab; and some say there are certain men among the children of men who entered Paradise alive. The King said to him: "Who are they?" He replied: "**Enoch**; and **Serah**, the daughter of Asher; and **Bithiah**, the daughter of Pharaoh; **Hiram**, the King of Tyre; and **Eliezer**, the servant of Abraham; and **Ebed-Melech** the Ethiopian; and the **servant of Rabbi Judah**; and **Jabez**; and **Rabbi Joshua ben Levi**; and all the **descendants of Jonadab**; and the bird *Mileham*."

The King said to him: "Tell me why these escaped from the Angel of Death." And **Rabbi Joshua ben Levi**, because he was also perfectly righteous and a friend to the Angel of Death. Once he said to the Angel of Death: 'Show me Paradise.' The Angel replied: 'Gladly, come with me.' On the way, the Rabbi said: 'I am afraid of you, lest you kill me with your sword against your will. If you love me and wish me to go with you, give me your sword into my hand until I have gone with you and you have shown me Paradise, until I have looked around and we return to the gate.' The Angel said: 'Very well.' He led him there immediately. What did Rabbi Joshua do? He stood at the entrance of Paradise until he began to see inside, then suddenly jumped and entered Paradise. He also had the knife of the Angel of Death in his hand and kept it for seven years until the Holy One, blessed be He, said: 'Joshua ben Levi, you have done a great thing; return the knife to the Angel of Death.' When he had jumped away from the Angel and entered Paradise, the Angel of Death gave a great cry and wanted to destroy the world, but he was silenced until, after seven years, the Rabbi returned it to him. **Hiram**, the King of Tyre, was brought into Paradise by the Holy One, blessed be He, because he built the Temple, and he was at first—

<note>original Hebrew: מתחילה ירא אלהים... This section recounts the legends of Hiram, Jonadab, and the Phoenix.</note>
Initially, he <note>Referring to Hiram, King of Tyre.</note> was God-fearing and lived in the Garden of Eden for a thousand years. Afterward, he became proud and said, "I am a god," as it is said: *Son of man, say...* <note>Ezekiel 28:2, where the Prince of Tyre is rebuked for claiming divinity.</note> Therefore, he was expelled from the Garden of Eden and entered Hell. The generation of Jonadab, son of Rechab: because he wrote all the matters that are in the book of Jeremiah and was a righteous man who rebuked Israel, he lives in the Garden of Eden. And the generation of the bird *Milcham* <note>original: *Milcham*; identified in Jewish tradition as the Phoenix.</note>: When Eve ate from the Tree of Knowledge and gave also to her husband and he ate with her, she was jealous of the other creatures and fed it to everyone. She saw the bird *Milcham* and said to him, "Eat of this, from which your companions have eaten." He said to her, "Is it not enough for you that you have sinned before the Blessed Name and caused others to die, but you come to me to entice me to violate the command of the Holy One, Blessed be He, that I should eat and die? I will not listen to you." Then he rebuked Eve and all the creatures. Immediately, a heavenly voice <note>original: *Bat Kol*</note> went out and said to Eve and Adam, "You did not keep my commandments and you sinned, and you came to the bird *Milcham* to make him sin as well; but he did not accept it and feared me, even though I did not command him. Because he kept my decree, he and his descendants shall never taste the flavor of death."

That is, **the Angel of Death** 
does not only lack rule over the lineage of the bird Phoenix, but 
there are also those of the lineage of **Jonadab**, as well as—according to 
some accounts—certain other people who, during 
their lifetimes, entered Paradise. Then he (namely **Nebuchadnezzar**) spoke to 
him: "Which ones are they?" He answered him: **Enoch**, 
and **Serah** the daughter of **Asher**, and **Bithiah** the daughter of **Pharaoh**, 
and **Hiram** the King of **Tyre**, and **Eliezer** the servant 
of **Abraham**, and **Ebed-Melech** the **Ethiopian** <note>original: *Mohr* (Moor); used historically to refer to people from Africa.</note>, and the servant of **Rabbi Judah**, 
and **Jabez**, and **Rabbi Joshua ben Levi**, and the entire 
lineage of **Jonadab**, as well as the lineage of the bird **Phoenix**.

<margin>The reason why these did not die.</margin>
Thereupon the King said to him: "Tell me the reason why

Then Adam answers: "I have committed only one sin and have been punished, but you have committed many sins."

<margin>How the Angel of Death examines the dying person, and when a person dies a gentle death or has a hard death.</margin>
In the book *Nishmat Hayyim* <note>original: "The Breath of Life," a 17th-century work on the soul by Menasseh ben Israel</note> it is also indicated on folio 77, columns 1 and 2, in the 20th chapter of the second part, how the Angel of Death examines the person, and how the person must be prepared if he is to die a gentle death; and it is written there as follows: "At the hour when a man departs from the world, it is not enough that he is terrified by the Angel of Death—who is entirely full of eyes and has his drawn sword in his hand—but the Angel also asks him: 'Did you occupy yourself with the Torah and with acts of loving-kindness? Did you acknowledge your Creator as King? And did you treat your neighbor with a tranquil spirit?' If these things are found in him, the Angel drops that drop into his mouth, and his soul goes out without pain, like pulling a hair out of milk. But if these things are not found in him, his soul goes out of his body like dragging thorns out of wool." <note>original Hebrew: בשעה שהאדם נפטר מן העולם לא די שנבהל ממלאך המות שכלו מלא עינים וחרבו שלופה בידו אלא שואל אותו כלום עסקת בתורה ובגמילות חסדים והמלכת לקונך והמלכת את חבירך בנחת רוח אם יש בו דברים הללו זורק אותה טיפה לתוך פיו ויוצאת נשמתו בלא צער כמשוך נימא מחלב. ואם אין בו דברים הללו יוצאת נשמתו מגופו כגרירת קוצים מן הצמר</note> That is: In the hour when a person departs from this world, it is not enough that he is terrified by the Angel of Death—who is full of eyes and has his naked sword in his hand—but the same also asks him: "Have you also studied the Law <note>The Torah</note>, and applied yourself to good deeds (or *the demonstration of mercy* <note>term: Gemilut Hasadim</note>), and recognized your Creator as your King, and allowed your fellow human to rule with gentleness?" When these things are found, then he lets the drop (of gall, which was mentioned before) fall into his mouth, and his soul departs without pain, like a thread pulled out of milk. But when such things are not found in him, then his soul goes out of his body like one pulls thorns out of wool.

On the conversation of the dying with Adam, and how they see God.

But as for the conversation between the dying person and the first man, Adam, and how the dying person sees God, it is written thus in *Bammidbar Rabba* <note>original: "Numbers Rabbah," a collection of ancient Jewish homilies on the Book of Numbers</note>, folio 224, column 4, and folio 225, column 1, in the 19th *Parashah* <note>section</note>, regarding the words of Proverbs 10, verse 3: **"The Lord will not suffer the soul of the righteous to famish"**:

> This refers to the first man, Adam, for death is decreed upon all the righteous who descend from him. They do not depart this life until they see the face of the Divine Majesty <note>original Hebrew: *Shekhinah*</note> and rebuke the first man, Adam, saying to him: "You are the cause of our death." But he answers them: "I committed only one sin, but among you there is not one who has not committed more than four sins." And from where is it proved that they see the face of the Divine Majesty and rebuke the first man (Adam)? Because it is said (Isaiah 38:11): "I said, I shall not see the Lord, even the Lord, in the land of the living; I shall behold Adam <note>The Hebrew text here uses *Adam*, which can mean 'man' in general or the specific person 'Adam'</note> no more with the inhabitants of the world." The righteous are punished with death for minor sins so that the first man, Adam, should not be blamed because of them, as it is said: "The Lord will not suffer the soul of the righteous to famish." <note>original: Hebrew text from Numbers Rabbah</note>

That is, **This (Righteous One) is the first man, Adam; for death is decreed over all the righteous who descend from him. These same ones do not die until they see the face of the Divine Majesty and have given a rebuke to the first man, Adam, saying to him: "You are the cause of our death." But he answers them: "I have committed one sin; but among you there is no one who has not sinned more than four times." But how is it proven that they see the face of the Divine Majesty and give a rebuke to the first man (Adam)? Because it is said (Isaiah 38, verse 11): "I said, I shall no longer see the Lord, the Lord, in the land of the living; I shall no longer look upon Adam" (for it should be interpreted this way according to the meaning of the quoted words, though it here signifies 'mankind' in general, as the word *Adam* here is not a proper name but a common noun) "with the inhabitants of the world." The righteous, however, are punished with death because of minor sins, so that the first man, Adam, might not be held responsible by them, as it is said: "The Lord does not let the soul of the righteous suffer hunger."**

<margin>Why the Jews pour out the water when a dead person is in the house.</margin>
The Jews are also accustomed to pouring out the water in a house in which a person has died; the reason for this is explained in the *Sepher Minhágim* <note>original: "Book of Customs," a guide to Jewish religious practices</note> folio 13, column 2:
<gloss>For we wish to know why the water is poured out. It is because when a person departs, his soul goes out from him where the blood is, for the blood is the soul itself. One sees a drop of blood there, which belongs to the Angel of Death <note>original Hebrew: *Malach ha-Mavet*</note>, who commands it upon his knife. Some say it is based on the verse "And Miriam died there, and there was no water for the congregation" (Numbers 20:1), for when she died, Israel had no water.</gloss>
That is, I will tell you why one pours out the water when a dead person is in the house: in former times, one blew a horn when someone had died, so that people would know a death had occurred. For one does not like to speak bad news with the mouth. Therefore, one pours out the water so that the neighbors may see that someone has died. Some say that the Angel of Death <term>Angel of Death <note>In Jewish folklore, the Malach ha-Mavet is the figure who extracts the soul, often depicted with a many-eyed form or a sword</note></term> washes his knife in the water. Others, however, say it happens because of the words of **Numbers 20, verses 1 and 2: And Miriam died there, and the congregation had no water.**

<margin>What the Jews write concerning the voice of a dying person.</margin>
Concerning the voice of a dying person, it is written in the *Jalkut chádasch* <note>original: "The New Collection," a 17th-century compendium of Kabbalistic and midrashic teachings</note> folio 124, column 3, number 53, under the title *Mitha* (or *Misa*) <note>meaning "Death"</note> as follows:
<gloss>When a person departs from this world, his voice travels from one end of the world to the other, wandering throughout the whole world until it enters and hides in the clefts of the rocks and in caves. When a person cries out and lets his voice go, that original voice echoes back against him—which in the German language is called a *Wiederschall* <note>meaning "echo"</note>—but it ceases immediately and does not linger like a human voice, because it has no place where it can spread out.</gloss>
That is: When a person departs from this world, his voice goes from one end of the world to the other, and travels around the whole world until it goes into the clefts of the rocks and into caves, and hides itself there. Now, when a person cries out loudly and lets a voice go forth, his own [past] voice lets itself be heard against him, which in German is called a **Wiederschall** (echo). It has, however, a quick end and does not draw out long like the voice of a [living] human, because it does not have enough space to expand. Thus, according to the foolish teaching of the Jews, the echo comes from the voices of deceased persons.

<margin>Three voices are said to go from one end of the world to the other.</margin>
In the Talmudic tractate *Jóma* <note>The tractate concerning the Day of Atonement, Yom Kippur</note>, however, it is said on folio 20, column 1, and folio 21, column 1, that three voices go from one end of the world to the other, and the following is read therein:
<gloss>The Rabbis taught: Three voices go from one end of the world to the other, and these are: the sound of the orbit of the sun...</gloss>

# What the Jews teach about the Angel of Death and Death. 677

<margin>...heard from one end to the other.</margin>
These are the voices: the sound of the sun’s globe, the sound of the tumult of Rome, and the sound of the soul at the hour it departs from the body; and some say also the sound of birth; and some say also the sound of Ridya. And our Rabbis sought mercy for the soul at the hour it departs from the body, and they abolished it. <note>original Hebrew: "הֶן קוֹל גַּלְגַּל חַמָּה..." This passage lists cosmic sounds that are said to vibrate through the entire universe, though they remain inaudible to human ears.</note> That is, **Our Rabbis teach:** There are three voices that go from one end of the world to the other, namely the voice of the sphere or globe of the Sun, the voice of the noise of Rome <note>In Jewish tradition, the "noise of Rome" often refers to the bustling, chaotic sound of the great city, which was seen as a terrestrial counterpart to the music of the spheres.</note>, and the voice of the soul at the time when it departs from the body. Some also say (the voice) of birth. Others also speak of (the voice of the angel) Ridya <note>term: Ridya; an angel in Jewish folklore who is said to be in charge of rain and the irrigation of the earth.</note> (who is set over the rain and the moistening of the earth). But our Rabbis have prayed for mercy for the soul when it departs from the body (so that it may no longer happen with such a great cry) and have caused it to cease, so that it occurs no more.

<margin>Rabbi Eliezer, however, teaches that there are five of them.</margin>
In the Chapters of Rabbi Eliezer <note>referring to the *Pirke De-Rabbi Eliezer*, an 8th-9th century midrashic work on the Torah</note>, it is read in the 34th chapter that five voices go from one end of the world to the other, with these words:

Five voices go from one end of the world to its other end, and their voice is not heard, and these are they: when a fruit-bearing tree is cut down, the voice goes from one end of the world to the other and the voice is not heard; and when the snake sheds its skin, the voice is not heard; and when a woman is divorced from her husband, the voice goes from one end of the world to the other and the voice is not heard; and when a woman is with her husband for the first time, the voice goes from one end of the world to the other and the voice is not heard; and when the child comes out of its mother’s womb, the voice goes from one end of the world to the other and the voice is not heard; and when the soul departs from the body, the voice goes from one end of the world to the other and the voice is not heard; and the soul does not depart from the body until it sees the Divine Presence, as it is said, "For no man shall see me and live." <note>original Hebrew: "חֲמִשָּׁה קוֹלִין הוֹלֵךְ..." quoting the Pirke De-Rabbi Eliezer and Exodus 33:20.</note> That is, **There are five things whose voice goes from one end of the world to the other, and yet their voice is not heard, and they are the following.** At the time when a fruitful tree is cut down, the voice goes from one end of the world to the other, and is not heard. And at the time when the snake sheds its skin, the voice is not heard. And at the time when a woman is divorced from her husband, the voice goes from one end of the world to the other, and yet is not heard. And when a woman is first touched by her husband <note>a reference to the loss of virginity</note>, the voice goes from one end of the world to the other, and is not heard. And at the time when a child comes out of its mother’s womb, the voice goes from one end of the world to the other, and is not heard. As also at the time when the soul departs from the body, the voice goes from one end of the world to the other, and is not heard. The soul, however, does not depart from the body until it has seen the Divine Majesty <note>original: *Göttliche Majestät*, referring to the Shekhinah, or the dwelling presence of God</note>, as is said in (Exodus 33, verse 20): For no man will live who sees me.

# Chapter XIX of the First Part of *Judaism Unveiled*.

<margin>Death / and why it happens.</margin>
The cause is indicated in the *Yalkut Chadash* <note>term: Yalkut Chadash; a 17th-century collection of Jewish legends and Kabbalistic teachings</note>, folio 124, column 2, number 47, under the title *Mita* (or Death) with these words: <note>original Hebrew: "בני אדם מתים בלא זמנם הוא שאינם נזהרים כשמוציאין מת לבית הקברות הם מתערבים בין הנשים..."</note> "The reason that most people die before their time is that they are not careful when a corpse is carried out to the cemetery; they mingle among the women. For the Angel of Death dances among the women from the hour the corpse is taken out until they return to their homes; and this has been the case since the time he seduced Eve. A man should be careful not to look at the faces of women at all until they have returned to their homes. When he walks, he should walk in front of them; but if that is not possible, he should walk behind them, so that in any case he does not look into their faces until their final return to their homes. And if a man is careful in this, he merits a long life." For this reason—namely, to guard oneself against the accusation of the Angel of Death—it was the custom in the days of the Talmudic sages

to die before their time comes, because they do not take care, when a dead person is carried out for burial, that they do not

mingle among the women. For the Angel of Death dances [among them] as long as it takes for them to return to their houses; and this has happened from the time that he seduced Eve. Therefore, a man must guard himself so that he does not look at the women at all until they have come back to their houses. But when he walks, he should walk in front of them; however, if it is not possible, he should walk behind them, so that he in no way looks into their faces until they are completely back in their houses. And when a person is careful in this matter, he deserves a long life. If, however, someone encounters them, what remedy should he use (so that no harm comes to him)?

But if one encounters such a thing, what remedy must he use (so that it [does not harm him]...)?

### What the Jews teach about the Angel of Death and the dead.

...suffer misfortune? He must jump four cubits <note>original: "Ellen"; a cubit is an ancient unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger</note> away from his place. If there is a river there, he should cross over it. If there is another path, he should take that one. If there is a wall, he should stand behind it; but if not, let him turn his face away and speak (the words of Zechariah 3:2): "And the Lord said to Satan, the Lord rebuke you, O Satan," until they (namely the evil spirits) have passed by him.

<margin>For what reason he dances.</margin>
The reason why he <note>the Angel of Death</note> dances is shown in the *Yalkut Chadash* <note>a 17th-century collection of Kabbalistic legends</note> folio 107, column 4, under the title *Keschafim* <note>original Hebrew: "כְּשָׁפִים"; Sorceries</note>, with these words: <note>original Hebrew: "כשאמר הק"בה עליו להמית את האדם הוא עצב אלא שמראה עצמו כדי להראות שמקיים מצות השם בשמחה ולכן מרקד לפני הנשים כאלו הוא שמח להראות ששמח לעשות רצון מאריה אבל עיקר דעתו לשמוע ההספד שהנשים עושות"</note> "When the Holy One, blessed be He, gives him the command to kill a person, he is sad; however, he presents himself as joyful to show that he fulfills the command of God with joy. Therefore, he dances before the women as if he were happy, to demonstrate that he joyfully performs the will of his Master. But the main point of his intention is that he may hear the wailing of the women."

<margin>Why the Jews bury their dead immediately and do not let them lie overnight.</margin>
The Jews are not accustomed to letting their dead lie overnight, but rather bury them quickly. Why this is done can be seen from the *Zohar* <note>the foundational work of Jewish mysticism, the Kabbalah</note>, in the *Parashat Emor* <note>the weekly Torah portion titled "Emor"</note>, folio 88, column 2 of the Sulzbach edition, where the words read as follows: <note>original Aramaic/Hebrew: "נשמתא לא עאלת קמי הק"בה ולא יכלא למהוי בגופא אחרא עד דיתקבר קדמאה וגו' וכל מה דגופא לא אתקבר צערא הוא לנשמתא ורוח מסאבא אדמין לשריא עלוהי ולסאבא לההוא גופא. וכיון דההוא רוח מסאבא אדמין לא לבעי ליה לאינש למיבת ההוא גופא לילא חד פגין דרוח מסאבא אשתכח בליליא ואשתטח בכל ארעא לאשכחא גופא בלא נפשא לסאבא ליה ולאסתאב יתיה"</note> "The soul does not enter before the Holy One, blessed be He, (namely, into Paradise) nor can it be in another body (or be moved into one) until the first (body) is buried, etc. As long as the body is not buried, it causes pain to the soul, and the spirit of impurity is ready to linger over it and to defile that body. Because the spirit of impurity is ready (to soil it), a person should not desire to let the body lie overnight, since the spirit of impurity is present at night and spreads over the entire earth to find a body without a soul in order to defile it; and (such a body) becomes greatly contaminated."

In the book *Zijoni* <note>a 14th-century Kabbalistic commentary by Menahem Zion ben Meir</note> on folio 101, column 1, the following is also read regarding this: <note>original Hebrew: "ועוד יש לך לדעת כי קבורת המת נחת רוח לנשמה וכל זמן שהמת לא נקבר אין מכניסין אותו למחיצתו של הק"בה כמו שאמרו ח"זל במדרש רוח כל זמן דגופא לא נחית בדוכתיה אף"</note> "And you should further know that the burial of the dead is a comfort to the soul, and as long as the dead is not buried, they do not bring it into the partition <note>the celestial dwelling place</note> of the Holy One, blessed be He, as our Sages of blessed memory have said in the Midrash: 'The spirit, as long as the body has not rested in its place, even...'"

880 The First Part of *Judaism Unmasked*, Chapter XIX.

<note>original Hebrew: "א הכי הוא. ע"א ע"ד סוד לעיבור כדי שלא לאחר גזירתו של הק"בה כי כל עוד שלא נקבר לא יתגלגל:" "Thus it is. On page 71, column 4, regarding the secret of Ibbur, so as not to delay the decree of the Holy One, blessed be He; for as long as one is not buried, one shall not transmigrate."</note> This is to say: Furthermore, you must know that the burial of the dead is pleasant to the soul (or creates rest for it). As long as the deceased is not buried, the soul is not brought into the dwelling of the Holy One, blessed be He, as our Sages, of blessed memory, have said in the *Midrash Ruth* (or the allegorical interpretation of the Book of Ruth): As long as the body does not come to its place <note>the grave</note>, the spirit (or the soul) likewise does not come to its place.

There is also another reason (why one should be buried quickly, namely) because of the "Secret of the Impregnation of Souls" (which is called *Ibbur* <term>Ibbur: literally "impregnation," a mystical concept where a soul enters an existing body to perform a specific task or undergo further refinement</term>, which will be dealt with in the first chapter of the second part), so that the decrees of the Holy One, blessed be He, are not delayed; for as long as the body is not buried, the soul cannot enter into another body.

So it is also taught in the first part of the book *Avodath hakkodesch* <note>The Service of Holiness, a 16th-century Kabbalistic work by Meir ibn Gabbai</note>, which is called *Chélek hajichud* <note>The Part of Unity</note>, in the 27th Chapter, 45th column, 1st section: <note>original Hebrew: "כל עוד שכל זמן שהגוף לא נח והוא שלא נקבר גם הנפש לא נח מנוח לכף רגלה ואינה זוכה לגן עדנה עד שיקבר ויגנז הגוף בקברו ואז תעלה ותשוב הנפש אל מנוחתה:"</note> "That is: We also learn that as long as the body does not rest and is not buried, the soul likewise finds no rest for the sole of its foot, and is not worthy of Paradise until the body has been buried and laid in its grave; only then does the soul first ascend to its rest."

<margin>
What occurs at a person's death, and how he is judged.
</margin>

Regarding what is said to happen to a person immediately during and after their passing, and how they are judged straight away, it is written in the *Sépher jorchot-chaim* <note>The Book of the Paths of Life</note>, number 66, in the following manner: <note>original Hebrew passage describing the moments of death and judgment</note> "In the hour when a person is judged in this world, and at the departure of his soul from the body, the *Shekhinah* <term>Shekhinah: The Divine Presence of God, often envisioned as a feminine aspect of the divine</term> stands over him. If Torah and good deeds are found within him, then happy is this man, for he clings to the *Shekhinah*, and his soul is worthy to ascend to the holy place. But woe to him from whom the *Shekhinah* distances itself and who does not cling to it. And in the hour when they carry the man out to the grave, all the deeds that he performed in this world are all prepared and ready, and they sit before him. And three heralds cry out: one before him, one to his right, and one to his left, saying: 'This is the certain person who served our Creator, the Ruler above and below and in the four corners of the world.' Immediately, through the Torah and the commandments, they see his deeds; they see how good it would have been for him had he not been created <note>if he lived wickedly</note>. And before he reaches his grave, all the dead tremble and quake in their places because of him; if they are wicked, woe to him who is buried with the evil deeds he performed. Also, all the deeds he performed stand over him at the hour of his departure and walk before him to the grave and stand over his body. And the soul also goes and wanders over him, even unto the body from which it has separated. And when they have buried him, the Angel *Dumah* <note>The angel in charge of the souls of the dead</note> stands there, and three angels also come forth from under his hand for the *Hibbut ha-Kever* <term>Hibbut ha-Kever: The "Beating of the Grave," a traditional belief that the soul is questioned and purified through a physical-spiritual struggle shortly after burial</term>, and three rods of fire are in their hands, and they judge the soul and the body together. Woe to him on that day! Woe to him for his evil deeds! And there are several judgments that judge a man when he departs from this world: The first, when his soul departs from the body. The second, when his deeds go before him and herald him. The third, when they bring the body into the grave. The fourth, the judgment of the Beating of the Grave. The fifth, the judgment of the worms. And after three days that the body has lain in the grave, it splits and bursts open, and there come forth..."

<note>original Hebrew: "מבטנו ונוטלים המעים עם התינוק שבהם וטורפין אותו על פניו ואומרין לו טול מה שנתת במעים שלך כמה שאכלת ושבית בכל יום ולא נתת מהן לעני ואביון כלום מכל חגים ומועדים שעשית כל יום כמ"ש וזריתי פרש חגיכם על פניכם. ואחר ז' ימים דנין הנשמה והגוף יחד. ובשביל כך נמצאת הנשמה למטה בארץ כל ל' יום שאינה הולכת למקומה כאשה נדה שיושבת בחוץ כל ימי נדתה. הו' דין של גיהנם. הז' שנשמתו הולכת ומטורפת לשוט בעולם ולא מצאה מקום מנוח עד שישלימו ימי ענשה. לו הו' דינין חולפין ובאין על האדם. סימן לדבר והלכתי עמכם בחמת קרי ויסרתי אתכם שבע על חטאתיכם :"</note>

-># Chapter 19 of the First Part of *Judaism Unveiled*.<-

<note>original Hebrew: "א הכי הוא. ע"א ע"ד סוד לעיבור כדי שלא לאחר גזירתו של הק"בה כי כל עוד שלא נקבר לא יתגלגל:"</note>
This is so. Furthermore, you must know that the burial of the dead is pleasing to the souls (or creates rest for them); but as long as the deceased is not buried, the soul is not brought into the dwelling of the holy, blessed God, as our Sages of blessed memory have said in the *Midrash Ruth* <note>A homiletic commentary on the Book of Ruth</note> (or in the allegorical interpretation of the Book of Ruth): "As long as the body does not come to its place, the spirit (or the soul) also does not come to its place." There is also another reason (why one should be buried quickly, namely) because of the mystery of the "composition of souls" (which is called <term>Ibbur: literally 'impregnation,' a kabbalistic concept where a soul enters an existing body to assist or fulfill a commandment</term> *Ibbur*, that is, a pregnancy, which shall be dealt with in the first chapter of the second part), so that the decrees of the holy, blessed God are not delayed: For as long as the body is not buried, the soul enters into no other body. Thus it is also taught in the first part of the book *Avodath hakkodesch* <note>Holy Service, a 16th-century Kabbalistic work by Meir ibn Gabbai</note> which is called *Chelek hajichud* <note>The Part of Unity</note>, in the 27th Chapter, page 45, column 1: <note>original Hebrew: "נו עד שכל זמן שהגוף לא נח והוא שלא מקבר גם הנפש לא נחה מנוח לכף רגלה ואינה זוכה לגן עדנה עד שיקבר וינח הגוף בקברו ואז תעלה ותשוב הנפש אל מנוחתה:"</note> that is, "We also learn that as long as the body does not rest and is not buried, the soul also finds no rest for itself, and is not fit for Paradise until the body is buried and laid in its grave; only then does the soul ascend to its rest."

<margin>What occurs at the death of a human, and how they are judged.</margin>
Regarding what is said to happen to a person immediately during and after their passing, and how they are judged at once, it is written in the *Sefer Orchot Hayyim* <note>OCR reads "Jochattaim," likely referring to the "Paths of Life," an ethical work</note>, number 66, in this manner: <note>original Hebrew: "באותה שעה נדון האדם בעולם ובצאת נשמתו מן הגוף השכינה עומדת עליו אם נמצא בו תורה ומעשים טובים ואשרי לאדם דבק בשכינה ונשמתו זוכה לעלות למקום קדוש. ואוי לאותו שמרחיקין השכינה ממנו ולא דבקה בה. ובשעה שמוציאין האדם לקבר כל המעשים שעשה בזה העולם כולם מוכנים ומזומנים ועומדים לפניו. ושלשה כרוזים מכריזים אחד לפניו ואחד מימינו ואחד משמאלו ואומרים זה הפלוני בקננו המושל למעלה ולמטה ובארבע רוחות העולם מרד בתורה ובמצוות ראו מעשיו וראו כמה טוב היה לו שלא נברא. וקודם שיגיע לקברו כל המתים חרדים ורוגשים ממקומם בשבילו ואומרים אוי לו לזה שנקבר עם מעשיו הרעים שעשה. וגם כל המעשים שעשה שעומדים עליו ביום פטירתו מקודם והולכין לפניו עד הקבר ועומדין על גופו. וגם הנשמה הולכת ומשוטטת עליו ובוכה על הגוף שנפרדה ממנו. וכאשר קברוהו המלאך דומה עומד וגם יוצאים מתחת ידו שלשה מלאכים על חיבוט הקבר ושלשה שרביטים של אש בידם ודנין הנשמה והגוף יחד אוי לו על אותו הדין אוי לו על מעשיו הרעים. וכמה דינין שדנין האדם כשיצא מזה העולם. הראשון כשנשמתו יוצאת מן הגוף. הב' כאשר מעשיו הולכין לפניו ומכריזין עליו. הג' כשמכניסין הגוף בקבר. הד' דין של חיבוט הקבר. הה' דין של תולעים ואחר ג' ימים ששוכב הגוף בקבר פריקו בקיעת כרסו ומעיו יוצאים"</note> "At that hour, the person is judged in the world, and as his soul leaves the body, the <term>Shekhinah: the Divine Presence</term> stands over him. But woe to him from whom they distance the Shekhinah and who did not cling to it. ### 882 Of the 1st Part of Judaism Unmasked, Chapter XIX.

the third is when the body is laid in the grave. The fourth is <term>Chibbut hakkėfer<note>Hebrew: "the beating of the grave"</note></term>, which is the beating in the grave. The fifth is the judgment of the worms. And after three days, while the body lies in the grave, its belly is ripped open, and its intestines come out of its paunch; then the entrails, along with the filth that is within them, are taken and struck against his face, and it is said to him: "Take what you put into your entrails, from that which you ate and drank every day, yet you shared nothing with the poor and needy from all your feasts and festivals which you held every day"; as it is written in <note>Malachi 2:3</note>: **And I will cast the dung of your festivals into your faces.** After these three days, however, the person is judged in his eyes, hands, and feet, which committed the sins, until the thirtieth day; and in all these thirty days the soul and the body are judged together; for this reason, the soul is found here below on the earth for all thirty days, so that it does not go to its place (where it belongs), just like an unclean woman who sits outside for all the days that her impurity lasts. The sixth is the judgment of Hell <note>Gehenna</note>. The seventh is that his soul wanders and is driven to run about the world, and finds no place where she can rest until the days of her punishment come to an end. These seven judgments occur and come upon a person. This is signified (by the words in <note>Leviticus 26:28</note>): **So will I also walk contrary to you in fury, and will punish you sevenfold for your sins.** Concerning these seven judgments, the book <term>Nishmath Chajim<note>Hebrew: "The Breath of Life," a work on the soul by Menasseh ben Israel</note></term> by Rabbi Menasse ben Israel may also be opened at folio 84, column 1, in the 24th chapter of the second part.

<margin>Description of the judgment called <term>Chibbut hakkėfer</term>.</margin>
As for the fourth judgment, which is called <term>Chibbut hakkėfer</term>, in which the dead person is severely beaten in the grave by the Angel of Death, it is written thus in Elijah’s <term>Tishbi<note>A 16th-century dictionary of Talmudic and Rabbinic Hebrew by Elijah Levita</note></term>, folio 31, column 1:

<margin>In the <term>Midrash<note>Ancient Jewish homiletic teachings and commentaries on the Bible</note></term>:</margin>
> <unclear>Rabbi</unclear> Isaac ben Parnach: His disciples asked Rabbi Eliezer: "How is the judgment of the beating of the grave performed?" He said to them: "When a <unclear>person</unclear> departs from the world, the Angel of Death comes and sits upon his grave. Immediately, his soul enters his body, and he makes him stand upon his feet and beats him." ### Chapter XIX of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked. ###

Regarding the sixth judgment, which takes place in Hell, it will be dealt with in detail below in the 6th chapter of the second part. However, regarding the seventh judgment—in which the soul must wander about without rest—detailed information will be provided in the first chapter of the aforementioned second part.

<margin>
The dead are also said to speak with one another and do other things that are performed by the living.
</margin>
According to the teachings of the Rabbis, the dead are also said to speak with one another and perform other actions that occur among living people; regarding this, the following story is read in the Talmudic tractate *Berakhot* <note>meaning "Blessings"</note> folio 18, column 2:

> It happened that a certain pious man gave a denarius <note>original Hebrew: *דינר*; translated in the German text as a "shilling"</note> to a poor man on the eve of the New Year <note>Rosh Hashanah</note> during a year of drought <note>original Hebrew: *בצורת*</note>, and his wife provoked him with her anger. He went and spent the night in the cemetery and heard two spirits <note>the souls of the deceased</note> talking to each other. One said to her companion: "Come, let us wander through the world and hear from behind the Curtain <note>original Hebrew: *הפרגוד* (Pargod), the heavenly veil that separates God's presence from the world</note> what punishment is coming to the world." Her companion replied: "I cannot, for I am buried in a mat of reeds <note>a sign of a very poor person's burial</note>. But you go, and whatever you hear, tell me." She went, wandered about, and returned. Her companion said: "My companion, what did you hear from behind the Curtain?" She replied: "I heard that whoever sows during the first rainfall, the hail will strike his crops." The man went and sowed during the second rainfall. Everyone else's crops were struck by hail, but his were not. The next year, he went and spent the night in the cemetery and heard the two spirits talking. One said: "Come, let us wander the world and hear from behind the Curtain what punishment is coming." Her companion said: "Did I not tell you I cannot? For I am buried in a mat of reeds. But you go, and whatever you hear, come and tell me." She went, wandered, and returned. Her companion asked: "What did you hear from behind the Curtain?" She replied: "I heard that whoever sows during the second rainfall, the blight <note>original Hebrew: *שדפון*</note> will strike it." The man went and sowed during the first rainfall. Everyone else's crops were blighted, but his were not. His wife asked him: "Why is it that last year everyone else's crops were struck but yours were not, and now everyone else's are blighted but yours are not?" He told her the whole matter. Not many days passed before a quarrel broke out between the pious man’s wife and the mother of that [deceased] girl. The wife said to her: "Come, and I will show you your daughter, who is buried in a mat of reeds!" The next year, the man went and spent the night in the cemetery and heard those spirits talking. One said: "My companion, come, let us wander the world and hear from behind the Curtain what punishment is coming." The other replied: "My companion, leave me be; the things that passed between us have already been heard among the living."

### Chapter 19 of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked. 886

<margin>
Proof from the Talmud that the dead speak with one another.
</margin>
As for how it is proven that the dead speak with one another, it is read as follows in the cited place of the Talmudic Tractate *Berakhot* <note>The tractate on "Blessings"</note>, folio 18, column 2: <note>original Hebrew: אמר רבי שמואל בר נחמני אמר רבי יונתן מניין למתים שמספרים זה עם זה שנאמר ויאמר י' אליו זאת הארץ אשר נשבעתי לאברהם ליצחק ליעקב לאמור מאי לאמור אמר הקב"ה למשה לך אמור להם לאברהם ליצחק וליעקב שבועה שנשבעתי לכם כבר קיימתיה לבניכם</note>—that is, Rabbi Samuel, the son of Nachmani, said that Rabbi Jonathan said: From where is it proven that the dead speak with one another? Because it is said (Deuteronomy 34:4): **"This is the land that I swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, *to say* (lemór)"**—that is, saying: (I will give it to your seed.) What does the word *lemór* ("saying") signify? The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses: "Go and say to Abraham, Isaac, and Joseph: The oath which I swore to you, I have already fulfilled for your children." Here, according to the erroneous teaching of the Talmud, the word *lemór*—which is a gerund <note>A verbal noun typically translated as "saying"</note>—must be an imperative <note>A command: "Go, say!"</note>, which is against all reason and the nature of the Hebrew language; it is done only so that it might be forced to mean that the dead speak, since Moses was supposed to say the cited words to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

<margin>
They are also said to know those things which occur in the world.
</margin>
The aforementioned Talmudic words are also found in Rabbi Bahya’s <note>Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century Spanish scholar</note> commentary on the five books of Moses, folio 229, column 4, in the <term>Parashat V'Zot HaBerakhah</term> <note>The final weekly Torah portion, found at the end of Deuteronomy</note>, and shortly thereafter it follows that the dead also know the things which happen in the world; the words run thus: <note>original Hebrew: למדונו החכמים ז"ל בכאן בפירוש שהמתים יודעים אפילו עניינים שבעולם הזה ומה שהוצרך משה להודיעם כדי שיחזיקו לו האבות טובה עם זה שהם כבר ידעוהו דבר זה אף על פי שכבר ידעוהו הם</note>—that is, the Sages, of blessed memory, teach us clearly here that the dead also know the things which are in this world: but that Moses was compelled to make such known to them (namely, to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob), happened for this reason: so that they would give him thanks for having made the matter known to them, even though they had already known it previously. In the Judeo-German <note>Literally "German-Hebrew," referring to Yiddish printed in Hebrew characters</note> *Sefer Minhagim* <note>Book of Customs</note>, printed in Dyhernfurth in the year 452 (that is, in the year of Christ 1692), it is also read on folio 55, column 1, under the title *Hilkhot Aveilut* <note>The Laws of Mourning</note>: <note>original Yiddish: מיר לערנן אין דר גמרא דז דייא מתים וויסן וואס מן אויף דער וועלט דרום מוז מן זיין זהיר זיין זיין זיא זלן נישט ח"ו דייא לייא זאגן דס דר פסוק זאגט והמתים אינם יודעים מאומה דס איינט דיא רשעים דיא הייסן מתים</note>—that is, "We learn in the Gemara <note>The part of the Talmud containing rabbinical analysis and commentary</note> that the dead know what one does in the world; therefore one must be careful [that they do not speak ill of us]. And if one should say that the Scripture says (Ecclesiastes 9:5): 'But the dead know nothing,' this refers to the <term>Resha'im</term> <note>The wicked</note>, who are called 'dead' [even while they live]." Therefore one should see

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the three parts of the human soul (Nephesh, Ruach, and Neshama) and their fate after death, specifically citing the "Midrash Ruth" and the "Zeror Hammor" to explain how these parts eventually reunite in the afterlife.</meta>

### Chapter XIX of the First Part of Judaism Unmasked.

...the *Ruach* <term>Ruach: Generally translated as "Spirit," representing the middle level of the soul associated with emotions and moral character.</term>, that is / Spirit / and that according to his works he becomes worthy of a higher glory / which is called *Neshama* <term>Neshama: The highest part of the soul, representing the divine breath or pure intellect.</term>. When the perfectly righteous person departs from the world / then the *Neshama* returns without any delay to its place / and the *Ruach* or Spirit goes / according to the words of the Midrash <term>Midrash: Ancient rabbinic commentaries that explain and expand upon biblical verses.</term>, which I have written / into the lower Paradise. The *Nephesh* <term>Nephesh: The lowest level of the soul, often called the "animal soul," which is closely tied to the physical body and its life force.</term> however remains by the body / until it decays / and the flesh is consumed. And this is / what has been brought forward in the Midrash (from the Book of Ruth, chapter 1, verse 17) / when it is said: **"Death must part [us],"** / <note>The text cites Ruth's oath to Naomi: "Where you die I will die... if anything but death parts me from you."</note> which refers to the time / in which the flesh is still present. But when it has turned back to dust / and has decayed / which is death / which parts it (namely the soul / which is called *Nephesh*) / and the body from one another / then the *Ruach* or Spirit rests in Paradise from its visitation (and ceases that same visitation / through which he visited the body / as long as it was still whole [and undecayed] / because of the *Nephesh* that remained with the body) / and then the *Nephesh* joins itself with the *Ruach*, and the *Ruach* with the *Neshama*. And in the Midrash of Rabbi Shimon ben Jochai <note>A 2nd-century sage to whom the Zohar, the foundational work of Kabbalah, is traditionally attributed.</note> / upon whom be peace / it is taught (regarding the words of 1 Samuel 25:29) / **"So shall the Nephesh, that is / the soul of my lord, be bound in the bundle of the living with the LORD your God."** It should have said / the *Neshama* of the Lord / but it is (constituted) as we have said. The portion of the righteous is righteous / for everything is bound together; the *Nephesh* to the *Ruach*, and the *Ruach* to the *Neshama*, but the *Neshama* to the Holy and Blessed God / therefore it is found / that the *Nephesh* is bound into the bundle of the living / as is mentioned in the Book of Ruth.

<margin>
Further report on the three souls.
</margin>

In the same way, the three mentioned souls are written about in the book *Zerór hammór* <note>The "Bundle of Myrrh," a late 15th-century Torah commentary by Abraham Saba.</note> folio 3, column 1, in the Section *Bereshith* <note>The first portion of Genesis.</note> as follows:

# 894 The First Part of Judaism Unveiled, Chapter 19

was not satisfied with returning into her grave until **Abraham** personally led her by the hand back to **Adam**. After this, **Abraham** buried **Sarah**. This means that once **Abraham** took it upon himself to satisfy the Holy and Blessed God on their behalf, **Adam** returned to his place. Then **Abraham** buried **Sarah**—the Hebrew text says <note>original: "את שרה"</note> **éth Sara**, which is interpreted here as "with Sarah" (though this is a misunderstanding of the grammar). The text does not say <note>original: "לשרה"</note> **Le-Sara**, meaning simply "Sarah," but **éth Sara**, meaning "with Sarah," in order to include **Eve** in the burial. (For the little word **éth** is not only a marker of the accusative case, but also means "with," so the intended meaning is that **Abraham** buried **Eve** along with **Sarah**), because **Abraham** had brought her back in to **Adam**.

And this is the meaning of the words in Genesis 2, verse 4: "These are the generations of the heavens and the earth <note>original: "בהבראם"</note> **behibbareám**, that is, when they were created." Our Rabbis of blessed memory say that the word **behibbareám**, through a rearrangement of the letters, means the same as <note>original: "באברהם"</note> **be-Abraham**, that is, "through Abraham." By this, it is given to be understood that **Adam** and **Eve**, who are the "generations of the heavens and the earth" (and not of men), were only ashamed because of the righteousness of **Abraham**, who brought them rest so that they would no longer have to feel shame in the future life. 

Are these not, however, once again strange perversions of Holy Scripture? Regarding the conversation of the dead, more can be read in the **Sepher Chasidim** <note>Hebrew: "Book of the Pious," a 12th-13th century Jewish ethical and mystical text</note>, numbers 196 and 452, as well as in the 113th chapter of the **Maase-Buch** <note>Yiddish: "Book of Tales," a collection of Jewish legends and folktales</note>. Concerning the knowledge possessed by the dead, the entire twenty-second chapter of the second part of the book **Nishmath Chayim** <note>Hebrew: "The Breath of Life," a work on the soul by Menasseh ben Israel</note>, folios 80 and 81, may be consulted.

the same is true, of which it is written in the aforementioned book <term>Nishmat Hayyim</term> <note>Hebrew: "The Breath of Life," a work by Menasseh ben Israel on the soul</note> folio 88, column 2, in the 26th chapter of the second part:
<margin>Secrets revealed.</margin>
When the righteous rest in their resting places, the secrets of those above and those below are revealed to them; but if one is buried near them who is not equal to them in their dignity, those above (who dwell in heaven) diminish their speaking and revealing of secrets to them—secrets from which they otherwise derive such delight as if they were eating all the best things of this world. <note>original Hebrew: כשהצדיקים נחים על משכנותם מגלין להם רזי עליונים והתחתונים וגו׳</note>
That is, when the righteous rest in their **bed-chambers** (that is, their graves), the upper and lower secrets are revealed to them. But when someone is buried with them who is not equal to them in their dignity, then the upper ones (who dwell in heaven) no longer announce and discover the secrets to them as often (as they are otherwise accustomed to do), from which they feel such delight as if they were eating the best of this world. Similar things are also to be found in the small <term>Yalkut Reubeni</term> <note>A collection of mystical midrashim</note>, number 4, under the title *Zuka*. As for what concerns the reading of books by the dead, this was treated above in the first chapter.

In the <term>Sefer Hasidim</term> <note>Hebrew: "The Book of the Pious," a primary text of the medieval German-Jewish Pietists</note> a leaf is printed, the title of which is *Zavvaoth Rabbi Yehuda he-Hasid*, that is, the *Instructions of the Pious Rabbi Judah*, wherein at number 1 it is also written:
<margin>One should not bury two dead people together who hated each other in life.</margin>
One must not bury two dead people near each other who hated one another during their lifetimes, for they will have no rest together. <note>original Hebrew: אין לקבור שני מתים זה אצל זה שהיו שונאים בחייהם וגו׳</note>
That is: One must not bury two dead people near each other who hated one another in their lifetimes, for they have no rest together. Furthermore, in the same place at number 5, one reads:
<margin>A dead woman who ate children during her lifetime should have her mouth filled with earth.</margin>
When one buries a woman who used to eat children during her life, if one sees her mouth open, it is certain that she will continue to do so for a year after her death; therefore, one must fill her mouth with earth, and then she will do no more harm. <note>original Hebrew: כשקוברין אשה שהיתה אוכלת ילדים בחיה וגו׳</note> <note>This refers to folk beliefs concerning "child-eating" spirits or individuals suspected of witchcraft/vampirism who were thought to harm the living from the grave.</note>
Further, in the same place at number 11, it is read:
<margin>No dead person should be buried in another city.</margin>
If there are graves in a city, one should not transport the deceased to another city for burial, for the dead who lie there will be angry, as it is a disgrace to them. <note>original Hebrew: אם יש קברות בעיר לא יעבירו המת לעיר אחרת וגו׳</note>

# Corrections for the First Part.

Page 3, line 20: for *aleph* <note>original: אלף; likely meant as a number or a specific term</note> read *ella* <note>original: אלא; meaning "but" or "rather"</note>. Page 9, line 3: for Daniel 17, verse 4, read Daniel 4, verse 14 <note>The book of Daniel contains only 12 chapters, so this corrects a significant citation error</note>.
